candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe frequent fights, bullying, shootings/threats, drug pressure, sexual harassment, chronic hallway loitering and teacher assaults at circle schools alongside repeated claims that staff and administration fail to enforce rules or adequately protect victims (examples: “there are fights all the time,” “bullies run the school,” “over 40 school shooting threats,” and “staff...was not interested in even attempting to resolve this”). This bucket groups reports about incident frequency, bystander cultures, and ineffective adult responses rather than formal rules or facilities issues.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger formal: These comments emphasize institution-level control tools and strict punishments at circle schools—metal detectors, daily scanning, rigid uniform/device bans, demerit/LaSalle systems, all‑day detentions, phone confiscation with parent pickup, and withheld privileges—often described as routine or onerous (examples: “scanner school…metal detectors,” “no cell phones…improper clothes may lead to detention or even suspension,” “4 demerits equal a 3 hour detention,” and “make the parents pick it up”). This bucket captures formalized surveillance and disciplinary systems (policy, procedures, and punishments) distinct from reports of incident prevalence or administration culture.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more robust advanc: These reviews highlight AP/honors offerings, dual/concurrent enrollment, formal college partnerships, high college‑placement statistics and outcome anecdotes, plus classroom technology integration (examples: “many different AP classes… She will start college as a Sophomore,” “Nearly 90% of eligible juniors and seniors take college classes,” “99–100% college placement,” and “MacBooks and iPads…3D printing/program design”). This bucket groups programmatic academic strength, credentialed pathways and documented student outcomes, not general teacher behavior or discipline.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: These reviews describe governance and leadership problems at circle schools—frequent turnover or temporary principals, nepotistic hiring, donor-driven favoritism, politicized school boards, rudeness to parents, cover‑ups, and resource misallocation (examples: “teachers/relatives were hired,” “constantly hit up from more money,” “attend a board meeting and they argue…,” and “The Principal ignores and disrespects the parents”). This bucket captures structural/personnel/policy-level breakdowns in administration distinct from classroom instruction or extracurricular programming.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader extracur: These comments point to a wide array of clubs, extensive varsity and non‑cut sports, active parent/volunteer engagement, strong band/music programs, alumni pride, and faculty-supported student‑initiated clubs at circle schools (examples: “over 30 clubs…25 Varsity sports,” “no cut sports, no pay to play,” “alumni connections are very strong,” and “faculty willingness to sponsor clubs created by kids”). This bucket groups schoolwide extracurricular capacity, community/alumni involvement, and accessibility of activities rather than funding complaints or administrative favoritism.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, more v: These reviews repeatedly cite concrete advanced programs, outcomes and tech (e.g., ‘IB program…top 3%’, ‘Every student gets a MacBook’, ‘over 60 free college hours…’, ‘AP students matriculate to Ivy League’, vocational tracks like culinary/medical/Beta Tech, internships), whereas square reviews rarely name comparable AP/IB/dual‑enrollment/vocational offerings or measurable college-placement evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive tea: Square reviewers frequently describe classroom-level failures—teachers who ‘don't teach,’ don’t return work, give no feedback, force students to retake classes, or provide little remediation—while circle reviews more often describe available tutoring, after‑school help, or named teachers who give individualized support.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviews contain repeated operational/governance complaints—enrollment/class-placement errors, principals ‘making up rules’, district mismanagement, administrators moved between schools, parent lawsuits and charges of unethical conduct or fund misallocation—issues square reviews do not generally document.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more safety and st: Multiple circle reviews describe concrete safety incidents and ineffective responses—‘lockdowns every other week,’ ‘several sexual assaults with no action,’ bullying ‘swept under the rug’ or staff participating—whereas square reviews seldom describe comparable violence or systemic non‑response.
candidate_defs.circle entries show stronger, more activ: Circle reviewers more often document organized parent clubs, fundraising foundations, active alumni involvement and tight tradition/ritual (class rings, mandatory volunteer hours), and also describe the corollary social dynamics (hovering parents, booster cliques, pay‑to‑play favoritism); square reviews more often report community apathy or resistance (levy refusals) instead.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups reviews that describe repeated physical fights, gang incidents, sexual assault allegations, widespread bullying/victim‑blaming, lockdowns, and accounts that staff/administration ignore or inadequately respond (e.g., “Constant fights breaking out,” “Sexual assault, bullying, and racial bias are rampant and under addressed,” victims punished while aggressors get light consequences, and reports of lockdowns/parents not informed). It captures safety climate and failure-to-respond evidence rather than tone of the review.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger or expa: This covers reviews noting broad AP/honors availability, named academies and career pathways, trade/Votech offerings, tutoring/expanded supports, dual‑enrollment/early graduation and concrete scholarship/college outcomes (e.g., “more than twenty AP and honors courses,” “Biomedical, Technology, Business, and Skills Trade Academies,” “full scholarship,” and “concurrently enrolled in college”). It groups program breadth/depth, vocational options, and demonstrable postsecondary outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Included here are reviews alleging hostile/retaliatory principals and boards, religious/sectarian control of governance, cover‑ups or swept‑aside accusations, transcript/financial holds, and formal policy failings such as not following IEP/504 plans (e.g., “The Principal fired all the teachers who raised concerns,” “School Board (all mormon) will not stand up,” “will not release your final transcripts… if debt remains,” and “Does not follow through with IEPs have to fight the system”). This bucket focuses on governance, policy compliance, and retaliatory administrative behavior.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frontline sta: This groups complaints about rude front‑office staff, intimidating or bullying teachers, nepotism/clique favoritism, and athletic favoritism determining privileges or resources (e.g., “Front office staff is VERY RUDE!!!”, “it’s all about who you are and who your dad is,” “Unless your child is on a sports team…your child is not ever going to get fair treatment,” and reports of coaches privileging favored players). It captures day‑to‑day staff conduct and unequal enforcement by adults.
candidate_defs.square entries report more chronic facil: This bucket groups reviews that emphasize rundown buildings, pest problems, overcrowded classes and cafeterias, broken infrastructure or inadequate HVAC, and broader resource shortfalls (e.g., “campus is run down and dirty,” “mice problem and had a shooting outside,” “up to 35 kids in my class,” and repeated notes of dated facilities and insufficient books/equipment). It covers physical plant, capacity, and material resource deficits.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: These reviews describe concrete curriculum and outcome strengths at circle schools — frequent references to IB/DP and honors/AP offerings, substantial dual‑credit opportunities and paid tuition, explicit college‑credit tallies (e.g., “18 credits”), high graduation/college‑acceptance rates and named awards/rankings — while square reviews more often cite remediation, failing exit‑exam patterns or NCAA ineligibility (examples: “IB Diploma/Certificate”, “99+ per cent college acceptance”, versus square’s “doesn't even prepare you for college” and NCAA course ineligibility).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Circle reviews contain recurring accounts of widespread fights, bullying, drug‑selling, expulsions, ethnic/racialized harassment and claims that discipline is uneven or protective of athletes/insiders (e.g., “fights all the time,” “totally infected with kids that sell drugs,” “bullies often get lesser punishments”), while square reviews generally describe isolated or more effectively handled threats rather than systemic safety breakdowns.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviewers repeatedly allege leadership problems and biased governance — nepotistic hiring/favoritism, administrators who are rude/unresponsive, opaque behavior during inspections, arrested staff retained, and contested uses of funds or misallocation to athletics (examples: “they play favoritism to employees' children,” “funds...not being put to good use,” and defensive actions when state inspectors visit) — whereas square reviews rarely make these governance or financial‑misuse claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries report richer extracurric: Many circle reviews cite a broad, high‑quality set of out‑of‑class programs — CTE pathways, state/national championship teams, Broadway‑level theater and top‑tier music ensembles, formal leadership programs and strong alumni/parent fundraising — and link them to school spirit and awards (e.g., “career and technical education programs…some of the best,” “state champion teams,” “Carnegie Hall‑worthy music”), while square reviews tend to emphasize a narrower set of programs or report program cuts.
candidate_defs.circle entries report smaller enrollment: Circle reviews frequently describe low student‑to‑teacher ratios, small total enrollment, close advisor/mentor relationships and one‑on‑one teacher interventions (examples: “minimal amount of kids (300–500)”, “class advisors…more than teachers…invited us into their homes,” “teachers work with students hands on”), whereas square reviews more often report overcrowding, high class ratios and teacher disengagement (e.g., “ratio as high as 36:1,” “Teachers are uncaring”).
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger advanc: These reviews describe concrete programmatic strength (AP/IB/STEM/dual‑enrollment, 1:1 tech, honors classes) and named outcomes (Ivy/Intel finalists, high AP/ACT/SAT scores, scholarships) that reviewers link to real college readiness—e.g., “offers great STEM programs, IB/AP, dual enrollment,” “students accepted into all 8 Ivy League schools,” and “lead the area in test scores,” whereas square reviews rarely cite such program breadth or quantifiable high‑end outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report higher day‑to‑day: Square reviews repeatedly credit consistent, hardworking teachers, coherent leadership, and classroom support (after‑school help, teacher availability, college‑prep culture) while criticizing few rogue staff—examples include “great administrators, teachers, and staff at EHS,” “teachers offer after school assistance,” versus many circle comments about inexperienced or disengaged teachers: “new teachers right out of college… have no idea what they're doing” and “teachers are not engaged.”
candidate_defs.circle entries document broader, higher‑: Circle reviews routinely list extensive clubs, competitive sports/band, internships, volunteer placements, strong fine‑arts programs, and community patron support—e.g., “fantastic sports program… top 25,” “band program is excellent,” “internship opportunities… Botanical Garden, Civil Court house,” and “business community… very supportive”—whereas square reviews seldom enumerate comparable extracurricular breadth or external partnerships.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more bureaucratic: Many circle reviews cite school‑board or district indifference, inaccessible administrators, patronage hiring, failure to follow mandated reporting, and even demands to re‑staff or shut down the school—examples: “no phone calls back from Principal… The school board is a disappointment,” “they hire… based on who they know,” and “should be shut down or totally re‑staffed,” while square reviews provide fewer or milder governance/central‑office failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more constructiv: Circle reviews frequently highlight character education, supportive/restorative discipline, welcoming atmospheres and community norms (e.g., “Character building is central,” “they lovingly discipline the student,” “students have lots of pride”), whereas square reviews more often report harsh punitive enforcement, exclusionary incidents, or poor classroom control (e.g., denying graduation over facial hair, “classes are never under control,” and calls out authoritarian discipline practices).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: This bucket captures reviews that describe pervasive safety problems at the school (frequent fights, gang activity, drug‑selling/vaping, sexual harassment) together with staff/security non‑response or ineffective anti‑bullying enforcement—e.g., “Fights every single day…kids vaping in the bathroom,” “I personally witnessed drug deals on school grounds,” and “I called them twice…security never came.” These items indicate an unsafe student conduct climate and routine failure to enforce rules or protect students that is reported far more often in circle reviews than in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups reviews alleging unequal treatment, politics, and poor governance (‘good‑ole‑boy’ hiring, favoritism toward athletes/wealthy donors, biased counselors, withheld records, punitive tuition/ refund practices, and rude/incompetent front‑office behavior) — e.g., “The district suffers from cronyism…he has a few favorites,” “they would have withheld his records,” and “secretaries are very rude…attendance office forgetful.” These are concrete governance and fairness failures (policy abuse, biased discipline, record/refund disputes) described much more often in circle entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger small‑sch: This bucket covers reviews emphasizing a close, family‑style school culture with teachers knowing students by name, extensive one‑on‑one help, active parent/mentor programs, multigenerational alumni involvement, and signature arts/extracurriculars (marching band, mariachi, award‑winning drama)—e.g., “the faculty know every student by name,” “multigenerational ties…proud to be an alumni,” and “the best mariachi in the nation.” These concrete community/individualization and extracurricular strengths are far more prominent in circle reviews than square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more advanced/spec: This bucket groups evidence of substantive programmatic rigor and measurable outcomes—AP/IB offerings, engineering or pathway programs, AVID and SAT/AP prep, dual‑credit/college acceptances and AP test passes—e.g., “AP Statistics, AP Calculus…students accepted to top colleges,” “Pathways to Engineering program,” and “he's passed two AP tests!” These concrete advanced‑program features and college‑readiness outcomes are reported more often in circle entries than in square entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more overcrowding,: This bucket captures reviews describing scale and facility/operational strain—extremely large classes (30–40+ students), overcrowded buildings, impersonal/anonymous student experience, and scheduling/space misallocation—e.g., “horribly overcrowded…more than 30 students in each class,” “had a class with 40+ students…had to sit on the floor,” and comments that the school is ‘so large’ and cliquey. Those structural/space/scale problems appear significantly more often in square reviews than in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, broader: These reviews describe concrete academic depth and offerings (AP/IB/honors, dual‑credit, magnets, ROTC, VPA/arts, CTE, STEAM/biomed) plus 1:1 devices and lab/tech investments, and link them to heavier workloads and measurable college outcomes (examples: many APs, 'IB program is very challenging', 'each student is issued a laptop', alumni admitted to selective colleges). Square entries rarely list comparable specialized pathways or device‑rich resources and instead note weaker AP preparation or missing textbooks.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: Multiple circle reviews cite sustained bullying, daily fights, vaping, weapons/drug incidents and administrators who ignore or inconsistently enforce discipline (examples: 'fights on campus almost daily', '17 fights in one day', 'drug distribution at this school', 'administration turned a blind eye'). Square reviews either omit these severe safety claims or describe better order/anti‑bullying enforcement.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviews contain many allegations of nepotism, favoritism (especially toward athletes or connected families), policy or legal violations, manipulative district politics, and unresponsive or unprofessional staff (examples: 'nepotism and sports', 'Athletes get away with things', 'the school board allows the district to break laws', 'Admissions Director is horrible', 'counselors never respond'). Square reviews may call for leadership change but contain fewer claims of systemic politicization, legal breaches, or persistent governance manipulation.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more facility, cap: Reviewers describe chronic physical‑plant and capacity problems—extremely overcrowded hallways, negligent custodial service, broken plumbing, removed library books after laptop rollouts, 'swim team without a pool', chaotic transportation and grading/attendance processing failures—whereas square reviews rarely combine such pervasive facility/operational breakdown claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries show much greater interna: Circle reviews frequently swing between glowing, outcome‑focused endorsements and extreme condemnations for the same school (examples: 'I absolutely love Pace' vs 'hands down the worst school'), and contain conflicting accounts about administration, teacher quality, safety and supports; square reviews are comparatively consistent in their themes and present fewer such stark contradictions about the same institution.
candidate_defs.circle entries have more specialized col: These reviews describe concrete, structured academic pathways (IB diploma, early‑college/associate degree programs, AP/dual‑enrollment, formal college partnerships, measurable score/scholarship evidence) tied to alumni success—examples: ‘opportunity to earn an associate degree while attending high school,’ ‘IB Diploma Programme,’ ‘both my kids got above a 31 on the ACT and qualified for Bright Flight,’ and multiple accounts of dual‑credit/college transfers; Square reviews rarely list these formal pipelines or the same level of measurable college outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries have more frequent report: These reviews describe heavy‑handed enforcement by staff and administration—physical grabbing or threats, intrusive searches and mandatory hair drug tests, strict dress‑code/search penalties, punitive expulsions or withholding of records/privileges—e.g., ‘yelled and threatened to lock her in the room,’ ‘pulled on students clothes and hair,’ ‘requires drug testing upon admission by hair analyst & does random drug tests,’ and ‘denied the sabbatical… attempted a search that was so bare and unprofessional.’ Square reviews do not report this cluster of invasive, punitive procedures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews document peer violence, racial/LGBTQ+ harassment, hazing, weapons and repeated threats, suicidal ideation and other clinical mental‑health crises, and descriptions of staff ignoring or inadequately responding—examples include ‘students bringing weapons to schools and suicidal students,’ ‘bullying goes around a lot especially if you're black,’ ‘hazing… failed to inform the public,’ and ‘teachers nor principal or vice principal did anything to stop it.’ Square reviews tend not to present the same volume or severity of unresolved safety/mental‑health incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: These reviews allege cronyism and biased governance (husband/wife administrators, ‘parents run the school’ selection, board politics favoring a faction), opaque or punitive fee practices (hidden charges, receipts withheld), and favoritism in team/program selection—examples: ‘assistant superintendent and special ed coordinator are husband and wife,’ ‘they give free rides to athletes while the rest pay,’ and ‘charges a dollar for each temporary id… refuses to put on the receipt’; Square reviews include far fewer or no such consistent claims.
candidate_defs.square entries have more consistent desc: Square reviews more often describe visible administrative engagement, proactive counseling or parent outreach, facility/upgrading narratives and district‑level improvement (rising grades/A+ ratings, newer campuses, supportive counselors), and organized college‑prep advising—examples: ‘we get better in school every year,’ ‘Under new administration OHS has improved greatly,’ ‘Counselors and teachers care about their students,’ and ‘fairly new school… the lunch food is very good.’ These kinds of steady improvement, accessible‑support, and resource investment narratives appear more in Square than in Circle.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger/more nu: This bucket captures reports that a school offers substantive programmatic pathways (AP/IB, multiple academies, dual‑enrollment/AA credit, magnet/communications/JROTC programs, college centers) and quantifiable outcomes (rankings, scholarship totals, Ivy/elite admits) — e.g., Circle cites IB/AP offerings, a college center and a 700 readiness metric, dual‑enrollment/$40 concurrent credit, and Newsweek/US News rankings, while Square lacks these concrete program/placement claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more uneven and of: This bucket groups evidence about in‑class teaching quality and staffing stability: complaints about 'hit‑or‑miss' teachers, weak core departments (chemistry/biology/math), many first‑year teachers or subs, mid‑year teacher departures, and inconsistent remediation versus isolated reports of extra help; e.g., Circle notes weak core instruction, multiple first‑year teachers in a semester, and failing students 'making up' grades, whereas Square more often praises steady, experienced teachers.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket covers reviewer accounts of unsafe student behavior and inadequate handling: recurring bullying, fights, everyday smoking/drugs, theft and harassment, plus descriptions of administration not intervening or handling incidents poorly (and occasional reactive measures like exit‑door alarms); e.g., Circle documents daily bathroom smoking, widespread bullying, unaddressed assaults and race‑based harassment, whereas Square rarely lists this breadth/severity of misconduct.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute facilit: This bucket groups concrete physical and logistical conditions: overcrowded classes and portable classrooms, flooding/no AC/rodents/sewer smells, lack of basic supplies, transportation and busing distance problems, or conversely visible renovations and 1:1 tech rollouts — e.g., Circle complains of trailers, yellow/brown water, no air conditioning, and rodent infestation, while Square typically omits such facility failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures systemic leadership and policy complaints: alleged staff misconduct and cover‑ups, favoritism toward wealthy families or athletes, IEP/special‑education noncompliance, revolving superintendents/layoffs, contested spending decisions, and refusal to remedy grievances — e.g., Circle alleges a teacher criminal scandal and confidentiality/legal violations, favoritism for donors/football, and lack of IEP follow‑up, whereas Square contains fewer or different governance accusations.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger academic: This bucket groups reviews where circle reviewers describe rigorous curricula, AP/Honors/magnet/STEM/vocational tracks and documented alumni college success (e.g., ‘Classes challenge students and prepare them for college,’ named magnet/Academy programs, vocational shop schedules, and alumni reporting Dean’s List or college completions), whereas square reviews emphasize weaker or uneven academics and limited long‑term outcome claims (e.g., complaints about declining test scores and only isolated AP credit).
candidate_defs.circle entries report worse student safe: This bucket captures reviews that describe pervasive peer harassment, tolerated racial slurs, underage smoking/drug use, weapons/gang incidents, even suicides, plus staff/administration failing to stop or selectively enforcing discipline (e.g., ‘Respect is missing…racial slurs,’ ‘there’s always lots of security and police,’ and reports that staff ignore or laugh at bullying), in contrast to square reviews which generally do not report such sustained safety crises.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege greater administra: This groups entries describing governance problems at circle schools — allegations that leadership is unresponsive, cloaked by an insular board, tolerates favoritism/donor-based privileges, covers up incidents and mishandles clerical processes (e.g., ‘nepotism is tolerated,’ ‘upper admin doesn’t follow up…cover up,’ ‘office staff never answers the phone’), whereas square reviews rarely make these combined claims of opaque capture and patronage.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe richer physical: This bucket captures reviews that enumerate concrete nonacademic assets at circle schools — new buildings, auditoriums, extensive band/choral/theatre programs, career‑tech shops, international travel and many clubs (e.g., ‘incredible auditorium,’ ‘choir, Moonlight Jazz, orchestra, dental assisting, graphic communications’), while square reviews either omit such breadth or call out narrower/less developed extracurricular offerings.
candidate_defs.circle entries mention more frequent fai: This groups reviews that describe denial of accommodations, exclusionary special‑education placements, lawsuits to obtain services, counselor shortages or ineffective advising, and contested accommodation decisions (e.g., ‘we had to sue to get him services,’ ‘administration can be un‑cooperative with inclusion,’ and rotating counselors), whereas square reviews rarely report systemic special‑education denials or legal disputes.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: This bucket captures reviews where circle schools are portrayed as having robust honors/AP/IB offerings, dual‑credit/college‑credit opportunities, higher standardized/test outcomes and clear college‑prep supports (e.g., ‘‘honors and AP classes,’’ ‘‘graduated with 21 college credits,’’ ‘‘more students accepted to top universities,’’ ‘‘higher ACT scores, national merit scholars’’) while square reviews lack comparable evidence of consistent advanced coursework, dual credit, or measurable college placement.
candidate_defs.circle entries document broader, high‑ac: Includes circle reviews listing extensive arts/athletics/NJROTC success, state championships, outstanding music/theater programs, large facilities and heavy fundraising tied to sports, plus claims that athletes or big donors receive protected treatment (examples: ‘‘phenomenal athletic facilities,’’ ‘‘NJROTC recognitions,’’ ‘‘wrestling state championships,’’ and ‘‘football players get passing grades / donors protected’’); square reviews generally do not present the same program breadth, competitive awards, or linked favoritism.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups reviews alleging chronic peer violence, racial/homophobic slurs, gang presence, vaping/drug problems, and staff/administration failing to protect victims or enforce policy (examples: ‘‘lots of gang activity,’’ ‘‘students use the n‑word with no repercussion,’’ ‘‘bullying is the norm,’’ ‘‘vapes are the craze’’ and reports that teachers/admin side with aggressors), whereas square reviews lack or contain far fewer such sustained safety claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries document greater administ: Covers reviews describing leadership churn, unreturned parental communications, obstruction of records or special‑education services, retaliatory behavior toward critics, nepotism/cliques and calls for state intervention (examples: ‘‘fourth principal in five years,’’ ‘‘no one answers the phone,’’ ‘‘refused to transfer credits,’’ ‘‘small clique runs the show,’’ ‘‘why hasn’t the state taken this school?’’); square reviews rarely assert the same level of governance breakdown or active suppression.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute facilit: This bucket captures tangible infrastructure/resource problems and imposed costs described in circle reviews — overcrowding, mold/sewage/heat/A/C failures, outdated textbooks, missing computer labs, Chromebook mandates without home internet, missing athletic fields, and heavy mandatory fees/tuition/fundraising (examples: ‘‘sewage smell,’’ ‘‘no air conditioning,’’ ‘‘forcing chrome books whether families can afford them,’’ ‘‘yearly $300 raffle tickets / $700+ monthly tuition’’) — issues that square reviews mention far less or not at all.
candidate_defs.circle entries report far more acute saf: This bucket covers reviews that describe violent or recurrent safety incidents at the school — e.g., riots, weekly lockdowns, weapons found/metal detectors, pepper‑spray/chemical control by police, frequent physical fights, gang activity, on‑campus sexual activity, thefts, and teen‑pregnancy clusters — claims repeatedly present in circle but absent or explicitly contradicted in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more and better‑do: This groups pieces that list concrete program breadth and high‑end facilities (multiple AP/dual‑enrollment courses, named academies/CTE pathways, robotics/STEM labs, award‑winning band/arts, NAVY JROTC, unique academies, documented college credits/outcomes), i.e., circle reviews frequently inventory programmatic assets and college‑prep pipelines that square reviews do not.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger small‑s: Includes reviews emphasizing small class sizes, highly invested teachers/staff, structured in‑day remediation (Power Hour), regular after‑hours tutoring, hands‑on counselors, individualized counseling/IEP advocacy or parental partnership, and administrators who personally know students — patterns more commonly asserted in circle than in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Covers complaints about unfair discipline/athlete favoritism, administration prioritizing sports over academics, withheld records/transcripts, excessive fees/fines, staff fear/retaliation, censorship, refusal to process paperwork, and opaque budget allocation — governance‑level dysfunctions and perceived monetization invoked in circle far more than in square.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent in: This bucket captures reviews that portray stable, uniformly positive operational performance — clear behavior policies or zero‑tolerance enforcement, reliably solid teachers, well‑implemented AP/honors pathways, strong ACT/AP results and alumni college success — themes that square reviews assert more consistently than circle reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews repeatedly describe harassment, fights, drug/alcohol/vaping use, teacher‑student sexual relationships, and even lethal violence or threats on/near campus, plus claims that staff/administration "do nothing" (e.g., “The bullying is bad…they do nothing to help,” “Drugs and drinking… used condoms around campus,” “two... succumbed… shootings”); Square reviews rarely raise comparable safety severity or systematic nonresponse.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more extensive for: Circle reviews list broad AP/IB/honors, dual‑enrollment/Running Start, explicit 9th‑grade career pathways, vocational/CTE offerings, and concrete matriculation/test metrics (e.g., “all AP class options,” “Running Start… Clark College,” “100% college bound,” “AP Calc BC… got a 5”), whereas Square reviews more often lack that programmatic breadth or concrete outcome figures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Multiple Circle comments allege district politics, hidden testing/environmental findings, nepotism and donor‑priority treatment, protected tenured staff, bungled transfers/records, and opaque fundraising/fee practices (e.g., “they choose to do nothing because he/she is tenured,” “Where does the bingo money go?”, “sent all records back… kept my student active”), claims that are largely absent from Square.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive sta: Square reviews often accuse teachers and administrators of not caring, failing to help struggling students, counselors being a 'no show', and poor teacher accountability (e.g., “Teachers do not care…counselors were a no show,” “if your child is a struggling student...MOVE”), while Circle reviews more frequently describe teacher availability, active counseling, or targeted supports.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger small‑sch: Circle reviewers repeatedly praise small classes, teachers who stay after school and mentor students, wide arts/club/sports offerings, attractive/new facilities and active parent fundraising/alumni involvement (e.g., “small size…individual attention,” “bands and choirs win competitions,” “library…like stepping into Hogwarts,” “huge support by the parents via The Shark Fund”), characteristics that Square reviews mention far less or counterpoint with crowding and limited extracurricular breadth.
candidate_defs.circle entries report pervasive safety,: These reviews describe frequent peer violence, daily bullying, sexual exploitation, drug incidents, weapons, staff‑perpetrated harassment and claims that administrators do nothing (e.g., “bullying is unbelievable…the administration does nothing,” “girls selling their bodies…drugs…staff incapable,” reports of drug busts and weapons). This bucket captures pieces that portray school safety and student‑climate breakdowns plus explicit failures to address them.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews cite measurable outcomes and programs—dual enrollment and large college‑credit counts, AP/IB/High AP scores, National Merit, large scholarship totals and alumni matriculations to selective colleges (e.g., “entering college as a sophomore because of dual credits,” “National Merit Scholars,” “85 seniors won $7.5 million”), presenting clear college‑prep capacity that square entries generally lack.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege entrenched favorit: This cluster covers claims that staff hire relatives/ex‑students, protect connected families, give favored students special treatment, and shield problematic faculty (examples: “hires ex‑students…good old boy attitude,” “if you have a certain last name forget getting any help,” coaches/athletics favoritism), i.e., systematic personalism affecting discipline, opportunities, and personnel decisions.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent, w: These reviews emphasize proactive principals and counselors, stable/committed teachers, effective family outreach and responsive communication (e.g., “principal is very involved and supportive,” “the counselors are off the charts fantastic,” “weekly progress reports, Renweb”), portraying a school where leadership and staff reliably support students — a pattern less evident in circle entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries provide far more concrete: This bucket groups reviews that narrate specific operational facts—1:1 device programs (iPads/netbooks), explicit budget crises and planned deep cuts, renovation notes, aging buildings or recent capital upgrades, and contested spending priorities (e.g., athletic upgrades vs. textbooks) — i.e., granular evidence about facilities, technology, and finances that square entries seldom supply.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe concrete safety failures inside the building—frequent fights, weapons, drug/alcohol use, sexual activity, unchecked physical bullying, and claims that complaints go unaddressed or are defended by administrators (e.g., 'they have kids with guns... fight almost every day', 'Bullying is awful... complaints often go unaddressed', 'The bully's run this school!!!'). That pattern is far stronger in circle reviews than in square reviews, which rarely catalogue weaponized violence or systemic non-response.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more extensive adv: Circle reviews repeatedly list concrete, institutional programs and outcomes—AP/IB expansion, CTE/shop programs, dual‑credit/associate degree pathways, award‑winning arts, championships, one‑to‑one devices, and documented college acceptances/metrics (e.g., 'AP programs... more students succeeding on AP exams', 'students graduating with associate degrees', 'award winning IPAD learning school', 'drama and music programs astounding'). Those programmatic breadths and claimed measurable outcomes appear substantially more often in circle than in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more proactive,: Many circle reviews give concrete teacher practices—staying late, lunch tutoring, creating extra help groups, frequent phone/email outreach, schedule accommodations and one‑on‑one remediation (e.g., 'stayed late, worked through lunches', 'phone calls home at least 3 times per week', 'worked with her to catch her up'), while square reviews more often report teacher disengagement or inconsistent help.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more institutional: Reviewers in circle accuse leadership and governance of biased treatment—principal/staff favoritism toward friends or athletes, nepotism, board weakness, administrators living outside the district, and conflicts (administrators as coaches) that undermine accountability (e.g., 'The nepotism and favoritism are beyond belief', 'the principal shows favoritism', 'School board doesn't hold certain teachers to a standard'). These governance‑and‑accountability complaints are markedly more frequent in circle than in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more operational a: Circle reviews repeatedly cite concrete resource and logistics problems—classes of 35–42 students, schools >100% capacity, program eliminations tied to budget, lack or shortfall of lunches/busing, precarious temporary teacher contracts, and mixed reports of outdated or overly locked devices despite some 1:1 deployments (e.g., '110% well over capacity', 'lunch food is horrid... PGCPS has financial challenges', 'laptops... so locked down', 'many teachers don't have contracts'). These operational/capacity issues appear far more often in circle reviews than in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete, doc: This bucket groups reviews where circle schools provide named advanced-course pathways, dual‑credit/AP/IB options, explicit college‑credit or placement evidence and alumni outcomes (e.g., “many students graduate with college credit,” “the number of AP classes has increased,” “my daughter received her Bachelors and Masters,” “MAP/SAT/ACT scores have continued to rise”), whereas square reviews typically lack comparable measurable outcome claims or named advanced‑program listings.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent, sev: This captures reviews that describe pervasive student-on-student violence, racial/anti‑LGBTQ+ harassment, staff inaction or protection of bullies, and explicit safety incidents (e.g., “Bullying is rampant… teachers look the other way,” “misgendering and deadnaming on a regular basis,” “code greens… special needs student needs restraining,” reports of weapons/fights), whereas square entries do not present the same level of systemic harassment or staff‑protected bullying.
candidate_defs.square entries report more teacher disen: This bucket covers reviews emphasizing poor classroom instruction, non-teaching or uncertified staff, and teachers who do not prepare or follow up (e.g., square: “There are very few teacher who do their job well,” “some teachers just sit there and do nothing,” and mentions of uncertified instructors), contrasted with circle reviews that more often describe accessible, caring, or named standout teachers and routine teacher outreach.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete faci: This groups reviews that list explicit physical/operational features and supports—longer school year/day, semester block schedules, uniforms, small class sizes, on‑site medical clinic, tutoring programs, vocational/CTE shops and recent capital projects (e.g., “new building opened in 2013,” “computers in each classroom,” “tutoring available during lunch and after school”), while square reviews focus less on these concrete structural offerings and more on programmatic/classroom issues.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more active parent: This bucket collects reviews that foreground parental/alumni mobilization, explicit tuition or fee discussions, families relocating to attend, referenda or alleged use of students in political campaigns, and local socioeconomic dynamics (e.g., “Fairmont Parents must become Active…,” “I am paying 7 Thousand each year,” “we moved to Stillman to avoid...”), whereas square reviews rarely emphasize that level of community/tuition/political involvement.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report broader and deeper: These reviews repeatedly name concrete program offerings and pathways—IB and AP sequences, dual‑credit/dual‑diploma options, early access to high‑school classes for 8th graders, career academies and expanding specialized programs—while square reviews lack comparable program breadth (examples: IB, dual credit, 'two diplomas,' 'high school classes for 8th graders' versus square's generic or absent advanced-course descriptions).
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more uneven instru: Many circle reviews document polarized classroom practice and failed supports—'half of the teachers are good, half are bad,' teachers not teaching, cheating enabled by laptops, remediation errors on state tests, and detailed IEP/504 implementation failures—whereas square entries rarely describe pervasive special‑education or testing‑integrity breakdowns.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more persistent sa: Numerous circle reviews recount widespread bullying, vulgar social media behavior, drug use, sexual harassment and even assaults with ineffective security or ignored incidents ('DRUGS are horrible', 'bullied with zero action', 'assault IN FRONT OF the security guard'), while square reviews do not present this breadth/severity of safety and discrimination failures.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviews frequently accuse leadership of biased enforcement, protecting favorites (athletes/donors/staff relatives), nepotistic hires, covering up problems and being absent or rude—plus high turnover and district blame—contrasting with square reviews that emphasize different, less systemic administrative complaints or praise for particular administrators.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more detailed mate: Circle reviews both identify physical/resource failures (missing textbooks, poor food, HVAC, Chromebooks/internet, parking and logistical failures, itemized tuition/fees/fundraisers) and enumerate high‑participation extracurricular achievements, parent/alumni mobilization and selective-access dynamics (auditioned arts, sports dominance, scholarships), a mix of richer extracurricular life plus stark funding/operational inequities not similarly documented in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger and bro: These reviews emphasize concrete programmatic breadth and measurable outcomes (AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, specialized academies, vocational certifications, college counseling, national awards, 1:1 tech). Examples: circle reviewers cite “many AP classes,” IB/academies, a Blue Ribbon award, one‑to‑one tablet programs, JROTC, strong marching band/theatre showcases, large scholarship totals and college placement—features square reviews do not assert as reliably.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize athletics, pare: These reviews foreground school life organized around sports, volunteer/parent coaches, and athletic championships as a central institutional feature. Illustrative evidence: square reviews repeatedly note parent coaching and CIF/league football success, community-run logistics for teams, and a locally dominant football culture—claims that stand out versus circle reviews which more often highlight academic/arts programming.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more overcrowding,: These entries document space and operational failures (severe overcrowding, insufficient classrooms/desks for large students, HVAC/building failures, mold, unhygienic bathrooms, and cuts to busing) that directly impair daily instruction and safety. Example notes include “overpacked with students” and thousands moving at once, 20‑year‑old textbooks, broken heating/cooling, trailers, chronic bathroom/soap shortages, and budgeted cuts to student transportation.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more teacher/staff: These reviews describe personnel behaviors and classroom practices that harm students: teachers insulting or bullying students, assigning little real instruction, systemic grade inflation, IEPs not followed, and staff favoritism (often toward athletes). Representative examples: “teachers insult you and call you worthless,” “IEP which the school and teachers would not follow,” reports that “NO child can fail…no grade below a C,” and accounts of staff‑level profanity and harassment.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more active govern: These reviews highlight district/board strategy, politicized enrollment decisions, and tight family networks that shape who benefits—claims of gerrymandering, recruitment/expansion plans, fundraising push for athletics, and ‘everyone's related’ nepotism recur. Examples include accusations of school‑zone gerrymandering, billboard fundraising for a new football field, multi‑generation family dominance of staffing, and explicit statements that leadership is pursuing expansion or strategic enrollment changes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, broader,: This bucket captures claims that Circle schools provide concrete advanced‑course access, organized magnet or conservatory tracks, technical/STEM electives, AP/IB/dual‑credit pathways, and documented college outcomes (e.g., '20 hours of college credit,' 'AWARD WINNING... AP tests,' 'arts‑magnet with daily art classes,' 'Organic chemistry... Apple Class') that Square reviews do not substantively document.
candidate_defs.circle entries portray a smaller, more i: Includes reports of small school size, close‑knit atmosphere, spirited student sections, high extracurricular breadth, long‑term alumni ties and frequent one‑on‑one teacher support (e.g., 'small, friendly atmosphere,' 'teachers will go the extra mile,' 'ample opportunity for student involvement,' 'family like atmosphere', student‑section/tailgating descriptions) that Square does not emphasize.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Groups reviews that describe hostile peer climates, physical fights, racial and homophobic harassment, organized threats or serious safety incidents (guns/kill lists/bomb threats), and teacher‑ignored assaults (e.g., 'students are rude, violent, racist and homophobic,' 'kill lists and bomb threats,' 'When a student brings a gun to school')—problems Square reviewers call out more often than Circle reviewers.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This covers allegations of lost attendance/credit records, billing lawsuits, cherry‑picked funding, nepotistic hiring/promotion, and unfair or punitive discipline practices (e.g., 'I have received 4 phone calls... I don't have a daughter,' 'lawsuit filed against them for billing my son,' 'favoritism plays a role,' 'promoted unqualified staff') which appear more frequently in Circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive sta: Includes Square reviewers' accounts of uncaring or rude teachers, guidance staff who 'don't care' or 'devalue' students, classrooms lacking direct instruction or accountability, and sustained teacher turnover/mediocrity (e.g., 'There are only a few teachers there who care,' 'guidance counselors didn't care,' 'teachers are for the most part not great'), which distinguish Square from Circle on adult instructional engagement and responsiveness.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced-: This bucket groups differences where reviewers of circle schools describe explicit AP/dual-enrollment/early-college pathways, tutoring, test-prep and concrete postsecondary outcomes (scholarships, high matriculation rates, associates/bachelor pathways), while square reviews lack or criticize those pathways. Examples: circle: “over 25 AP courses, Dual Enrollment, Early College/associate degree, SAT prep, many students go to college”; square: no comparable AP/dual-credit breadth and complaints about dwindling honors/AP classes or poor college preparation.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures safety and student-behavior patterns: circle reviewers repeatedly describe frequent fights, drugs, bullying, gang presence, normalized rule‑breaking and either large police/K9/search programs or lax adult enforcement; square reviews rarely report such pervasive behaviours. Examples: circle: “fights are very frequent, drugs are an issue,” “K9 thing along with random searches,” “students smoking in front of adults”; square: mentions occasional incidents but frames them as rarer and managed.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups operational and governance problems attributed to school leadership and district processes: reviewers of circle schools raise chronic mismanagement, nepotism/favoritism, contested principals, calls for removal, mishandled testing/placement/transcripts, hidden fees and poor responsiveness. Examples: circle: “administration needs to be completely removed,” “put into wrong class / transcripts not sent,” “teacher nepotism/Good ole boys club,” whereas square seldom documents these systemic operational failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more disrespectful: This bucket covers classroom-level staff conduct and instruction where square reviewers emphasize uncaring or disrespectful teachers, inconsistent grading, weak pedagogy and poor responsiveness to students/parents compared with circle. Examples: square: “The teachers are disrespectful... 'Well you're still passing aren't you?'” and “some teachers just suck,” whereas circle reviews more often cite caring, available teachers and concrete extra-help programs.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe better facilitie: This bucket captures resource, program breadth, and community support contrasts: circle reviewers frequently praise new/clean buildings, many clubs, competitive athletics and active parent organizations, while square reviewers report underfunded arts, broken instruments, dropped electives and minimal clubs. Examples: circle: “beautiful facilities, lots of clubs, amazing FFA, band program, strong town support”; square: “we couldn't buy new music, over 100 instruments were broken,” “clubs and activities are minimal.”
candidate_defs.Circle entries report stronger advanced: This groups reviews where Circle emphasizes durable academic rigor and explicit college-prep supports (AP/IB/AP-credit, SAT/ACT prep, guidance help, vocational certs) with named outcomes — e.g., “Over the years, more AP classes have been added,” “Both my kids graduated with over 21 college credits (AP), high ACT scores,” and seniors matriculating to selective universities — claims that Square reviews do not substantively make or directly contradict.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more pervasive stu: This groups reviews that describe concrete safety/discipline breakdowns in Circle — recurring fights, normalized drug use, bus assaults, death threats, pervasive bullying and weak/no effective administrative response or misuse of punitive policies (Zero Tolerance) — e.g. “BIG problem with drugs,” “bullying was out of control,” “my daughter has gotten hit on the bus,” and administrators who 'do nothing' when victims report.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more administrativ: This groups reviews where Square specifically faults top-level governance and leadership trust — criticizing the school board, district leadership, and principal-level oversight or advising prospective families against enrollment — e.g. “The school board runs the district poorly… those at the top are unimpressive,” “I beg you to not let your kids go here,” and repeated distrust of administrators and district policy decisions.
candidate_defs.Circle entries document more concrete, d: This groups Circle reviews that give concrete statements about physical plant and resourcing — both investments (new facilities, passed levies, multi‑million dollar stadiums, detailed media/tech inventories) and constraints (broken faucets, pests, overcrowded halls, parking nightmares) — e.g. “recent levy (to build new facilities) passed,” “cameras, tripods, Adobe…”, and “most of the bathrooms having broken water faucets.”
candidate_defs.Circle entries report higher parental/co: This groups Circle reviews that emphasize organized parent involvement, alumni/ multi‑generational continuity, active PTO/festivals and local advocacy alongside insider effects (who‑you‑know admissions, nepotism, favoritism) — e.g. “The PTO is active,” “I taught there for 37 years…we have many graduates,” and complaints like “Who You Know Policy… spots are saved for the friends and family.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent stud: These reviews document higher rates of fights, gangs, drug use, sexual-assault allegations, theft, chronic bullying, and both punitive and absent discipline — often saying administration ‘did virtually nothing,’ ‘didn't care about bullying,’ or used long suspensions to remove students (examples: “infested with gangs, drugs,” “I had to pull child out… due to bullying,” “there are mostly fights in the school”). This bucket captures reviewer evidence about unsafe student conduct and a failed or inconsistent in-school response to protect students or prevent recurrence.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more governance, l: Reviews grouped here name board conflict, calls to fire superintendents/principals, secrecy, donor/parent-clique influence, and nepotistic protection of students/staff (examples: “Superintendent … should be fired,” “We get a new principal every school year,” “A student must have the correct last name…”). This bucket covers structural/political problems outside classroom instruction — board behavior, leadership churn, secretive or biased decision-making, and community/parent influence that reviewers tie to inequitable treatment.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more operational,: This cluster captures concrete deficits in school infrastructure and core instruction: broken HVAC/boilers and unsanitary bathrooms, nonfunctional metal detectors and computers, chronic teacher turnover and inexperienced hires, archaic or absent special‑education practice, heavy chronic absenteeism and low on‑time graduation, and poor subject-level outcomes (math/scores) — e.g., “no working AC… rooms reaching 95°F,” “Teacher turnover is high. Attendance is low,” “annual math test scores were dismal,” and “Text books need to be an option… computers fail.”
candidate_defs.circle entries highlight stronger, conce: These reviews emphasize specialized program excellence and concrete achievements — arts-focused curricula, championship bands and athletic successes, IB/AP/dual-credit pathways, technology rollouts, and documented college matriculation or awards (examples: “marching band has won many STATE competitions,” “graduates attend Harvard/Columbia,” “partnership with Ivy Tech… graduate with associate degrees,” “All students have iPads”). This bucket groups programmatic strengths, awards, and explicit college-readiness evidence reported more often in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent, v: Square reviews more often describe hands-on administrators and teachers, clear communication systems, lower bullying reports, and narratives of steady improvement or professional responsiveness (examples: “The Deans and all administration are out all day…,” “They have worked diligently to accommodate his different learning style,” “there has been barely any bullying”). This bucket captures evidence that square schools present as better‑managed day‑to‑day, with dependable adult–student relationships and an overall safer, more supportive environment.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, concret: These reviews explicitly name hands‑on and articulated pathways—woodshop/culinary/home economics, JTED/medical‑magnet programs, many electives and dual‑credit/AP listings, partnerships placing students in internships and college courses—whereas square reviews rarely enumerate equivalent CTE/dual‑enrollment opportunities (examples: Circle mentions 'home economics, woodshop, Business Education,' 'many Dual Credit, AP courses,' 'partners with companies to give graduates internships'; Square does not).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe and sy: Many circle reviews document high‑severity incidents and repeated safety lapses—bomb threats, gang activity, physical assaults (teacher in a coma), repeated property crime, pervasive vaping/drugs and bathroom misconduct—and allege denial or slow/inadequate administrative response; square reviews may note misbehavior or vaping but do not describe this scale or repeated unaddressed violence (examples: 'lots of bomb threats,' 'gang activity... prevalent,' 'My Niece was brutally attacked... Noone helped her').
candidate_defs.circle entries document more systemic st: Reviews grouped in circle repeatedly allege nepotism and favoritism determining student treatment and extracurricular access, teachers kept despite misconduct or tenure protection, privacy breaches (GPAs announced in class), lost/manipulated official records, inconsistent or dismissive principal behavior and administrative unresponsiveness—claims that go beyond square's critiques (examples: 'must be born in Russell... if you don’t have the right last name... you will not fit in,' 'administration has been well informed about his inappropriate behavior but has opted to continue to employ him,' 'they had lost over half of her school records').
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pronounced fa: Circle reviewers cite concrete building/hygiene failures (filthy water fountains, broken locks, overcrowded lunchrooms), recurrent supply shortages, waiting lists or overcapacity, and specific budget/prioritization complaints (new gym while textbooks are decades old; money diverted to sports), whereas square reviews less often describe this combination of poor maintenance plus contested spending (examples: 'desks and equipment outdated,' 'ran out of printer paper,' 'District builds a new gym... while textbooks are so old').
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger social: Circle reviews frequently describe status‑based access (family names, wealth, 'if you’re an athlete you’ll do well; if not you’ll be miserable'), parental complicity or harassment, active community mobilization or sustained volunteerism, and many families transferring out or homeschooling as remedies—social patterns that square reviews do not foreground (examples: 'You have to be born in Russell to be happy,' 'parents encourage this behavior...harass Deerfield residents,' 'Glad my children transferred out... I now home school my kids').
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews emphasize concrete curricular breadth and results—AP and dual‑enrollment offerings, high AP pass rates, students earning 40+ college credits, specific scholarship and direct‑admit examples, and repeatedly‑cited college placement metrics (e.g., “AP test scores and the college placement successes are outstanding,” “dual enrollment…Spanish college credits,” “our son was offered direct admission…and a scholarship”). In short, circle school texts present systemic, programmatic rigor and documented outcomes more often than square texts, which tend to lack such program detail or measurable metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive bul: Many circle reviews recount repeated peer abuse, racial slurs, fights, students roaming halls, and parents withdrawing kids for safety—often paired with claims that administration fails to stop offenders (e.g., “constant bullying…teachers don't deal with the bullies effectively,” “fights are regular,” “students run the place,” and parents: “I had to pull 2 of my daughters out due to bullying”). These safety/discipline narratives appear far more frequently and with concrete incidents in circle entries than in square entries, which are more likely to describe a controlled or improving discipline climate.
candidate_defs.circle entries contain more reports of s: Circle reviewers give multiple concrete allegations of teacher/administrator misconduct—forgotten tests, public grade disclosure, favoritism for athletes/connected families, retaliation against involved parents, calls for district investigation, and frequent principal/teacher turnover (e.g., “teachers…gave out each student’s grade to the entire class,” “if a parent dares to get involved…will make sure their children pay for it,” and “absurd principal and administrative turnover”). These governance and professionalism complaints are more numerous and specific in circle entries than in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries showcase broader extracur: Circle reviews repeatedly list expansive programmatic breadth and campus assets—award‑winning band and athletics, vocational/AG/CTE offerings, skate parks, huge theaters, pro‑team practice use, Astroturf fields, and many clubs or national competition teams (e.g., “marching band…state competition 33 times,” “woodshop, auto shop, AG program, FFA national level,” “skate park, HUGE theater”). Square entries seldom enumerate this combination of extracurricular variety and facility richness.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more proactive s: Circle reviews cite institutional remediation and communication practices—mandatory programs for failing students, added tutoring periods and lunchtime tutoring, named reading specialists and counselors who respond to parents, and explicit claims of strong school‑to‑home communication (e.g., “they added 2 tutoring periods,” “The level of communication from school to home is by far the best,” “Ms. Tina Leach is the reading specialist,” and ‘Counselors really answer parents’ questions on time’). These operational, school‑provided supports and outreach are reported more often in circle entries than in square entries, which more frequently describe reliance on private tutors or limited counselor engagement.
candidate_defs.circle entries report systemic favoritis: These reviews describe governance and personnel practices that protect favored staff and donors and prioritize elite families/athletes — e.g., claims that 'once a teacher is accepted... it is very hard for them to be fired,' athletes and donor families 'get treated so much better,' and 'nepotism is an issue.' This bucket captures complaints about hidden favors, hire/retain-protection, donor-driven preferential treatment, and board-level misprioritization of spending toward image/athletics rather than accountability.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, named ac: These entries name concrete program strengths and credentialed outcomes — e.g., high AP pass rates and AP exam success, large scholarship totals ('won over $28,000,000 in merit based scholarships'), vocational/CTE certifications and college credit, SciTech/Scholars/STEM programs, FBLA state competition, and documented college matriculation without remediation. This bucket groups specific, program-level evidence of advanced coursework, CTE credentials, dual‑credit/AP outcomes, and specialized scholars magnets.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe a closer, small‑: Reviews in this bucket emphasize small‑campus intimacy, mandated family volunteering/lotteries, strong alumni ties and local multi‑generational engagement — e.g., 'all schools on one campus... everyone knew everyone,' 'each family serve 10 hrs of volunteering,' 'Alumni Association is stronger,' and parents reporting active PTA/community support. It covers patterns of high parental expectations, visible school spirit, and formalized family participation.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student safet: These entries document on‑campus misconduct and failures of supervision or response — e.g., multiple fights and drug use, 'students steal and sell drugs,' sexual manipulation of younger students, theft of personal property, and claims that administration 'fails to address' these incidents or fails to notify parents of injuries. This bucket groups concrete safety incidents, pervasive bullying/violence reports, and inadequate enforcement or remediation.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more accessible, i: This bucket captures reviews that cite hands‑on teacher availability and formal supports — e.g., teachers' cell phone numbers and PowerSchool grade portals, 'a ton of tutoring programs' and required teacher 'help nights,' one‑on‑one registration counseling, proactive guidance counselors, and personalized senior scheduling. It covers direct parent contact, structured academic help, mentoring/after‑school project support, and concrete transitional supports for military/transient families.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, more n: This bucket captures claims that Circle schools offer tangible advanced-course pathways and college-readiness (AP/IB/honors, magnet/STEM/CTE academies, dual-enrollment, Running Start, large scholarship totals and named college acceptances) and report higher test/AP results or consistent college matriculation; examples include 'The IB Program is exceptional,' 'Our seniors earned $2,000,000 in scholarship offers,' 'students earned enough AP credit to skip a year,' and named university matriculations—contrasting Square's reports of weak preparation, lower college attendance, or limited AP offerings.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, deeper, a: This bucket covers Circle reviews that enumerate many extracurriculars, strong daily music/arts, NJROTC, FFA, engineering and career academies, extensive athletic participation and state championships and booster engagement—evidence such as 'award winning band, chorus, robotics, FFA with state championships,' 'great NJROTC program,' and 'many teams play and win'—whereas Square reviews lack comparable program breadth or named successes.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more frequent an: This bucket groups accounts of ongoing unsafe student behavior and incidents plus claims that staff/administration ignored, minimized, or mishandled them—for example, reports of weapons and chemicals brought in, restroom drug offers while administration 'does nothing', routine daily bullying and racial slurs, theft captured on camera with no remedy, and claims administrators covered up assaults—contrasting Square reviews which rarely report comparable safety crises.
candidate_defs.circle entries contain more concrete fac: This bucket captures Circle reviewers' frequent, specific notes about buildings, capital projects, 1:1 technology, underused expensive labs, overcrowded buses, cafeteria food safety/quality, remodeling or deterioration, and schedule/transport logistics (e.g., 'MacBooks for every student,' 'million dollar lab used by 20 students,' 'buses with kids standing,' 'needs theatre and locker room remodeling'), while Square tends not to provide this level of facility/operational granularity.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive sta: This bucket groups reviewer claims about personnel and governance problems that undermine schooling: teacher favoritism and grade manipulation, administrators bullying or harassing staff/parents, ignored parent communications, counselors who harm graduation prospects, mass teacher departures, and allegations of misused funds or politicized board decisions (e.g., 'teachers change grades,' 'administration harasses parents,' 'decades of poor top-down culture'), which are described far more often in Circle than in Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete acad: These reviews call out explicit program architecture and outcome metrics (course lists, academies, dual‑enrollment partners, IB/AP, vocational certification pipelines and state/graduation/ACT figures). Examples: circle reviewers name 'Dual credit classes… AP classes,' 'scholars program… dual enrollment paid by the school,' 'The IB Program… best in the state,' and cite graduation/ACT data and grade‑inflation concerns—details that Square reviews typically omit or discuss only generically.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These comments describe repeated violent incidents, gang/drug exposure, ongoing bullying and harassment, and claims that staff or administrators failed to address them (suspensions, inaction, or punitive mishandling). Illustrative evidence from circle: 'Bullies receive little consequences,' 'see someone get beat up… blood on the walls,' 'pressure into gang activity, beaten and robbed multiple times,' and parents hiring lawyers after administration 'did nothing.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups allegations about leadership behavior, opaque or dishonest practices, and unequal enforcement that reviewers attribute to senior staff decisions. Examples: circle claims that administrators 'manipulate school data,' 'protect favorites/teachers’ children,' 'refused to pull up book return list and forced me to pay $119,' accusations of nepotism in scholarship/tryouts, and secretive firings—charges largely absent from Square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete faci: These reviews contain actionable facility/capacity evidence (new buildings or renovations, dirty restrooms, overcrowded classrooms, undersized PE with wait lists, cameras/security upgrades, and contested spending priorities). Examples from circle: 'The school is dirty… food splatters on the walls,' 'PE program is poor and too small—wait list,' 'lots of ongoing construction… math building, pool,' and 'spent $15,000 to refinish court while safety issues neglected.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report more organized, in: This grouping captures reviews that cite concrete, repeatable support practices: before/after‑school and weekend tutoring, peer tutoring programs, coordinated nurses/guidance counselors, breakfast-in-classroom, and teachers who reserve extra time for students. Representative circle evidence: 'continuous open door policies—early morning, after school and weekend tutoring,' 'the nurses and guidance counselors worked together,' 'teachers will help no matter the situation' and 'breakfast in the classroom,' contrasts Square reviewers frequently describe weaker or inconsistent counseling/support.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reports of widespread peer misconduct and safety incidents plus claims that staff/administration ignored or mishandled them — e.g., multiple Circle reviews cite chronic bullying, weekly physical fights, visible drug deals, an open campus that enables skipping, and parents saying the office ‘did nothing’ or relied on police instead of intervening. It is distinct from administrative corruption (see bucket 3) because it centers on student behavior, violence/drug exposure, and the school’s front‑line safety response rather than governance or favoritism.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, higher‑: This bucket groups concrete programmatic breadth and high‑level outcomes: Circle reviews repeatedly name full IB/Cambridge programs, extensive AP and Dual Enrollment completion, career‑tech academies, state athletic championships and award‑winning band/fine‑arts, and large scholarship/college‑matriculation figures (e.g., Dual Enrollment credits, millions in scholarships). It merges advanced academic rigor with extracurricular/athletic achievement because the raw evidence ties both to institutional program strength and student outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures governance and ethical complaints: Circle reviewers allege principals/staff protected one another, favored wealthy families or athletes, hired friends/relatives, threatened or harassed parents/students, and described pressure to pass or alter grades (‘teachers told to put in minimums’). These items are about leadership behavior, corruption and unfair insider practices and are kept separate from operational process failures (bucket 5) and classroom instruction quality (bucket 4).
candidate_defs.square entries report more chronic teach: This bucket collects square reviewers’ concrete instructional criticisms: frequent claims that many teachers ‘don’t care,’ classrooms are unorganized or unruly, core instruction (especially math/English) is ineffective, and guidance/counseling fails to prepare students for college (students getting A's in AP but struggling in college). It focuses on pedagogy, teacher responsiveness and counseling effectiveness rather than governance or program breadth.
candidate_defs.circle entries contain more specific, co: This bucket covers tangible, day‑to‑day operational evidence: Circle reviews frequently enumerate parent portal problems, dated/accurate grade systems, lost credits, counselor scheduling failures, night school/irregular calendars, overcrowding or recent renovations, cafeteria hygiene or meal praise, one‑laptop programs, and detailed transit/attendance logistics. It is distinct from administrative misconduct (bucket 3) because it addresses systems, processes and infrastructure rather than ethical or favoritism issues.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews portray circle schools as offering more AP/IB/dual‑enrollment options, routine college‑credit accumulation, concrete scholarship and selective‑college placements (e.g., named IB/dual credit, students earning 26–32 college hours, full‑ride scholarships, UC/Berkeley law placement), whereas square reviews lack comparable program breadth or documented alumni college success.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, higher‑: Circle reviews repeatedly name award‑winning band/theater/visual arts, strong CTE and STEM pathways, ROTC/JROTC and competitive athletics plus recent construction/technology upgrades (e.g., state band wins, engineering/independent research programs, new stadium/library/field house), while square reviews rarely list equivalent organized, high‑level extracurricular breadth or capital improvements.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Circle accounts contain frequent concrete safety and wellbeing failures — fights, overdoses, gang presence, high local suicide warnings, unchecked bullying — paired with explicit SPED/IEP/504 noncompliance and poor mental‑health support (e.g., 'they don't follow IEPs and 504s', psychiatrists advising removal), whereas square reviews do not report this constellation of severe safety and accommodation problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent gove: Circle reviewers describe chronic principal turnover, school‑board/district corruption or politicization, nepotism/legacy favoritism, and operational mismanagement (lost transcripts, late hires, skewed security vs counselor staffing, budget misallocation), with examples like '6 or 7 different Principals in the last 5 years,' alleged corruption, and donor/alumni reinstatement of misbehaving students; these governance‑level complaints are far less present in square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviews emphasize staff unresponsiveness and unprofessional conduct — indifferent principals, rude or non‑communicative counselors and teachers, failing to return emails, and classroom misconduct (mocking, storming out) — and frame student support systems as ineffective, complaints that are much more common in square than in circle entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, explic: This bucket captures reviews that report organized, high‑level academic pathways (IB/AP/dual‑credit/early college, extensive AP participation, subject‑specific honors, measurable test/college outcomes) and explicit college‑readiness metrics in circle schools (e.g., IB/IB academy, ‘ACT 34’, ‘SAT 200 points over national average’, early 9th‑grade college prep, many students to selective universities), contrasted with square reviews that note fewer AP/rigorous options, lower test readiness, or single anecdotal alumni success.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent seve: This bucket groups reviews describing pervasive student misconduct and safety incidents in circle schools—daily fights, drug/alcohol use, regular police presence, rampant bullying, systemic racism/homophobia/sexual harassment, and threats to student safety (examples: ‘fights everyday’, ‘kids coming to school drunk and high’, ‘racism runs wild’, ‘students led off in handcuffs’), whereas square reviews more commonly describe fewer or more contained disciplinary issues and clearer rules or improving climate.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more consistent,: This bucket covers reviews that emphasize dependable teacher help, routine outreach, effective counselors, and organized family communication in square schools (e.g., ‘guidance and counseling department is very quick’, ‘Almost every teacher I had was wonderful’, ‘regularly scheduled parent‑teacher conferences’), in contrast to circle reviews that more often allege counseling incompetence, slow responses, or spotty teacher follow‑through.
