candidate_defs.circle entries document greater administ: This bucket groups reviews reporting managerial failures and unfair administrative practices in circle schools—unresponsive principals, favoritism/nepotism, punitive dress‑code/tardy policies, misrecorded grades/attendance, blocking transfers, alleged falsified credits or vendetta‑driven staff removals (examples: ‘They lie about what they offer’, ‘suspended me so many times because of dress code’, ‘One counselor messed up my attendance and grades’, ‘drove out one of the best teachers for a personal vendetta’), while square reviews raise fewer of these specific administrative abuse or recordkeeping allegations.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader on‑site: This bucket captures reviews that list extensive physical and co‑curricular assets at circle schools—state‑of‑the‑art gyms/stadiums, IPads/laptops, greenhouse, many languages, career/CTE pathways, numerous clubs, and competitive music/athletic honors (examples: ‘built with state‑of‑the‑art technology’, ‘golf, wrestling, football, marching band, greenhouse’, ‘each child has an iPad’, ‘in‑house CTE/BOCES’), whereas square entries more often describe narrower offerings, outdated labs/textbooks, or fewer advanced extracurricular resources.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews repeatedly name concrete, high‑level academic offerings and outcomes in circle schools—e.g., “opportunity to take 40+ college credits,” extensive AP rigor, IB/full‑diploma counts, active guidance counselors who secure scholarships and college placements—while square reviews more often report poor preparation, lack of counseling, or only a few dual‑enrollment mentions. Falling into this bucket means the school narrative centers on formal advanced-course availability, heavy homework/rigor, documented college credits/scholarships, and active college‑prep counseling (examples: 10 APs/31 college credits, guidance counselors providing scholarship assistance).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent seve: Circle reviews include graphic accounts of sexualized misconduct, physical assaults, LGBT‑targeted harassment, repeated fights, and thefts plus descriptions of either weak enforcement or escalatory punitive responses (metal detectors, SRO citations, expulsions for off‑campus parties), e.g. explicit sexual/assault anecdotes and claims of weekly fights versus claims of punitive detentions/suspensions. Content falls here when reviews focus on on‑campus violence/bullying incidents, harassment with mental‑health harm, plus a disciplinary approach that is either lax/inconsistent or severe and law‑enforcement‑oriented.
candidate_defs.square entries document more chronic res: Square reviews more consistently call out underfunding, large class sizes, lack of basic materials and overcrowding (e.g., no money for books or desks, AP class with 45 students, 'not enough money for paper'), whereas circle reviews more often describe program expansion, capital bonds, or 1:1 tech. A review is classified here when it emphasizes persistent material/resource shortfalls, capacity limits, and routine operational shortages affecting instruction and scheduling.
candidate_defs.circle entries display greater polarizat: Many circle reviewers praise named teachers, close advisor relationships, and high parent communication while other circle reviewers report verbal attacks by staff, administrative harassment/censorship, favoritism toward athletes or alumni, grade‑changing, and rapid leadership churn; examples include named advisors who 'truly cared' alongside allegations that 'they change your child’s grades' or 'she harasses the strongest teachers.' This bucket captures reviews where staff behavior is highly mixed and unpredictable—either highly personal and supportive or punitive, biased, and disorderly—rather than uniformly good or uniformly bad.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger extrac: Circle reviews frequently foreground a distinctive school identity—arts magnets with intensive rehearsal, state‑championship athletics, audition/admissions rules, alumni/parent volunteerism, booster culture, faith‑based programming or single‑sex rationales—while square reviews focus less on a singular identity and more on general programs or vocational breadth. A review fits this bucket when it highlights institutional specialization, demonstrated extracurricular success, active alumni/parent fundraising, or an explicit religious/single‑sex mission shaping student life.
candidate_defs.circle entries document stronger, cleare: These reviews explicitly name AP/IB/AICE pathways, academies, dual-enrollment and credential partnerships and cite concrete results (valedictorians, Ivy/college admits, scholarships, state certifications), whereas square reviews mostly mention generic college-prep or lack comparable program detail (examples: circle lists IB diplomas, Biotechnology/BACE certification, many AP classes and documented college placements; square only generically notes college-prep courses).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Many circle reviewers describe daily fights, gang and drug presence, sexual harassment and racist harassment and allege adults either ignore, protect perpetrators, or punish victims; square reviews lack these sustained safety claims (examples: '40+ fights last year', 'principal protects gang members', 'sexual harassment is common', and reports of administrators doing nothing).
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more administrat: Circle reviews frequently allege an unresponsive or nepotistic principal/office, lost transcripts/scheduling errors, punitive bans of complainants, and even claims of purging students or fabricating data to inflate metrics; square reviews rarely make such sustained operational accusations (examples: 'principal will NOT return parents' calls', 'lost test records', 'restricted me from campus for one year', 'clearing failing students to raise stats').
candidate_defs.circle entries portray more active, indi: Circle reviewers repeatedly report teachers who provide after-hours study sessions, daily progress updates, proactive counselors and quick parent communication—concrete behaviors distinct from system-level praise—whereas square reviews more often record limited or inconsistent teacher outreach (examples: 'daily updates of her progress', 'AP teachers provide weekend workshops', 'teachers are available after school and respond within 24 hours').
candidate_defs.circle entries surface sharper facility,: Circle reviews describe pronounced infrastructure issues (crowding, falling-apart buildings, lunch/bus shortages) alongside accounts of major athletic/arts facilities or active construction, or clear imbalances in resource allocation (examples: 'almost 4,000 students/overcrowded', 'buildings are falling apart after failed levy', and conversely 'wonderful football field but only one classroom copy of books'); square reviews do not present this same degree of facility/capacity extremes.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more acute safet: These reviews report concrete safety crises and staff non‑intervention at circle schools—physical assaults, gang activity, frequent fights, drug circulation, ignored self‑harm, bed‑bug infestations and even police arrests—examples include “My son has been beaten up four times,” “gang activity…in plain view,” and complaints that guards/staff ignore cutting; square reviews lack comparable reports of assaults, gangs, sexual‑harassment mishandling, or police overreach.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more punitive, arb: Circle reviews repeatedly describe leadership that enforces rules unevenly, protects insiders, or responds vindictively—examples: church‑linked favoritism, board nepotism (high‑paid hires tied to board members), strict arbitrary dress/attendance/grade punishments, and claims that complaints go unresolved; by contrast square entries rarely allege systemic nepotism or politicized retaliation and contain more mixed or stable accounts of discipline and governance.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more concrete, n: Many circle reviews enumerate specific, high‑detail programs and outcomes—AP/College‑in‑High‑School/dual enrollment, explicit CTE pathways (welding, culinary, audio production, career center partnerships), strong music/theater with pro partnerships, 1:1 take‑home laptops and measurable alumni/college success—evidenced by lines like “College‑in‑High‑School classes granting community college credits,” lists of electives (Welding, Video Game Design), and alumni scholarship/degree claims; square reviews rarely supply this same level of concrete program names or documented long‑term outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger instituti: Square reviews more often highlight consistent AP/honors offerings, upward academic trends, involved principals, and capital improvements—examples include praise for AP courses and college readiness, a new science/math building and athletic facilities, ‘grades improved dramatically,’ and examples of active counselors—whereas circle reviews more often describe academic unevenness, leadership turnover, or facility decay.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize closer small‑sc: Circle reviews frequently describe intimate, family‑like cultures, small class sizes, teachers who provide one‑on‑one mentoring and out‑of‑class tutoring, and active parent involvement—e.g., “teachers know every single student,” “dozens of teachers open their rooms before and after school,” and “fantastic parent involvement”—while square reviews tend to depict broader programmatic structures, larger‑scale dynamics, and advice that students must be self‑motivated to thrive.
candidate_defs.circle entries report far worse student: This bucket captures reports of violent or dangerous student behaviors and weak/ineffective responses (e.g., gang violence, drug use, fights, a student overdose, death threats, PSAT lockdowns, rampant bullying) and administrators/staff tolerating or failing to stop them — examples include “received death threats,” “Gang violence … Do not ever take your child here,” and “Bullying is a huge issue… it's brushed under the rug.” These items distinguish schools where safety and discipline climate is a dominant, recurring problem in the building and surrounding community.
candidate_defs.circle entries depict greater administra: This groups reports about leadership problems — sustained lack of follow‑up, dishonesty or reputation control, retaliation toward parents/students, part‑time/interim leaders, biased favoritism, and punitive top‑down climates (e.g., “superintendent will lie straight to your face,” “ignored with NO response,” “principals fire the good teachers,” “retaliatory atmosphere toward parents”). These differences signal schools where district/school leadership quality and accountability are cited as primary operational failings.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: This bucket covers concrete programmatic academic strength: multiple AP/IB classes, extensive dual‑enrollment/college‑credit opportunities, multilevel course tracks and measurable college outcomes (e.g., “many AP as well as concurrent college credit… graduate with over 40 hours of college credit,” “offers HONORS PROGRAMS and IB integration,” “college dual-credit arrangements”), distinguishing schools with explicit advanced-course access and documented postsecondary gains.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more teacher/staff: This groups staffing problems described in reviews: high turnover and mass departures, inexperienced or misassigned teachers (Teach For America or teachers teaching subjects they lack credentials), poor grading/record‑keeping, and unprofessional behavior (e.g., “taught Spanish 1 year then left,” “they hired a music‑degree teacher to teach geometry,” “teacher played with his phone during parent conference,” “teachers do not grade papers”), indicating personnel reliability and instructional professionalism are core differences.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize broader extracu: This bucket captures descriptions of abundant clubs/CTE/arts and high‑level performing-arts or sports facilities (stadiums, pools, auditoriums) alongside disputes over spending or athletics favoritism (e.g., “many activities/clubs/sports,” “marching band, JROTC,” “brand new stadium,” and complaints like “we never had textbooks but funded a football team” or “athletic director only cares about football”). These items distinguish schools with pronounced extracurricular infrastructure and contested resource/prioritization choices.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reviews that describe frequent bullying, fights, gangs, substance use, violent incidents, and supervisory failures (e.g., bus drivers ignoring bullying, students 'rule the school', 'fights everyday', 'someone was shot at a football game') together with administrator inaction or victim‑blaming; square entries do not describe this level of pervasive safety breakdown and instead report fewer or improving incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: This groups reviews that emphasize broad/rigorous programming and demonstrable outcomes—AP/IB and tracked curricula, career academies and industry certifications, award‑winning music/robotics/athletics, dual‑credit/adjunct faculty and students accepted to top colleges (e.g., multiple acceptances to UCLA, 'entered college with 40 college credits')—while square entries typically lack those concrete programmatic breadths or outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Includes reviews alleging preferential treatment for donors/friends, office favoritism, principals who back teachers '100%', leadership that bullies staff or misuses surveillance, politicized board decisions/COVID mismanagement, and punitive/exclusionary enforcement (e.g., student barred from summer school over a bounced check); square entries lack or counter these kinds of governance/favoritism allegations.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more failures in s: This covers reviews alleging IEP/504 paperwork and implementation failures, incompetent or damaging guidance counselor actions (e.g., 'messed up my profile', 'refused to help my son'), and neglect of student mental health (reports of self‑harm, 'they do not take mental health seriously'); square entries are less likely to describe systemic breakdowns in these student support services.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete faci: Groups evidence of physical and operational resource problems—deteriorating buildings and sanitation ('restrooms are broken down', inedible cafeteria food), lack of transportation in rural contexts, antiquated student technology, missing electives and supplies, fundraising reliance and budget shortfalls, and administrative access problems (e.g., refused parent‑portal access)—whereas square entries rarely document this breadth of facility/resource failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, more con: This bucket captures claims that circle schools list specific AP/IB/Pre‑AP, dual‑enrollment, academy/CTE/certification pathways (e.g., AP offerings, IB, dual‑credit, community‑college IT academy with C++ certs, students graduating with college credits or associate degrees) and concrete college matriculation evidence (acceptances to Duke/UNC, high graduation/college‑going rates), whereas square reviews lack comparable program detail or measurable outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more concrete te: This groups reports of teachers routinely tutoring before/after school, formal mentoring programs and teacher‑run clubs (e.g., tutoring, 'homework hall,' ROTC, 'Band of Brothers' mentor assignment, teacher‑led clubs and coaching), and explicit teacher credentials/mentorship, contrasted with square reviews that offer praise but fewer concrete examples of sustained teacher availability or structured teacher‑run supports.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive bul: This bucket covers repeated accounts of severe student‑on‑student and staff‑perpetrated abuse (racism, homophobia, targeted attacks, sexual assaults), daily or rampant bullying, and reviewer claims that administrators/staff routinely fail to remediate or cover up incidents — themes that appear far more frequently and with greater severity in circle reviews than in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report a stronger athleti: This groups claims that athletics dominate school priorities (sports glorified over arts/academics, budget skew to football/basketball, recruitment allegations, disciplinary leniency for athletes, athletes receiving scholarships/priority) — patterns emphasized in many circle reviews while square reviews do not show the same systemic athletics‑first criticisms.
candidate_defs.square entries portray more consistent,: This bucket captures square reviews’ recurring theme of reachable teachers/principals, deans who respond, a family‑like or safe atmosphere, and steady college‑preparation claims (e.g., teachers stay late to help, principal/counselors are helpful, 'safe & welcoming' environment), in contrast to circle reviews which are often internally polarized, report inconsistent responsiveness, or document harsher safety/leadership failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger formal: These reviews repeatedly cite concrete school-level academic offerings and outcomes (AP/IB/honors, dual‑enrollment/college credit, A+ or API scores, internship/STEM partnerships) and alumni college acceptances—e.g. “IB program…super difficult,” “earned over 19 credits of college credits,” “hit a 714 API score,” “accepted to every college he applied” — claims that Square reviews do not consistently provide or that Square often lacks.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: Many Circle reviews document fights, gang presence, in‑class drug use, sexual/physical abuse, psychiatric crises, and repeated bullying plus administrators who ignore or mishandle complaints (e.g. “fights everyday,” “drugs running rampant,” “I was sexually harassed…went into psychiatric care,” “numerous complaints about bullying were made and were disregarded”); Square reviews by contrast rarely report comparable violent/drug/safety crises or systemic adult inaction.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more consistent,: Square reviews more often praise steady, helpful teachers, engaged counselors, and a warm principal (e.g. “teachers are all very understanding… principal is warm,” “teachers come in on weekends to tutor”), whereas Circle reviews more often report variable or unprofessional teachers, higher turnover, favoritism, or staff misconduct.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger extrac: Circle reviews frequently note prominent athletics, award‑winning arts, marching‑band/athletic rankings, funded facilities or cosmetic athletic investment, and both broad and exclusive club/team access (e.g. “athletic programs are excellent,” “arts programs are well funded and award winning,” complaints about money spent on stadium lights or expensive uniform vendors), whereas Square tends to foreground general clubs and college/prep breadth without the same elite athletic/arts prominence or funding narratives.
candidate_defs.circle entries document greater operatio: Circle reviews contain many concrete operational complaints (moldy/decaying buildings, split‑campus logistics, lost transcripts or scheduling errors, constant solicitations for money, enrollment lottery breakdowns, nepotistic hires — e.g. “ceiling tile fell off,” “office won’t transfer grades,” “constantly asked for money,” “principle had her sister‑in‑law working as an assistant principal”), while Square reviews rarely assert comparable systemic operational mismanagement.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: These reviews repeatedly cite concrete advanced-offering and outcome evidence (AP/IB/Honors, dual-credit and early‑college pathways, specialized academies/high‑tech programs, high ACT/scholarship totals and Ivy/elite acceptances) that square reviews do not; examples include claims of many AP/IB courses, credit-acceleration programs, students accepted to top colleges, and large scholarship awards versus square's lack of comparable college-placement evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more persistent st: Many circle reviews describe repeated safety events (fights, code reds, gang activity, weapons, visible substance use, hate symbols) and administrators failing to stop or properly sanction offenders, whereas square reviews contain far fewer or more managed safety anecdotes; representative lines include reports of swastikas, beer bottles/tampons on campus, regular threats of violence, police presence, and bullying left unaddressed.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviewers more often accuse leadership of turnover, favoritism (athlete/parent shields), ideological or religious coercion, targeted shaming by principals, contract/labor disputes and claims that 'the administration lies'—including calls for principals to be fired or removed—while square reviews show fewer of these governance/political-abuse allegations.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more facility, res: Circle texts contain numerous concrete service-and-resource failures—poor building condition, sanitation problems and pests, no air conditioning, bad cafeteria food and extra family fees, transportation and bus-lane incidents, lost CTE/vocational programs and shortages of instructional materials—whereas square reviews rarely describe such systemic physical or operational deficits.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, more con: Multiple circle reviewers describe passionate teachers who 'go above and beyond,' very small classes and one‑on‑one attention, clear special‑education/IEP supports and measurable remedial gains (reading level jumps, successful transfers), contrasting with square reviews that more often lack claims of individualized help or show mixed teacher responsiveness.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures school-safety and day-to-day student-behavior problems: multiple circle reviews describe frequent fights, gang activity, severe bullying, vandalism, criminal incidents, and concrete examples of staff mishandling self-harm or harassment (e.g., “fights every week,” “gangs are formed,” staff ignoring racial hazing, and using suspension to avoid services), whereas square entries rarely report that level or frequency of violent/unsafe incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries document broader, named a: This groups programmatic substance—explicit AP/honors counts, magnet/CTE majors (aviation, engineering, computer science), dual‑enrollment and credential pathways, STEM/maker resources, and cited test/graduation/college‑matriculation metrics—that circle reviewers repeatedly enumerate (e.g., ‘nation’s only high school…Private Pilot license,’ ‘11 AP classes,’ ‘several academies and dual enrollment,’ and state test/graduation claims) while square reviews lack comparable detailed program lists or outcome statistics.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize small-school pe: This bucket covers evidence that the school operates as a close, family‑style community: circle reviewers frequently report small classes, named beloved teachers, after‑school help, strong alumni networks and parents volunteering in daily operations (concession stands, committees), and explicit school‑spirit traditions, whereas square reviews less often describe enduring alumni ties, pervasive personalization, or daily parent-run operations.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more responsive,: This captures differences about district and administrative leadership: many square reviews praise active principals, superintendents, parent‑teacher engagement and invitations to attend board/PTA meetings (“stellar interactions from Superintendent down”), whereas circle reviews more often allege politicized boards, unaccountable leadership, or calls to shut down the school, signaling a contrast between square’s responsive governance narratives and circle’s governance criticism.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete oper: This bucket groups logistics/facilities evidence: circle reviewers provide explicit operational metrics and cite problems or assets—bus lateness, one‑hour pickup delays, bad lunches, bathroom issues, trailer classrooms, 1:1 laptop rollouts or classroom tech, and explicit enrollment/crowding numbers—while square reviews generally omit those granular operational data or report different facility themes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more explicit adva: These reviews describe concrete, programmatic college pathways in circle—AP/IB classes, dual‑enrollment ("you take college courses in 12th grade," "IB classes," "free 4 years at hunter college"), documented matriculation and scholarship statistics ("99% go on to college," "full scholarship," Ivy counts)—whereas square reviews tend to offer generic praise of 'great academics' without named advanced curricula or school‑level outcome metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent stud: Many circle reviews detail recurring fights, drugs, assaults, severe bullying and racial harassment and allege staff inaction or punitive/uneven discipline (e.g. "kids are getting assaulted every single day," "PCBs...teachers diagnosed with cancer," "the school promotes Bullying... the bully gets away with it"), while square reviews largely describe fewer systemic safety incidents and administration that enforces rules or is caring and responsive.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, higher‑vi: Circle reviews catalogue extensive arts, music, band and competitive sports programs and public accomplishments (marching band honors, state championships, strong music/theater departments) and also frequent complaints that resources and attention are diverted to athletics ("All of our resources are pulled...football," "put all of the money into the football program"), whereas square reviews rarely list that same breadth of arts or program prestige and emphasize a more balanced set of academic supports.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more facility, fun: Circle reviewers repeatedly cite concrete infrastructure and resourcing failures—outdated/infested buildings, leaking ceilings, HVAC/AC failures, overcrowded lunches/parking, lost credits, budget shortfalls and explicit accusations of financial mismanagement—("ceilings still leak," "ridded with roaches and rats," "over crowded...adding a second Senior High," "They pocket the funds"), while square reviews seldom report similar breadth or severity of facilities/funding breakdowns.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent, a: Square reviews more often describe caring, accessible administrators and counselors and orderly staff stability ("Administration...are generally caring and helpful," "assigned counselor and programs"), contrasting with many circle reviews that accuse leadership of turnover, unresponsiveness, retaliatory or politicized decisions, and counseling failures ("many, many meetings with school 'leadership' and nothing has improved," "Our counseling is awful..."), so square entries emphasize steadier adult supports while circle entries more often record leadership instability or unresponsiveness.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews recount frequent physical fights, gang activity, on-campus substance use, threats and pervasive bullying plus explicit failures to respond (e.g., “watch/be in a fight every other day,” “the gangs run the town and the schools,” “people smoke in the bathrooms,” and administration that ‘did very little’ after assaults), while Square reviews rarely describe systemic safety collapse—so this bucket groups substantive, recurring safety/discipline failures and under‑enforced anti‑bullying policies.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize a faith‑centere: Circle reviewers repeatedly describe integrated religious formation, selective or tuition-funded enrollment, and narrow demographics (e.g., “foundation in Christ,” “you pay almost $10,000 every year,” “you’re either rich, religious, or you’re nobody,” and ‘selective… you have to apply’), whereas Square contains no comparable claims, so this bucket captures institutional religiosity, choice/tuition admission, and exclusionary socioeconomic or denominational cultures.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, broade: Circle reviews list concrete program strength (career/technical pathways, automotive shop, theater academy, on‑campus college courses, CTE/FFA, and named AP/dual‑enrollment opportunities) and outcome claims (scholarships, top‑tier college admits and articulated AP/college credit examples), while Square focuses less on such structured program breadth or clear, positive placement evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more administrat: These items describe front‑office rudeness, refusal to return calls, suppression of referrals, hiring for denomination, favoritism (legacy/athlete privilege), punitive/inconsistent discipline, and spending priorities that favor athletics or administrators over students (e.g., “went to office and was not even acknowledged,” “they don’t want them reported so NO ONE FINDS OUT ABOUT IT,” “budgets favor sports,” and “hiring based on the 'correct' religious denomination”), while Square contains fewer of these governance‑level accusations.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more consistent, i: Many Circle reviews name caring, high‑quality teachers and concrete supports (small classes, Questar/autism program praise, scheduled remediation periods, effective college counseling and frequent one‑on‑one help — e.g., “AMAZING teachers who ALWAYS go the extra mile,” “my son is in the 10th grade Questar Program… I love his Questar teacher,” and “Extra help is always available”), whereas Square reviews more often describe mixed or disengaged teacher experiences, so this bucket groups teacher‑level dedication and individualized student support.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: These reviews describe concrete curricular breadth and outcomes — AP/IB/ECE classes, named academies (Pre‑Law, Biotechnology, Medical), dual‑credit, robust CTE/shop/Welding/culinary programs, internships and career-placement supports — and cite measurable college outcomes (AP scores, Ivy/full‑ride admits, alumni degrees). Examples: multiple circle items praise outstanding AP/IB and ECE coursework, vocational pathways, hands‑on shop/half‑year schedules, internship placement, and explicit college matriculation, whereas square reviews emphasize only basic course variety or report poor college readiness.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe and re: These reviews document repeated, concrete safety incidents (daily fights, gang bullying, hospitalizing assaults, widespread drugs/alcohol, theft) and claim staff protect or ignore perpetrators and fail to enforce anti‑bullying policies. Examples: circle reviewers recount gang members bullying their child daily, students ‘jumped’ and hospitalized, pervasive drug/alcohol presence and surveillance gaps, and administrators who 'did nothing' — contrasts that square entries generally lack or describe far less frequently.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater overcrowdi: This cluster covers capacity and physical‑resource problems: chronic overcapacity (schools built for X with 25–30%+ excess enrollment, 30+ students/class), mobile classrooms, leaking roofs/poor HVAC, dirty facilities, understaffed custodial support, weak technology and budget cuts. Examples: circle reviewers cite specific overcrowded classes, mobile units for middle school, no air conditioning/roof leaks, 'very dirty' buildings and cuts to gifted programs, while square reviews more often highlight newer or state‑of‑the‑art facilities.
candidate_defs.circle entries contain more detailed rep: These reviews provide specific, case‑level descriptions of special‑needs services, 504/IEP management, and one‑on‑one remediation — sometimes praising effective individualized supports and successful transitions, and other times documenting abandoned 504 plans, poor case management, or lack of inclusion. Examples: circle items include a special‑needs student who became honor‑roll after targeted supports and also report parents who never reached a case manager or had plans abandoned; square reviews rarely describe such detailed special‑education outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger commun: This group captures school–community integration: multigenerational attendance, family‑like small‑school atmosphere, town traditions (powderpuff, civic support), strong alumni return/mentorship, and named external partnerships that support programs. Examples: circle reviewers describe tight knit 'home away from home' communities, three‑generation family ties, town events and municipal support for school projects, and formal partnerships (NAF, PLTW, Strathmore), while square reviews do not repeatedly report these multigenerational/community‑embedded features.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: This bucket groups reviews where circle schools describe concrete, higher‑level academic programming and measurable college/career outcomes (AP/IB/AICE/Cambridge, early‑college partnerships, dual enrollment, CTE/Tech center offerings, STEM/medical lab affiliations, scholarship totals and test‑score claims) that square reviews do not. Examples: circle mentions Cambridge/AICE diplomas, early‑college agreements, in‑house college credit, expansive AP stacks, vocational nursing/EMT/Welding tracks, and multi‑million dollar scholarship totals, while square lacks comparable programmatic depth or measurable outcome claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more proactive, in: This bucket captures reviewers saying circle schools provide responsive teachers, frequent parent communication, one‑on‑one tutoring/after‑school help, successful IEP implementation, and whole‑child supports, in contrast to square reviews that describe unresponsive counselors or IEP failures. Illustrative evidence: circle reviews praising teachers who call parents, provide individualized tutoring, and run strong special‑needs programs, versus square accounts of ignored IEPs, an unavailable guidance counselor, and families relocating for support.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups reports of active bullying, violent student assaults, drug problems, frequent fights, ineffective security measures (e.g., metal detectors that don’t stop contraband), and administration/staff failing to intervene—claims that appear far more in circle reviews than in square reviews. Examples: circle accounts of nine‑girl attacks, students 'thrown lunchboxes,' 'major bullying problem,' and staff who 'did nothing,' contrasted with square reviews that largely lack repeated, detailed safety‑incident narratives.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader extracurri: This bucket collects reviews describing abundant clubs, fine‑arts concentrations, audition‑based arts magnets, strong sports programs and school spirit in circle schools, together with recurring complaints of nepotism, no‑tryout team access, PTA gatekeeping, or preferential treatment for athletes or vocal parents—patterns not prominent in square reviews. Examples: circle lists numerous arts academies, marching band/highly lauded sports, and also claims that 'to play you need the right last name,' PTA‑controlled tryouts, or athletic resource priorities.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more material, fac: This bucket contains reports that circle schools face underfunding, contested budget allocations or corruption, tuition/recurring fees, program cuts (especially arts/music), scheduling/enrollment logistics failures, library or facility access limits, credit/transfer problems, and messy administrative turnover—issues emphasized more in circle reviews than in square. Illustrative items include claims of rising tuition and fees, lost textbook/resources while nonacademic purchases occur, building renovations or cleanliness complaints, lost credits requiring summer school, and allegations of district misappropriation or imminent state takeover.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more persistent ad: This bucket captures leadership and operational failures described in Circle reviews—confused or rude principals and front offices, counselors and administrators who are unavailable or unhelpful, scheduling and event mismanagement (e.g., forgotten buses, chaotic graduation/ticket handling), and policy/fiscal choices (athletics prioritized over academics, booster-funded trips) that disadvantage families; Square reviews do not describe these systemic operational failures. Examples: 'The main office seems confused,' 'They forgot to order buses for the senior class trip,' 'administration is unavailable and incompetent,' and complaints that arts are left to boosters while money goes to athletic facilities.
candidate_defs.circle entries report worse teacher and: This bucket covers classroom and coach-level performance and behavior problems that Circle reviewers name—ineffective, rude, or incompetent teachers and poor athletic coaches—whereas Square reviewers generally praise classroom staff or note mixed teacher quality without widespread allegations of incompetence. Examples: 'Some of the teachers are terrible at their job and rude to kids,' and 'The coaches are terrible coaches and worse teachers, especially in football and boys basketball.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report more safety proble: This groups reports that Circle schools have unsafe climates, frequent bullying/ostracism, snobby or elitist student social norms, formal 'parting' practices, and explicit racism/homophobia/ableism—issues Square reviews describe less or frame as isolated incidents in otherwise orderly settings. Examples: 'very racist and homophobic slurs...withinthe earshot of teachers,' 'this school is not safe at all... Hope the kids stop bullying each other,' and 'very snobby, loud, obnoxious, self-entitled' students.
candidate_defs.circle entries present stronger document: This bucket collects Circle reviews that cite concrete, quantifiable academic gains, external rankings, and formal pathway/extracurricular programs (e.g., US News ranking, ACT increases, scholarship placements, AFJROTC, Trio, orchestra)—claims Square reviews lack or only describe subjectively, with no comparable metrics or named programs. Examples: 'US News has Lane Tech ranked #5 in Illinois,' 'attendance has increased by 10%,' 'average ACT score of 23,' and named programs like 'AFJROTC' and 'Trio Gear up.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report smaller class size: This bucket describes Circle reviews that emphasize low enrollment, small classes, a personal/safe environment, large campus/facilities, and embedded volunteer or community-run supports (breakfast programs, grandparents volunteering), whereas Square reviews do not foreground small classes, extensive volunteer integration, or claims of superior facilities. Examples: 'classes are small so I can get individual help,' 'The campus is great and huge. The community is also very involved,' and 'I volunteer for the breakfast program...All of the volunteers contribute.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket covers accounts of an unsafe student climate in which reviewers describe frequent fights, gang presence, rampant bullying, vaping/drug use, theft, and concrete failures of adult supervision or protection (e.g. “Fights, bully's… this school needs to be shut down,” “A LOT of fights… gang activity is present,” “welcomed with the gross smell of vapor”), contrasted with square entries that do not describe pervasive on-campus violence or that frame misbehavior as isolated or external.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stricter, more p: This bucket groups reports of authoritarian rules, punitive zero‑tolerance discipline, restricted parent/campus access, and complaints of favoritism in enforcement (e.g. “DON'T WALK ON THE GRASS,” suspension for tardiness, athletes 'not punished at all,' and nepotism claims), whereas square entries lack this combination of heavy-handed policy plus inequitable enforcement.
candidate_defs.circle entries document stronger, concre: This bucket captures detailed programmatic offerings and outcomes that reviewers tie to school quality — AP and high AP load, extensive dual‑credit/paid concurrent enrollment, trade/vo‑tech pathways, JROTC, arts conservatory programs and explicit college‑matriculation metrics (e.g. '40+ college credits paid by school,' 'trade programs such as brick laying, autobody, welding,' 'one of the highest ACT averages'), while square entries typically lack comparable, reviewer‑verified evidence of broad dual‑credit/AP/trade pipelines or show specific college‑prep failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more consistent, p: This bucket includes reviewer evidence of hands‑on teacher involvement, long‑running mentorship, effective counselor interventions, and tailored remediation that produced student turnaround (e.g. 'teachers go out of their way,' 'counselor bent over backwards... Today he finally graduated!,' 'Saturday Academy/24hr online tutors'), in contrast to square entries which more often describe limited or inconsistent adult follow‑through.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more facility and: This bucket groups concrete physical‑resource and capacity issues — overcrowded classes and trailers, mold or restroom problems, underfunded arts/academic materials, and explicit claims that money is prioritized for sports over classrooms (e.g. 'up to 35 kids in my class,' 'no money for music/arts but funded a football team,' 'Bunch of trailers on parking lot'), while square entries rarely center reviews on the same cluster of crowding, infrastructure decay, and resource‑misallocation.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews emphasize concrete, school‑level academic assets (IB diploma, many AP classes, dual‑enrollment/AA outcomes, external rankings and documented college acceptances) that square reviews do not; examples include “full IB… earned college credit,” “daughter taking 11 AP courses,” and “ranked #2 in Georgia,” showing institutional pathways and measurable college readiness that are largely absent from square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report tighter small‑scho: Circle reviewers repeatedly point to small size, lifelong alumni ties, religious or town identity, high parental involvement, and personalized relationships (e.g., “everyone is just one family,” “extraordinary parental involvement,” “multigenerational attendance”), whereas square reviews more often describe a large, impersonal campus with limited parental/alumni continuity.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviews disproportionately document concrete process failures—lost transcripts, rude secretaries, punitive credit-transfer and summer‑school costs, enrollment/lottery mismanagement, busing problems, poor lunch/cleanliness and deferred maintenance (e.g., “went three times…to get my son release paper,” “lost over half of her school records,” “roaches,” “bus stops are very far”), issues that square entries do not raise.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: Circle reviewers more often describe frequent fights, drug problems, stabbings, sexual‑harassment mishandling, police overreach, and administrators failing to address safety (e.g., “fights every week,” “police…arrested me over a rumor,” “bullying is a HUGE issue…staff didn’t do anything”), while square entries rarely document such pervasive or extreme safety incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater staff favo: Many circle reviews allege preferential treatment for athletes/insiders and staff relatives, biased counselor placements, teacher retaliation, grade manipulation and workplace unprofessionalism (e.g., “if you’re not a football player or a teacher’s offspring you will be treated terrible,” “teachers do fake assignments to raise grades,” “teachers take complaints out on your student”), patterns that square reviews do not consistently assert.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive saf: This bucket captures reviews that describe routine peer violence, gang/drug activity, sexuaI threats/assaults, and school tolerance or ineffective response (e.g., “GANG ACTIVITY... kids being assaulted,” death threats, reports that bullying is ignored, reliance on police). Falling into this bucket means the review cites recurring safety incidents and/or staff/administration failing to stop or adequately discipline them (metal detectors rendered ineffective, peer assaults unaddressed, students walking away from campus).
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger and bro: This bucket groups reviews that list concrete advanced or alternative academic offerings and outcomes — AP/IB/magnet programs, career/technical majors, industry certifications, dual‑enrollment, and standout arts/music conservatory tracks (e.g., Cambridge/Graphic Arts praise, Cosmetology/OSHA certifications, dual credit/associate‑degree graduates, award‑winning band). Belonging here means the review emphasizes program breadth/depth and quantifiable postsecondary results (high scholarship totals, high graduation/college‑acceptance rates, early college credit).
candidate_defs.circle entries highlight teachers provid: This bucket covers reviews that point to teachers or specialists doing extra‑mile work for individual students — frequent teacher availability, morning/after‑school IB review sessions, intervention specialists, tailored schedules to keep students on track, help transferring to another school (e.g., teacher came in early with donuts to review for IB; 'they put me on a schedule to keep me on track'). Falls here when the review documents hands‑on, personalized academic or emotional interventions that directly changed a student's outcome.
candidate_defs.square entries report more visible, stab: This bucket contains reviews that praise steady principals, proactive administration, district support, and organized improvement/turnaround efforts (e.g., 'The principal is amazing,' 'Dr. Davison's vision,' leadership‑driven rank rises and alumni feedback sessions). A review fits here when it emphasizes coordinated leadership, staff teamwork, and deliberate schoolwide improvement rather than isolated teacher actions or operational breakdowns.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more concrete op: This bucket groups reviews reporting administrative and material breakdowns — counselor unresponsiveness and 6+ month credit transfers, attendance/recordkeeping errors, missing textbooks/uniforms, peeling paint, no required teachers (e.g., 'No Spanish teacher yet Spanish is required to graduate'), overcrowding/capacity strain, and poor cafeteria/food. A review belongs here if it details recurring misadministration or tangible resource/facility deficiencies that impede students' daily schooling.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, more ext: This bucket groups raw items where reviewers describe concrete program capacity and outcomes (AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, honors, PLTW/STEM tracks) and cite quantifiable results (ACT/college‑credit totals, large scholarship sums, high graduation/college‑matriculation rates); examples include circle notes of multiple AP classes, dual enrollment and millions in scholarships or 100% graduation claims versus square’s limited or missing AP/advanced-course evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This bucket collects reports of peer violence, systemic bullying, racism/transphobia, on‑campus sexual activity, gang/criminal incidents and reviewers’ claims that staff/officers ignored or covered up problems (e.g., sex in school areas, students sent to the ICU, pervasive homophobic/racist behavior and administrators who ‘laugh off’ issues), contrasted with square entries that rarely describe comparable severe safety failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive ins: This groups evidence about poor classroom instruction (out‑of‑field or uncertified teachers, rote/test‑teaching, homework without explanation), teacher disengagement (phones, minimal effort), plus operational failures tied to staff (lost doctor’s notes, unreturned counselor/office calls, scheduling/testing mistakes), which appear repeatedly in square reviews but far less in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more visible facil: This bucket captures contrasts in infrastructure and resource evidence — circle reviewers frequently cite new construction, renovated campuses, security cameras and 21st‑century tech, whereas square reviewers more often call out missing athletic infrastructure, awful cafeteria food, outdated textbooks or poor lab funding.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more institutional: This groups accounts of selective enforcement and inequality (athletes or wealthy/connected families ‘getting away with’ behavior, hiring favoritism/nepotism, lunch lines that stigmatize low‑income students, active fundraising that creates quasi‑private advantages, and tightly exclusionary cliques), patterns attributed to school politics and parent-status that appear far more often in circle reviews than in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: These reviews emphasize named rigorous academic offerings (IB, many AP classes, honors, dual‑enrollment and free ACT prep), higher test/exit scores, and concrete post‑secondary outcomes (college acceptances, scholarships) that square reviews do not document; examples include claims of IB adoption, a 22+ ACT average, and alumni receiving large tuition waivers versus Square’s lack of comparable program/outcome evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, better‑: Circle reviews repeatedly list extensive, well‑supported programs (magnet/academy internships, strong band/theater, state‑champion athletics, large CTE/career‑center offerings and trade‑to‑work pathways) while Square reviews lack comparable program breadth or high‑level competitive achievements.
candidate_defs.circle entries display higher parental/a: Circle reviewers report active PTA/alumni giving, parents relocating or returning for the school, small‑school familiarity and long‑running community ties—e.g., parents saying they’ll always support the school, multi‑child families and alumni who moved back—whereas Square reviews rarely document organized parent/alumni involvement or enduring local loyalty.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent stud: Square reviews more often describe repeated fights, pervasive bullying, serious safety events (guns, assaults) and administrative inaction or poor response to incidents, e.g., 'fights every other day,' 'a gun was brought to school,' and victims being punished or ignored—conditions that circle reviews do not emphasize to the same degree.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater leadership: Circle reviewers more often allege rapid principal turnover, mass teacher departures, reconstitution, nepotism/favoritism in hiring or athletics, budget misallocation and governance failures (accusations of corruption, fabricated metrics, or administrators driving out staff), contrasted with Square’s reviews which seldom document such systemic leadership/turnover patterns.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more persistent sa: This bucket captures reviews that describe ongoing student-safety problems (daily fights, bomb threats/lockdowns, robbery/threats, drug distribution and smoking, sexual-assault allegations) together with claims that staff/administration ignore or inadequately address them ("there are fights all the time","there's always lots of security and police","administration turned a blind eye"). Examples include explicit drug distribution, gang protection allegations, repeated bullying left unresolved, and reports of police presence — contrasts repeatedly drawn against Square, which rarely describes ongoing safety crises and often describes improvements or stronger adult responses.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, organi: This bucket groups reviews that list institutional, structured academic offerings and measurable postsecondary outcomes — AP/IB inventories and diploma recipients, STEM programs, CTE pathways, National Merit scholars and named college matriculations (e.g., 'IB FULL DIPLOMA RECIPIENTS', 'one of the first presidential scholars', 'many go on to Ivy League/Top colleges'). These entries emphasize curricular rigor and concrete results (AP/IB/college acceptances) that Square reviews do not consistently document.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more extensive and: This bucket captures reviews that highlight robust, high‑quality out‑of‑class programs — award‑winning choir/band, First Robotics, state championship teams, thriving theater/production/CTE activities and year‑round events (pep rallies, fairs). Many Circle reviews emphasize abundant clubs, arts and competitive athletics (sometimes noting D‑1 placements), whereas Square reviews rarely enumerate equivalent high‑achieving extracurricular breadth.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket collects descriptions of governance and operations problems: allegations of nepotism/corruption, favoritism (athlete/relative advantages), decades of misused funds, district incompetence, broken registration/scheduling systems, missing textbooks, pest/cleanliness issues, antiquated tech and Wi‑Fi failures. These are managerial, logistics and resource failures ("blatant nepotism","no oversight of the budget","waiting in line for hours to register") that Circle reviewers raise far more often than Square.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive tea: This bucket groups reviews that describe widespread low instructional quality and nonresponsive classroom staff in Square — teachers who "punch the clock," give busywork, fail to respond to parents or students, and produce inconsistent grading or counseling, e.g. "There are a couple of really good instructors. The rest punch the clock," and "counselors... are really a waste." These claims about routine teacher disengagement and poor classroom practice appear more often in Square than in Circle.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more embedded ad: This bucket captures concrete programmatic breadth in circle reviews—explicit mentions of IB, in‑house college credit (Hunter College), High Tech/credit‑acceleration academies, robust CTE/automotive/agriculture/shops, arts majors, and internships—whereas square reviews emphasize a narrower set (AP or single strong programs) and lack comparable embedded dual‑enrollment or hands‑on career pathways. Examples: circle’s repeated IB/dual‑enroll/High Tech/automotive comments vs. square’s focus on AP/band/JROTC without embedded college or shop programs.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistently: This bucket groups staffing and leadership stability/quality that reviewers attribute more to square: reliable guidance counselors, caring/dedicated teachers, an ‘outstanding’ principal, and accessible staff who follow up—contrasted with circle’s mixed or unstable accounts of turnover, unresponsive counselors, or widely variable teacher quality. Examples: square testimonials praising consistent staff support and leadership vs. circle’s recurring complaints about high turnover and nonresponsive front‑office.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more persistent sa: This bucket covers reports of unsafe climate and broken discipline systems that appear more often in circle: frequent fights, vaping/drug incidents, gang activity, systemic bullying, staff complicity or ignoring of abuse, or conversely heavy authoritarian punishments that are applied unevenly—while square reviews lack comparable chronic safety crises. Examples: circle’s claims of daily fights, hospitalization, rampant bullying/drugs and administrators who ‘look away’ or threaten legal action vs. square’s absence of such systemic safety failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete faci: This bucket groups tangible infrastructure and resource deficits that circle reviewers describe: out‑of‑date tech, no/poor cafeteria service, missing textbooks, severe overcrowding, and district underfunding—whereas square reviews generally describe better facilities or do not raise the same scale of resource failure. Examples: circle’s complaints about no textbooks, moldy lunches, two labs for 1,400 students, and outdated equipment vs. square’s ‘modern and clean’ building claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more nepotism, fav: This bucket captures patterns of unequal treatment and insider advantage in circle reviews—hiring relatives, preferential treatment for athletes/honors/magnet students, program‑level segregation (rotc/athletes getting better teachers), and arbitrary or biased discipline—that reviewers tie to systemic unfairness, unlike square where such internal nepotism/favoritism is rarely reported. Examples: circle’s multiple anecdotes about staff family hires, athletic/AP favoritism, and ‘you must be friends with admin to get ahead’ vs. square’s lack of comparable nepotistic claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews repeatedly cite IB/AP/Honors, selective magnet/dual‑enrollment pathways, specialized STEM/arts tracks, and concrete college matriculation (Ivy/Stanford/Division I, high AP/ACT performance) as defining features of circle schools (examples: IB/AP rigor, DASH/medical‑magnet, early college/dual credit, 'All 250 students continued to college'). Square reviews lack comparable, consistent evidence of school‑wide advanced offerings or measurable college-placement outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more pervasive s: Many circle reviews report repeated bullying, daily fights, drug use, sexual harassment, racism and poor administrative handling (examples: 'Bullying is not only overlooked…often it is encouraged,' 'too much bullying and fights happen every other day,' 'racism goes unnoticed,' 'sexual assault & harassment…teachers had favorites'). Square reviews rarely describe that level of ongoing violence or identity‑targeted harassment and more often do not depict institutionally tolerated danger.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more facility, ope: Circle reviews frequently call out flooded or dilapidated buildings, dirty/unsupplied bathrooms, no AC, unlocked doors/security gaps, extreme overcrowding, food‑safety complaints, and heavy mandatory tuition/fees or fundraising tied to participation (examples: 'school gets flooded…no air conditioning,' 'bathrooms had no soap,' 'massively overcrowded…illegal to remain open during covid,' 'you have to pay 9k for tuition…mandatory fundraisers'). Square reviews contain far fewer of these concrete infrastructure/resource failure reports.
candidate_defs.circle entries highlight stronger multig: Multiple circle reviews emphasize small‑town, family‑like cultures, active parent organizations and fundraising (parent‑run 'School Power', fathers/mothers clubs), town‑wide attendance at games, and broad volunteer engagement (examples: 'everybody is treated like family,' 'the community takes a lot of pride…whole town comes to games,' 'very high parental involvement'). Square reviews more often report weaker community endorsement or parents removing children due to problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more administrativ: Circle reviews contain repeated claims that office staff and administrators show biased treatment, protect athletes/connected families, tolerate nepotism, manipulate grades or policy, and sometimes flout legal/confidentiality rules (examples: 'If a student has a high ranking parent…gets special treatment,' 'nepotism is tolerated,' 'an honestly earned D is magically turned into a C,' 'The school board allows the district to break laws'). Square reviews include few or no comparable allegations of systemic favoritism or governance/legal breaches.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive saf: These reviews describe frequent fights, gang/drug activity, rampant bullying, theft, and even allegations of staff-student sexual misconduct alongside claims that administrators "turn a blind eye" or fail to enforce policy (examples: “Violence and drugs are rampant,” “First 3 months at least 12 fights,” “BULLYING IS VERY HIGH… administration does little to help,” and reports of gangs and police inability to control incidents). A school falls in this bucket when reviewers describe endemic physical-safety or bullying problems and ineffective/absent administrative intervention rather than isolated episodic incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger formal ac: Many circle reviews highlight concentrated programmatic rigor and outcomes—IB/AP breadth, university credit, National Merit recognition, Ivy/Intel finalists, and large scholarship totals (examples: “Full IB Diploma… one of the best,” “graduating with 18 credits,” “earned nearly $1,000,000 in scholarships,” “students accepted into Ivy League schools,” and “many students graduate with college credit”). This bucket captures entries that emphasize institutional academic strength, advanced-course offerings, and concrete postsecondary placement or award metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more accessible, i: Circle reviewers frequently cite timely teacher communication, scheduled tutoring, responsive counselors, active PTO/alumni fundraising, and local business or career-center partnerships (examples: “Communication is wonderful… teachers reply quickly,” “free math tutoring twice a week,” “strong alumni support provides top‑notch facility,” and career-center/academy partnerships). Use this bucket for reviews that point to consistent one‑on‑one help, parent engagement, and community-funded resources supporting students.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege governance, financ: These entries level board- or district‑level critiques—claims of nepotism, misallocated budgets, legal exposure, fired staff without mandated reporting, or direct blame of the board/superintendent (examples: “The board of education is also at fault,” “They pocket the funds,” “Chef paid $95K—board president’s live-in boyfriend,” and predictions of ACLU/litigation). This bucket groups reviews that attribute school dysfunction to governance decisions, fiscal mismanagement, or elected‑board malpractice rather than classroom- or teacher-level causes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more teacher disen: Square reviews more often describe uncaring or ineffective teachers, patchy remediation, counselor failures, staffing instability, and resource shortfalls that leave students behind academically (examples: “terrible teachers… don’t care,” “stays after school almost every day… 'help' loosely and still struggling,” “college counselor left… seniors harmed,” and “most of the teachers are substitutes”). This bucket captures reviews that attribute weak student outcomes to disengaged staff, poor follow-up, and operational neglect rather than active safety or governance crises.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups differences about student misbehavior and school-safety failures: circle reviews repeatedly describe daily or frequent fights, vaping/drug use, assaults, gang activity, ignored bullying, lockdowns and threats, and law‑enforcement citations (e.g., 'fights every single day', 'huge vaping, drug, and bulling problem', 'a person...overdosed', 'WAY TO MUCH BULLYING and teachers seeing it and do NOTHING'), whereas square reviews typically describe a safer, better‑managed student climate. Content falls here when reviews document prevalence of misconduct, unaddressed safety incidents, or systemic tolerance of risky student behavior.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe richer and more: This bucket captures curricular and outcome differences: circle reviews provide detailed, structured academic offerings and measurable outcomes — AP/AICE/Cambridge programs, multi-level honors tracks, ACT/region/test rankings, engineering/STEM partnerships, dual‑enrollment/associate‑degree pathways and explicit college placements (e.g., 'ACT prep course', 'AICE Diploma', 'already has earned three college credits', 'ranked number one in the Region'), while square rarely lists comparable programmatic detail. Include reviews describing advanced coursework, structured remediation or support centers, IEP/special‑education inclusion, and explicit college‑prep outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, more acti: This bucket groups descriptions of extracurricular breadth and culture: circle reviews repeatedly enumerate extensive clubs, daily music participation, award‑winning band/orchestra, many varsity sports and championships, and strong coach mentorship (e.g., 'extensive music program', 'won many championships', 'Coach...made me try as hard as I could'), but also document athlete‑favoritism and boosters mismanagement ('They cater to the athletes and let them get away with everything', 'boosters or someone is stealing money'). Place reviews here when they report program breadth/quality in arts or athletics or when they link athletics to social status or funding priorities.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers leadership and personnel patterns: circle reviews frequently allege moved 'problem' administrators, high teacher turnover, retaliatory firings, nepotism/favoritism, staff fear of speaking up, and inconsistent or biased discipline (e.g., 'they send their problem administrators to hide them', 'ten teachers have left... said to get my child out', 'created a climate where people are afraid to speak up', 'A LOT of favoritism'), while square reviews contain fewer or different governance accusations. Use this bucket for reviews describing systemic governance failures, opaque decision‑making, or widespread staff morale/retaliation problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater variabilit: This bucket groups operational evidence about building condition, resources and logistics: circle reviews include both explicit recent capital investments and many concrete shortages or logistical failures — renovated/new buildings, 1:1 tech, or conversely 'very dirty... smells like sewage', 'no accreditation', overcrowded classes, meal‑debt withholding of records, long uniform wait times, and rural transportation gaps (e.g., 'Excellent new building in 2019', 'the school is old and outdated', 'holding his last report card until it is paid', 'parents have to arrange two buses'). Put reviews here when they document facility condition, funding constraints, custodial/food/tech problems, overcrowding, or transport/logistics barriers.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: This bucket captures claims of higher academic rigor and concrete post‑secondary results in circle reviews — e.g., repeated mentions of AP/IB and honors courses, unique academies or CTE tracks, 1:1 MacBook/iPad programs and updated STEM labs, and explicit scholarship/college matriculation (letters from Harvard/Yale, full‑ride scholarships). Square reviews lack comparable systematic evidence of advanced programs or consistent college outcomes and instead emphasize uneven instruction or remediation struggles.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, more acce: This groups circle evidence about abundant clubs (’over 100 clubs’, welcoming club culture), award‑winning fine arts and athletics, visible student media and community fundraising, and named community backing (cookouts, strong turnout at orchestra), whereas square reviews either omit such breadth or present extracurriculars as narrower/less welcoming.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent seve: This bucket covers circle reports of everyday fights, bullying, gang activity, drug problems, pepper‑spray/police interventions, and parents’ complaints that administration watered down punishments or ignored incidents — contrasted with square reviews that seldom describe routine violence and more often report isolated behavior or prompt handling.
candidate_defs.circle entries exhibit more polarized an: Circle reviews frequently include both glowing, personal accounts of teachers/counselors who ‘stay until 4 or 5 to help’ or ‘know students’ names’ and sharply negative, named allegations (humiliating deans, teacher name‑calling, political bias, favoritism, grade‑tampering), producing a visibly polarized staff profile; square reviews tend to present more uniform statements about staff (either generally positive or generally critical) without the same pattern of extreme, named contrasts.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups square evidence about misassigned schedules and periods, poor guidance counseling (not informing students of college visits, incorrect course placement), credit recovery or transcript delays, and weak parent/portal communication about classes — a pattern of academic‑administration logistical breakdowns that is less frequently and less systematically described in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more chronic stude: These reviews describe frequent physical fights, drug/alcohol presence, pervasive bullying, gang-like social groups, and direct safety incidents (e.g., '17 fights in one day', 'drugs and alcohol are widespread', 'boys harass her on a constant bases') — patterns repeatedly present in circle but absent or minimized in square, which more often emphasizes community pride and safety.
candidate_defs.circle entries document broader and bett: Circle reviews list concrete, structured program offerings and results — IB, dual‑credit programs, specialized academies, award‑winning band/athletics, and explicit college matriculation metrics (e.g., 'IB program is very challenging', 'academies count as college credit', '100% of seniors graduate and 98% go to college') — whereas square tends to mention fewer distinct specialty academies or measurable program expansions.
candidate_defs.square entries report higher classroom i: Square reviews more often credit teaching quality, classroom rigor, and AP/IB instruction that prepared students for post‑secondary work (examples: 'Kids are well taught', 'The quality of the classroom and staff so far has been excellent', reports of AP preparation leading to college readiness), while circle reviews include many reports of weak day‑to‑day instruction, busywork, and under‑prepared teachers.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete faci: Circle reviews provide specific facility and resource complaints and operational breakdowns — moldy ceilings, 'no air in the summer, and no heat in the winter', 'the food is inedible', outdated textbooks, attendance/record‑keeping errors and long bus commutes — details that square reviews rarely enumerate or emphasize.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle contains repeated allegations about leadership failure and misuse of authority — favoritism toward donors/insiders, withholding transcripts, underreporting incidents, blocking transfers, administrative harassment or bullying, high turnover and unresponsiveness — while square reviews give fewer governance‑level corruption claims and more often describe engaged or improving administration.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These circle reviews repeatedly describe frequent fights, gang/drug activity, bullying, off‑campus assaults, broken or mishandled security, restrictive/jail‑like policing, and either overly punitive suspensions or ineffective enforcement (e.g., “one of the biggest drug problems,” “the kids fight,” cameras/school police that make it feel like a jail,” and restrictive restroom/closed‑campus policies), whereas square reviews rarely report pervasive violence and instead emphasize a safer, family-like atmosphere.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater administra: Circle reviewers more often accuse school leaders and front‑office staff of incompetence, favoritism, selective discipline, sweeping accusations under the rug, harassment, or biased refusal of services (examples: “leadership is weak,” “admin only discipline people they dislike,” “assistant principal not willing to work with me,” and reports of office staff gossiping/ignoring), while square reviews contain few or no sustained claims of cover‑ups or systemic administrative favoritism.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, more-do: Circle reviews frequently list concrete program breadth (AP/IB/dual enrollment, magnets, CTE, band/arts, 30+ clubs), measurable metrics or awards (graduation/ACT/AP statistics, US News recognitions), and specific facility/tech assets (pools, multiple theatres, iPads/DTEN panels, new campuses), e.g. “over 95% move on to college,” “three theatre spaces, two gyms,” and “many electives including dual credit,” while square reviews provide fewer program metrics or detailed facility lists and emphasize different local constraints.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent, u: Square reviews commonly convey concordant praise for caring counselors/teachers, individualized support in a small/safe environment, and a welcoming school climate (examples: “Counselors and teachers care about their students,” “a very diverse school, everyone is friends,” and “safe sending my child”), whereas circle reviews show far more mixed testimony about staff caring and community welcome.
candidate_defs.circle entries show higher internal vari: Circle concatenations frequently contain sharp, contradictory accounts within the same school—praise and condemnation of the same programs, reports of both strong leadership and recent decline, or wildly different department/teacher quality (e.g., “very troubled school” alongside “teachers go above and beyond,” reports of both strong counseling and counselor shortages, or ‘B→A’ turnaround claims next to failing-score claims), while square reviews are comparatively consistent and concordant.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, more c: This bucket captures reports that circle schools provide concrete, person-level academic and socioemotional supports (small class sizes, routine tutoring lunch/after‑school, counselors who call home, teachers who stay after school and know students by name) while square reviews emphasize uneven or unresponsive staff. Examples: circle reviewers cite 'IGETC and Associates degree pathways,' 'tutoring during lunch and after school,' 'class size was only 3 in one class,' and 'teachers are always willing to help,' contrasted with square comments like 'teachers totally gave up on me' and 'admin listens, but you must be active about it.'
candidate_defs.circle entries document more extensive c: This bucket groups concrete programmatic offerings and measurable academic pathways described more often in circle reviews — dual‑enrollment/college‑credit programs, AP/IB availability, vocational tracks (culinary, construction, CTE), robotics/3D‑printing/astronomy labs, and ROTC outcomes — whereas square reviews lack or understate those pathways. Examples: circle mentions 'dual enrollment…IGETC and Associates degree,' '3D printing lab, robotics lab,' 'named Chef Mac culinary program,' 'Towson University ROTC pathway' and 'IB/bio‑medical programs,' while square reports 'nowhere close in preparing me for college' and no comparable program detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize athletics as a: This bucket captures circle reviews that portray sports as central to school life and resourcing — athletics overshadowing academics, preferential treatment of athletes, selective tryouts, and logistics/transport mismanagement — while square reviews either highlight nonathletic offerings or do not depict athletics as overriding academic priorities. Examples: circle reviewers say 'The school revolves around sports,' 'Athletes are frequently excused…,' 'sports teams practically require Olympic athletes,' and 'forgot to get us a bus to away games,' whereas square highlights arts, academic programs, and winning teams without alleging athletics-driven favoritism over academics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups concrete allegations of repeated bullying, fights, tobacco/drug use, sexual‑assault allegations, lockdowns/gang fights, and claims that staff or administration fail to remediate (swept‑under‑rug, superficial punishments, ignored reports), while square reviews contain fewer or more isolated safety incidents. Examples: circle contains 'several sexual assaults within the school with no action,' 'kids bring tobacco…lots of fights,' 'constant bullying…police reports ignored,' and 'administration didn't respond to harassment complaints,' whereas square typically lacks such systemic safety allegations or reports stronger staff intervention.
candidate_defs.circle entries show deeper local family/: This bucket groups descriptions of an engaged, sometimes insular community around the school — active parent volunteer networks, principal‑parent outreach, alumni ties, community protests/board fights, but also favoritism, 'good ol' boy' hiring, and affluent/snobby student cliques — distinct from internal staff responsiveness or programmatic offerings. Examples: circle reviewers report being 'warmly embraced by the parent community,' named community campaigns ('#savepotts'), 'favoritism given to members of the church and/or staff's children,' and 'very snobby, rich‑kids' social stratification, whereas square reviews do not present the same intensity of local volunteer coordination or community‑level favoritism.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report substantially stro: These reviews repeatedly name formal programs, rigorous coursework, and college outcomes (AP/IB/Dual‑credit/CTE articulations, students entering college with 12+ credit hours, IB Diploma, industry certifications), whereas square reviews omit or question comparable program depth (square notes few/failed AP offerings or remedial gaps). Example evidence: circle lists wide AP/IB offerings, aviation/CTE magnets, and documented college credit; square highlights lack of program detail and first‑year remediation issues.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more pervasive stu: Many circle reviews describe routine peer bullying, cyber‑bullying, racism/homophobia/ableism, staff or coaches protecting popular athletes, and administrators failing to intervene (families transferring, student anxiety/medication as consequence), while square reviews more often describe a safer/family atmosphere or isolated incidents. Representative items: accounts of racist/homophobic slurs within earshot of teachers, cheerleader harassment, protected athletes escaping discipline, and anti‑bullying programs described as compromised.
