candidate_defs.Circle entries emphasize an athletics‑fi: Circle reviewers repeatedly report that athletics dominate school priorities (significant grants/bleacher spending, athlete privileges, preferential discipline), alongside frequent winning records and state titles; square reviews discuss extracurricular variety or criticize coaching bias but less often portray school identity as athletics‑first. Examples include claims that ‘everything revolves around athletics’, athlete free‑lunch/tolerance, and multiple state championships.
candidate_defs.Circle entries describe greater variabil: Circle reviews show wide teacher quality swings (some outstanding teachers vs. many unqualified/unmotivated), chronic classroom management issues (cell phones, busywork), overreliance on laptops with little teacher guidance, and concrete IEP/counseling breakdowns; square reviews more often praise consistent teacher responsiveness and classroom help. Illustrative complaints: teachers ‘just hand out assignments via laptop,’ counselors ‘disjointed,’ inconsistent grade updates, and IEPs not followed.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe more cohesive, f: Square reviews frequently characterize the school as a close, supportive community where staff ‘treat students like family,’ parents feel heard, and students from diverse backgrounds stick together, whereas circle reviews are far more likely to report snobbery, entrenched cliques, or polarized experiences. Examples: square notes strong staff outreach, family atmosphere, and students ‘stick together’ despite economic diversity, contrasting circle’s frequent reports of exclusion and long‑standing cliques.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, more div: These reviews emphasize concrete program breadth and outcomes at circle schools (AP/IB and named academies, engineering/STEM/Ag/vocational pathways, dual‑credit/college courses, abundant extracurriculars and championship teams) and cite alumni/college‑matriculation evidence (e.g., multiple AP/Honors enrollments, 98–100% college‑going claims, named partnerships and students matriculating without remediation), whereas square reviews lack sustained program depth and measurable outcome claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: Many circle reviews recount gang activity, shootings, metal detectors/lockdowns, pervasive bullying (including racial/LGBTQ+ targeting), vaping/drug concerns and hazing, and describe staff or discipline systems that fail to protect victims; square reviews contain far fewer or less severe safety incidents and more examples of effective interventions or lower incident rates.
candidate_defs.circle entries report worse overcrowding: Circle reviewers frequently cite extreme class sizes (e.g., 30–43 per class), no science labs, overcrowded or K–12 consolidated buildings, pest/ bathroom/AC/heating problems and inadequate lunch services, while square entries more often reference renovated or well‑maintained facilities and do not raise comparable space or sanitation crises.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more organized,: Circle reviews often name and praise proactive principals/superintendents, cite coordinated leadership actions (principal outreach during crises, superintendent approachability, planned renovations, community work days) and describe organized anti‑bullying or onboarding efforts; square reviews more commonly report district neglect, standoffish administrators, or resistance to system‑level improvement.
candidate_defs.square entries report more uneven teache: Square reviews document mixed or many weak teachers, teachers who are disengaged or 'cruise' during class, morale/turnover concerns, and poor counseling/teacher responsiveness, whereas circle reviews more often describe consistently dedicated, responsive, and student‑supportive teachers (named mentors, frequent tutoring, successful special‑needs accommodations).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reviews that describe widespread peer aggression, drug problems, suicides or fights and a school that fails to stop them (e.g., “I've seen kids get followed after school & beaten bloody,” “lots of drugs...overdosing,” monthly drug-dog lockdowns, and “the number of suicides...shocking”) and explicit claims that staff/leadership refuse to address complaints; square entries rarely raise systemic safety or unaddressed bullying and instead tend to describe a safer climate or isolated incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more teacher/admin: This bucket groups concrete operational and personnel complaints: allegations of uncertified teachers, verbal abuse/cursing by staff, grading and record‑keeping errors that damaged GPAs, leadership protecting staff or ignoring misconduct, and violations of special‑education follow‑up (e.g., “most... should not have any certification,” “teacher forgot I turned in work,” “leaders protect each other,” “against federal regulations”); square reviews rarely allege pervasive staff misconduct or protected staff networks and more often report at least some responsive, qualified staff.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more persistent fa: This bucket covers concrete resource and building deficiencies cited in reviews—lack of books and up‑to‑date materials, overcrowded classrooms, unsanitary bathrooms and pests, broken HVAC, and explicit funding/shortage pleas (e.g., “we don't have books,” “ant infested,” “no air conditioning,” requests to pool resources or pass bonds); square entries seldom describe chronic pest/cleanliness or basic-resource failures and often emphasize adequate facilities or recent investments.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, higher‑vi: This bucket groups specific programmatic and community features: multiple named strong programs (band/choir/theater awards, FFA, robotics, PJAS), active parental fundraising and volunteerism, multigenerational alumni ties and district events, and distinctive community connections (military families, regional commuters) (e.g., “First FFA board,” “drama club trips to Broadway,” “parents still volunteering 20 years later”); square reviews mention some activities but do not repeatedly document the same breadth, competitive recognition, or organized alumni/parent mobilization.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, more con: This bucket captures claims of rigorous AP/STEM tracks, structured college counseling/dual‑enrollment, scholarship totals and named alumni success used as evidence (e.g., “AP track oftentimes as or more difficult than college undergrad,” “STEM certified program,” “students have earned over $3 million in scholarships,” “graduates attending Binghamton/University of Chicago”); square entries more often lack this kind of documented college‑prep infrastructure or measurable alumni outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries document stronger and mor: These reviews describe concrete program breadth and college-prep results (AP/IB/dual‑credit, STEM academies, vocational shops, robust arts/athletics) and cite outcome metrics (associate degrees, high college matriculation, scholarships). Examples: multiple Circle notes of many AP/dual‑credit classes, STEM/vo‑tech opportunities, and graduates entering university or earning college credit, contrasted with Square’s lack of comparable AP/dual‑credit evidence and complaints about poor college preparation.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent seve: This bucket groups reviews that document assaults, bomb/lockdown threats, gang/drug activity, repeated bullying, staff boundary violations, and claims that security/administration failed to act. Examples: Circle accounts of on‑campus assaults in front of guards, bomb threats, teachers grooming students or leaking private complaints, and administrators refusing to hold perpetrators accountable — incidents not present in Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more consistent: These reviews report teachers/staff who provide one‑on‑one remediation, timely communication, AVID/Guidance scholarship help, effective special‑education supports, and nurturing small‑school relationships. Examples: Circle testimonials of teachers emailing back promptly, individualized tutoring, strong AVID/guidance scholarship assistance, and special‑needs students ‘blossoming,’ whereas Square reviews more often describe uneven or absent individualized follow‑up.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures complaints about board politics, superintendent/principal mismanagement, lost or mis‑sent records, favoritism, litigation, and unreturned communications. Examples: Circle claims of district hiding reports, records sent to wrong schools, principals belittling staff, lawsuits from parents and ‘smile‑to‑your‑face/stab‑you‑in‑the‑back’ leadership — contrasts with Square which lacks comparable district‑level governance allegations.
candidate_defs.circle entries supply more concrete oper: These reviews contain specific, actionable operational evidence — new or state‑of‑the‑art buildings, overcrowded lunches/classrooms, inventories of lab/media tech, bus failures, explicit pay rates, and quantified student/teacher ratios or turnover rates. Examples: Circle notes of brand‑new $75M facilities or lack of hot water, explicit starting pay for aides, ‘almost 4,000 students’ or 8:1 vs 15:1 disputes, and mid‑year teacher attrition; Square reviews generally do not provide this same level of concrete operational metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: These reviews emphasize concrete academic breadth and results (AP/IB/dual‑credit, academies, national awards and quantified alumni success) — e.g., “nearly 20 AP classes,” IB scores and ‘wall‑to‑wall IB’ expansion, dual‑credit hours, 98% college acceptances, and alumni who earned scholarships and high salaries — while square entries lack comparable named programs or measurable long‑term outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more proactive,: Circle reviews repeatedly cite organized in‑school supports: a named, supportive counseling team, upperclassmen mentoring freshmen, multiple tutoring pathways, teachers staying after or available by phone until 9pm, and counselors who ‘know every single student,’ whereas square reviews do not highlight this same level of structured, consistent student‑support services.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Circle contains numerous concrete safety and misconduct claims — frequent fights and assaults, sustained bullying K–12, explicit racial threats by staff (e.g., teacher who 'would kill all Black people'), drugs/vaping, sexual‑misconduct scandals, and failures to notify parents of injuries — problems that square reviews generally do not document at the same frequency or severity.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more administrativ: Circle reviewers report systemic governance issues: nepotism/’good ol boy’ politics in selections, grade‑inflation promoted by administration, gaming awards, coverups, punitive fee enforcement (withholding caps/gowns/yearbooks), pay‑to‑play coach corruption, and opaque spending decisions (cosmetic buys over textbooks), claims largely absent from square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater extracurri: Circle reviews detail wide extracurricular offerings and high‑visibility program success (award‑winning FFA, competitive band, state‑qualifying teams), strong athletic facilities or recent rebuilds, intense fan/community spirit, and cases of families relocating for the school — while square reviews rarely describe comparable scale or prominence of extracurriculars and facilities.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: These reviews describe concrete programmatic rigor and quantified outcomes at circle schools (AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, high SAT/CST scores, graduation rates, scholarship totals, alumni at selective colleges), while square reviews rarely cite comparable metrics; examples include circle claims like “3 AP tests…passed,” “85 seniors won $7.5 million in scholarships,” “IB classes available,” and “98% graduation rate.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe and re: Circle reviews contain numerous specific safety incidents and organized threats (kill lists, bomb threats, shootings, drug busts, fights, weapons, bullying including targeted/vulnerable-student cases) and staff boundary violations or alleged assaults, whereas square reviews lack that cluster of acute safety allegations; examples include “two drug busts…one student going to the hospital,” “students fighting constantly and being weapons,” and a teacher who “assaulted a student.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: These items document governance and staff-behavior failures at circle schools—grade manipulation pressure, nepotism, administrators who ignore or threaten critics, selective enforcement of rules, and poor parent communication—while square reviews less frequently assert entrenched cronyism; supporting evidence includes “favoritism has a home,” “administrators that will threaten to sue you for speaking up,” and “teachers are resigning because they are being told to alter grades.”
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize broader and hig: Circle reviews repeatedly list extensive extracurricular breadth, top-tier sports/JROTC, notable facilities and regional/national athletic recognition—and sometimes criticize athletics crowding out academics—whereas square reviews tend to emphasize a narrow set (e.g., choir/arts) or lack comparable breadth; examples include “athletics are phenomenal,” “their JROTC program is top notch,” and complaints that “most funding is spent on the sports.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report more inconsistent,: Many circle reviews cite concrete special-education failures (IEP noncompliance, understaffed special ed, denied services, lost testing, or students 'falling through the cracks') as well as isolated positive therapy supports, while square reviews seldom document detailed special‑needs program failures; examples include “The teachers do not understand the concept of an IEP… refused my requests,” “Special ed is over worked, understaffed,” and “he receives speech therapy at school.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, concrete: These reviews list named AP/honors/IB/majors, dual‑enrollment and vocational certifications, teacher names and program specifics and cite measurable outcomes (ACT/college admits, scholarships). Examples: reviewers cite “many AP classes,” “Both my kids got above a 31 on the ACT and qualified for Bright Flight,” dual‑enrollment credits, named award‑winning bands and magnet career strands—details and outcome metrics that square reviews generally lack.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Circle reviews contain repeated concrete safety incidents (students bringing weapons, repeated shooting threats, suicidality, stalking), widespread bullying and harassment, and claims that administrators fail to protect victims or cover up incidents. Illustrative quotes include “Students brought guns… were not expelled,” “BULLYING is out of control,” and “When a stalker was reported, nothing was done,” patterns that appear far more often in circle than in square entries.
candidate_defs.square entries foreground community pove: Square reviewers more frequently ascribe issues to local socioeconomic conditions, failed levies, low tax base and low teacher pay (e.g., “lack of funding… low income town. Low pay = low taxes paid,” and “hard time trying to pass levies”), framing resource scarcity and compensation as root causes rather than leadership or culture alone.
candidate_defs.circle entries depict stronger local com: Circle reviews routinely describe tight-knit, multi‑generation family ties, active PTO/business partnerships, alumni pride and organized calls to improve the school (e.g., “Nine out of twelve of my nieces and nephews have attended this school,” “The PTO is active,” and rallying language like “we all should stand up and do something about it”). Those community‑cohesion signals and organized pride are far more present in circle than square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more concrete fa: Many circle reviews cite recent or new capital investments—brand‑new buildings, stadiums, updated computer labs, visible security cameras and facility renovations—often with enthusiastic detail (for example “BRAND NEW Stadium. GO MUSTANGS!!!,” “new computers and computer labs,” and “taking every step to have our new school build by January 2013”), whereas square reviews more often describe older/dilapidated facilities or do not mention such upgrades.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced/: This bucket groups pieces that describe concrete advanced-course and credit offerings and school-level outcomes more often in circle than square (examples: ‘‘honors, AP, IB, dual-enrollment/college-credit classes,’’ magnet/career academies, high exit‑exam/pass-rate claims, scholarship and college matriculation anecdotes like a ‘full ride to Univ of Alabama’). It captures program breadth and documented outcome metrics (test/graduation/college placement) as a substantive school feature rather than opinion.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent seve: This groups reviews that describe recurring, concrete safety/discipline incidents and poor institutional handling—e.g., fights, arrests/handcuffs, daily police presence, on‑campus sex/drug use, hospitalizing assaults, and claims that bullying is tolerated—attributes attributed to circle far more than to square. It bundles both the incidence of harm and the school’s weak or punitive/inconsistent responses as a unified operational climate issue.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader and better: This cluster collects descriptions where circle schools list many staffed, specialized extracurriculars and in‑school career resources (marching band, award‑winning arts, JROTC/ROTC, engineering/IT academies, FFA, robotics, on‑site bank/culinary labs, field trips, vocational certifications) and simultaneously note athletics-driven resource/favoritism dynamics (football/ROTC privilege, athletic scholarships), patterns that appear in circle reviews more than in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries show greater polarization: This bucket covers repeated circle claims of hit‑or‑miss teacher quality, high turnover/burnout, wildly different rigor between sections, arbitrary or inflationary grading practices, and contradictory reviewer outcomes (some students thrive, others fail) — a pattern of unstable, uneven educational delivery that distinguishes many circle reviews from the more consistent accounts in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger physical: This groups reports describing tangible facility and service advantages more often in circle: newer buildings/central air or active construction, technology integration or campus clinics, structured parent programs/PTO and parent liaisons, and regular parent communication/follow‑through (e‑mail reminders, PupilPath, PTO/festivals). It captures concrete investments and community engagement that reviewers cite as operating features of the school environment.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, better‑r: This bucket captures claims that one school offers rigorous honors/AP/IB pathways, on‑campus college courses, Vanguard/academy feeders, measurable score/acceptance gains, and explicit college‑prep infrastructure (college center, AP passes, dual‑enrollment partnerships); examples: circle reviews cite 'more than twenty AP and honors courses,' 'on‑campus college courses,' 'students admitted to UCs/CSUs and Ivy peers,' and clear test‑score/college‑readiness metrics, while square reviews report limited advanced options, declining grades after transfer, or uneven AP/IB results.
candidate_defs.circle entries document broader, higher‑: This groups reports of extensive, well‑supported extracurricular life (daily arts classes, formal theatre academies, championship athletics, new fields/gyms, booster/partnership activity, 1:1 laptop rollouts and campus modernization) that reviewers tie to student engagement; examples: circle reviewers list '2D/3D Art, Jazz Band, theatre academy, state championship teams, new football field and Cleveland Clinic partnership' while square reviews rarely cite comparable arts/athletics breadth or recent capital upgrades.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive bul: This bucket covers sustained accounts of peer and staff harassment, targeted discrimination, sexual harassment or assaults, riots/fights/lockdowns/pepper‑spray, death threats, and frequent claims that reports were ignored or mishandled; examples: circle reviews describe 'homophobic bullying with clinical‑level depression,' 'sexual harassment and coverups,' 'riots and pepper‑spray in hallways,' and 'reported threats that school did nothing about,' whereas square reviews lack comparable severe safety or systemic non‑response accounts.
candidate_defs.square entries portray more consistently: This bucket collects evidence that reviewers describe prompt teacher/counselor responsiveness, active college/career counseling, visible and supportive principals, structured staff development, and collaborative leadership; examples: square reviews mention 'teachers return emails quickly,' 'counselors and staff were very helpful,' and 'principal is loved and accessible,' while circle reviews more often report administrative hostility, refusal to release records, absent leadership, or chaotic counselor communication.
candidate_defs.circle entries report entrenched favorit: This bucket captures recurring claims that staff or trustees favor connected students (athletes, children of staff/board members, co‑religionists), protect favorites from discipline or low grades, and apply discriminatory discipline or religious pressure; examples: circle reviewers allege 'athletes get preferential treatment,' 'teachers hire ex‑students and protect them,' 'students favored for being Church of Christ,' and 'principal punishes only non‑white children,' whereas square reviews do not report these systemic favoritism or nepotism patterns.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced/: These reviews describe explicit AP/IB/dual-enrollment offerings, systematic test prep, capstone senior projects and a heavy nightly homework culture (e.g., “they have added AP courses… We get lots of ACT training,” “IB program… workload caused depression,” “loads of homework…done by 10–11pm”)—a substantive pattern of college-focused curriculum and high expectations that square entries do not emphasize.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more visible, name: Many circle reviews name counselors, advisors and teachers who provide after‑school help, para‑professional or one‑on‑one interventions and structured mentorship (e.g., “Secondary Campus Guidance Dept., Dr. Lyons and Mrs. Graham…genuinely concerned,” “teachers stay after school…helped bring grades from C to A”), a pattern of concrete, personalized student support largely absent from square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more systemic safe: Circle reviews more often document pervasive peer violence, hate‑motivated attacks, racial/homophobic slurs, and disciplinary favoritism for athletes/wealthy students—plus examples of administrators failing to intervene (e.g., “combat zone…had to fight daily,” “I was hate‑crimed multiple times,” “they let the guilty party get away with bullying if they are good at sports”), a school‑climate pattern square reviews rarely describe.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater difference: Circle entries repeatedly reference concrete resourcing — both positive (new buildings, MacBook/iPad 1:1 rollouts, state‑of‑the‑art campus, award‑winning band) and negative (cafeteria food complaints, overcrowding, pest problems) — and a wider array of clubs/competitive programs (JROTC, band, performing arts, vocational offerings) as distinguishing features that square reviews do not enumerate.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This cluster covers concrete governance/operational issues described in circle reviews—administrative unresponsiveness, retaliation/fear of speaking up, image‑management over student safety, strict punitive policies (deme rits/meal denials/graduation‑portfolio threats), lawsuits and district constraints (open enrollment, busing, budget deficits) — items square reviews mention far less or not at all.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe concrete safety problems inside and around the school—frequent fights, gang activity, pervasive drug use, sexual exploitation, and daily bullying—plus parents urged to 'transfer out when you can' and accounts that security/discipline is uneven or ignored (examples: 'Bullying and rumors run rampant,' 'It is full of drugs and violence,' 'the bullying is out of control').
candidate_defs.circle entries document more administrat: Multiple circle reviews allege leadership problems and governance failures—'the administration lies,' 'closed door policy,' backing teachers regardless of complaints, conflict‑of‑interest (administrators who are coaches), calls to fire superintendents and warnings of state/district takeover—showing systemic accountability and transparency issues absent from square examples.
candidate_defs.circle entries highlight stronger, concr: Reviewers point to named advanced programs, magnet/STEM/CTE tracks, AP and dual-enrollment offerings, certifications, high-profile alumni college placement and upgraded facilities/1:1 device rollouts (examples: 'amazing magnet school,' 'AP classes and college credit,' 'brand new school... excellent facilities,' 'students aiming for Ivy League and getting in').
candidate_defs.circle entries report more individualize: Several circle reviews cite concrete, realized supports—small class sizes and individualized attention, effective Questar/autism programs, scheduled help periods, Saturday tutors, on‑campus clinics, free meals and migrant-center services—indicating operational, student-level accommodations and remediation that square reviews rarely describe.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistently: Square reviews more often describe dependable, engaged adults—'teachers go above and beyond,' 'guidance and teachers are going above and beyond,' 'the counselor makes you feel welcome,' and principals described as 'absolutely wonderful'—portraying steadier teacher/counselor responsiveness and relational support than the mixed or dysfunctional staff reports in many circle reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report far more systemic: This bucket groups cases where reviewers describe pervasive student misconduct, physical assaults, weapons/drugs, lockdowns, tolerated bullying, and frequent fights—e.g. “students roam the hallways…physical attacks…bomb threats,” “drugs are used very often on campus,” and “kids with guns…fight almost every day,” claims absent from square reviews. It captures both violent incidents and chronic enforcement failures (no follow‑through on bullying, security indifference, quotas preventing reports).
candidate_defs.circle entries describe greater administ: This captures reports of unresponsive or rude front offices, dishonest or opaque leadership, nepotism/athlete/donor favoritism, bungled registration/records, and cover‑ups—e.g. “Don’t expect to get any response,” “principal takes the side of his teachers,” “where does the bingo money go?,” and lost transcripts/erroneous billing. It bundles governance, communication, and integrity problems at the admin/district level rather than teacher performance or student behavior.
candidate_defs.circle entries document stronger and mor: This bucket includes explicit programmatic offerings and outcomes such as AP/Dual Enrollment, early AP access, high college placement/test scores, and concrete metrics—e.g. “99–100% college placement,” “graduated with four college classes through Dual Enrollment,” “performing very well in SOL testing,” and named AP/dual‑credit pathways—features square reviews generally lack. It focuses on institutional course offerings, credentialing, and measurable postsecondary results.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more consistent te: This groups evidence that teachers provide hands‑on instruction, before/after‑school tutoring, prompt parent communication, small classes and mentoring—e.g. “teachers stay after school to help students,” “class sizes…one or two students,” “mentoring starting in 6th grade,” and specific ‘devoted educator’ praise—where square reviews more often describe uneven or unresponsive teaching. It concerns day‑to‑day instructional attention and teacher‑driven supports rather than formal program offerings.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize richer extracur: This bucket captures descriptions of high‑quality or high‑resource extracurriculars and facilities (state championships, top band/theater, skate parks, large campus amenities), selective admissions/lotteries and tuition/fee structures, plus sports‑centered social status—e.g. “very competitive Track…excellent music program,” “admission by lottery…waiting list,” “pay almost $20k,” and “if you don't play sports you are looked down on.” It groups resource intensity, exclusivity/selection, fee/donor influence, and the extracurricular culture that shapes student status.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete curricular depth and student-facing academic help at the school (e.g., many AP/IB/dual‑enrollment courses, teachers with masters/doctorates, one‑on‑one tutoring, SMART nights, measurable college credits and scholarships). Circle reviews give repeated examples of advanced course breadth, early college credit, and teacher-led remediation, while Square reviews either lack comparable program breadth or report students graduating unprepared despite honors/AP labels.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe a smaller, famil: These items emphasize institutional scale and social capital — small enrollment, ‘family’ atmosphere, active parent clubs/fundraising/scholarships, multigenerational attendance, and organized parent forums; circle reviews frequently cite parents and alumni as partners and boosters, whereas square reviews do not report the same close, community-driven parental/alumni involvement.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, higher‑pr: This bucket captures concrete program breadth and external achievement: state titles and competitive teams, award‑winning bands, robotics placements, robust CTE/ROTC/NAVY JROTC programs, and named arts/theater productions or travel opportunities. Circle reviews repeatedly cite such competitive and programmatic accomplishments; Square reviews instead emphasize different vocational/alternative tracks or criticize extracurricular quality without the same record of high-level success.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent/seve: Grouped here are reviews naming discrete safety and conduct events (drugs, smoking/hookah in class, organized fights, weapons/chemicals, thefts, bathrooms with no locks, racial harassment) and claims that these incidents were pervasive or mishandled; many circle reviews give concrete incident examples and describe ineffective or protective responses by staff, while square reviews do not present the same pattern of repeated, severe on‑campus safety incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries report more hostile, obst: This bucket gathers reviews that portray administrators and counselors as actively harmful or obstructive—examples include hostile treatment of students (public humiliation), prolonged re‑enrollment barriers, ‘uninformed/terrible’ counselors, secretaries with bad attitudes, retaliation against involved parents, and counseling that discourages college aspirations; these management and counseling failures are much more commonly asserted in Square reviews than in Circle reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket covers reviews that describe ongoing, schoolwide safety and climate breakdowns in circle schools — e.g., ‘bullying is out of control,’ ‘fights everyday,’ students ‘smoke in the bathrooms,’ harassment of Deerfield adults, racial profiling, and students pushed toward dropout or jail — contrasted with square reviews that do not report these pervasive safety failures or describe staff actively addressing incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more concrete, d: This groups circle reviews that list specific program breadth and outcomes — AP/IB expansions, dual‑credit/50+ college credits, vocational/Votech classes (culinary, HVAC, health tech), thriving JROTC and award‑winning band, documented college matriculation (Duke/UNC/Yale examples) — whereas square reviews typically lack these named programmatic successes or measurable college outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more responsive, s: This bucket captures square reviews that emphasize steady leadership, prompt parent/teacher communication, visible supportive principals and caring teachers (e.g., ‘the new principal is a rock star,’ ‘teachers go out of their way’), and fewer reports of administrative turnover or operational mismanagement compared with circle reviews that allege frequent leadership churn, unreturned calls, or punitive admin behavior.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more systemic favo: This groups circle reviews describing institutional favoritism and protection of athletes/donors — e.g., ‘football stars are favorited by the principal,’ ‘big donors’ kids get away with things,’ labs torn down for weight rooms, and families ‘parted’ for not fitting in — contrasted with square reviews that do not attribute unequal discipline or programmatic favoritism to school leadership.
candidate_defs.square entries report more overcrowding,: This bucket contains square reviews that emphasize large‑school logistical breakdowns — simultaneous lunch for thousands, closed/filthy bathrooms, packed hallways, late bus/long rides and chaotic scheduling — whereas circle reviews more often describe small‑school scale, recent capital improvements, or named facility/program investments rather than the particular crowding/scheduling hygiene failures called out in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries show stronger, measurable: These reviews repeatedly cite concrete AP/honors/dual‑enrollment offerings, test‑score gains, and elite postsecondary outcomes for circle schools (e.g., “I took 10 AP courses…entered college with 31 credits,” “over 60 free college hours,” “increase their CCRPI score by over 10 points,” and ‘alumni are phenomenally successful’), while square reviews describe fewer named advanced pathways or report that dual credit/PSEO felt easy and under‑preparatory.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more hands‑on, i: Circle reviewers emphasize teachers and staff who give one‑on‑one help, after‑school tutoring, active guidance/IEP supports, small learning communities/houses, and frequent parent communication (examples: “teachers go above and beyond,” “weekly updates from Skyward,” “The Houses help students bond,” and special‑needs supports like an Enrichment Center), whereas square reviews more often report unresponsive or inconsistent teacher/counselor follow‑through.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive unc: Square reviews contain multiple accounts of daily harassment, bullying that required therapy, ongoing peer substance use and fights, and leadership failing to stop or remediate these harms (e.g., “daily harassment and bullying of my child,” vaping in bathrooms, and administrators who ‘do nothing to stop’), in contrast to many circle reviews that describe effective discipline or a safer small‑school deterrent.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe facili: Circle reviews frequently document concrete physical and process failures—accreditation risk and ‘falling down’ buildings, bedbug infestations, lost/late transcripts, lunch/payment/accounting errors, bus pickup failures, outdated/no AC, and unreliable classroom technology—issues not present or less severe in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more explicit ad: Circle reviewers more often accuse leadership of playing favorites or prioritizing athletics/families, enforcing punitive dress/search policies, integrating Bible‑based or mission/faith instruction, and perpetuating racial/identity discrimination or targeted surveillance (e.g., “favoritism plays a role,” ‘Textbooks from Bob Jones University,’ ‘random searches of girls purses,’ and ‘a school operated by WHITE people getting rich off of our children’), whereas square reviews rarely allege systemic nepotism or curricular religiosity.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, more con: These reviews describe tangible college- and career-facing offerings and outcomes (e.g., extensive AP/IB/Cambridge classes, dual‑enrollment and college‑credit programs, JTED/vocational academies, robotics/STEM labs, students graduating with 50 college credits or national scholarships, and numeric performance metrics) that circle schools advertise more often than square schools, which typically lack the same documented AP/dual‑credit breadth or measurable postsecondary results.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent, sev: Many circle reviews recount recurring physical fights, robberies, drug sales, police responses or arrests, racial slurs and homophobic harassment, and unresolved bullying (e.g., daily fights, students followed/robbed, racial slur + light punishment), whereas square reviews rarely describe that level of violence or persistent, unaddressed harassment.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater administra: Circle reviews repeatedly document concrete operational failures—unreturned calls, lost records, late hiring, counselor/scheduling errors, layoffs, perceived overpaid/underperforming staff, donor/nepotistic favoritism, and teacher morale/walkout threats—while square reviews provide fewer or milder examples of systemic unresponsiveness and personnel mismanagement.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more explicit reso: Examples include claims that districts build new gyms while textbooks are outdated, heavy tuition and fundraising demands or scholarships linked to athletics, donor/funder families receiving preferential treatment, out‑of‑zone athletes dominating teams, and gendered underfunding of girls’ sports—specific resource/prioritization disputes more frequently called out in circle reviews than in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more problems with: Circle schools are described with concrete inclusion failures—special‑education students separated into their own classrooms and excluded from electives, budget‑driven cancellation or denial of services, long delays for ADHD/IEP supports, and poor physical‑disability accommodations—issues that appear far more often in circle reviews than in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger academic: These reviews describe programmatic strength (AP/Honors/IB, STEM, magnet arts, dual‑credit, NJROTC, vocational CTE) and cited outcomes (state/national rankings, high ACTs, high college matriculation and scholarships) — e.g., Circle notes ‘‘AP and Honors classes,’’ ‘‘ranked 155 in the nation,’’ and ‘‘97% enter post‑secondary,’’ whereas Square rarely documents consistent AP/IB breadth or outcome metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more proactive,: Circle reviews repeatedly point to teacher availability, consistent tutoring/catch‑up interventions, small class/counselor caseload advantages, and principal/parent communication (examples: teachers helping before/after school, ‘‘counselors have more time to speak with students,’’ principal outreach), while Square reviews more often report unreturned calls, limited guidance, and weaker one‑on‑one follow‑through.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater capital in: Circle mentions new/modern campuses, green certification, new weight rooms/auditoriums, underused high‑cost labs, and visible donor/athletics funding alongside explicit tuition/fee/fundraising burdens (e.g., ‘‘platinum green building,’’ new athletic complexes, ‘‘football is a huge money maker,’’ high tuition and relentless donation requests), whereas Square lacks these consistent facility/upgrade and donor/tuition narratives.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent seri: Circle contains concrete incidents and systemic safety failures — filmed students in restrooms, sexual‑harassment mediation only, gangs/drugs, repeated bullying and retaliation, and security/administration inaction (examples: ‘‘videoed in restroom,’’ ‘‘mediation with counselor only,’’ ‘‘infested with gangs, drugs’’), while Square generally documents fewer or more isolated safety events.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviews disproportionately describe rude or unhelpful office staff, teacher churn or underqualification, lost student work, punitive/high‑stakes grading and scheduling errors that delay graduation (examples: ‘‘many staff members are very rude,’’ ‘‘grossly underqualified teachers,’’ ‘‘had to repeat a 5th year due to mismanaged credits’’), whereas Circle reviews more often describe organized supports and staff stability.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: This bucket groups raw items where circle reviews cite concrete advanced‑academic and career pathways (AP/honors, dual enrollment, on‑campus college credit, CTE/vocational majors, credit‑recovery/early‑college programs) and nameable postsecondary outcomes (scholarships, Ivy/elite admits, direct program placements), e.g. “8 AP courses…college credits transferred to Rutgers,” “offered direct admission into an architecture program and a scholarship,” and “school for second chances…finish with 9 college credits.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive bul: This bucket captures reviews documenting frequent student safety incidents and targeted harassment plus weak or failing institutional responses—examples include repeated bullying and racial slurs, students being punched, claims that “bullying is out of control,” reports of homophobia/racism and that the anti‑bullying policy “isn’t effectively being implemented,” even where visible security/metal detectors are present but problems persist.
candidate_defs.circle entries depict poorer staff and l: Included here are reports of administrative rudeness, counselors not returning messages, nepotistic hiring/protection of relatives, decisions seen as image/finance‑driven, punitive parent/discipline actions, and mass teacher resignations (e.g., “Nepotism is an issue,” “the counselor has not returned any messages in 9 months,” “All the best teachers are gone,” “administration is very rude” or runs the school “like a prison”).
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater material,: This bucket groups concrete complaints about building systems, supplies, and fiscal crises: HVAC/boiler failures and extreme classroom temperatures, insufficient textbooks or take‑home materials, lack of equipment, failed levies or looming deep cuts, late buses and cafeteria problems (e.g., “no working AC…rooms reaching 95°F,” “does not even have enough science books to take home,” and warnings that funding cuts will ‘cut the band…fire half the staff’).
candidate_defs.circle entries describe a more extracurr: This bucket covers reports that extracurriculars—especially sports and band—dominate school priorities, enforce heavy after‑school commitments, and generate favoritism or exclusion (e.g., “Sports is number one priority, not education,” band leadership discouraging participation in other activities, selection unfairness in athletics, and policies tying team membership to grades).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent bull: This bucket groups accounts of student-on-student violence, systemic bullying (including racial and LGBTQ+ harassment), weapons/metal-detector incidents, drug use/vaping, bus assaults, and repeated reviewer claims that administration ignored or mishandled complaints (e.g., “Bulliying runs rampant… administration has done NOTHING,” weapons found at metal detectors, students vaping in hallways). It captures school-safety climate problems and failures of corrective action that appear far more often in circle reviews than in square reviews, which instead tend to describe fewer/isolated incidents and more visible principal intervention.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more teacher/sta: This bucket covers reports of teacher racism/abusive discipline, punitive faculty behavior, mass staff departures, micro-management, coercion of staff, and allegations of union or district-level mismanagement (e.g., “Teachers do not stay… Over half leave every year,” “some teachers are very racist,” “politics and bullying by Administration”). It groups personnel- and leadership-level breakdowns (misconduct, credential worries, threatening or demoralizing supervisor behavior) that distinguish circle reviews from square’s comparatively more consistent praise of teachers and visible, engaged principals.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more formalized,: This bucket groups descriptions of structured, branded academic pathways (IB, organized academies, robotics/technology tracks), consistent college-prep supports and measurable outcomes, and a youthful/visible principal who is lauded for hands‑on support (e.g., “IB programming,” “Principal Thilman is highly visible,” school-level outcome stats). It captures square’s tendency to report organized, recognized academic programs and centralized instructional leadership versus circle’s more fragmented mix of vocational/arts/early-college examples and variable administrative narratives.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger local: This bucket groups reports of multi‑generational attendance, strong local alumni/parent attachment, high community event participation, and small-town cliquishness/nepotism or socioeconomic exclusion (e.g., “multiple children across three generations attended,” “Community is well involved,” alongside “If you come from a low income family you... aren’t accepted”). It captures how circle reviews frequently characterize the school’s social ecology—deep local roots and parental loyalty that coexist with tight cliques and insider advantages—whereas square reviews do not foreground that same local legacy dynamic.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete oper: This bucket captures specific, actionable failures in school operations and resources—lost or withheld transcripts, denied credit transfers, opaque or punitive fees, overcrowding/seat-capacity problems, building-condition complaints and equipment failures, and schedule/office staffing dysfunction (e.g., “they almost cost my child his diploma by not giving him English 12,” “overcrowded due to many students using other peoples address,” “we were overcharged/charged hidden fees”). These concrete logistical and facilities problems are far more prominent in circle reviews than in square reviews, which tend to describe steadier operations or single resolved incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews repeatedly cite concrete curricular strength (AP/IB/honors offerings, named STEM/Scholars programs, academies, dual‑enrollment, and advanced STEM teachers) and alumni outcomes/college matriculation or scholarships for circle schools (examples: multiple AP/IB mentions, a dedicated Scholars/engineering track, and named graduates in STEM/grad school), whereas square reviews lack comparable, consistently strong evidence of advanced programming or measurable post‑secondary success.
candidate_defs.square entries report more reliable, ins: Square reviews more often describe consistent, committed supports (counseling availability, follow‑through on IEP/504 needs and remediation), while circle reviews contain numerous specific complaints of neglected lower‑functioning special‑needs students, 504 noncompliance, punitive mishandling of disabled students, and parents 'fighting' the special‑ed department.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Many circle reviews recount frequent bullying (including racial slurs), drug/alcohol prevalence, visible unsupervised misconduct, rapid student withdrawals tied to harassment, and administration inaction — concrete safety incidents (e.g., repeated use of the N‑word, students smoking at campus entrances, students leaving due to bullying) appear far more in circle than in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger, more: Circle reviews frequently describe teachers who go beyond duties (phone outreach to absent students, after‑school tutoring, private instrument lessons, coaches attending competitions), close teacher‑student familiarity, active band/theatre/band mentorship, and multigenerational parental/alumni loyalty or families relocating to attend — patterns that square reviews do not consistently show.
candidate_defs.circle entries contain more concrete ope: Circle reviews more often name specific operational programs and problems (1:1 laptops and iPad policies, HVAC/mold/rodent reports, high tuition or tuition‑value complaints, bus tardy lockouts, removal of college‑prep classes, and claims that funding disproportionately favors football), whereas square reviews rarely offer that level of concrete resource or daily‑policy detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger instituti: These reviews describe circle schools as having broader advanced-course infrastructure (IB/MYP, abundant AP/Honors, dual‑enrollment, pathway/STEM programs), formal external partnerships, 1:1 device programs and vocational/co‑op pipelines that yield concrete college and certification outcomes (e.g., 'IB program...MIT, Penn matriculations', 'school issued laptops', 'concurrent classes tuition paid' and 'intern program at the Franklin Institute'), whereas square reviews lack comparable program breadth or documented postsecondary results.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent, sev: Circle reviews repeatedly document on-campus violence, student assaults, pervasive bullying, racial homophobia/transphobia, suicide-related incidents, and easy access to drugs/alcohol (e.g., 'Three assaults on three different teachers', 'bullied because of the texture of hair', 'kids are high and drunk in school regularly', 'suicide investigation'), while square reviews either do not report these issues or describe a safer, better-managed climate.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater administra: Many circle reviewers point to chronic leadership problems—secretive personnel actions, cronyism and athletic favoritism, lost credits or botched recordkeeping, inconsistent/punitive discipline, IEP violations, and calls for state intervention (e.g., 'They keep everything a secret... fired a great teacher', 'as long as you're part of the football team you can do whatever', 'lost my credits', 'why hasn’t the state taken this school?'), whereas square reviews contain fewer or more localized leadership complaints.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger small‑s: Circle reviews frequently emphasize a family-like, multi‑generational community, visible parental fundraising and volunteerism, alumni tradition, and local pride that supports programs and events (e.g., 'Hometown feel', 'parent‑run groups raise funds', 'many generations of families attended', 'we moved to Richmond specifically for this school'), while square reviews tend not to foreground that same level of local cohesion or organized community fundraising.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent st: Square reviewers more often describe accessible, caring teachers and counselors, organized supports (consistent K–12 preparation, effective counselor outreach, proactive student follow‑up) and instructional reliability (teachers who 'help before and after school', 'counselors are off the charts'), contrasting with circle reviews that more often allege teacher inconsistency, unresponsiveness, or instructional avoidance.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, more s: These reviews emphasize concrete programs and results at circle schools—AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, early‑college or vocational/CTE certifications, high SAT/ACT averages, scholarship totals and named college matriculations—whereas square reviews lack comparable program detail or measurable outcomes (examples: dual‑credit/associates programs, millions in scholarship offers, vocational healthcare placements vs. square’s general/uneven academic claims).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: Circle reviews contain repeated accounts of fights, code‑reds/lockdowns, physical assaults, expulsions, pervasive bullying and claims that discipline or administrative responses are inconsistent or inadequate; square reviews rarely detail comparable violence and instead focus on lesser discipline concerns or isolated incidents (examples: stabbings with pencils, students thrown through windows, 40+ fights vs. square’s 'usual fights' or general monitoring complaints).
candidate_defs.circle entries exhibit more problematic: Circle entries more often allege teacher/administrator misconduct, protected tenured staff, grade‑favoritism, staff hostility or slurs, widespread turnover/long‑term substitute use, and failures to implement IEPs, whereas square reviews more frequently describe stable, caring teachers and responsive staff (examples: teacher racial/sexist slurs, 'teachers play favorites', IEPs overlooked, ‘many classes without teachers’ vs. square’s praise of committed teachers).
candidate_defs.circle entries document more pronounced: Circle reviews include concrete facility and operational conditions—aging buildings or newly renovated campuses, overcrowding/hall congestion, lack/underuse of classroom tech or 1:1 laptops, food/pest problems—and explicit complaints about budget allocation (funds moved to athletics/coaches teaching classes) not seen in square entries, which tend to emphasize program/faculty rather than such infrastructure/resource controversies.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe richer extracurr: Many circle reviews highlight extensive, organized extracurriculars, active boosters/alumni and community fundraising, formal mentoring/peer programs and internship/civic partnerships that engage students outside class; square reviews rarely describe this depth of community/extra‑curricular integration and instead focus more on classroom or safety issues (examples: national‑champion music, extensive clubs, board fundraising to save the school, Band of Brothers mentor process versus square’s sparse club descriptions).
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, more c: This bucket captures reviews that cite explicit academic programs and measurable postsecondary outcomes at circle schools—AP/IB/dual-enrollment, organized distance learning/AP test prep, documented scholarship/college-placement statistics (e.g., '$3.8 million in 2014', 'many national merit semifinalists'), and named curricular models—while square reviews lack comparable program detail or quantified college outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, better‑re: Includes claims of fully funded arts, high-participation clubs, championship athletics, large spectator football culture, CTE/shop programs, and sports‑scholarship outcomes (e.g., state champions, fully funded arts/sports) that circle reviewers emphasize more than square reviewers, who rarely list comparable department breadth or trophy/participation counts.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more pervasive s: This cluster groups reviews alleging frequent bullying (including cyberbullying), racial/sexist/homophobic discrimination, physical assaults and gang/drug activity, sexual‑assault warnings, and incidents where administration overlooked threats or allowed unsafe conditions—claims that appear far more often in circle reviews than in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report worse governance,: Covers systemic, institutional complaints about school boards and leadership—poor parent communication, cover‑ups, biased/exclusive enforcement, forcing passes, special‑education IEP failures, alleged gerrymandering or donor influence—that reflect policy/decision‑making breakdowns in circle reviews more than in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries cite more individualized: Encompasses reviewers who name specific teachers/coaches, describe one‑on‑one attention, tutoring and mentoring, proactive counselor/teacher contact, and concrete support programs (e.g., credit recovery, free dual enrollment, take‑home devices), signaling teacher‑driven, personalized supports that appear more often in circle reviews than in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reports that circle schools have chronic, concrete student-safety issues—frequent fights, underage smoking/drinking/partying, threats/violence, thefts, teen pregnancy, students off-campus during the day, and weak enforcement (e.g., cameras/security absent, staff not intervening). Representative evidence: “every week there are at least 3 to 5 fights,” “every kid smokes and dips in class,” “DEATH threats from varsity football players,” and “reporters walked in…no questions asked,” contrasted with square reviews that emphasize a safe, caring environment and few or no recurring fight/drug incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: This bucket groups reports that circle schools offer more AP/IB/dual-enrollment/scholars programs, formal academies, frequent AP/IB coursework and higher test/API results and clearer college-placement anecdotes (including Ivy/top-college matriculation) than square schools. Examples: “variety of AP and honors classes,” “IB academy program are very challenging,” “highest high school API scores,” and concrete alumni outcomes (students at top universities), whereas square reviews more often emphasize limited advanced options or mixed readiness despite some AP mentions.
candidate_defs.circle entries report a sports-dominant: This bucket groups claims that circle schools prioritize athletics over academics (resource allocation, coach-first behavior, recruiting/favoring athletes, fundraising for football) and that athletic status shapes student inclusion and discipline. Illustrative items: “Everything revolves around sports,” “teachers who are coaches prioritize winning,” “giant billboard soliciting funds for the new football field,” and “if you are on the football team you could get away with anything,” while square reviews focus more on academics/AP pressure or balanced extracurriculars.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures recurring, concrete governance problems in circle schools—corruption claims, nepotism/’good‑ol’ boy’ hiring, retroactive policy changes, mis‑managed records, calls for district intervention, unresponsive or hostile front-office staff, and polarized leadership/turnaround narratives. Examples include “the corruption and flaws outweigh the progression,” “retroactive 4.0 GPA scale applied without notice,” “Because 98% of these people are related they won't address negative issues,” and repeated calls to have the district investigate or replace staff; square entries more often describe proactive communication or improving leadership.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent fail: This bucket contains concrete allegations about poor IEP/504 implementation, minimal counseling, missing therapies, parents forced to fight for services, and students with learning differences being targeted or inadequately prepared for independence—contrasted with square reviews that rarely report IEP failures and sometimes report effective special-education supports. Representative evidence: “they do not follow through with IEPs,” “Counselors do minimal amounts of counseling,” “trying to get a child with Special Needs any form of help is like jumping through rings of fire,” and “they are not preparing him for real work and independence.”
candidate_defs.circle entries show stronger, more-syste: These reviews describe institutional academic strength at scale in circle schools — broad AP/IB offerings, named academies, CTE pathways, dual-enrollment/Running Start, counselor-driven scholarship drives, and concrete alumni/college-placement metrics (e.g., high AP participation and pass rates, SAT/ACT scores well above average, ’100% college‑bound’ claims, Running Start credits) — whereas square reviews lack sustained systemwide college-prep evidence and instead contain isolated AP anecdotes or reports of unequal preparation.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more governance op: Many circle reviews detail opaque boards/central offices, nepotistic/local‑hire cultures, favoritism/protection of staff, alleged cover‑ups and privacy breaches, and even solicitation of positive reviews, while square reviews usually criticize administrative bloat or policy enforcement but do not allege the same level of secrecy, corruption, or deliberate reputation‑management misconduct.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater overcrowdi: Circle reviewers repeatedly cite overcrowded classes and trailers, locked/restroom/vandalized bathrooms, lack of air conditioning, outdated textbooks/technology, and choices that prioritize athletic/stadium or cosmetic upgrades over security and instructional materials (e.g., new weight equipment or TVs but missing cameras or textbooks); square reviews rarely report this combined pattern of capacity strain plus misallocated capital.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more discriminator: Circle reviews contain repeated allegations of racism, homophobia, social insularity toward nonlocals, active newcomer ostracism, and documented special‑education failures (IEP/504 noncompliance, ‘warehousing’ autistic students, legal threats), while square reviews do not present this consistent cluster of exclusionary behavior and systemic SPED mistreatment.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent stud: Square reviews more often describe pervasive behavior problems, tolerated bullying, frequent fights/theft, weak classroom control and ineffective consequences (e.g., ‘ISS is a joke,’ principals failing to punish), and parents/students seeking transfers for safety — in contrast to many circle reviews that either claim strict enforcement, visible security/cameras, or far fewer violence incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report far more severe st: This bucket covers concrete accounts of on-campus danger and adult failure to protect: Circle reviews describe unresponsive security, frequent fights, drugs, gang violence, strip‑show/sexualized dance incidents, students pushed into psychiatric care, and teachers or counselors perpetrating or ignoring abuse, whereas Square offers at most occasional intolerance or isolated incidents rather than a pervasive safety crisis.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, more s: Circle reviews repeatedly list formal advanced tracks (IB, many APs, dual‑enrollment, early‑college pathways), external rankings and college-placement anecdotes (scholarships, associate degrees), and explicit college-readiness practices, while Square's comments lack comparable program breadth, measurable outcomes, or elite-program claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistently: This bucket captures reviewer claims about reliable adult responsiveness and support: Square reviewers praise visible principals, fair administrators, caring teachers, proactive counselors, and useful parent-notification systems, while Circle reviews more often document administrative absenteeism, lost records, politicized governance, or broken follow‑through.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more punitive, e: Circle reviewers report hardline or capricious discipline—spanking suggestions, suspensions for technicalities, disenrollment for off‑campus behavior, strict uniforms/metal detectors, or sending bullied students to independent study—whereas Square generally criticizes either lax enforcement or isolated harsh punishments but not this pattern of institutionalized punitive policy.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pronounced so: This bucket groups claims about who is included or favored: Circle reviews describe surname-based privilege, athlete/cheerleader favoritism, gated access to prestige programs, explicit racial/religious homogeneity and exclusion, and elite parent foundations, whereas Square's comments emphasize broader inclusion or do not foreground systematic social gatekeeping.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reviews that describe frequent fights, bullying, sexual harassment, drug/dealer activity, weapons/violent incidents, suicides, and routine failures to enforce discipline (e.g., ‘‘Students fight a lot in the hallways,’’ ‘‘Weed is super popular,’’ ‘‘a little boy got beat up with brass knuckles,’’ reports of sexual harassment and administrators who do nothing). These items also include evidence of recurring lockdowns/metal-detector use and claims that disciplinary systems are ineffective or punish defenders instead of aggressors; square reviews lack comparable accounts of systemic student-safety breakdowns and instead describe safer, more orderly environments.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: This bucket groups reviews reporting robust AP/IB/early-college offerings, named academies, internships/fellowships, honors placement, and high measurable outcomes (National Merit, high SAT/ACT, high college matriculation or scholarships) — e.g., ‘‘lots of APs available,’’ ‘‘early college program/partnerships,’’ ‘‘over 95% of students proceed to college,’’ and specialized career academies. These circle claims contrast with square entries that emphasize weaker or mixed college-readiness, fewer measurable high-achievement indicators, or post‑graduation struggles.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more adult-level p: This bucket covers allegations about staff and leadership conduct: hiring and promotion based on connections, tenured teachers bullying students, protected or unaccountable staff, administrative rudeness or capture by the board, criminal incidents (e.g., ‘‘at least one teacher arrested for sexual relations with a student’’), and coach/athletics favoritism that skews opportunities. These are governance/personnel problems distinct from student-behavior issues; square entries do not contain the same cluster of entrenched favoritism, nepotism, or protected misconduct allegations.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger family/co: This bucket captures reviews emphasizing a tight, family‑style school culture, active parental volunteerism and decision-making roles, faith-based identity/mandated spiritual programming, and long multigenerational alumni ties (examples: ‘‘we are not just a school but a family,’’ parents serving as class advisors, ‘‘faith based… chapel and Bible classes,’’ and multiple-generation attendance). Square entries, by contrast, more often lack these consistent reports of sustained parental/community cohesion or organized faith identity.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pronounced fa: This bucket groups concrete, non-instructional resource and operations issues and assets that circle reviewers call out — both positive and negative — including one-to-one iPads and smartboards or ‘‘brand NEW’’ buildings, alongside sanitation/food/pest problems, overcrowding, limited bus schedules, pay-to-play fees, hidden tuition, and scheduling/counseling breakdowns (e.g., ‘‘one to one iPads,’’ ‘‘animal waste on campus,’’ ‘‘no soap in bathrooms,’’ ‘‘pay-to-play for sports,’’ ‘‘limited bus schedule’’). These are physical, funding, and operational realities distinct from classroom pedagogy or staff conduct; square reviews do not present the same range of conspicuous facility/fee/operational contrasts.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reviews describing repeated peer violence, harassment, vaping/drug use, gang/weapon incidents, sexual misconduct, and claims that staff ignore, blame victims, or punish unfairly (examples: ‘frequent fights,’ ‘kids doing drugs in the bathroom,’ ‘security took a gun out of a locker,’ ‘My child was beaten up several times, teachers simply turned their backs,’ and ‘Bullies often get lesser punishments if they are in sports’), contrasts that with Square reviews which rarely report systemic safety failures and instead describe a safer, more orderly environment.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger college: This groups comments about high academic rigor, heavy homework, dual enrollment or AP credits, named career academies and industry certifications, and explicit selective/admissions or weeding practices (examples: ‘entering college as a sophomore because of dual credits,’ ‘wide variety of career academies,’ ‘expect 3 hours of homework a night,’ and ‘we weed out all of the non conformers to preserve 100% college acceptance’), distinguishing them from Square reviews that emphasize more modest offerings or weaker college-prep outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers reviewer claims about unresponsive or condescending administrators, manipulated or unreliable school data, nepotistic promotions, unqualified principals, refusal to address complaints or special‑education needs, and bureaucratic delays (examples: ‘School data is not reliable due to manipulation from new principal,’ ‘If you have a problem the Supt and principal will not address,’ ‘promoted an unqualified administrator,’ and ‘refused therapeutic support’), whereas Square reviews contain fewer or milder governance/transparency accusations.
candidate_defs.circle entries report worse physical inf: This groups concrete facility and capacity evidence — leaking hallways through light fixtures, bat/rodent infestations, no air conditioning, crumbling roofs, severe overcrowding and 35–40 students per class, lack of books or materials — contrasted with Square reviews which rarely list such severe maintenance, pest, HVAC, or material shortages and sometimes note facility improvements instead.
candidate_defs.circle entries portray a stronger, tight: This bucket captures social‑culture evidence that reviewers emphasize small‑town/family atmosphere, strong alumni networks and pride alongside reports of elitism, preferential treatment for athletes or wealthy families, constant fundraising demands, and closed/cliquish parent communities (examples: ‘family atmosphere’ and ‘brotherhood,’ plus ‘If you don't have the last name or the money you are a nobody,’ ‘teachers favor athletes and alter grades,’ and ‘constant fundraisers’), while Square reviews are less likely to describe both the same degree of tight local identity and the same depth of exclusionary favoritism.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: This bucket captures reports of frequent fights, gang activity, weapon threats, in-class drug use, repeated bullying and explicit assaults plus broken or lax security (old metal detectors, open campus, poor supervision) and inadequate on-the-ground responses; examples include "There is a lot of gang activity... safety is ALWAYS an issue," daily gang bullying, students 'stabbed' with no follow-up, and malfunctioning security equipment — contrasts where square reviews describe students feeling safe or do not raise gangs/violence.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger curricu: This groups claims about robust academic pathways (IB/AP/dual‑enrollment, college-credit agreements, science research, CTE and vocational options), concrete college counseling and scholarship outcomes, and explicit test/ranking evidence (e.g., IB diploma recipients, full-ride scholarships, Running Start/college partnerships) that circle reviewers cite more often than square reviewers.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, higher-ac: This bucket covers both positive breadth/quality of clubs, arts, competitive teams and alumni/competitive achievements (nationally ranked orchestra, many clubs, successful band/theatre) and complaints that athletics dominate culture (football pedestal, lowered GPA for players, counselor favoritism toward athletes); circle reviews contain many concrete program lists and athlete-privilege allegations that square reviews do not.
candidate_defs.square entries report more punitive or i: This captures square reviewers' recurrent descriptions of administrators as indifferent, punitive, politically/or image‑driven, slow or unhelpful counselors, failures to protect student mental health, and administrative mismanagement (e.g., 'principals enjoy dealing out over‑the‑top punishments', 'administration doesn’t care about mental health' and poor counseling access) — a distinct governance/fairness pattern not emphasized in circle entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more extreme facil: This bucket captures concrete operational patterns tied to space, funding and community choices — overcrowded buses/cafeterias and being well over capacity, or conversely new state‑of‑the‑art buildings; 1:1 device programs and technology integration; tuition tradeoffs and school‑of‑choice boundary effects; and local political or parental migration for/against the school (families moving into the district, alumni returning) — all described more often in circle reviews than in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries show more top-down admini: These reviews describe stronger, explicit admin-driven controls at circle schools (strict attendance rules that can block approved trips, intrusive searches, sudden shop-placement rule changes, and leadership-driven schedule changes like a four-day week), whereas square reviews more often describe weak on-campus enforcement; examples include circle accounts of a student denied a sabbatical and an "attempted a search...so bare and unprofessional," and circle crediting a four-day week with decreased discipline and higher attendance.
candidate_defs.circle entries report weaker subject-lev: Circle reviews combine claims of vocational/technical strengths or specialized programs with concrete instructional failures and worse outcomes—e.g., strong trade/technical mentions alongside complaints about an "awful" math department, ineffective foreign language teaching, rushed state-test pacing, and higher dropout/illiteracy—while square reviews describe better college preparation and successful student academic outcomes and conventional AP/fine-arts offerings.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student disen: Circle reviews frequently describe widespread student apathy, relational drama, fights, and racial/social segregation (e.g., 'majority of the students...don't really want to learn,' frequent fights, and 'student body is very racially segregated'), whereas square reviews emphasize a 'nice blend' of students and 'great kids' with fewer reports of pervasive disengagement or violent misconduct.
candidate_defs.circle entries show more explicit organi: Multiple circle reviews document active faith-integration and proselytizing pressure (pressure to attend specific church colleges, one-on-one administrative admonitions about college choices, claims that 'Christ is at the center of everything we do') and religion-linked grooming rules affecting students, while square reviews contain no similar evidence of institutional proselytizing or religion-enforced policies.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize parental respon: Circle reviews urge parents to take primary responsibility for academics and behavior and note parent-facing administrative practices—real-time attendance/grade monitoring tools, aggressive admin fundraising/solicitation, and frequent admin contact—while square reviews do not foreground home-as-primary-responsibility or report aggressive parent solicitation (examples: circle reviewers: 'Don't always put your trust in the School...reinforce...at home,' and 'The admin is aggressive about contacting parents for fundraising,' plus 'robust, real time look at my kid's attendance and grades').
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete, nam: This bucket groups raw items where Circle reviews list explicit program names and pathways (Early College, Cambridge/AICE, IB, AP, CTE tracks, Dual‑enrollment, majors like Computer Science/Engineering) and concrete outcomes (associates degrees, valedictorian, Ivy/UC acceptances, high AP/ACT performance). Examples: Circle notes an Early College associate's outcome and named academies, specific AP pass/college matriculation anecdotes, and career‑academy lists, whereas Square rarely provides comparable program names or measured student outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures instances where Circle reviewers describe recurring physical fights, lockdowns, K‑9/random searches, police presence, theft, and chronic bullying with ineffective enforcement. Examples: Circle claims “17 fights in one day,” “lockdowns every other week,” 'Police there every week,' and 'bullying occurs at every grade level,' while Square reviews rarely document such persistent safety incidents or law‑enforcement measures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent st: This groups cases where Square reviews describe reliable teacher availability, functioning counseling and IEP/504 support, structured tutoring/study supports, and proactive administrator follow‑up, in contrast to Circle accounts that claim neglected special‑education services or unresponsive counselors/teachers. Examples: Square says 'teachers and staff are committed' and recommends persistent parental advocacy successfully met, while Circle includes claims like 'You can forget a 504 or IEP' and 'they REFUSED elevator accommodation despite doctor notes.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups reports of biased enforcement, preferential treatment for athletes/wealthy/donor families, withheld diplomas/records over unpaid fees, PTA secrecy, and school‑board cliquishness. Examples: Circle alleges 'rules don't apply to the athletes,' 'we will withhold yearbook/cap/gown/diploma until $100 paid,' 'football program gets all funding,' and 'school board members act like they are in high school themselves,' whereas Square contains few such governance/favoritism allegations.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, better‑re: This bucket covers Circle reviews that enumerate extensive physical resources and extracurricular breadth — multiple gyms/theaters/pools, renovated LEED campuses, robotics/STEM electives, comprehensive arts/music success, CTE buildings and vocational pathways — claims absent or less detailed in Square. Examples: Circle lists 'three theatre spaces, two gyms, a professional dance studio and a pool,' 'new C.T.E. building,' 'Organic chemistry, Apple class, build your own PC,' and strong state‑level arts/athletics achievements, while Square rarely matches this level of facilities or program infrastructure detail.
