candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reports about campus safety and enforcement: circle reviewers frequently recount recurring bullying, physical fights, drugs, cyberbullying, guns, police/drug‑dog lockdowns and staff/administration ignoring or failing to remediate them (e.g., “students bully each other… staff did absolutely nothing,” “A gun was brought to school,” “drug dogs walk by lockers”). Square entries, by contrast, rarely describe ongoing violence and often say bullying is handled or rare (e.g., “Bullying is very rarely an issue,” “there has never been a genuine attack”).
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, more co: This bucket groups curricular and pathway evidence: circle reviews repeatedly name AP/dual‑enrollment, vocational certification and career‑center partnerships, award‑winning fine arts, robotics/STEM labs, internships and concrete college matriculation examples (e.g., “dual‑enrollment that gets you college credit,” “medical assistant certification,” “award‑winning fine arts,” “sons attended Centre College”). Square entries tend to emphasize general college‑prep rhetoric or a few programs (AP/IB/magnet) but with fewer named vocational or outcome examples.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more inconsistent: This bucket captures unequal enforcement and capture of school decisions: many circle reviewers allege teachers/coaches protect popular athletes, donors/wealthy parents get special treatment, appointed student councils, and selective dress‑code or grading enforcement (e.g., “shining stars get away with it because teachers and coaches protect them,” “If you are a parent with deep pockets they will do anything for you,” “Favoritism is a huge thing there”). Square reviews do not present repeated, systemic accusations of nepotism or wealth‑based favoritism.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more facility, cap: This bucket groups physical‑plant and resourcing claims: circle reviewers frequently cite overcrowded classes (e.g., 43 students in a class), sewage/cleanliness problems, lack of space for athletics, budget cuts and misallocated funds (e.g., “very dirty… smells like sewage,” “Budget cuts… left the school system in serious trouble,” “overcrowded due to many students using other peoples address”). Square reviews seldom raise these concrete facility or systemic funding complaints and more often highlight up‑to‑date tools or newer buildings.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more proactive, in: This bucket covers active staff/leadership outreach and individualized supports: circle reviews repeatedly describe teachers/staff who adapt instruction for struggling students, named principal initiatives and outreach (e.g., “The Principal is amazing,” “Coffee with Potts,” 12th‑grade capstone projects and internships), structured parent programs (School Site Council, ELAC, PIQE) and concrete guidance/college‑application help. Square reviews, by contrast, more often complain of hard‑to‑reach or unresponsive administration/counseling and lack the same catalogue of named, proactive programs.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize structured coll: These reviews describe concrete academic systems at circle — AP/IB offerings, extensive dual‑enrollment and college credit, adjunct‑professor instructors, strict grading/accountability, Saturday tutoring and retake policies — and often cite high SAT/ACT/test rankings and alumni college placements (e.g., ‘many AP and Dual Credit Classes,’ ‘entered college with upwards of 40 College Credits,’ ‘scored the highest in the county on the ACT’); square reviews lack sustained evidence of those formal college‑prep structures and metrics and instead emphasize more mixed or uneven academic supports.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: Multiple circle reviews recount frequent fights, drug/vape deals, public sexual behavior, severe bullying (including of special‑needs students), bus safety incidents, and staff or admin inaction or inconsistent discipline (e.g., ‘fights almost every day,’ ‘girls getting groped,’ ‘students use vapes on the bus,’ ‘administrators stood back watching’), whereas square reviews rarely describe pervasive safety incidents or systemwide enforcement failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more administrat: Circle reviews repeatedly cite front‑office unresponsiveness, lost or denied credits/transcripts, billing and diploma withholding, hiring by connections, biased discipline/athlete favoritism, and calls for leadership change (e.g., ‘they would not receive credit… half a year shy,’ ‘they hire coaches… who they know,’ ‘made me Pay $119 for books I already turned in’), while square reviews more often describe accountable communication systems and fewer large‑scale record or nepotism problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries highlight sharper facilit: Reviewers of circle both praise modern, high‑tech facilities and inventories (smart boards, cameras, Adobe suites, welding/culinary/wood shop) and document capacity/maintenance problems (severe overcrowding, 4 bathrooms for 400+ students, no heat/AC in seasons, broken Chromebooks or pest issues), whereas square reviews do not present this combined pattern of new‑facility investments paired with acute overcrowding or facility failure.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, more o: Circle reviews frequently list extensive clubs, award‑winning music and state‑level sports, internship and leadership programs, active parent fundraising/portals and alumni networks (e.g., ‘band, robotics, Chicago/AP trips, alumni reunions, parent‑run School Power’), and sometimes a selective or tuition‑funded faith identity that shapes access; square reviews rarely report the same breadth of organized extracurricular infrastructure, selective admissions, or pronounced alumni/parent financial engagement.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews emphasize concrete academic offerings and outcomes (AP/honors/IB, dual‑enrollment, high AP/ACT results, district/state rankings, explicit graduation/college‑matriculation statistics) for circle schools while square reviews lack those specifics and describe stagnation or poor college readiness; examples include circle mentions of “top 7% by US News,” “11 AP classes,” “dual enrollment/College on Campus,” and 100% or near‑100% graduation claims contrasted with square’s anecdotes of students being unprepared for college and only rising API without sustained metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, better‑su: Circle reviews repeatedly enumerate well‑resourced, diverse extracurriculars and public achievements (traveling band/choir, championship teams, award‑winning arts, JROTC, magnets/vocational shops) and note strong community support, whereas square reviews either omit these programs or mention only a few isolated activities; illustrative items include circle’s traveling band and state FFA championships, robotics/3D labs, and named JROTC instructors versus square’s limited extracurricular references.
candidate_defs.circle entries report athletics/extracur: Many circle reviews allege that sports and high‑profile activities receive disproportionate resources, protection and preferential treatment (e.g., coaches/athletes getting better grades, alumni/donor influence reinstating students, selection based on legacy or coach relationships) whereas square reviews do not document systemic athletics‑driven favoritism; concrete claims include athletes bribing teachers, alumni donations reversing expulsions, and 'legacy' kids getting leadership and team slots.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: Circle reviews contain detailed, repeated accounts of peer violence, in‑class drug use, gang proximity, chronic bullying, and teachers/principals failing to stop or properly implement anti‑bullying policy, while square reviews rarely describe that breadth/severity of safety incidents; examples are reports of regular fights, 'kids doing drugs in class,' anti‑bullying policy 'not effectively implemented,' and inadequate dean investigations.
candidate_defs.circle entries document greater administ: These reviews describe managerial dysfunction—administrative invisibility, refusal to document complaints, covering up or retaining staff after criminal incidents, hostile or censoring leadership, routine non‑responsiveness to parents and high staff turnover—distinct from but sometimes contributing to safety or program problems; cited evidence includes principals 'running it like a prison,' arrests with retained staff, 'administration lies,' missing complaint records, and pervasive non‑returned calls/emails.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent, sev: These reviews describe concrete, repeated safety incidents and weak enforcement at the school—e.g., “We have a couple of fights every week,” “Drugs are horrible problem,” “GANG ACTIVITY... kids being assaulted,” thefts of personal property, and allegations that administration protects dealers or fails to intervene—whereas square reviews do not document this level of physical/criminal disorder or regular violent incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe substantially st: Multiple circle reviews cite AP/IB/dual‑enrollment/STEM tracks, early‑college and associate‑degree programs, large scholarship totals, and alumni college credit/placements (examples: full IB/college credits, ‘over $9 million in scholarships,’ ‘graduate with over 40 hours of college credit’, STEM‑certified programs), while square reviews lack comparable program breadth, formal dual‑credit pathways, or documented scholarship/placement metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more staff and adm: Circle reviewers repeatedly allege teacher/admin wrongdoing and unequal treatment—harassment and interrogation of students/parents, racist or abusive teachers, favoritism for athletes/relatives/appearance, excessive suspensions and shaming, and claims that staff ‘bully’ kids—charges that are largely absent or far less frequent in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger parent‑fa: Circle reviews frequently note operational transparency and proactive outreach—PowerSchool/grade portals, direct teacher email, online lunch payments, active PTA/foundation fundraising (e.g., eagleacademyfoundation.org), visible principal presence, coordinated athletics/community turnout, and explicit college‑prep advising—features square reviews rarely document.
candidate_defs.square entries report more peer‑driven s: Square reviewers disproportionately describe popularity‑based hierarchies and social exclusion—‘popular kids rule the roost,’ students ‘mocked on Facebook,’ ‘asked to prom as a joke,’ ‘holy water thrown at me in the halls’—portraying a peer culture of cliques and interpersonal cruelty that circle reviews more often characterize as cohesive or family‑like.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, more con: This bucket captures when reviewers describe day‑to‑day staff who proactively help students and parents (e.g., “caring teachers,” ‘‘staff always listens to parents,’’ routine parent‑teacher conferences, web notification systems, counselors who "will work with you"). Square entries, by contrast, tend to describe mixed or unresponsive staff behavior (e.g., unanswered emails, slow schedule changes) and do not foreground routine, systematic teacher/counselor outreach.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This groups reports of serious on‑campus safety problems in circle (e.g., constant fights, gang fights and lockdowns, in‑class overdose, student thrown through a window, athletic hazing, sexual exploitation), whereas square entries lack comparable accounts of repeated violence, overdose, hazing, or mass lockdowns.
candidate_defs.circle entries document broader, more co: This covers reviews that list specific curricular and co‑curricular strengths and outcomes in circle—AP/IB/dual‑credit, CTE/early‑college partnerships, professional arts mentorships, award‑winning clubs, scholarship totals and college placements (e.g., dual enrollment leading to sophomore standing, US News rankings, Broadway teaching partnerships)—while square entries typically make fewer or vaguer claims about concrete program partnerships or measurable postsecondary outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more specific faci: This bucket includes concrete, tangible facility/resource evidence in circle (e.g., black mold and pest/centipede infestations, no air conditioning, disgusting bathrooms, versus praise for new gyms/brand‑new buildings, MacBooks/iPads and renovation projects), whereas square entries seldom enumerate a similar range of concrete facility problems or recent capital/technology details.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more systemic ineq: This groups reports of institutional unfairness appearing in circle—nepotism, donor/athlete favoritism and grade alteration, selective discipline or punishment of victims, IEP violations and special‑education noncompliance, politically charged or image‑focused administration—while square entries rarely allege this kind of pervasive policy bias or governance‑level misconduct.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more pervasive s: This bucket captures reports that the school tolerates frequent bullying, physical harassment, daily fights, drug/vaping problems, easy skipping and open campus security, and generally ineffective or punitive discipline responses (e.g., “Fights all the time,” “kids do drugs there, vape etc.,” “They allow bullying… administration has done NOTHING,” and repeated accounts of violent incidents and unsafe drop‑off/traffic). These accounts emphasize recurring student misbehavior plus staff/administration failures to prevent or reliably remediate it, in contrast to square reviews which rarely describe sustained, episodic violence or pervasive safety breakdowns.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more systemic favo: This bucket groups evidence that discipline and opportunity are distributed unequally—big‑donor kids, athletes, or those with the ‘right’ last names receive preferential treatment while complainants/others face retaliation or harsher penalties (examples: “big donors kids get away with a lot,” “You are only someone if your last name is Mild…,” “The only people who get support are football players,” and “If you complain your child becomes a target”). These items emphasize protected adult networks, favoritism in resourcing and discipline, and nepotistic culture, which square reviews do not describe at the same systemic scale.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more institutional: This bucket covers reviews alleging explicit school endorsement or enforcement of religious/ideological norms and identity‑based exclusion—forced religious practices, contracts limiting LGBT expression, Church‑of‑Christ favoritism, and faculty ignoring racial slurs (e.g., “They force students to sing about a Christian god,” “I had to sign a contract that I could not be gay,” and “racism is non stop… administration will do nothing”). These are substantive claims of policy or practice that privilege religious conformity or discriminate against protected groups, which do not appear in the square material.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger academi: This bucket groups concrete claims that the school provides rigorous honors/AP/IB/CTE pathways, visible college matriculation and scholarship outcomes, extensive program tracks, and routine one‑on‑one academic support (e.g., “The college course selection and AP curriculum… is way beyond,” “both of my children graduated…doing very well in a four‑year university,” “EVERY teacher has after school extra help hours,” and named AP/IB/CTE academies). Square reviews more often emphasize unchallenging instruction, missing courses/staffing gaps, and weaker college preparation, so this contrast captures program strength and tangible outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries more often reflect a tuit: This bucket captures structural differences in how reviewers describe school funding, governance, and admissions—circle reviews frequently note high tuition, multigenerational alumni boards, selective/lottery admissions, hidden fees, or strong alumni/private support (“the tuition is legendary,” “board of directors… many teachers are former students,” “large waiting list/lottery”), whereas square reviews are framed as public district schools with mixed socioeconomic enrollment, levies/fee complaints, program cuts due to public funding, and open enrollment issues. These are school‑level operational models (private/selective vs. public/district) and their concrete effects on resources and access.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups reviews that describe frequent bullying, harassment (including ethnic/LGBT-targeted and sexual), gang activity, fights, vaping/violence, and claims that staff or administrators fail to stop or improperly handle incidents (e.g., “Bulliying runs rampant and unchecked,” “many sexual assaults... not taken care of,” “There was one day when we had 5 or 6 fights in the same day,” and accounts of mediation or swept‑under‑the‑rug responses). It also captures restrictive or punitive day‑to‑day discipline practices tied to those safety dynamics (e.g., automatic suspensions, restricted restroom access) when reviewers tie them to safety/behavior failures rather than routine orderliness.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: This bucket captures reviews reporting broader AP/dual‑enrollment/college‑credit access, organized college supports and counselor scholarship help, external recognitions, and high college placement (examples: “8 AP courses, and college credit courses,” “dual enrollment... free,” “named 'Best High Schools'…,” and lists of students going to Ivy/elite schools). It groups concrete programmatic evidence of college prep and outcome metrics that reviewers cite as distinguishing features of the school.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more individualize: This bucket covers evidence of small‑school personalization, teacher availability outside class, named supportive teachers and counselors, mentor‑style coaches, and formal in‑day remediation structures (e.g., Power Hour, before/after‑school tutoring, teachers who 'email you back in a timely manner,' coaches as mentors, and curriculum adjustments putting a student on an advanced track). It groups hands‑on, person‑level practices that reviewers describe as directly supporting individual students.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket collects reviews alleging principal/board unresponsiveness or harassment, nepotism and protected staff, grade manipulation or pressure to pass students, privacy breaches and swept‑under‑the‑rug investigations, commercial/vendor kickbacks, and unstable leadership/turnover (examples: “horrendous nepotism… one family runs the place,” “they push some of the kids thru to force them to graduate earlier due to money,” and “administration will do anything to save face”). These are governance‑level problems distinct from classroom teaching or extracurricular strength.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger extrac: This bucket groups reviews that highlight robust performing‑arts and music programs, high‑level marching band/arts/athletics success, broad extracurricular variety, and visible parent/faculty/alumni advocacy (e.g., “The marching band is amazing… one of the top in our state,” “students, faculty, parents, and alumni joined forces and were able to stop the merger,” and extensive club/activity lists). It captures the school's public identity and community activism around non‑academic programs and school preservation.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete safety crises and adult non‑response in circle schools (drugs, stabbings, assaults, suicides ignored, threats, pervasive bullying and students 'running the school') versus square reviews that mention only isolated fights or better staff intervention; examples include circle claims of a stabbing, widespread drug problems, ignored student suicides and ineffective disciplinary response compared with square's far milder accounts of fights and principal-led searches.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more chronic facil: This captures building- and infrastructure-level problems that circle reviewers raise more often—mold, bed bugs and mice, broken HVAC and computers, poor wifi, terrible cafeteria food, overcrowding and broken equipment—whereas square reviews rarely mention these problems; examples include repeated circle notes of bedbugs, moldy buildings, 'no air conditioning', 'wifi sucks', and packed buses/40‑student classes.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize a smaller, clos: This bucket collects circle reports of small class sizes, tight student–teacher relationships, multi‑year continuity programs (e.g., 6‑year arts), robust alumni ties, high parental volunteerism and individualized supports (lower student–teacher ratios, scheduled tutoring), contrasted with square's portrayal of a larger, more impersonal campus; examples include circle statements like 'class size about 15', 'you feel like family', many alumni returning to teach, and 'parent engagement above any school you've ever worked with.'
candidate_defs.circle entries document more entrenched: This groups instances where circle reviews describe nepotism, booster‑parent cliques, politicized school-board fights, withheld services over fees, favoritism in scholarships/athletics, pressuring teachers to pass students, and rude/unresponsive front‑office staff—issues presented far more frequently in circle than in square; examples include claims that scholarships go to well‑connected families, board politicization over levies/COVID policy, and 'front office staff is VERY RUDE!!!'.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent in: This bucket captures square reviews that emphasize reliable teacher quality, active college counseling, monitored grades/parent portals, and coherent academic programming (IB/honors/college counseling), whereas circle reviews are more mixed on instructional consistency; examples include square praise for 'excellent staff', 'grades are actually watched by the school and by parent portal', and counselor help with college applications contrasted with circle's repeated accounts of uneven preparation and missed guidance.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe substantially st: These reviews say circle schools list many named, high‑value programs and measurable outcomes (AP/IB seats, Cambridge/IB, running start/dual enrollment, NJROTC/JROTC awards, industry certifications, large fine‑arts centers and high AP/college matriculation rates) while square reviews mention fewer advanced pathways and weaker college‑prep credibility (limited AP/IB, struggles with IB diploma, or narrow CTE mentions). Examples: circle cites ‘many AP classes…98% go to college,’ ‘Cambridge IGSCE, band/choir, magnet programs,’ ‘OSHA/industry certifications, Running Start,’ whereas square lacks comparable program breadth or outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent, sev: Circle reviews frequently describe violent incidents, weekly lockdowns/code‑reds, gang‑related shootings, metal‑detector/scanner policies and students fearing for their safety, whereas square reviews tend to focus on isolated fights, policy neglect or mental‑health concerns rather than repeated, severe safety events. Examples: circle: ‘weekly NYDP lockdowns,’ ‘gang related shooting,’ ‘scanner school/metal detectors’; square: ‘administration cares more about vaping than sexual assault/mental health’ or only occasional fights.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more proactive,: Many circle reviewers emphasize hands‑on remediation, timely counselor/teacher responsiveness, small class mentorship and concrete advising (e.g., early college planning, weekly progress tools, teachers staying after class), while square reviews more often report counseling gaps, lost credits, or weaker newcomer placement. Examples: circle: ‘counselors helped seniors apply to college,’ ‘teachers reply to texts/emails, 12:1 ratios, caught transfer student up’; square: ‘weak newcomer placement guidance,’ ‘lost some of my credits while i was there.’
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more administrativ: Circle reviews repeatedly accuse leadership of cronyism and rigged selections (family/alumni picks for teams/opportunities), selective charter/admissions/exclusion of special‑needs students, hidden program cuts or pocketed funds, and cover‑ups, whereas square reviews do not present comparably detailed allegations of systemic nepotism or financial misconduct. Examples: circle: ‘favorites based on last names,’ ‘charters choose their students/could not accommodate disabled child,’ ‘They pocket the funds,’ ‘cover for inappropriate behavior,’ and parent demands to fire district leaders.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete faci: Circle reviewers give repeated operational complaints—old/dusty buildings, no AC causing fainting, overcrowded classrooms, last‑minute bus cancellations, poor cafeteria portions, and heavy family fees—while square reviews more often praise up‑to‑date facilities or do not report those systematic operational failures. Examples: circle: ‘no AC…students faint from heat,’ ‘40 kids in a class,’ ‘sent bus cut notices one day before school,’ ‘Sparta entrance fee $1,000/monthly fees,’ versus square’s ‘incredible facilities’ and modern campus notes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student-safet: This bucket captures reviews that describe concrete safety and climate harms (bullying, sexual misconduct, large fights, gang presence, on-campus/off-campus assaults, alcohol/drug prevalence and malfunctioning security) and note administrators/staff failing to stop them — e.g. “need to crack down on bullying,” “Drugs and alcohol are widespread,” staff smelled of alcohol, “A LOT of fights… gang activity is present,” a robbery causing concussion, and repeated claims that complaints were ignored or victims told to "be a problem solver."
candidate_defs.circle entries report more explicit adva: This groups reviews that list concrete curricular structures and outcomes — multiple named academies and pathways (Biomedical, Technology, Business, AG/FFA, woodshop/auto shop), IB/AP/Honors and dual‑enrollment/AA attainment, and numeric outcome claims (GPAs, ACT/IB counts, scholarship dollars) — e.g. “Biomedical, Technology, Business, and Skills Trade Academies,” “IB Program is exceptional,” “walk with her AA Degree,” and explicit ACT/college matriculation statistics, which square reviews rarely provide.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more problems with: This bucket covers concrete, staff‑and-leadership operational effects described in reviews: counselor scheduling errors threatening graduation, rude/unhelpful counselors, high teacher turnover and leadership churn, administrative retaliation or nepotism, favoritism in athletics and discipline, and also specific claims of deeply caring teachers — e.g. “Counselor was inefficient… check to make sure your child has what is needed to graduate,” “Over 50% of the teachers have left,” “Jeremy Jackson will make sure their children pay for it,” and numerous accounts of teachers staying after school to help students.
candidate_defs.circle entries contain more specific, co: Reviews placed here offer tangible, on‑the‑ground facility/resource claims rather than generalities — examples include brand‑new or state‑of‑the‑art buildings and new computer labs (“brand new school buildings… recently been updated with new computers”), or explicit failures (“the back half is sliding down the hill,” broken restrooms, old/ malfunctioning metal detectors, insufficient cafeteria seating), whereas square reviews rarely provide such specific facility detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger parent/: This bucket groups reviews that report active PTAs/PTSAs, multigenerational/alumni traditions, explicit religious programming (retreats, weekly liturgy, faith‑based hiring or moral formation), links to community poverty or military demographics, or tuition/financial‑aid realities — e.g. “very good and involved PTSA,” “Kairos retreat… Catholic,” “small community with lots of poverty,” “tuition… financial aid available,” and deep multigenerational ties — topics square reviews generally omit or treat differently.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger structure: These reviews describe concrete program offerings and measurable outcomes (AP/IB course depth, 4x4/AP scheduling issues, dual‑enrollment credits, CTE/Tech center classes, IB/advanced program reputations, and quantified college credits or scholarship results) that are more frequently documented in circle entries (e.g., “graduated with 21 college credits,” “offers more Advanced Placement Courses… produces more national merit scholars,” “outstanding STEAM/biomedical offerings”) than in square entries, which rarely list the same combination of advanced pathways and documented postsecondary outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Many circle reviews allege systemic leadership failures—frequent principal turnover or disliked transitions, calls for district investigation or wholesale re‑staffing, manipulated metrics, nepotistic protection of favorite students/staff, front‑office unprofessionalism, and suppression tactics (e.g., alleged fire alarm pull to stop protest)—whereas square entries less often present coordinated claims of corruption or administrative cover‑ups and instead give mixed or specific operational criticisms.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe a worse student: Circle reviews contain repeated, concrete accounts of peer violence, racist/homophobic slurs, gang presence, weapons or police involvement, on‑campus drug/sexual activity, and claims that staff/administration tolerated or mishandled reports (e.g., bruising from fights, a gun removed from a locker, tolerated racist slurs), while square entries seldom present this cluster of severe safety incidents and systemic non‑protection.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, higher‑qu: Circle reviewers more often enumerate extensive clubs, strong music/arts programs, high‑achieving teams, service requirements and thriving ASB traditions (e.g., ‘amazing arts program,’ state‑champion teams, ‘something for everyone’), yet also cite concrete participation fees and exclusionary shop/fee practices; square entries more often lack that level of breadth or note program decline rather than the combination of high quality plus fee barriers.
candidate_defs.circle entries contain more explicit, co: Circle reviews frequently provide specific counselor/IEP anecdotes—overloaded guidance caseloads, refused testing accommodations, dramatic IEP transfer recoveries, or staff who ‘go out of their way’ to support a special‑needs student—whereas square entries rarely include this degree of concrete, actionable detail about counseling, accommodations, or special‑education practice.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, progra: These circle reviews repeatedly list concrete advanced offerings and outcomes—IB Diploma, many AP/dual‑credit options, industry academies, SAT/ACT prep, high AP pass rates and named college matriculations—while square reviews more often report missing AP/GT options, no SAT prep, or weak college readiness (e.g., “no ACT/SAT prep,” “not prepared to apply for colleges”).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: Many circle items document intense bullying, racial harassment, assaults, on‑campus drug activity, lockdowns and claims that administrators ignore or punish victims (e.g., racial slurs, students punched, marijuana sold at school, lockdowns during PSATs), whereas square entries are often silent on or explicitly claim fewer/contained bullying incidents and more administrative effort to improve climate.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more pervasive a: Square reviews frequently point to entrenched leadership failures and mismanagement—principals/superintendents described as absent or hostile, transcripts withheld for debts, cronyism or retaliation, chaotic scheduling and lost paperwork—claims that frame school problems as systemic governance/operational breakdowns rather than isolated classroom issues.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize consistent, per: Circle reviews often highlight low student–teacher ratios, teachers who give personal hands‑on help and run extra tutoring (Saturdays/evenings), strong parental and alumni ties, and community internships/experiential STEM—contrasting with square reviews that describe more uneven or impersonal teacher attention and larger crowding.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize athletics‑first: Numerous circle reports say athletics and image drive school priorities—‘academics come second,’ sports/family name determines playing time, pay‑to‑play fees, and arts cuts—while square reviews more often describe broader extracurricular access or do not depict sports as the dominant organizing force.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, broader: This bucket captures reviews that emphasize concrete program breadth and rigor (IB, AP, Honors, academies, dual‑enrollment, CTE pathways, award‑winning arts/athletics, scholarships and elite college placements) that appear repeatedly for circle but are absent or weaker in square (examples: “the IB program...top 3%...USA's #1 high school debate team,” extensive CTE and Running Start partnerships, “millions in scholarship money annually,” versus Square’s lack of comparable named programs and elite placement claims).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups reviews describing concrete safety breakdowns and enforcement failures that circle reviewers single out (e.g., “students bringing guns,” “two students succumbed to shootings,” “fights every day,” pervasive bullying and racism, failure to notify parents of injuries), contrasted with square reviews that generally do not document that level or frequency of violent/safety incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more personalized,: This bucket covers accounts where circle reviews repeatedly describe one‑on‑one teacher support, teacher availability, dedicated coaching involvement, and systematic parent communication (examples: “teachers were always there… took extra time,” “coaches take girls to games,” “grades updated a few times a week; teachers reply to concerns”), while square reviews more often lack or dispute those consistent reports of individualized teacher care.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups concrete managerial and office‑level failures that reviewers attribute more to square (examples include counselor/office ignoring requests, lost doctor’s notes, poor record‑keeping, refusal to resolve grade/placement complaints, and claims about administrators protecting staff and being rude), distinguishing these operational stewardship problems from classroom‑level teacher behavior.
candidate_defs.circle entries report sharper facility/r: This bucket collects reviews that describe concrete physical and operational conditions in circle schools (both positive: new SmartBoards, maintained pools, active construction, booster funding, free transit or college shuttles; and negative: extreme overcrowding, no science labs, short lunches, parking/drop‑off enforcement, tuition/fee complaints and questions about budget allocation), whereas square reviews rarely present that same mix of named facility investment and specific operational policies.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger academic/: These schools' reviews describe concrete curricular depth and recognized outcomes — many circle entries name AP/dual‑enrollment classes, career/CTE pathways (healthcare, AFROTC, Academy of Finance), district/state awards and rising test‑score rankings or college placements (e.g., “named an A+ School of Excellence,” “students can earn a year of college,” “ranked by U.S. News”), whereas square reviews lack comparable program breadth or measurable college‑prep claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more engaged, indi: Circle reviews repeatedly describe teachers who stay after to help, stable same counselors across years, one‑on‑one attention and low student:teacher ratios (e.g., “willing to stay after…,” “same counselor from day one,” “15:1”), whereas square reviews more often report large classes, limited individual support, or unresponsive staff.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: These circle reviews document governance and HR failures—protected/entrenched staff, nepotism/local‑hire culture, difficulty firing ineffective teachers, withholding transcripts for financial reasons, and calls for school‑board accountability (e.g., “very hard for them to be fired,” “refused to give me transcript…didn't want to give up any money,” “school board needs to reevaluate”), a theme that distinguishes them from square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent stud: Circle reviews often list concrete safety incidents and pervasive student misconduct (regular fights, drug use, chronic bullying, even shootings or staff‑student relationships) and describe inadequate or punitive responses (long suspensions, lack of follow‑through), whereas square reviews provide fewer reports of sustained violence or pervasive bullying.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater visible co: Many circle reviews emphasize active parent volunteering, donor/alumni bases, broad extracurriculars (band, missions, FBLA, state competitions), and visible facility/technology investments (new gyms, iPads, maker labs), while square reviews less often describe this kind of sustained external support or wide activity roster.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, concrete: These reviews describe tangible academic offerings and results (AP/Advanced classes, dual‑enrollment/transferable college credit, CTE/vocational majors, organized ACT/college prep) and cite measurable outcomes (graduation‑rate gains, college matriculation, early graduation) that square reviews do not; examples include statements about AP/dual enrollment, technical centers, vocational majors (auto tech, Fashion Design), and explicit metrics like a 25% graduation‑rate increase or strong SAT/ACT averages.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Circle entries more often recount ongoing bullying, daily fights, drug use, heavy police/security patrols, and either ineffective responses or overly punitive/arbitrary discipline (suspensions, blanket punishments, 'boot camp' discipline) whereas square entries lack the same breadth or severity of these reports; supporting evidence includes repeated claims of unchecked bullying, frequent fights, police patrolling halls, students doing drugs, and inconsistent/harsh punishments.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more individuali: Many circle reviews emphasize small class sizes, one‑on‑one teacher help, morning help labs, proactive tutoring/teacher interventions, responsive counselors, and successful IEP inclusion – concrete staff‑student supports and personalization that square reviews report less consistently; illustrative items include reviewers noting small cohorts, 'one on one time with teachers,' functioning guidance teams, and successful special‑needs mainstreaming.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more administrativ: Circle reviews contain numerous governance‑level complaints—administrative cover‑ups of incidents, political/family ties affecting fairness, donor/donation pressure determining awards or placements, hidden fees and financial penalties (fines for parents), and board/district mismanagement—that square reviews do not emphasize; examples include reports of cover‑ups, calls to 'weed out political and family ties,' parents paying/being solicited, and punitive fee enforcement or opaque billing practices.
candidate_defs.square entries report more athletics‑cen: Square reviews more frequently describe a culture and resource allocation that privilege athletes and powerful parents—funding and attention to football, coach/athlete favoritism, cutting drama/arts to support sports—leaving non‑athletes marginalized; supporting examples include explicit complaints about prioritizing the football team, resources funneled to athletics, and non‑athletic programs being cut or underfunded.
candidate_defs.circle entries show stronger advanced ac: This bucket groups reviews that attribute concrete programmatic rigor and post‑secondary results to the school (AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, STEM/career academies, high SAT/ACT/National Merit counts, scholarships, alumni at selective colleges), claims that these offerings produce measurable college‑ and career‑ready outcomes. Representative evidence: statements like “consistently produces National Merit Scholars,” “STEM Academy,” “dual enrollment / BACE certification,” and detailed alumni/scholarship examples (students at MIT, WPI, Bright Flight/other scholarships).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups reviews describing frequent on‑campus misconduct (vaping, drug use, tobacco incidents, assaults, sexualized behavior, severe bullying) coupled with claims that staff/administration tolerate or under‑enforce rules. Representative evidence: “Students vape in the bathrooms between every class,” “when I was attacked in a blind spot… they told me I was a liar,” reports of drugs and assaults, and claims athletes ‘get to bully kids n get away with it.’
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more administrat: This bucket covers accounts of unresponsive or evasive administrators and staff, underreporting of incidents, nepotism/favoritism, and failure to implement legal or individualized supports (IEP/504 noncompliance, ignored parental concerns). Representative evidence: complaints that administration “did not even call his mother,” “bullying report… always reads ZERO infractions,” “teachers will not follow IEP/504,” and “it’s all about who you are and who your dad is.”
candidate_defs.circle entries document more operational: This bucket captures concrete operational failures and resource constraints (transportation/bus shortages, budget/levy shortfalls and cuts, poor maintenance or temporary classrooms, problematic 1:1 device rollouts) as distinct from pedagogy or staff behavior. Representative evidence: “needs more buses… unequal allocation,” “the laptops… impair learning,” “budget troubles… impacts the students,” and repeated facility/maintenance complaints or construction/upgrade notes tied to service disruption.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe a smaller, more: This bucket groups statements about school size, social fabric, parental/alumni involvement, and program emphasis (close‑knit/familylike feel, multi‑generational attendance, booster/grassroots fundraising, athlete privilege and strong local athletics or high‑profile extracurriculars). Representative evidence: “smaller school so everyone is on a more personal level,” “we're not just a community but family,” alumni/career pipelines and fundraiser appeals, plus claims that athletics dominate social life or that there are nationally competitive teams.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews emphasize concrete curricular/program strengths at circle schools — e.g., AP/IB/honors availability, Early‑College/dual‑enrollment and selective magnet arts programs, vocational/Broadcasting/CTE pathways, 1:1 laptop/iPad rollouts, and large senior scholarship totals/state ratings — whereas square reviews rarely cite equivalent, school‑level academic metrics or breadth of advanced/technical offerings (examples: ‘AP program is outstanding’, ‘college professors on campus… graduate with your associate’s degree’, ‘each student issued a laptop’, versus square’s absence of comparable school‑wide claims).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent stud: Many circle reviews recount recurring safety incidents and normalized peer abuse plus ineffective/cover‑up administrative response — e.g., daily gang bullying, students beaten up, weapons/assaults, students smoking/hooking up in bathrooms, and principals blamed for covering incidents — while square reviews more often describe isolated incidents or portray a safer, better‑managed climate (examples: ‘My son was bullied by gang members EVERY DAY,’ ‘teachers laugh along with bullying,’ ‘principal tried to cover the incident up’).
candidate_defs.circle entries show more operational/adm: Circle reviews contain repeated, concrete service‑delivery failures (missing/late grade entry, counselors who never return calls, schedules not ready, students not entered in system, unreliable buses, months‑long plumbing leaks, IEP/504 accommodations not implemented), whereas square reviews contain fewer or different administrative complaints and more examples of timely staff follow‑up (examples: ‘teachers don’t put grades in timely’, ‘look at the website’ deflection, ‘buses will not show up five days a week’, ‘no one answers the office phone’).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more selective/fav: Reviews of circle schools repeatedly describe exclusionary practices and politicized access — e.g., selective admissions/waitlists, favoritism toward staff/church families, volunteer‑tied or pay‑to‑play access to sports and traditions, manipulated award paperwork, and wealth‑based social exclusion — while square reviews do not center these systematic access‑barriers (examples: ‘FAVORITISM given to members of the church and/or staff’s children,’ ‘If parents aren’t willing to work volunteering forget your kid starting in sports,’ ‘they pull teachers to fill Blue Ribbon paperwork’).
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger local com: Many circle reviews highlight a tight‑knit, small‑school or faith‑oriented community and concrete family supports — e.g., chapel/Bible classes and daily spiritual practices, parents funding clubs, alumni returning, campus clothing closets/bookstores and in‑school therapists, and staff who ‘know every child by name’ — whereas square entries less often emphasize integrated faith life, alumni return‑migration, or explicit wraparound social supports (examples: ‘Chapel…Bible taught daily,’ ‘they have a clothing closet and help families with food bags,’ ‘many alumni moved back when they started having children’).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: These reviews describe concrete safety failures (daily fights, arrests/handcuffs, pervasive vaping/drugs, sexual‑harassment mishandling, negligent weather protocols) and repeated staff/admin inaction (SRO conflicts, ignored bullying, ineffective discipline). Example evidence: “I got arrested without prior notice because of a /rumor/,” “Fights occur almost everyday,” and “There is no bullying prevention,” whereas Square contains only limited mentions of misbehavior and no comparable police/arrest or sexual‑harassment incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more formal advanc: Many Circle reviews list programmatic offerings (AP/IB, Running Start/dual enrollment, named academies and early‑college partnerships) and document high‑tier matriculations and scholarship totals (Ivy admits, nearly $1,000,000 in scholarships). Example evidence: “Running Start with Clark College,” “Both girls take nearly all AP classes,” and “We have kids going to Stanford/Northwestern,” while Square generally lacks dual‑credit/early‑college claims and reports weaker or uneven college preparation.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater extracurri: Circle frequently cites richly resourced/competitive extracurriculars (state‑rated band and choir, professional‑level orchestra, repeat athletic state championships, standout theater and marching‑band performances), e.g. “band and choir constantly receive high reviews at state contest” and “wrestling program…won its fifth straight 2A state championship,” whereas Square’s reviews rarely document sustained contest‑level arts or multi‑sport championship records.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle contains repeated governance‑level allegations (corruption, nepotistic favoritism, tyrannical or absent principals, board decisions that undermine staffing/facilities, stolen fees, unresolved grievances) such as “the Superintendent just resigned due to harassment charges,” “scholarships go to well‑connected insiders,” and “the board nixed expansion in favor of mobiles,” while Square’s criticisms focus more narrowly on individual school administrators and lack the same level of district/board corruption or organized favoritism claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more small-school,: A distinct subset of Circle reviews emphasize small class sizes, highly accessible counselors/teachers, proactive pastoral care and strong parent communication—e.g. “class sizes are no more than about 10,” “when I call the school they know who my daughter is,” and guidance checking in after a bereavement—features Square reviews do not similarly document and which point to a more personalized, family‑like school experience.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute student: This bucket groups reviews that describe frequent physical fights, organized social-media fighting, pervasive bullying/harassment (including racial and homophobic abuse), on‑campus drug use/overdose, sexual activity/assault incidents, and administrators/staff who fail to intervene (e.g., “last year there were a lot of fights,” “had to switch schools due to bullying,” “a person overdosed,” “he was beaten and nobody would help”). It captures both the unsafe incidents themselves and the school's ineffective mitigation/response as reported by reviewers.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more governance an: This bucket captures concrete management and policy failures: frequent principal turnover or absentee leaders, ad hoc rulemaking, suppression of incident referrals, nepotism/favoritism, billing/credit mistakes, PTA/legal disputes, and alleged manufacture of positive reviews (e.g., “principal is rarely there,” “he makes up his own rules,” “checks bounced…lawsuit filed,” “Most of the good reviews here are fake,” “they messed up all my credits”). These items describe how district/school governance and routine operations harm student outcomes or fairness.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more consistent te: This bucket groups reviews that describe small classes, teachers who volunteer extra help, long‑term mentoring, attentive counselors, strong teacher–parent communication and programs like parent nights or counseling outreach (e.g., “Teachers honestly care…can watch them more carefully,” “The teachers really do try to talk to parents,” “counselors educating parents at all times”). It covers concrete instructional/caring practices that produce measurable student social‑emotional and academic gains.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger and mor: This bucket includes explicit programmatic offerings and results: AP, IB, advanced STEM courses, dual enrollment/college credit, career/technical certifications (ROTC, Ag, carpentry), district outreach programs, remediation initiatives, and documented college matriculation or scholarships (e.g., “AP math, science, computer science,” “IB program is wonderful,” “graduated with an Electronics certification,” “students now attend UC/Cal Poly”). It bundles advanced-course breadth, vocational pathways, systematic college‑prep efforts, and their reported outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete faci: This bucket groups reports of physical and program resources—new or renovated school buildings, superior technology or device programs, on‑campus amenities (theaters, skate parks), extensive clubs/teams, and active facility upgrades—as well as notes about funding or underfunding when tied to program offerings (e.g., “a beautiful new High School,” “way more technologically advanced,” “skate park, HUGE theater,” “many opportunities to participate in after school activities,” alongside funding warnings like levies failing). It covers tangible school infrastructure, tech, and extracurricular capacity differences.
candidate_defs.circle entries report far worse student-: This bucket captures reviews that describe concrete safety failures and a hostile peer climate—frequent on- and off-campus fights, gang protection by staff, pervasive drug use/odors, violent assaults with bystander failure, and tolerated racial/homophobic slurs—claims repeatedly attributed to circle schools (e.g., “there is always a fight, EVERYDAY!”, “Drugs in this school huge issue!!!!”, “My Niece was brutally attacked … Noone helped her,” “Homophobia and Racism is common”) while square reviews do not report comparable severe safety incidents and often describe kinder, closer-knit student communities.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, more e: This bucket groups reviews that give programmatic evidence (IB adoption, AP/dual‑enrollment, academic centers, quantified test/scholarship metrics, graduates accepted to selective colleges, college credits earned) and claim concrete college-readiness outcomes—examples include circle notes like “we went through…to get the International Baccalaureate,” “Class of 2014 … received more than $5 million in scholarship offers,” and “students graduate with 20 hours of college credit,” whereas square reviews lack equivalent concrete program/outcome evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater teacher ac: This bucket covers evidence-heavy claims that circle schools are smaller/single-campus with one‑on‑one attention, proactive teacher outreach, rapid parent–teacher email responses, structured onboarding/mentorship, and sustained family ties (e.g., “kids get one on one support,” “Send the teacher an email and have a response by the end of the day,” “recently hired…everyone was helpful and encouraging”), contrasting with square reviews that more often describe students feeling lost, counselors/teachers who dismiss concerns, and weaker personalized follow‑up.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more authoritarian: This bucket groups reviews documenting concrete punitive policies and enforcement at circle schools—granular uniform policing, phone‑confiscation/fees, coercive testing/graduation enforcement, locked bathrooms and restricted parent drop‑offs, and tight surveillance (e.g., “if you are not wearing their school logo shirt you will miss an entire day,” “lock the students phones in a pouch…pay TWELVE dollars”), whereas square reviews depict either more lenient discipline or administrative indifference rather than systematic authoritarian policing.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more nepotism, fav: This bucket collects complaints that circle schools practice cronyism and inequitable treatment—hiring former students/relatives, protecting favored students from discipline or low grades, athletic/playing‑time favoritism, and race‑ or class‑based exclusion from advanced tracks (e.g., “The school hires ex-students… the 'good old boy' attitude continues,” “if you don't have the right last name then you don't get playing time…”, “most of my honors and AP classes were at least 75% white”), claims that square reviews do not make as a consistent pattern.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger/expanded: These reviews repeatedly name AP/IB/honors, dual‑enrollment and vocational pathways, quantifiable outcomes (scholarship totals, college matriculation, test scores) and school–college or hospital partnerships (e.g., IB scores, early concurrent enrollment with Cal Poly Pomona, AP/IB pathways, ‘$8M in scholarships’, college credit through St. John’s). Falling into this bucket means the school narrative centers on explicit program offerings and concrete postsecondary metrics that reviewers credit with preparing students for college and careers.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe and pe: Multiple circle reviews describe gang presence, daily fights, alcohol/drug/vape epidemics, systemic bullying, and tolerated racist/homophobic language (e.g., ‘Fights everyday,’ ‘Vapes are the craze,’ ‘you will hear racial slurs…a majority of the staff lets this all slide’). Content in this bucket documents unsafe student behavior and a weak or inconsistent safety response by staff or administration.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more institutional: Circle reviewers frequently allege staff/pastor favoritism, nepotism, administrators who threaten critics or ignore complaints, punitive discipline or expulsions tied to attendance/credits, and decisions protecting staff‑related students (e.g., ‘spots are saved for friends and family,’ ‘administrators that will threaten to sue you,’ ‘booted out…forced into homeschooling’). Items in this bucket highlight that the school’s problems are organizational and political—complaint processes, hiring/enrollment practices, and discipline are handled in ways reviewers call biased or punitive.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize athletics‑cente: Many circle reviews note a strong sports culture and sport-driven outcomes (football emphasis, D‑1 placements, sports scholarships) along with budget choices that favor athletics over classroom resources and evidence of overcrowding or lack of instructional materials (e.g., ‘spending so much money on the football team,’ ‘no textbooks but funded a football team,’ ‘overcrowded buses and 35+ class sizes’). Content in this bucket signals a visible mismatch in resource priorities—well‑funded athletics or facilities coexisting with shortages that impair teaching and learning.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent, c: Square reviews more often describe teachers who ‘genuinely care,’ accessible tutoring/after‑school help, reliable counselor and IEP supports, and proactive parent communication (e.g., ‘teachers are always willing to help,’ ‘went above and beyond…gets more personalized help,’ ‘IEP staff are really concerned’). Material in this bucket centers on responsive, individualized instructional and family‑facing practices that reviewers credit with supporting struggling students and fostering college readiness.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: This bucket captures reviews that describe pervasive on-campus safety failures (sexual assault, rampant bullying, drug use, racialized harassment), inadequate adult response, and victims blamed or ignored; examples include allegations of sexual assault and racial bias left unaddressed, students using drugs in bathrooms, and repeated reports that “if you are a person of color you will NOT feel safe here.” These accounts are distinct from facility or program complaints because they focus on student conduct, harm, and insufficient protective responses.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, named ad: This bucket covers reviews listing concrete curricular and co-curricular strengths (AP/IB, academies, ROTC, nationally ranked orchestra/theater, vocational and engineering pathways, dual‑credit/college credit totals) and documented college placements or scholarships (Newsweek rank, Ivy/arts conservatory acceptances), e.g., multiple circle reviews citing IB/AP breadth, orchestra national rankings, ROTC commissioning, or large scholarship totals. These items are about program availability and measurable student outcomes rather than teacher demeanor or building condition.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more consistentl: This bucket groups reviews that emphasize teachers/staff who go ‘above and beyond’ (named reading specialists, tutors, counselors who drive progress), mentorship and family‑like school culture, and proactive principal communication (podcasts, visible outreach), for instance reports of teachers helping struggling students to 90s and an accessible principal podcast. It is distinct from program breadth (above) because it focuses on staff behaviors, responsiveness, and student-level support rather than formal program existence.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more facility, ope: This bucket captures concrete operational problems: HVAC failures/overheated classrooms, pest and cleanliness complaints, overcrowded/mobile classrooms and lost transcripts, lunch shortages and no nurse, and inconsistent maintenance or recent renovations noted as uneven, e.g., accounts of 85°F classrooms, roaches/bedbugs, running out of lunches, and multi‑lunch schedules due to extreme enrollment. These are physical and process failures distinct from safety climate or curricular strength.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups reviews alleging structural unfairness and governance problems—‘who you know’ admissions, preferential treatment or grade inflation for athletes, nepotism/cliques, adversarial or litigious administrations, and inconsistent/punitive discipline systems (demerits, public humiliation), such as claims that football players get grades, teachers are told to alter grades, or parents sued the district for denied special‑education services. These governance and priority‑allocation complaints are separable from individual teacher helpfulness and from facility or safety issues.
candidate_defs.circle entries report far more severe st: This bucket captures concrete reports of safety and student‑on‑student harm: multiple circle reviews describe ongoing bullying, daily physical assaults, gang presence, repeated bomb/shot‑threats, widespread drug use, and reviewers linking bullying to clinical anxiety and depression; square reviews largely lack these claims or explicitly describe a safer, controlled environment (e.g., ‘there has been 4 fights in 3 years’ and competent incident responses).
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, more fo: This groups concrete programmatic evidence: circle reviews repeatedly cite specialized academies, magnet/IB/AP growth, dual‑enrollment and community‑college certification pathways, robust arts and band programs, and named college/athletic placements or scholarship outcomes; square reviews rarely list such structured program suites and instead mention limited advanced-class options or general extracurricular shortfalls.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Here reviewers point to tangible management failures — lost student records, mis-scheduled transcripts, ignored IEPs, arbitrary or vindictive discipline, administrators who ‘won’t answer’ parents, and district‑level political conflict — while square reviews contain fewer or contrasting examples of such systemic administrative breakdowns and often emphasize accessible/engaged leaders.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more explicit athl: This bucket groups repeated, concrete allegations that school resources and discipline are skewed toward sports — money spent on fields, athletes receiving special treatment (free lunches, lenient discipline), coach bullying/favoritism, and parent pressure around youth sports — patterns that are absent or far less prominent in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries exhibit greater variabili: Many circle reviews describe both ends of the staffing spectrum — teachers who provide one‑on‑one help, before/after support, and close small‑class attention alongside accounts of frequent turnover, uncertified instructors, grade inflation, and teachers who ‘don’t know how to teach’ — producing a wider, more polarized pattern than square’s generally more consistent teacher‑quality reports.
candidate_defs.square entries report more stable leader: This bucket captures reviews that portray square schools as having steadier, approachable principals and responsive counselors and office communication, whereas circle reviews more often report deficient or inconsistent administrative responsiveness. Illustrative square evidence: 'counselors are off the charts fantastic,' 'principal was willing to help,' and 'teachers were easily accessed by email' contrasted with circle complaints about unreturned emails and unavailable counselors.
candidate_defs.circle entries show greater variability: This bucket groups content where circle reviews supply conflicting accounts across cohorts/years or striking splits within the same school (e.g., elementary praised while middle/high criticized), signaling high temporal and experiential inconsistency that square reviews report far less. Examples include direct contradictions in circle reviews ('I went there over 10 years ago' vs 'I attended two months'), claims of long‑term decline ('not the same school it was 20 years ago'), and level‑by‑level contrasts (excellent elementary vs terrible middle/high).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers concrete, practical breakdowns attributed more often to circle schools—lost or altered student records that block graduation, mis‑scheduled classes and enrollment/transfer mismanagement, attendance/credit recording errors, counselor unavailability, and consistent failure to notify or respond to parents. Representative evidence: 'they had lost over half of her school records... she wasn't going to be able to walk,' 'teachers don't really take attendance... that's why I "missed" soo much school,' and repeated reports of unreturned parent emails and bungled transfer/enrollment processes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student misco: This bucket groups reviews describing worse student safety/behavior (frequent fights, drug/gang reports, bomb/shooting threats, sexual manipulation), plus systemic inequities—preferential treatment for athletes or connected families, pay‑to‑play barriers, racial/sexist/transphobic discrimination, and clique‑based exclusion—occurring more often in circle entries than in square. Examples include allegations of rampant bullying and death threats, athletic GPA leniency/'country club' treatment for athletes, race‑ and gender‑based mistreatment, and claims that 'the only way to get ahead is to be friends with teachers or administration.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced/: These reviews describe concrete curricular depth (many AP/Honors/IB options, multi-level courses, IMP/unique electives), dual‑enrollment and college credit opportunities, vocational/CTE pathways, and cited outcomes (college acceptances, scholarships, high graduation rates). Examples: reviewers noting ‘plenty of AP options,’ ‘seniors can finish freshman year of college,’ ‘student received a FULL RIDE to USC,’ and ‘100% graduation rate,’ contrasted with square entries that complain of denied opportunity and missing instruction.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe richer extracurr: Circle reviews routinely name broad, high‑quality co‑curricular offerings and structures (large club lists, competitive arts and music trips, JROTC, varsity teams, mentorship/onboarding programs, national arts/science recognitions) and high student participation. Illustrative evidence: ‘13 different sports, 19 clubs,’ ‘orchestra to Juilliard,’ ‘choral group accepted to Carnegie Hall,’ ‘welcome dinner and assigned upper‑class mentor,’ while square reviews either omit such programs or report uneven/weak extracurriculars.
candidate_defs.square entries report pervasive teacher: These reviews allege classroom-level failures: teachers who rely on heavy homework/self‑teaching, sit through conferences on their phones, provide minimal instruction (PowerPoints only), misgrade or mishandle records, or are widely seen as ineffective—resulting in low test/pass rates and students being ‘pushed through’ without learning. Examples include ‘teachers give countless homework expecting students to teach themselves,’ ‘played with his phone the WHOLE time,’ ‘not enough one‑on‑one attention,’ and ‘students fail Regents,’ contrasted with circle reviews that more often praise teacher accessibility and mentorship.
candidate_defs.square entries report hostile, unrespons: Square reviews more frequently describe enrollment obstruction, punitive or image‑protecting administration, nepotism/favoritism, poor communication, mishandled crises, and IEP/504 noncompliance—concrete governance breakdowns rather than isolated teacher complaints. Representative claims: ‘administration is horrible… don’t reveal mental illness,’ ‘prolonged re‑enrollment obstacles in 2021,’ ‘husbands and wives run the school,’ ‘IEP was overlooked,’ and ‘administration looks the other way to protect image,’ whereas circle reviews more often report engaged or student‑knowing administrators.
candidate_defs.square entries report poorer physical en: Square reviews more often document dilapidated or aging facilities, overcrowded classes, broken HVAC/unsanitary conditions, service cuts, and contested funding choices (program cuts, transportation loss, mandatory fees), or describe the district as underfunded. Examples: ‘classes are overcrowded… 35–42 students,’ ‘no air conditioning,’ ‘gross bathrooms,’ ‘cutting busing,’ and ‘taxes too high for low quality,’ while circle entries more frequently call out newer/beautiful campuses or dedicated facilities.
candidate_defs.circle entries report far more pervasive: This bucket captures reviews that describe routine fights, gang activity, widespread bullying, heavy drug use, sexual misconduct and ineffective incident response (e.g., “infested with gangs, drugs, and gang violence,” “weekly/daily fights,” stalking ignored, resource officer mishandling reports). Falling here means the reviewer emphasizes on‑campus and neighborhood safety breakdowns and school inaction; Square reviews do not make these pervasive safety claims and instead often describe safer, more orderly environments or isolated incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, formal: This groups reviews that name concrete, credentialed programs and outcomes (IB programs, on‑campus dual enrollment, AP stacks that yielded college credit, associate degrees, major scholarships and Ivy admits — e.g., IB diploma candidates, 'graduated with associate degrees', on‑campus dual enrollment with NWFSC). Inclusion means the school review documents structured college‑prep offerings and verifiable postsecondary results that Square reviews either do not mention or describe only as advising/AP possibilities without the same documented outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize a pronounced ex: This bucket contains reviews that highlight broad or highly resourced extracurricular programs (many sports, marching band, championships, town turnout for football), along with claims that athletics are prioritized or protect athletes (funding skewed to football, athlete favoritism, awards and recruiting). Falling here means the reviewer foregrounds active community sports/arts life and either celebration of championships or critiques that athletics receive disproportionate attention and resources; Square reviews rarely present that same combination of breadth, funding visibility, and institutional prioritization.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more administrativ: This bucket groups reviews pointing to governance problems and unfair enforcement — e.g., students kicked off rolls to boost graduation metrics, punitive dress/PDA enforcement, favoritism/nepotism (teacher children winning awards), teacher/administrator harassment or retaliation, lawsuits and billing disputes, and rude or unresponsive front‑office behavior. Inclusion means the reviewer links leadership decisions, policy abuse, or misconduct to harmed students or skewed outcomes; Square reviews generally do not allege this pattern at the same scale.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater extremes a: This bucket covers reviews that point to stark contrasts in material conditions and program partnerships — examples include reports of 1:1 MacBooks and new state‑of‑the‑art buildings, strong CTE/industry/college partnerships and therapy/special‑education teams, alongside other reviews of leaking hallways, broken toilets, moldy food, trailers/overcrowding, and chronic network outages. Falling here means the review emphasizes concrete infrastructure or resourcing realities (positive or negative) and external partnerships/CTE pathways; Square reviews are less likely to show this same range of extreme facility/resource evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: These reviews emphasize concrete program breadth and outcomes (AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, large AP selections, honors, documented college credits, scholarship and admission figures) that square reviews do not: examples include “graduating with 18 credits,” “$3.8 million in scholarships,” “100% graduation rate,” high AP/IB/AP pass‑rates and AP‑driven competitive cultures vs. Square’s lack of comparable outcome metrics or program lists.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more proactive,: Circle reviewers repeatedly cite one‑on‑one tutoring, before/after‑school help, remedial programs (e.g., GAAP, SMARTS nights), multiple college counselors and hands‑on vocational partnerships that improve individual students, while Square reviews more often report little teacher help, limited guidance or no follow‑through from staff.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more safety/discip: Many Circle reviews document pervasive bullying, theft/assault incidents, students leaving campus, inadequate anti‑bullying enforcement or staff participation in abuse, often tied to administrators who are described as unresponsive, protective of insiders, retaliatory, or opaque (examples: teachers or admins excusing bullying, principal firing dissenting staff, nepotistic hiring practices), a cluster less present in Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete reso: Circle reviews contain abundant, specific operational complaints—pest infestations, broken/septic systems, no textbooks/heat cuts, overcrowded campuses, parking/shuttle safety, weak Wi‑Fi or severely outdated machines—(even when some Circle reviews note modern 1:1 programs), whereas Square rarely documents such the same breadth of physical/infrastructure failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize tight‑knit comm: Circle reviewers frequently highlight small‑town or family‑first culture, mandatory religious/character programs, tuition/grant dynamics, magnet/STEM/arts academies, strong school spirit and external partnerships (hospital links, business advisors, college seminars, marching band/athletic championships), attributes and institutional missions that Square reviews do not foreground.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reviews that describe frequent on-campus violence, pervasive bullying/harassment (including racism, sexism, homophobia), visible drug use/dealing/overdoses, fights, and administrators failing to enforce discipline or protect victims (e.g., “drugs are everywhere… I’ve seen drug deals,” “nine boys… bullying me on Facebook… investigation,” “smell of marijuana in bathrooms,” repeated accounts of racial slurs and sexual misconduct). These accounts are about student behavior, safety incidents, and the school’s inability or unwillingness to respond — distinct from programmatic, facility, or teacher-support complaints.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader and strong: This bucket groups reviews that emphasize available rigorous courses and articulated career pathways and concrete outcomes — AP/IB, dual-credit, CTE/vo‑tech, expanded AP offerings, scholarship totals, and students matriculating without remediation (e.g., “Dual credit… a full range of college level and AP classes,” “graduated with 50 credits… associate degree,” “A lot of scholarship money… attend top schools”). These comments concern curriculum breadth, college-prep structure, and demonstrable college/career gains rather than day-to-day instruction or extracurricular life.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent te: This bucket captures reviews in which staff-level problems predominate for the square school: explicit allegations of teacher prejudice, misogynistic or uncaring teachers, weak instruction or underqualified staff, and chronic staffing gaps (e.g., “teachers are prejudice… some teachers are not very good,” “many teachers grossly underqualified,” “there are not enough people”). These claims are specifically about classroom instruction quality, bias by staff, and insufficient staffing rather than administrative governance or student-safety incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent admi: This bucket includes reviews alleging unprofessional or power-tripping leadership, slow or absent responses to parents, refusal of alumni/donations, nepotistic hiring, deliberate protection of problematic tenured staff, punitive financial/privilege-withholding policies, and operational chaos (e.g., “administration is unprofessional… get the run around,” “they refuse alumni gifts,” “teachers feel threatened… could lose their jobs,” “policy: miss a tuition payment and privileges withheld”). These are governance/operational failures distinct from classroom teaching or student behavior.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger community: This bucket covers reviews describing an embedded community character — active parent volunteers, alumni returning to tutor, explicit faith-based programming and daily spiritual mentorship, multigenerational legacies, and highly polarized local reputations (some glowing endorsements vs. damning accounts) (e.g., “teachers prayed with him daily,” “generational alumni rate is astounding,” “we were volunteer parents… Off to college both girls,” and juxtaposed extremes like “BEST school… ” vs “worst experience”). These items concern community composition, religious identity, parental/alumni involvement and polarized local reputation rather than internal operations, instruction, or safety.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe a small, family‑: These reviews highlight small class sizes, strong parent/alumni ties, and routine individualized attention (e.g., “small enough so your child isnt a number,” “student to teacher ratio…4th grader went from 28 to 9,” “teachers and staff really care…go over and beyond”), whereas square reviews more often report overcrowding, transient populations, or only sporadic teacher care.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student safet: Many circle reviews recount concrete safety crises and ineffective follow‑up (death threats from athletes, drug distribution on campus, repeated hazing and racial slurs, and administrators who ‘looked away’ or blamed victims), while square reviews rarely describe this level of persistent, unaddressed student safety threats.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize broader extracu: Circle reviewers repeatedly name wide elective and extracurricular offerings plus high athletic achievement, but also complain that athletes receive special treatment and funding (examples: ‘won more than 75 state titles,’ ‘sports get all the funding,’ ‘if you play football, the scholarship is in the bank’), whereas square reviews tend to call out fewer electives or praise specific academic/career programs instead.
