candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, named ad: Many circle reviews list AP/IB/magnet/dual‑enrollment and concrete college credits or grads (‘20 AP classes,’ ‘dual enrollment…16 semester hours,’ graduates succeeding at top universities), while square reviews more often describe mediocre preparation, remedial college courses, or lack of advanced offerings.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more operational: These circle reviews cite chronic resource problems (mold, outdated computers, no textbooks, budget inequity favoring athletics), high teacher turnover and nepotism, hostile administrative actions or legal escalations, and enrollment/placement mishandling — concrete operational and governance failures that appear far more often in circle than in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute safety,: This bucket captures reviewer claims that circle schools face daily fights, robberies, gang pressure, weapon finds and metal detectors, threats/active‑shooter concerns, pervasive bullying (including staff-on-student bullying) and drug problems — e.g., accounts of metal detectors and knives confiscated, students "pressed into gang activity, beaten, and robbed," frequent fights, and reports that staff do nothing — while square reviews more often describe a safe environment or active administrative intervention.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more administrat: This groups critiques about leadership politics, cronyism, optics-first priorities, selective rule enforcement for athletes or connected families, punitive law‑enforcement citations, misuse of students for advocacy, and clerical/gradebook/transfer failures — e.g., reviewers describing textbooks unrecorded then charged, nontransparent substance testing, SRO misdemeanor citations, "good ol' boy" selection processes, and rude/obstructive front‑office handling — contrasted with square entries that generally lack these clustered operational and governance failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more consistent te: This bucket contains reports that teachers at circle schools frequently go above and beyond (after‑school tutoring, daily grade monitoring, one‑on‑one catch‑up, turnaround stories), with examples like students pulled up from failing through targeted help and teachers who "went out of their way," whereas square reviews more often emphasize uncaring or inconsistent teacher/counselor responsiveness.
candidate_defs.circle entries depict stronger, broader: This groups evidence that circle schools offer more AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, magnet and CTE pathways, internships/partnerships, project‑based STEM, and explicit college‑placement metrics (Ivy/elite matriculations, scholarships) — e.g., mentions of IB, dual credit, issued laptops, internships at the Franklin Institute, and concrete matriculation statistics — while square reviews tend to report weaker AP preparation, fewer formal pathways, or less-documented college outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize an explicit fai: This bucket captures cultural and community features: frequent religious/chapel programming and exclusionary faith norms, strong small‑town/sisterhood identity, prominent athletics reputation and budget/discipline favoritism for athletes, and active parent clubs or district pride (e.g., daily prayer, campus ministry, "well recognized state wide" sports, or "great parent club"), whereas square reviews do not foreground organized faith culture and instead focus on arts/program specifics or describe eroding spirit.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, better‑d: These circle reviews repeatedly cite concrete advanced offerings (IB, AP, Honors, STEM/Scholars magnets, dual‑credit/dual‑diploma programs, CTE certifications) and named postsecondary results (college admits, scholarships, alumni degrees), e.g. mentions of IB programs, 'two diplomas', private pilot licensure, AP/dual‑enrollment, and explicit college matriculation/scholarship examples—while square reviews rarely provide comparable program inventories or measurable postsecondary outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent seve: Many circle reviews describe repeated fights, students sent to the ER/ICU, rampant bullying (including targeted harassment of LGBT/PoC/disabled students), and claims that incidents were covered up or not properly disciplined (e.g. 'sent 3 students to ICU', 'Bullying is brushed off for lgbt and poc students', 'They covered up and disregarded the safety of the students'), whereas square reviews seldom describe this level of violent incidents or systemic non‑enforcement.
candidate_defs.square entries describe poorer day‑to‑da: Square reviews more consistently report instructional failures such as teachers who 'rarely get anything across', classes without teachers, movies in class, teachers who don't grade work, and underpreparation for college; circle reviews include many examples of individualized, high‑quality instruction and teacher praise that contrast with square's repeated accounts of weak daily teaching practices.
candidate_defs.circle entries more often note concrete: Circle reviewers frequently report principals/superintendents who know students by name, recent leadership‑driven improvements, proactive parent communication, or explicit turnaround narratives (e.g. 'new Principal has changed the school', 'principal knows each of the kids by name', 'superintendent is amazing'), while square reviews more often attribute problems to district leadership or report less personalized administrative engagement.
candidate_defs.circle entries provide more concrete, sp: Circle reviews repeatedly supply operational/facility specifics such as overcrowding and meal shortages, unsanitary restrooms and health hazards, calls for new buildings, or positive notes about renovations and 1:1 computing/online tutoring (e.g. 'overcrowded... lunch shortages', 'roaches in the school', 'beautiful renovation', 'chromebook provided for each student'), whereas square reviews rarely include this level of concrete facilities or resourcing detail.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger advance: Square reviews more often report concrete college-preparatory offerings and outcomes (AP/IB/CET classes, transferable college credit, high SAT/ACT scores, students admitted to top colleges) while Circle reviews in the same comparisons complain of ‘few AP classes,’ limited language options, or declining rigor; examples: Square notes “fantastic AP classes” and a 2230 SAT/30 college credits, contrasted with Circle statements like “Few AP classes & only 11th & 12th grades.”
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: Many Circle reviews independently recount robust advanced coursework, dual‑enrollment, measurable score gains and clear postsecondary placement (multiple APs, 1:1 tech, summer ACT prep, students attending UCLA), whereas Square contains no comparable metrics in those instances; examples: Circle cites ‘many A.P. classes, extra-curricular classes and sports’ and reports graduates accepted to UCLA and other top colleges.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more staff/adminis: Circle reviews frequently allege nepotism, selective enforcement, missing student funds, high teacher turnover, unresponsive teachers/administrators, and concrete special‑education mistreatment (504/IEP refusals or archaic pull‑out practices), while Square reviews lack these system‑level accusations; examples include Circle claims that the school ‘runs on nepotism & favoritism,’ teachers refusing to work with a student with ASD, and administrators who ‘never really follow through.’
candidate_defs.square entries describe a safer, more su: Square reviews repeatedly portray a family‑like, cohesive student community with caring teachers and fewer reports of gangs, severe violence, or unresolved bullying; in contrast Circle reviews (in the same comparisons) report gang activity, daily assaults, kill‑lists, or tolerated bullying—e.g., Square: ‘treated like family’ and ‘very unproblematic,’ versus Circle: ‘haven for gang thugs,’ ‘kids are getting assaulted every single day.’
candidate_defs.circle entries report more visible extra: Circle reviews more often enumerate concrete extracurricular programs, well‑funded athletic facilities, mandatory/centralized sports, boarding/dormitory populations, or school technology initiatives (marching band, JROTC, state championships, Apple laptops, new auditoriums), whereas Square reviews rarely list this breadth of infrastructure; examples: Circle lists ‘new weight room/wrestling room,’ ‘world class athletic program,’ and school‑issued laptops, while Square’s comments focus on academics and a smaller set of clubs.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, more e: This bucket groups reviews that report concrete academic strength (AP/IB/Cambridge, Dual Enrollment, STEM/First Robotics, honors/tracked curricula), higher test/graduation metrics, and explicit college‑prep coaching — e.g., Circle cites '11 graduates with 4.0…college level advanced courses,' 'Dual Enrollment — four college classes completed,' 'AP/IB options,' and 'increase their CCRPI score by over 10 points,' while Square contains repeated claims of being under‑challenging or failing to prepare students for college.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups reviews describing frequent peer abuse (bullying, racist slurs, sexual harassment, threats), unsafe climate effects (anxiety, psychiatrists advising withdrawal), and administrators/staff failing to protect victims or enforcing discipline unevenly — e.g., Circle: 'Bullying is out of control,' 'death threats…nothing was done,' 'racial slurs…do not recommend going to this school if you are not white,' and administrators who 'took that student's side,' whereas Square typically lacks these systemic safety complaints and sometimes reports a safe, 'zero tolerance' environment.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more staff/admin: This bucket captures allegations that staff or leaders favor elites/athletes/wealthy families, exhibit religious or anti‑LGBT bias, practice nepotism or protect problem administrators/coaches, or act unprofessionally — e.g., Circle: 'teachers pick favorites…homophobe,' 'administration treats wealthier students differently,' 'How can coaches be reprimanded when administration is a coach?,' and 'superintendent blocking parent safety programs,' while Square rarely levels these specific claims of systemic favoritism or protected conflicts of interest.
candidate_defs.circle entries contain far more concrete: This bucket groups reviews that supply specific, tangible operational conditions or resource claims (no textbooks, 1:1 iPads, broken boilers/95°F rooms, late buses, inedible lunches, smartboards, metal detectors/alarms), e.g., Circle: 'School does not provide text books,' 'every student gets an ipad,' 'no working AC…rooms 95°F,' 'late busses, terrible lunch,' and '40 cameras to monitor 8 hallways,' whereas Square generally omits such detailed facility/operational diagnostics.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize broader, better: This bucket covers explicit program breadth, prominence and prioritization claims — strong band/state championships/JROTC/FFA/shop/First Robotics, frequent trips/competitions, or athletics being prioritized over academics — e.g., Circle: 'high school band one of the best in the state,' 'JROTC…almost half the school,' 'shop programs and fantastic FFA,' 'sports are the priority,' and 'First Robotics is the school's best extracurricular,' while Square mentions activities but lacks the same depth, scale, or claims of program dominance.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more developed, fo: These reviews describe concrete institutional AP/Honors/Dual‑Enrollment structures, block scheduling and on‑campus college courses (e.g., “opportunity to take 40+ college credits,” “Both kids entered AP & Honors in 9th grade,” “various AP and Dual Enrollment programs”), whereas square reviews rarely list formal advanced programs or such detailed college‑prep pathways.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: Circle reviews repeatedly cite extreme behavioral and safety incidents plus ineffective remediation — drug use, gangs, stabbing, high local suicide concerns, homophobic and identity‑based bullying and students “coming to school drunk and high,” often paired with claims that staff/administration failed to protect victims — while square reviews do not describe this scale or severity of unaddressed harm.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more polarized a: Many circle reports show the same school praised for specific exceptional teachers but also condemned for mass turnover, alleged unqualified instructors, and rapid loss of good staff (e.g., “named, effective teachers” vs. “the great teachers are being run out,” “most should not have any certification”), producing a wide teacher‑quality gulf not evident in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more systemic admi: Circle reviews document governance problems and punitive rules — nepotism, favoritism to athletes/transfers, revenue‑focused decisions, withholding regalia for unpaid fees, invasive searches, IEP threats, secrecy and unreturned parent calls (even escalation to the school board/AG) — distinguishing them from square reviews that seldom allege this constellation of systemic administrative misconduct.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader extracurri: Circle reviewers list a wide, concrete ecosystem of extracurriculars and career pathways (robust band/choir/theatre programs, theatre academy, strong music, JROTC prominence, state athletic titles, work‑study, vocational magnets and internships), whereas square reviews offer far fewer or narrower program inventories and rarely report comparable arts/CTE depth or competitive achievements.
candidate_defs.Circle entries describe stronger organiz: This bucket captures reviews that cite concrete curricular offerings and measurable college outcomes—AP/IB classes, dual‑enrollment/tuition‑paid college courses, STEM and career-technical shops, medical or magnet academies, and documented scholarship/college matriculation (e.g., 'AP/IB and college credits,' 'tuition paid concurrent classes,' 'earned full scholarships', 'state‑of‑the‑art STEM facilities'). These comments signal institutional program strength and explicit college/career pathways that reviewers say are present in the circle schools but absent or limited in the square schools.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups reviews describing repeated student violence, bullying left unaddressed, drug/gang activity, underage smoking, racial slurs, and general unsafe/chaotic campus climates (examples: '12 fights in first 3 months,' 'bullying is rampant,' 'bathroom for underage smokers,' 'students with criminal records'), i.e., recurring, concrete safety incidents and failed enforcement that reviewers attribute to the school environment in circle schools more often than in square schools.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more staff/adminis: This bucket covers allegations about leadership and governance problems—administrative turnover, cover‑ups of scandals, favoritism/nepotism toward athletes or donors, misprioritized spending (athletics/cosmetics over academics), and administrators placating parents or protecting staff (examples: 'covering up bad things,' 'athletes regarded highest even with D's and F's,' 'board of education are yes-men,' 'administration admitted recruiting students for funding'). These are concrete managerial or ethical failings of adults and systems that reviewers attribute more to circle schools.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more operational a: This bucket includes practical, day‑to‑day service breakdowns—unresponsive guidance counselors, retroactive GPA policy changes, lost report cards/directories, poor testing/proctoring logistics, lunch shortages/food safety issues, lack of credit‑recovery programs, parking/overcrowding and custodial shortages (examples: 'Guidance Counselor rarely answers emails,' 'retroactive 4.0 scale,' 'not enough food for last lunch period,' 'doors opened late for standardized test'). These operational failures affect families' ability to navigate academic requirements and are reported more often for circle schools.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more hands‑on teac: This bucket groups reviews that recount teachers and staff who proactively tutor, communicate with parents, provide emotional support, succeed with students with disabilities, or sustain long‑term teacher retention (examples: 'teachers stay after school to help,' 'tutoring during lunch and after school,' 'special education department is second to none,' 'teachers are very communicative with parents,' 'many teachers still teaching from years ago'). These concrete accounts of instructional engagement and family outreach appear more often in circle reviews compared with square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups raw terms where reviewers describe frequent bullying, day-to-day fights, drug use, weapons/threats, and routine student misconduct—often saying 'fights every day,' 'drugs running rampant,' 'students beat up teachers,' or 'constant bullying'—contrasted with square entries that either do not mention such pervasive safety problems or describe bullying as isolated/incidental.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more administrat: This captures reports of governance problems like revolving superintendents, dishonest/unresponsive principals, nepotism and athletic/donor favoritism, politicized hires, opaque athletic/discipline handbooks, and punishment applied inconsistently—e.g., 'administration lies,' 'favoritism toward jocks,' and 'BOE president will not return email'—whereas square reviews emphasize stable, responsive leaders and fewer governance/politics complaints.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader and more: This bucket covers mentions of many concrete programmatic strengths—AP breadth, CTE pathways (welding, culinary, engineering), competitive arts and nationally ranked sports, state championships, and measurable college-placement/test-score claims—such as 'lots of APs,' 'choral program is top notch,' or 'state champs,' while square entries tend to be less specific about program breadth or competitive outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries include more specific, do: This groups reviews that give concrete IEP/counseling details, both positive (named counselors and mentoring programs, vocational paid-work for special needs) and negative (missing accommodations, procedural violations, refusal of services), e.g., 'special education in this school is a joke,' 'Ms. Nemeth and the team of counsellors are great,' and 'they collect little data,' whereas square reviews largely omit detailed special-education or counseling accounts.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete faci: This bucket groups evidence about physical capacity and operational choices—overcrowded halls and lunches, scheduling/block-schedule issues, misplaced capital spending (stadiums/TVs vs textbooks/security cameras), tuition or budget strain, food/facility deterioration, and renovation projects—e.g., 'hallways packed,' 'built a multi-million dollar football stadium,' 'scheduling is a nightmare,' and 'hard, bone-like substances in the meat'—details less frequently found in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries document broader, special: These reviews highlight structural academic breadth and measurable postsecondary results at circle schools (IB and dual‑language programs, expanded AP, vocational certifications like CDL, college credits, and cited graduation/college-acceptance statistics), e.g. “IB classes available,” “Great Schools shows Casa's graduation rate at 98%,” and “I got my CDL there,” while square reviews lack comparable program breadth or concrete college/career metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe richer, better‑r: Circle reviews repeatedly praise organized extracurricular strength and school spirit—nationally recognized music/theatre, competitive sports, travel and mentoring programs, and coach-led academic oversight—(examples: “#2 in the state for their music program,” “theatre department Mrs. Longshore is simply the best,” “coaches make sure students stay on top of grades”), whereas square entries emphasize academics/administration and do not report that same depth of arts/athletics prominence.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent, sev: Many circle reviews recount ongoing fights, vaping/drug incidents, racial/transphobic harassment, staff‑inflicted bullying or victim‑blaming, and claims that complaints are ignored or mishandled (examples: “bullies run the school,” “racially-motivated speech quite often,” “misgendering and deadnaming on a regular basis,” and repeated reports of fights/lockdowns), while square reviews rarely describe this level of systemic safety or identity‑based abuse.
candidate_defs.square entries report more chronic instr: Square reviews more often accuse the school of teachers who 'do not teach,' frequent teacher unpreparedness or turnover, punitive grading/policy enforcement, and poor parent communication (examples: “teachers do not teach and need to communicate better,” “staff leaves yearly,” and reports of students being withdrawn/denied credit), whereas circle reviews more commonly describe sustained instructional support and teacher availability.
candidate_defs.circle entries exhibit greater internal: Circle reviews contain highly polarized, co‑existing patterns—small, family‑like communities and very personal staff support alongside entrenched favoritism/nepotism, stark facility/resource extremes (privileged extracurricular facilities vs. peeling paint/ASB), and sharp changes over time or across majors (examples: 'small enough that everyone knows one another,' 'Good school if you're rich…', and both 'VERY privileged in curricular activities' and 'building is falling down'), while square entries present a more uniform, consistent set of problems or strengths.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe far worse studen: This bucket groups reviews where circle schools report acute safety breakdowns (riots, lockdowns, fights, guns, pepper‑spray), sustained bullying, racial/homophobic harassment, or staff tolerance of extremist behavior and where administrators fail to protect victims (e.g., victims moved to independent study or told to leave); Square reviews do not report comparable systemic violence or tolerated hate speech.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger academi: This captures reviews that highlight circle schools’ concrete curricular strength (AP/IB/honors breadth, specialized academies, dual‑enrollment), high test percentiles, National Merit/major scholarships and explicit college matriculation examples (e.g., named universities and scholarships), whereas square reviews lack the same volume of measurable advanced-course offerings and postsecondary outcome evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater teacher/co: This groups claims that circle schools provide consistent one‑on‑one teacher time, proactive counseling (scholarship/college outreach), after‑school/lunch help and small‑class personalization, with reviewers citing teachers who 'stay late', meet during breaks, and offer intensive IB/AP support; square reviews more often describe uneven or less available classroom help.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more administrat: This bucket covers reports of leadership shielding staff, nepotistic athletic hires, donor or donor‑based favoritism, ignored parental complaints, withheld records/grades for unpaid fees, mishandled IEPs or credit transfers, and alleged suppression of negative reviews — problems that circle reviewers raise repeatedly and that are more specific/structural than the briefer administrative complaints in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more chronic facil: This captures concrete infrastructure and resourcing problems described in circle reviews (filthy or dilapidated buildings, poor plumbing, outdated textbooks/computers, trailer classrooms, overcrowded halls, missing athletic fields, mandatory fees), plus patterns where athletics are prioritized over arts or electives are eliminated; square reviews do not show the same density of these material/operational failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews emphasize concrete program offerings and outcomes—abundant AP/IB/Honors, STEM magnets, dual‑enrollment/college‑in‑high‑school credit, CTE pathways, thriving band/ROTC/athletics, and large scholarship/graduation statistics (examples: 'abundance of advanced placement classes', 'over 60 free college hours', '85 seniors won $7.5 million in scholarships', 'marching band of 60–90', 'aviation magnet draws out‑of‑state families'). They contrast with square entries that rarely cite equivalent program depth, measurable outcomes, or the same level of extracurricular participation and external demand.
candidate_defs.circle entries report worse student safe: Many circle reviews document concrete safety and behavior problems (daily fights, food‑throwing, drug busts and hospitalizations, reported sexual assaults) plus either tolerant or highly punitive/inconsistent discipline regimes ('Several sexual assaults within the school with no action', 'two drug busts… one student going to the hospital', 'food fights like once per day', 'zero amount of freedom' with demerits and suspensions). Those square reviews do not portray the same combination of frequent serious incidents and either dismissive or uneven enforcement.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more staff unprofe: Circle reviewers repeatedly allege unqualified or unprofessional staff, explicit favoritism (especially toward athletes/locals), hostile staff behavior, and unstable staffing ('very unprofessional', 'hire anybody with the slightest degree', 'if you're not an athlete you don't get respected', 'teachers never stay longer than 3 years', 'teacher told me I was going to Hell'). Square reviews, by comparison, more often highlight consistently outstanding or engaged teachers and do not aggregate the same frequency of hiring, favoritism or mid‑year departure allegations.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe greater facility: Circle reviews include detailed infrastructure and resource deficits—mold/roaches/ceiling tiles, class sizes of 40+, daily bus crowding, insufficient event seating/restrooms, lack of textbooks, and explicit local underfunding or contested spending decisions ('riddled with roaches and rats', 'class with 40+ students', 'Everyday there are multiple kids standing [on the bus]', 'the students have no textbooks', 'spends below the state average per special education student'). Square entries lack this consistent pattern of material decay and crowding.
candidate_defs.circle entries report poorer student sup: Multiple circle reviews describe failures to follow IEPs, absent or ineffective counseling and mental‑health supports, discrimination/warehousing of special‑needs students, and weak onboarding for transfers ('They don't do anything to help struggling students, don't follow IEPs', 'counseling is lacking', 'If you have a child with autism DO NOT enroll', 'very little effort is given to helping students adjust'). Square reviews generally do not contain the same cluster of program‑level special‑education noncompliance and counseling breakdowns.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: This bucket captures claims about concrete academic programs and measurable postsecondary results — e.g., circle reviews cite paid dual‑credit hours, many AP/IB offerings, higher ACT scores, scholarship/full‑ride examples, and statements like “top AP school” or “everyone goes to college,” while square reviews lack comparable concrete credit/test metrics and often report mixed or pass‑oriented instruction.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: This groups descriptions of campus safety and student conduct problems and their consequences — e.g., circle excerpts include assault in front of security, pervasive bullying (including bullying of neurodivergent students), unresolved drug/vaping issues, suicidal ideation tied to school experience, expulsions for complaints, and reports of chronic truancy; square reviews generally do not document this level of acute safety or mental‑health crisis.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more administrat: This bucket covers systemic personnel/ethics problems reported by reviewers — examples include named nepotistic relationships (assistant superintendent married to special‑ed coordinator), coach/staff favoritism in athletics and arts, allegations of teachers in intimate relationships with students, deliberate favoritism based on wealth/family name, and leadership behavior that belittles or forces staff turnover; square reviews rarely make these specific ethics/nepotism charges.
candidate_defs.circle entries more often portray a smal: This groups structural and community characteristics — circle reviews frequently describe magnet/admissions requirements, small enrollment and low student:teacher ratios, named beloved teachers and one‑on‑one attention, tight school spirit and multigenerational alumni loyalty, whereas square reviews more often describe larger comprehensive schools without the same intimacy or selection.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more operational,: This bucket captures logistics, tech rollouts, scheduling, communication and resource allocation issues — e.g., circle reviewers note 1:1 iPad rollouts with no instructional plan, internet‑only report cards/newsletters that block access, block‑schedule complaints, transportation/pickup and tardy lockout failures, fundraising/tuition pressure and money skewed to athletics or facilities; square reviews seldom describe this particular cluster of operational/tech/policy failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader/stronger a: This bucket groups differences where circle reviews describe concrete program breadth and rigor — many AP/IB offerings, dual‑credit partnerships, specialized academies (e.g., engineering/CTA/Enviro/Academies), SAT prep and measurable college matriculation/Ivy‑level wins — while square reviews lack or portray fewer of these formal advanced pathways (examples: “many AP classes,” “partnership with Ivy Tech,” “students accepted to Ivy League” vs. square’s limited AP offerings or blocked acceleration).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive bul: This bucket collects safety/discipline reports where circle reviewers recount active bullying, sexual harassment, drug offers (even in restrooms), suicides, external intruder/violent incidents and administration that punishes victims or fails to intervene (e.g., “The bully's run this school!!!”, restroom drug offers with admin aware, multiple suicides), whereas square reviews either omit pervasive safety problems or describe them as isolated or better‑managed.
candidate_defs.circle entries report a stronger familyl: Here circle reviews emphasize close-knit small‑school identity, traditions/mascot apparel, sustained multigenerational enrollment, active parent organizations, strong alumni endorsement, and individualized teacher‑student relationships or regular after‑school tutoring (examples: “jacket pride,” “teachers and staff know everyone’s name,” active parent association), while square reviews generally describe a larger, less intimate environment with less multi‑generational community bonding.
candidate_defs.square entries report better facility co: This bucket captures facility/resource contrasts where square reviewers praise cleaner, newer or better‑maintained campuses and fewer space problems, while circle reviewers more often recount dirty/overcrowded buildings, outdated textbooks/technology, accessibility gaps and deferred maintenance (examples: square: “nice and clean environment,” vs. circle: “school is dirty…food splatters,” “WAY too crowded,” torn/old books).
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent te: This groups differences in staff/leadership where square reviews frequently describe effective, responsive teachers, engaged principals, lower turnover and reliable counseling/college guidance, whereas circle reviews more often allege tenure problems, high turnover, unprofessional conduct, poor training or administrative dysfunction that harms instruction (examples: square: “Most teachers are really great,” vs. circle: “Tenured teachers do whatever they want,” “teachers quit left and right,” slow/poor college counseling).
candidate_defs.circle entries document stronger advance: This bucket groups reviews that report concrete academic offerings and outcomes—AP/ECE/dual‑enrollment, IB or High‑Tech credit acceleration, named AP/STEM teachers, high AP participation/rankings, exit‑exam pass rates, scholarship awards and alumni college completion—which appear in circle reviews far more than in square (examples: “more than 25 AP courses…Dual Enrollment,” “Every year all of our Seniors pass the EXIT EXAM,” and alumni with masters/PhD or Hope scholarships). A school falls here if reviewers point to structural, programmatic college‑prep resources or documented student success metrics rather than only impressions of quality.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reviews describing recurring violence, bullying, gang activity, fights, weapons, assaults on students, routine lockdowns/metal detectors, and accounts that discipline or administrative follow‑through is inadequate (examples: “bullies ripped off his clothes… nothing has yet been done,” “fights every week,” “gangs, violence,” and reports of lockdowns/metal detectors). A review is in this group when it details tangible safety incidents or routine behavioral disruption plus failures or delays in corrective action.
candidate_defs.circle entries highlight broader, higher: This bucket groups reviews that emphasize extracurricular breadth and prestige—marching band traditions and championships, extensive clubs/CTE/robotics, large sports complexes—and also call out athletics’ institutional priority, booster fundraising pressures, or booster/athletics crowding out other programs (examples: “3‑time national championship winning band,” “sports complex is amazing,” “they are so focused on the athletic departments… boosters stealing money,” and scheduling conflicts displacing band). Content belongs here when it centers on extracurricular program scale, prominence, or resource/prioritization tensions tied to boosters and athletics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete oper: This bucket covers reviews documenting tangible infrastructure or instructional‑resource problems—no/old textbooks, 'Stone Age' curriculum, lack of AC, cockroaches, overcrowded classrooms, food safety, unmanaged student parking and traffic risks—often paired with mentions of renovation plans or funding shortfalls and staff paying out‑of‑pocket (examples: “lacks textbooks and reliable resources,” “the building is overcrowded…in desperate need of AC,” “cockroaches and worms,” and “undergoing renovation but lacks funding”). Include reviews that focus on physical or resourcing constraints, aging facilities, or technology/curriculum obsolescence rather than interpersonal or policy problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries reveal more staff/adminis: This bucket groups reviews that describe biased decision‑making and unprofessional staff practices—counselor favoritism, hiring nepotism, staff stereotyping/gossip, mismanaged records/billing, grade inflation or deliberate failing for revenue, discriminatory treatment of LGBTQ or nonconforming students, and high teacher turnover/unreliable substitutes (examples: “guidance counselor was only helpful to those she favored,” “principle had her sister‑in‑law…they favor any child that has a parent staff member,” “teachers give answer to final exams,” and “at LEAST two different teachers/long term substitutes”). Use this bucket for evidence of systematic personnel behavior or administrative processes that privilege some students, undermine fairness, or produce unstable staffing/communication.
candidate_defs.circle entries contain more concrete aca: These reviews list specific programs, courses and measurable outcomes (e.g., orchestra, MHSA/MYSO, pre‑calculus and AP calculus, TRANSTEM/TRANSTECH, aviation camps and industry visits, dual‑enrollment/Eastern University credits, drama club/choir) and even claim regular scholarship awards—details that Square reviews generally omit or describe only generically (e.g., “after school clubs”).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviews repeatedly cite operational failures and inequity at the administrative/district level—broken event/website coordination, principals unaware of events, intimidation of parents, hardship/enrollment favoritism (athletes/insider ties), and explicit blame of the board/superintendent—issues Square reviews do not raise or contradict with praise for the principal.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more staff indif: Square reviews contain multiple accounts of teachers/staff not caring or behaving discriminatorily (e.g., “Most of the staff do not care,” accusations of homophobic/Islamophobic teachers, students not being heard), contrasted in the corpus by Circle reviews that emphasize caring, hands‑on teachers who run clubs and tutoring.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: Several Circle reviews allege pervasive, high‑severity safety problems—kids with guns, daily fights, tolerated bullying, racial slurs in class, disruptive classrooms and a failing special‑needs program—claims that are either absent or much less frequent in Square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete oper: Circle reviews give concrete facts and complaints about money and facilities—tuition and lunch costs, ‘plastic’ food, explicitly outdated buildings, large athletic spending with poor results, single‑sex/male orientation and claims of no diversity—details Square reviews generally do not provide.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, broader: This bucket captures reviews that describe concrete curricular breadth and postsecondary results in circle schools—many circle entries list AP/IB/dual-enrollment offerings, predict or document college credit accumulation (e.g., “over 40 hours of college credit,” AP/dual credit with Arkansas State, IB program), and alumni college success (students at UNC Chapel Hill, Appalachian State). It groups any evidence of explicit advanced-course availability, early-acceleration opportunities, and measurable college placement that circle reviewers emphasize relative to square.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize higher-profile: This bucket groups instances where circle reviews highlight prominent, competitive extracurricular life—state/national championships, standout band/theater/robotics teams, extensive sports success (multiple state titles, large FFA success), or strong arts programming—i.e., program visibility, competitive wins, and broad extracurricular participation that circle reviewers call out more than square reviewers.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket covers concrete safety and climate problems described in circle reviews: frequent fights, gang activity, organized violent threats (kill lists, bomb threats), rampant vaping/smoking, cyberbullying, students filmed in restrooms, and claims that staff fail to control or meaningfully respond (e.g., 'bullying is out of control,' 'fights almost every day'). It groups evidence of unsafe student conduct and weak behavior enforcement inside classrooms and common areas that circle reviewers report more often than square.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more competent,: This bucket captures reviews that credit square schools with functioning leadership and institutional procedures—examples include active security protocols and guards checking IDs, competent incident handling (a bomb scare handled well), friendly/main-office staff, and administrators praised for responsiveness—contrasted with circle reviewers who report unresponsive or politicized governance, arbitrary or punitive discipline, secrecy, high leadership turnover, and administrative favoritism.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater operationa: This bucket groups concrete, day‑to‑day operational problems emphasized by circle reviewers: extreme overcrowding (40+ students in classes, gym classes >100), parking/traffic and open-campus logistics, building disrepair or cleanliness failures ('falling down', janitorial neglect), device/network/textbook access problems (unused iPads, network outages), PE/program capacity limits and busing/extreme‑weather failures. These are capacity, maintenance, and infrastructure issues circle reviews describe more often than square.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, more c: This bucket captures reports of classroom-level adult responsiveness and mentorship (teachers who 'stay after and help,' named supportive counselors like Bill Giles, long‑running advisor relationships, and individualized college counseling) that appear frequently in circle reviews but are contrasted with square reviews describing 'hit‑or‑miss' or disengaged teachers and ineffective guidance staff. Falling into this bucket means reviewers emphasize proactive, sustained teacher/counselor time, personal mentorship, and tangible help (tutoring, weekend AP workshops, one‑on‑one advising) as a defining feature of the school experience.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more administrat: This groups accounts where reviewers emphasize leadership and office failures (principals and counselors who 'do not return phone calls,' 'are rude or disconnected,' or whose offices respond negligently), selective/enforced favoritism, threats/harassment by administrators, and inconsistent discipline; these problems are much more commonly attributed to square schools in the data. Content belongs here when reviews highlight poor communication from the front office, bureaucratic neglect, administrative intimidation/favoritism, or a lack of coherent top‑down improvement strategy as central operational problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more extensive pro: This bucket covers reviews that emphasize abundant advanced coursework, IB/AP offerings, dual‑enrollment/AA attainment, National Merit and scholarship outcomes, award‑winning arts/STEM teams (FBLA, First Robotics, state competitions), and clear college‑prep infrastructure (college centers, measurable readiness metrics)—all repeatedly stressed in circle reviews and less often in square. Reviews fall here when the school is described by concrete program counts, competitive extracurriculars, or demonstrable postsecondary outcomes as a primary strength.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute facilit: This bucket groups concrete, service‑level complaints that reviewers tie to the school’s physical capacity and daily operations—for example classrooms of 35–42 students, 'XP' machines and heavily locked laptops, locked/unsanitary bathrooms, food shortages at lunch, hazardous bus incidents, and odd/ineffective schedules or night‑school requirements—items that are disproportionately reported in circle entries. Material fits here when the review details tangible infrastructure, maintenance, technology, transportation, cafeteria, or scheduling breakdowns that materially affect student experience.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe a more problemat: This bucket captures reports of on‑campus violence and safety breakdowns—explicit weekly physical fights, 'bullying is rampant,' gang presence, repeated bomb threats, on‑site probationers, pervasive smoking/drugs, and academic pressure linked to panic attacks or clinical‑depression risk—claims that appear repeatedly in circle reviews. Reviews belong here when the core concern is student behavior, peer toxicity, or documented safety/mental‑health incidents that undermine wellbeing and learning.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger/broader: These reviews emphasize concrete academic structures and measurable postsecondary results—IB/Academic Centers/AP breadth, dual‑credit and early‑college partnerships, vocational/shop scheduling, documented AP/IB scores, large scholarship totals and named college matriculations (e.g., IB score averages, $13.8M/$16M scholarship classes, students going to Penn State/Howard/Georgetown)—whereas square reviews typically mention only pockets of rigor or single AP successes without systemwide metrics or formal career/dual‑credit pathways.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more extensive, hi: Circle reviews repeatedly list many specialized extracurriculars and team achievements—state championships, long playoff streaks, large marching band traditions, multiple theatre spaces, professional‑level athletic facilities and visible fundraising (e.g., billboards for a new football field)—and also call out athletics‑driven funding/prioritization; square reviews by contrast give fewer program‑level achievements and more limited extracurricular descriptions.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Circle reviewers describe ongoing bullying, frequent fights, a growing drug problem, staff protection of bullies, intrusive searches/phone confiscations, retaliatory punishments and authoritarian measures (new gate, strict attendance rules, false accusations), painting a sustained safety/discipline climate; square entries tend to describe isolated incidents or administrative attempts to manage behavior rather than this pattern of pervasive misconduct combined with punitive/cover‑up responses.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize greater small‑s: Circle reviews frequently highlight small class sizes, highly accessible teachers and coaches, individualized interventions (tutoring, learning‑disability success stories), strong parent volunteerism and enduring alumni ties—specific, person‑level mentorship and hands‑on support that reviewers credit with student turnarounds—while square reviews seldom emphasize this degree of personalized, small‑school attention.
candidate_defs.circle entries raise more concrete admin: Many circle reviews call out biased office behavior, favoritism/nepotism, administrators protecting staff or hiding problems, superintendents blocking safety programs, chronic counselor non‑response and disputed funding priorities (staff paying out‑of‑pocket, wasted systems), requests for district investigations or leadership replacement—whereas square reviews focus more on programmatic complaints or individual administrator style rather than repeated allegations of governance misconduct and cover‑ups.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student-safet: This bucket groups reviews where circle schools describe frequent physical incidents (fights, thefts, mass brawls, drug incidents, vandalism) and reports that discipline or safety responses are ineffective, punitive in extremes, or inconsistently applied (e.g., 17 fights in one day; repeated fire-alarm pulling; drug busts and hospitalizations; administrators who fail to investigate bullying or mishandle self-harm). Square entries lack comparable reports of routine violence or documented failure-to-protect responses, so this distinction captures prevalence + response failures together.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced-: This bucket groups reviews that attribute concrete academic strength to circle schools—broader AP/IB/dual-enrollment offerings, magnet/21st-century career strands, formal college partnerships and test-prep, and cited alumni/metric success (AP participation rankings, ACT averages, high college-acceptance stories, dual-enrollment, free summer ACT prep). Square reviews generally do not document the same breadth of institutional pathways or measurable postsecondary outcomes, making this a program-and-outcome contrast.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more staff and lea: This bucket captures reviews alleging administrative/teacher problems at circle schools—rudeness, dishonesty, tenure-protected poor performers, blatant favoritism or nepotism, high teacher turnover and burnout, and parents ignored or intimidated by staff (e.g., administrators 'lied to my face,' staff hires tied to family, many teachers leaving and warning parents). Square reviews do not make comparable systemic misconduct or nepotism claims, so this groups governance/HR/professionalism failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater facility,: This bucket covers concrete infrastructure and resourcing problems emphasized in circle reviews—massive overcrowding and hallway congestion, locked/insufficient restrooms, malfunctioning Chromebooks/poor filters, outdated textbooks, withheld outlets or lab space, required laptop/family fees, and enrollment/lottery mismanagement. Square reviews typically do not document the same degree of space/technology/funding shortfalls.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more special-educa: This bucket groups reviews describing limited inclusion models, archaic pull-out special-ed practices, overworked special-education staff, insufficient autism/IEP training, counselors who impede services, and explicit denials or discouragement of accommodations. Square entries do not emphasize these targeted special-education failures, so this bucket isolates inclusion/service capacity problems distinct from general staff or academic-program critiques.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger measura: These reviews report concrete program and outcome evidence in circle: abundant AP/Honors and IB mentions, selective admission language, dual‑credit/CTE pathways, and measurable placements (e.g., '99–100% college placement,' Ivy League and National Merit examples, many AP scores), whereas square reviews lack comparable advanced‑course breadth or outcome metrics and often say the school 'does not prepare ANYONE for college' or has limited AP options.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student safet: Circle reviewers repeatedly cite fights, assaults, gang/drug problems, sexual misconduct, chronic bullying and property destruction and describe weak or punitive administrative responses (e.g., 'had to hire a lawyer,' 'bullies receive little consequences,' police presence ineffective), while square entries generally do not describe pervasive violence or failed responses.
candidate_defs.circle entries indicate stronger institu: Multiple circle reviews describe athletics receiving preferential treatment—facility investment and event closures, athlete immunity from discipline, scheduling/funding bias against arts and non‑athletes, and explicit statements that 'sports are the priority'—whereas square reviews do not portray athletics as the dominant institutional priority to the same degree.
candidate_defs.circle entries document greater communit: Circle reviews emphasize active PTAs, town or municipal support for projects, business‑academy partnerships, powerful alumni networks and multi‑generational enrollment ('my kids graduated and now my grandkids go'), while square reviews rarely report comparable sustained local partnerships, multigenerational ties, or formal advisory‑board collaborations.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more systemic fail: Circle reviewers give concrete examples of IEP noncompliance, denied accommodations, unresponsive or rude counselors (e.g., '3 minutes' meetings), students self‑harming, and lack of monitoring for neurodivergent students, whereas square reviews do not document this cluster of special‑education and mental‑health service failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger academi: This bucket captures reviews that attribute concrete academic strengths to circle schools—explicit mentions of IB diplomas, AP/honors offerings, dual‑enrollment/college credit, STEM/CTA academies, high ACT scores and scholarship totals, and alumni college/career outcomes (e.g., “IB program is really taking off,” “both my kids got above a 31 on the ACT,” “offers dual enrollment,” “named an A+ School of Excellence”). It groups evidence of course availability, programmatic pathways, and observable postsecondary success that circle reviewers emphasize more often than square reviewers.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups reviews describing recurring student misconduct and acute safety incidents at circle schools—systemic bullying, racial/sexual‑orientation harassment, on‑campus drug use, riots/lockdowns/pepper‑spray events, sexual harassment, and claims that staff or security ignored or mishandled these incidents (examples: “bullying is rampant,” “kids doing drugs in the bathroom,” “riot… peppersprayed,” “they did nothing about the bullying,” “racial slurs in the hallways”). These concrete safety and victim‑response failures appear far more frequently in circle reviews than in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket collects reviewer accounts of personnel and leadership problems at circle schools: unreturned calls and bureaucratic delays, blocking transfers, selective discipline or favoritism/nepotism, coercive demands on staff, recordkeeping and grading errors, and staff/administrative abusiveness (e.g., “they won’t let me switch my kid,” “good ol’ boy hiring,” “principal is never here,” “administration constantly ignores and laughs off real issues”). These reports focus on how adults and systems operate (or fail to), and they are disproportionately associated with circle entries versus square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more tangible faci: This bucket groups concrete, operational facility and resourcing complaints in circle reviews: pest infestations and unsanitary bathrooms, broken HVAC/temperature problems, late buses, inedible or terrible lunch service, overcrowded classrooms, outdated textbooks, or lack of athletic fields (examples: “highly infested with rats and roaches,” “no air conditioning…windows open,” “late buses, terrible lunch,” “teacher to student ratio 24-28:1,” “no athletic fields at all”). These material and logistical deficits show up more often in circle than in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries depict stronger local com: This bucket groups reviews that emphasize community life and social structure around circle schools—visible school spirit, long‑standing alumni traditions, heavy parental/community involvement, successful athletics and extracurriculars, faith/Catholic identity, tuition/assistance dynamics, and wealth/status‑based cliques or donor influence (examples: “annual canned food drive…won 75 state titles,” “family atmosphere,” “Catholic identity,” “many families pay tuition,” “the rich run the school,” “spirit week and Pumpkin walk”). These community/extracurricular and socioeconomic phenomena are described more often (and in richer detail) for circle entries than for square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive saf: This bucket captures reviews that describe frequent peer violence, ongoing bullying, drug offers, stalking, sexual assault, teacher/staff harassment or assault, and school inaction (e.g., “kids get followed after school & beaten bloody,” “There is a SEVERE drug problem… Teachers are told NOT to inform parents…,” “When a stalker was reported, nothing was done,” “This School has a teacher … who assaulted a student. They refuse to take disciplinary action”), contrasted with square reviews that emphasize friendlier students and safer climates.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, better‑d: This bucket groups reviews that cite concrete program offerings and outcomes—AP/accelerated courses, magnet/communications internships, CTE/certification wins, high scholarship totals and named alumni successes (e.g., “AOC… internships with professional radio stations,” “85 seniors won $7.5 million in scholarships,” “one passed her state exam in cosmetology and was accepted to a 4‑yr university”)—while square reviews generally mention program offerings without the same specific outcome metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more consistent, i: Reviews in this bucket describe named teachers who ‘go above and beyond,’ regular tutoring/after‑school help, low student‑teacher ratios, Talent Development/virtual accommodations and concrete counseling follow‑through (e.g., “Mrs. Furlong,” “teachers provide tutoring as needed,” “Talent Development program… one‑on‑one help,” “virtual school… teachers want the best for the student”), whereas square reviews more often describe uneven or insufficient one‑on‑one support.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater administra: This bucket covers structural and leadership complaints such as rapid principal turnover, perceived hiring favoritism or religion‑based bias, censorship, budget‑driven program cuts, and contested spending/administration (e.g., “four principals in the first year,” “tends to favor those who are members of the Church of Christ as employees,” “Due to state budget cuts, a lot of the programs are suffering,” “Superintendent … incompetent”), while square reviews less frequently allege this pattern.
candidate_defs.square entries report a more consistentl: This bucket captures square reviews that emphasize approachable administration and counselors, active parent communication, broad arts/music/club offerings and a generally safe, supportive environment (e.g., “The students on campus are really nice… Teachers at Garey are really cool,” “The counselors are always there to help you,” “very active concert and marching band program,” “administration communicates through weekly phone calls and emails”), in contrast to circle reviews that more often document safety, admin or communication failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced-: These reviews describe circle schools offering IB/AP/honors pathways, many advanced courses, visible AP/IB exam/college-credit outcomes and scholarships (e.g., “more than twenty AP and honors courses,” “IB Diploma … major college scholarships”), and concrete college‑readiness supports—claims that are far more frequent in circle entries than in square entries, which more often describe uneven preparation or isolated AP anecdotes rather than systemwide advanced-program strength.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more consistent, c: Circle reviewers repeatedly praise devoted, approachable teachers and routine extra help (e.g., “teachers really do care… many go the extra mile,” “EVERY teacher has after school extra help hours”), whereas square reviewers more often describe teacher burnout, poor instruction, staff who 'don’t teach,' high turnover, or unprofessional behavior (e.g., 'teachers are over whelmed', 'Some teacher stare…', 'case managers…USELESS').
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, better‑ma: Circle reviews frequently list award‑winning arts/band, well‑funded extracurricular pathways, new/modern buildings and technology, and organized career/vocational pathways (examples: 'band is award winning,' 'brand NEW! … latest technology,' 'Academy of Engineering'), while square entries either omit such breadth or emphasize curtailed/declining programs, limited extracurricular options, or older facilities.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive unr: Square reviewers include concrete unresolved safety incidents and claims of administration failing to address harassment or assault (e.g., a student 'racially harassed… then brutally assaulted… I could find no one to help me,' administrators who 'insist on keeping that math teacher that was in trouble'), and catalogue fights, bullying, and disciplinary breakdowns more often than circle entries that tend to describe either orderly classrooms or active anti‑bullying efforts.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater administra: Square reviews commonly accuse leaders of closed‑door unresponsiveness, protecting seniority over effectiveness, hiring/retaining poor staff, or mismanaging programs (e.g., 'prioritizes seniority over adaptability', 'administration bullies parents', credit/placement errors), whereas circle reviews more frequently document empowered PTO/PTA, transparent parent‑communication systems, lotteries/selective admissions, or community foundations supporting programming.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe and pe: This bucket captures accounts of bullying, fights, drug use, gang-related violence, police presence, sexual harassment, and repeated reports that administration or counselors tolerate or mishandle misconduct (e.g., “police are there almost every day,” “students are led off in handcuffs,” “bullying is tolerated,” victims threatened with suspension). These pieces of evidence show circle schools more often name concrete safety incidents and weak enforcement compared with square reviews, which rarely document this level or frequency of safety failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, more num: This groups reviews that describe formal AP/IB/honors/dual-enrollment/STEM programs, measurable college outcomes, scholarships, and also the heavy workload/college‑placement pressure that accompanies them (e.g., “Great Honors/AP/Dual enrollment programs,” “IB program is very challenging,” and “three hours of homework every night…panic attacks”). Circle reviews repeatedly cite structured advanced pathways and high-stress rigor, whereas square reviews tend to mention only general preparedness or lack comparable program detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries detail more concrete stud: These items reference counseling programs, private counseling, enrichment centers, dyslexia/special‑education services, Saturday tutoring, 504/IEP accommodation successes and also explicit denials or lawsuits over services (e.g., “Enrichment Center…ranked top 10,” “special counseling program…private and free,” and conversely “we had to sue to get him services,” “no help with 504 plan”). Circle reviews more often describe existence, structure, or breakdowns of student-support systems compared with square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries raise more concrete facil: This bucket covers explicit discussion of building condition, cleanliness, overcrowding, technology rollouts and costs, food service, uniform fees/enforcement, scheduling/logistics, and fundraising/tuition concerns (e.g., “very nice and clean school” vs. “bathrooms had no soap,” “parents had to cough up $700 for iPad,” “overcrowded,” “where does the bingo money go?”). Circle reviews disproportionately surface these tangible operational/resource topics, positive and negative, while square reviews seldom focus on them.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, better-do: This groups mentions of extensive extracurricular programs (championship band, ROTC, agriculture/shop, career academies, sports), active parent/alumni networks, community traditions, and explicit religious/faith programming or retreats (e.g., “best mariachi in the nation,” “large and engaged parent network,” “13 academies,” “Bible-based curriculum,” “campus ministry”). Circle reviews more often point to organized, signature extracurriculars and community/faith integration than square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, stronge: These reviews report concrete program breadth (AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, named academies, vocational pathways, magnets and certifications) and measurable results — e.g. “we have all core classes available in ap,” “Biomedical, Technology, Business, and Skills Trade Academies,” and claims like “All of my children went on to college” — while square reviews lack comparable comprehensive AP/IB/CTE stacks, college matriculation evidence, or named career pathways.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more proactive,: Circle reviews frequently document hands‑on supports and responsiveness (small class sizes, tutorial periods, teachers staying after, responsive principals and counseling follow‑up) — e.g. “current administration is wonderful and very responsive,” “successful tutorial period,” and counselors who ‘bent over backwards’ — whereas square reviews more often describe administrative indifference, punitive principals, and poor parent/teacher responsiveness.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent bull: Many circle reviews recount repeated peer bullying, cyberbullying, racial/homophobic hostility, teacher‑perpetrated bullying, fights and even sexual‑misconduct allegations (quotes include “This school is full of bullying,” “biased, racist, and homophobic people,” and multi‑year dropouts due to bullying), while square reviews generally do not present such pervasive or repeated harassment narratives.
candidate_defs.circle entries include more concrete fac: Circle reviews often name specific operational realities — ongoing renovations or passed levies, technology programs (iPads), pest/food‑safety issues, lost credits, meal‑debt record withholding, block scheduling, and scheduling/staff shortages — e.g. “no ac… students faint from heat exhaustion,” “new weight room… building an auditorium,” and “they also lost some of my credits,” whereas square reviews rarely provide this level of facility/operations detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more unequal disci: Circle reviewers repeatedly allege differential enforcement and resource allocation — favoritism toward athletes/cheerleaders or donors, ‘two sets of rules’ for honors students, donor pressure, and coerced seniors to protect ratings (e.g. “football players get all the attention,” “athletic placements… by which parents donate the most,” and “two sets of rules… athletes vs non‑stars”) — a pattern of inequitable treatment that square reviews do not commonly allege.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced-: This bucket groups reviews where circle schools provide clear, concrete academic-program strength and college‑readiness evidence (AP/IB/dual‑credit, accreditation, higher test scores, named college acceptances and scholarships) that square reviews lack; examples include circle claims of AP-heavy coursework and OGT/ACT/CST gains, WASC/ACCREDITED WITH DISTINCTION, dual‑enrollment/associate degree pathways, and documented scholarship/college placements versus square’s absence of comparable outcome metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute student: This cluster captures circle reviews that describe frequent, serious safety incidents and security breakdowns (regular fights, in‑class drug use, gang activity, sexual activity on campus, robbery/threats, even past shootings) and nonresponsive or ineffective security/staff responses — contrasts made against square reviews that do not describe the same level of violent or systemic security failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more administrativ: This bucket groups instances where circle reviewers report cronyism, protected staff behavior, nepotistic hiring/promotions, grade/GPA manipulation, removing students from rolls, retroactive policy changes, or retaliation and poor accountability, in contrast to square reviews which may note bureaucracy or too many administrators but do not allege the same level of corruption or nepotistic protection.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger, broad: This captures circle reviews that detail extensive program offerings and achievements — strong band/marching programs, award‑winning arts, CTE/technical pathways, ROTC/robotics, plentiful athletics and playing opportunities — and related resource/prioritization patterns (including parental fundraising and sports‑first budget choices) that square reviews do not attribute at the same scale or specificity.
candidate_defs.circle entries report superior physical: This bucket groups reports of circle schools having newer or better‑maintained buildings, up‑to‑date technology, renovated labs/fields and visible funding (state‑of‑the‑art facilities), whereas square reviews in the same comparisons detail underfunding, overcrowded classrooms, portable/AP course space limits, sanitation/food problems, transportation failures, and routine operational shortages.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews highlight concrete, higher‑level academic offerings and outcomes (AP/IB/dual‑credit, paid dual‑credit tuition, High Tech Academy, top national rankings, large scholarship totals and specific test scores) for circle schools more often than square; examples include: “He has taken many AP classes and scored a 34 on his ACT,” “ranked in the top 7%…by US News,” and “Our seniors earned $2,000,000 in scholarship offers.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report more robust, organ: Circle reviews repeatedly name program breadth and achievement (audition‑based fine‑arts magnets, daily arts classes, national marching‑band champions, state athletic titles, many sustained clubs) while square reviews are more generic about offerings; illustrative evidence: “Fine arts is a major concentration… audition,” “marching band… always makes the top 10,” and “athletics… often win the state championships.”
candidate_defs.circle entries describe greater teacher/: Circle reviewers more often report teachers who stay after school, provide one‑on‑one interventions, rapid parent contact, small class attention, and nurturing counseling compared with square reviews which emphasize unresponsive or uneven staff; sample lines: “Teachers will stay after school as long as you need them,” “JupiterGrades… teachers' cell phone numbers,” and “personal, caring school.”
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more administrativ: Many circle reviews accuse leadership of family‑based hiring, selective enforcement, bullying or cruel administrative behavior, confidentiality breaches and excessive punishments (searches, exclusion from graduation) in ways square reviews do not; examples include: “most all employees and teachers are related,” “The Principal… bully the students,” “He loves to tell you what he sees on his video cameras,” and denial of graduation participation under a vague '12 week' rule.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more operational a: Circle reviews more frequently document concrete material and operational failures — sanitation problems, lack of textbooks or PE, trailer classrooms, missing science/CTE teachers, failed iPad rollouts, and underfunding — whereas square reviews raise these issues far less; cited evidence: “elementary cafeteria is infested with ants,” “never had any textbooks in some classes,” “no science teachers… substitutes (babysitters) and virtual teachers,” and “unable to sign in to the programs… for a month or two.”
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews repeatedly cite concrete program access and measured postsecondary outcomes (AP/IB counts, CTE shops, concurrent‑credit totals, dual‑enrollment credit and scholarship listings) for circle schools—for example: “already has earned three college credits,” “opportunity to take 40+ college credits by graduation,” IB adoption and alumni attending Duke/Harvard/Med School—while square reviews lack those programmatic details or report weaker college preparation (students “far behind” or AP students left without teachers).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: Circle reviews document intense safety problems and failed responses—two TBIs, death threats, ‘fights everyday,’ recurring thefts, bus assaults, food‑throwing, and examples of bullied students being removed to independent study—whereas square reviews rarely present the same level or frequency of violent/safety incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries recount more visible, nam: Many circle reviews name principals and coordinators and describe active, approachable leadership and sustained family involvement—e.g., “The principal leads by example,” “Parent Coordinator, Ms. Monique,” parents volunteering and feeling the staff ‘treat my children like family’—while square reviews either omit such named, engaged leaders or describe weaker family connection.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more pervasive t: Square reviews commonly report classroom‑level dysfunction—teachers showing up late, forgetting to create tests, leaking grades, favoritism, poor explanations, and minimal academic help—(e.g., “GRADING IS HORRIBLE!!”, “teachers…teach for the paycheck,” “do not do their jobs”), whereas circle reviews more often describe consistent teacher commitment or offer concrete examples of strong instruction.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more operational/a: Circle reviews frequently list concrete administrative/operational failures—broken parent portals/Infinite Campus, repeated registration attempts, rude enrollment staff, poorly timed lunches, janitor shortages, classroom overcrowding or misallocated spending (lights/stadium over academics)—examples include “5 attempts to register my child,” “Parent Portal…updated only occasionally,” and “not enough janitors,” while square reviews less often document these specific logisitical failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger family‑st: These reviews describe tightly knit, multi‑generational school communities, high parent volunteering/attendance, and ongoing alumni ties (e.g., “small town school is like family,” “my kids have been there since day one,” “lots of parent involvement,” “we have 3 WHS graduates”) — patterns that appear repeatedly in circle but are absent or muted in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more concrete, h: Circle reviews repeatedly cite organized advanced programming, AP/dual‑enrollment, awards and explicit college outcomes (e.g., “over 50 college credits offered,” “100% college bound graduation rate,” state/national awards, alumni admitted to UGA/Naval Academy), whereas square reviews make general claims about preparation but lack comparable program detail or alumni evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, higher‑ac: Circle reviewers list extensive clubs, high‑achieving music and sports programs, championship teams and large community turnout at games (e.g., ‘excellent choir,’ ‘state champion teams,’ ‘stadium has thousands show up,’ ‘no‑cut sports’), while square tends to emphasize a smaller set of activities or a single vocational standout without the same breadth or community spectacle.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more socioeconomic: Many circle reviews allege preferential access tied to wealth, donors, athletes, or family names and report identity‑based abuse or IEP noncompliance (e.g., “if you don't have a lot of money…you will be a detriment,” “teachers hand out free passes to athletes,” “IEP failures,” “misgendering/deadnaming,” “staff will make sure your child can no longer come there because they don't want to lose financial support”), a cluster of exclusionary and inequitable practices largely absent from square.
candidate_defs.square entries report more systemic admi: Square reviews more often center on persistent leadership problems, unresolved safety incidents and litigation, poor admin communication/credibility and staff indifference (e.g., ongoing fights and a lawsuit, ‘the office does not care at all,’ ‘school administration is horrible and you are always lied to’), a sustained administrative/safety failure pattern that distinguishes square from circle.
candidate_defs.circle entries report a worse student-sa: This bucket captures reviews that describe recurring physical fights, tolerated substance use, gang presence, pervasive bullying (including targeted racial/LGBTQ abuse and autism bullying) and explicit accounts that staff or administrators ignore or mishandle reports (e.g., students 'carrying spit bottles,' 'Tobacco can be smelt through the school,' 'WAY TO MUCH BULLYING and teachers nseeing it and do NOTHING,' and administrators who 'did nothing' after threats). Items belong here when the primary distinction is a hazardous behavioral climate plus ineffective or absent protective response, as contrasted with square reviews that lack or downplay these safety failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more athletics/par: This bucket groups evidence that opportunities, discipline, and resources are unequally distributed because of athletic status, parental influence, or in‑group cliques—e.g., 'football players are put on a pedestal,' 'many teachers and coaches are the parents of the kids who get picked for teams,' 'if your kid does not play the sports then they are looked down on !!' and 'parents run it instead of the educators.' Use this bucket when reviews emphasize systemic favoritism/exclusion tied to athletics or family networks rather than neutral program shortages.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader and more c: This bucket captures reviews that list named AP/magnet/STEM/vocational programs, dual‑enrollment, plentiful clubs and sports, specialized labs/technology, clear college placement examples, or flagship athletic championships (e.g., 'BioMedical and Allied Health Magnet,' 'every kid has a tablet,' '2013 State champions,' 'Ivy League acceptances,' 'dual credit, AP courses, school to work options'). Items go here when the distinguishing evidence is tangible program breadth, facilities, or documented student outcomes/awards rather than commentary about teaching quality or safety.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more operational: This bucket contains reviews describing bureaucratic and managerial breakdowns—misregistration, unanswered phones and emails, lost medical documents, recurring principal turnover, opaque budget choices and program cuts (e.g., 'voicemail full and calls unanswered,' 'we get a new principal every school year,' 'budget cuts left us with only a few non‑sports extracurriculars,' 'idk where the budget goes'). Use this bucket for logistics, recordkeeping, scheduling, governance and fiscal‑priority problems distinct from classroom instruction or student behavior.
candidate_defs.square entries report poorer instruction: This bucket groups reviews whose primary distinguishing claims criticize classroom instruction and teacher practice—frequent comments that 'many teachers don’t know how to teach,' 'most teachers could care less,' lack of differentiation for gifted or struggling learners, and reports that graduates are underprepared for college. Assign here when the central issue is low instructional quality, limited academic rigor in practice, or uncaring classroom behaviors (as opposed to program availability, safety, favoritism, or administrative logistics).
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews frequently name concrete academic programs and outcomes (20 AP classes, IB, Early College/associate‑degree pathways, dual‑enrollment with UNH/UCONN, high AP/PSAT/state test results, and scholarship totals) that reviewers tie to students being better prepared for college—claims that Square reviews do not match and often counter with reports of low AP/pass rates and weak college guidance.
