candidate_defs.square entries describe more consistentl: Square reviewers repeatedly praise teachers as friendly, dedicated, and academically supportive and call out a ‘stellar’ principal and engaged coaches, while many Circle reviews describe teacher absenteeism, cell‑phone distraction, fake or unqualified licenses, routine cursing, or inconsistent instructional effort, making teacher professionalism and visible, steady school‑level leadership a distinguishing Square feature.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Circle reviews contain numerous concrete safety and climate failures—ongoing racial slurs, transgender and LGBTQ insults, frequent fights, drug odor/use in hallways, violent attacks, cutting/self‑harm ignored by guards, and critics of ineffective anti‑bullying or mental‑health supports—whereas Square entries rarely describe systemic safety failures or widespread ignored self‑harm incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader extracurri: Circle reviews list a wide, concrete set of nonacademic offerings and community investments (award‑winning band and drama, FFA/FFA championships, career‑technical majors, robust athletics competing at state/national levels, TV news programs, Broadway trips, booster‑driven facility upgrades and partnerships like Cleveland Clinic), claims of organized fundraising, and visible facility projects that Square reviews do not typically document.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater administra: Circle reviewers more often allege governance problems—dishonest superintendent/district messaging, school‑board coverups, nepotism/favoritism, politicized leadership, manipulated or misleading data, scheduling and credit‑management errors, active discouragement of AP testing, and punitive/transactional policies—issues that Square reviews seldom raise and which point to systemic admin/district mismanagement rather than isolated teacher problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe safety: This bucket captures reports of student safety and behavior crises that reviewers say are frequent and poorly addressed (e.g., “student fights are almost a daily occurrence,” “social media pages dedicated to fighting,” robberies/threats, widespread bullying and racial/immigrant harassment, and allegations of staff‑student sexual relationships). Many circle reviews also tie these harms to weak enforcement or administrative indifference (e.g., “it got to Fleming’s desk, and he did nothing,” “They protect bullies”), distinguishing them from square entries that lack or minimize these severe safety claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: This groups claims that circle schools offer concrete academically advanced pathways and measurable outcomes—IB/AP curricula, dual‑enrollment and CTE certifications, intense ACT/SAT prep, scholarships and lists of college matriculation (Harvard/Yale, top‑tier schools), and claims like “I went into college as basically a sophomore.” These circle reports also frequently note the tradeoffs of rigor (heavy nightly homework, grade deflation, stress), whereas square entries generally do not document comparable advanced program breadth or outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more staffing and: This bucket covers reviewer allegations about adults and governance: parents or staff changing grades, nepotistic hiring of coaches, administrators accused of unethical behavior (plagiarism, pushing early graduations for money), teachers allowed to bully students, and claims that complaints aren’t investigated. These explicit staff/admin‑level corruption and accountability failures appear far more often in circle than in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more personalize: This includes reports of small‑school/family atmospheres, teachers and leaders who ‘know every student by name,’ active PTO/alumni networks, named strong coaches and program leaders (e.g., NJROTC, specific coaches), many clubs/events, and organized extracurricular offerings that aid social integration—features reviewers contrast with square entries that do not emphasize this sustained personalization or community engagement.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more tangible faci: This bucket groups complaints about overcrowding and capacity strain, aging or unsanitary facilities, poor food and long meal lines, out‑of‑pocket fees, bus/transport gaps, failed levies and budget shortfalls, and uneven facility investments—evidence such as “so overcrowded you literally feel like cattle,” $500 registration complaints, roaches/sewage and no air conditioning. These concrete material and operational problems are documented more often in circle than in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reviews that describe sustained, severe student-behavior problems and ineffective responses — e.g., physical attacks on staff and students, sexual assaults left unaddressed, widespread vaping/drug use, and chronic bullying or racial/homophobic slurs with little enforcement. Representative evidence: “kids beat up teachers…,” “several sexual assaults within the school with no action,” “Vapes are the craze…,” and repeated claims that bullying is ‘swept under the rug,’ contrasted with Square’s reviews that more often describe calmer hallways, fewer pervasive drug problems, or isolated incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, more e: This bucket groups reviews that name concrete programmatic offerings and outcomes — career-technical pathways, dual-enrollment/AP access, hands-on STEM/tech labs, and explicit scholarship/college-success claims — e.g., lists of ‘Academy of Finance,’ culinary/PCA/BETA Engineering, ‘Every student has an iPad…3D printers,’ dual credit/AA-with-diploma anecdotes, and ‘full scholarship’ outcomes, whereas Square’s reviews tend to lack the same breadth of named pathways or measurable college outcome descriptions.
candidate_defs.circle entries report higher teacher tur: This bucket covers staffing patterns and hiring/accountability issues in reviews: frequent remarks that faculty are ‘a stepping stone,’ high turnover/reconstitution events, ‘questionable hiring practices,’ and specific claims that ineffective teachers are kept despite poor student outcomes. Examples include ‘High teacher turnover rate,’ ‘constant change of faculty,’ and ‘some teachers…never acceptable, yet they are allowed to keep their job,’ whereas Square reviews more often describe stable, engaged or consistently praised faculty.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups critiques of school/district leadership and operations: slow or nonexistent responses to parents, bungled transfers and records, refusal to validate discipline, alleged sweeping‑under‑the‑rug of accusations, legal/financial controversies, and claims of administrators who ignore or intimidate complainants. Illustrative items: ‘took over two months to meet the principal,’ ‘they flat lied saying my student had been withdrawn…,’ ‘Most accusations are swept under the rug,’ and PTA/financial lawsuits—claims far more prominent in Circle than in Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize athletics and e: This bucket captures reviews that report both strong extracurricular offerings and an institutional tilt toward sports (sometimes at the expense of academics), plus favoritism for athletes — e.g., well‑supported marching band/ROTC/film programs, travel clubs, and frequent complaints like ‘sports are their importance,’ ‘athletes get special treatment,’ or resources prioritized for athletics over arts/academics. Square reviews rarely combine both broad extracurricular breadth and the same repeated athlete‑privilege/funding complaints.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures reports about student-on-student harm and weak frontline enforcement: examples include circle reviewers describing weekly fights, gang‑affiliated youth, racial harassment chants, hazing on athletic teams, vaping/drug policy non-enforcement, unsupervised exits and metal‑detector/lockdown incidents—none or far fewer of which appear in square reviews. Items belong here when the review documents concrete safety incidents or describes school-level failure to prevent or respond to physical/psychological harm.
candidate_defs.square entries allege more leadership/go: This bucket groups claims about district or central-office failures rather than classroom practice: square reviewers accuse boards of silencing, corruption, administrative ineffectiveness, refusal to accept alumni gifts, and policy-driven IEP failures; they also describe enrollment policy shocks and district consolidation problems not raised by circle. Use this bucket for critiques tied to principals/superintendents, school boards, district decisions, financial mismanagement, or systemic governance breakdowns.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: This bucket covers explicit program breadth and outcomes: circle reviews frequently name full IB programs, many AP/dual‑credit classes, National Merit/AP success, biotechnology/healthcare academies, co‑op placement or FFA and direct college matriculation or testing‑out claims, whereas square reviews lack equivalent programmatic evidence. Include texts that highlight formal college‑prep or structured career pathways and concrete college/readiness metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more proactive,: This bucket captures reports of hands‑on staff responsiveness and tailored supports: circle reviewers describe teachers ‘bending over backwards,’ accommodating guidance counselors, frequent phone/email outreach, aides teaching organizational skills, and close transition supports; square entries more often report hard-to-reach counselors or adversarial/defensive staff. Assign items here when the emphasis is on teacher/counselor‑level responsiveness, individualized help, or consistent parent outreach.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger physical: This bucket groups reviews highlighting tangible assets and extracurricular breadth: circle reviewers cite major renovations, new auditoriums, school‑issued iPads/Apple computers, high‑quality bus/cafeteria service, thriving bands/arts and competitive athletics (and also itemized activity fees), whereas square reviews rarely document comparable capital upgrades or device programs. Use this bucket for concrete reports about buildings, equipment, device rollouts, named extracurricular programs, and explicit fee/participation costs.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent stud: This bucket captures descriptions of day-to-day safety breakdowns and weak or superficial staff/administrative protections (e.g., repeated physical assaults, drug circulation, racial harassment, mishandled sexual‑assault cases, and statements like “My child was beaten up several times, teachers simply turned their backs”), as well as explicit claims that administration tolerates or minimizes incidents; square entries generally do not document this level of recurring violence or administrative failure on safety and instead describe fewer or better‑handled incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more systemic favo: This groups reports that leadership and boards protect insiders and allocate advantages to athletes, staff relatives, wealthy donors, or favorites (examples: “FAVORITISM given to members of the church and/or staffs children,” “money ... misappropriated by the county,” and ‘admin/board comprised of the same people, no transparency’), plus allegations of corruption and privacy/coverup behaviors that square reviews do not raise.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more pervasive s: This bucket covers repeated claims about unanswered communications, rude front‑desk/guidance staff, failure to follow up on parent requests or paperwork, guidance-counselor errors, and classroom teachers refusing accommodations (e.g., “they refused to fill out a form I needed,” “guidance counselors didn't care,” “teachers wouldn't work with 504 kids”), whereas square reviews are more likely to describe proactive counseling and responsive staff.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more robust advanc: This groups concrete evidence of specialized, high‑level academic offerings and results in circle reviews — IB/AP expansions, Dual Enrollment completion, high national rankings, selective tracked pathways, and named program successes (e.g., “IB program… top 3%… Dual Enrollment: four college classes completed”) — while square reviews rarely cite comparable specialized programs or measurable college‑prep metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize material resour: This bucket captures claims about how physical resources are distributed and experienced — preferential funding for athletics and athlete privileges, cuts to arts, fundraising/tuition burdens, visible technology initiatives or one-to-one tablet/iPad programs, and widely reported facility conditions (from state‑of‑the‑art campuses to crumbling buildings and overcrowding) — a range of concrete resourcing and facility evidence that square entries mention far less or in different terms.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews repeatedly name concrete advanced offerings and outcomes (AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, college credits transferring to Rutgers, Ivy‑league acceptances, 96% daily attendance, 98% graduation) and also report heavy testing/homework pressure ("I have a test every day...", "homework till 11:00pm"). By contrast square reviews rarely cite sustained AP/IB pipelines or hard college‑placement metrics and instead report program failures or lack of consistent rigor, so membership means the review emphasizes concrete advanced coursework, measurable postsecondary results, and related academic intensity.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more frequent se: Square reviews include repeated accounts of pervasive fighting, juvenile‑delinquent atmospheres, bullying and discipline failures (e.g., ongoing fights, ankle monitors/police calls, students ‘miserable’ and depressed), whereas circle reviews are more often framed as small‑town safety or mixed on safety. Put another way, a review falls here if it foregrounds chronic violent incidents, gang/drug visibility, or routine armed/police patrols as an operational safety problem.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more consistent, p: Circle reviews frequently cite teachers/staff staying after school, proactive tutoring and test‑reward incentives, and parent‑facing accessibility ("teachers are always there to help", "staff have been wonderful and caring", counselors who "were always willing to work with you"). Square reviews more often describe counselor no‑shows, uneven teacher availability, turnover and lack of consistent follow‑through, so this bucket groups reviews that emphasize hands‑on, routine instructional help and responsive teaching staff.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger communi: Many circle reviews highlight multi‑generation ties, active alumni pride, high parental involvement and explicit religious or cultural fit ("being part of a family", "Chapel services EVERYDAY", "we have been at CAL 7 years"), and also describe insider advantages (parents employed at the school, athlete favoritism, program cliques). A review belongs here if it centers community cohesion, sustained alumni/parent networks, local cultural or faith identity, or social‑network favoritism as a defining school feature.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviews repeatedly document concrete operational breakdowns — lost or late transcripts, counselors who don’t respond, schedules not updated, added classes without teachers, broken website/communication systems — that impede student enrollment, course crediting and family engagement. This bucket groups reviews that foreground administration/office mismanagement, logistics failures and program roll‑out problems rather than classroom pedagogy or community culture.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader and stro: These reviews assert that circle schools offer more advanced-course pathways (AP, AICE, Cambridge, dual‑enrollment/Running Start), expansive CTE/vocational tracks (transportation/aviation, agriculture, welding, allied health), and richer arts/music/extracurricular offerings with concrete college matriculation examples (Georgetown, Harvard, state-level awards) — e.g., multiple citations of AP/dual‑enrollment success, thriving music programs, and national FFA/Beta competition that square reviews do not report.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: Many circle reviews recount systemic student-safety problems — recurrent fights, bomb threats/lockdowns, death threats, homophobic/racial harassment, police involvement and even pepper‑spray use — and describe staff failing to protect victims; these concrete safety and targeted‑abuse claims appear substantially more often in circle material than in square material.
candidate_defs.circle entries document greater administ: Circle reviewers repeatedly allege unavailable or misleading administration, arbitrary/coercive policies (forced AP placement, harsh uniform enforcement), favoritism (athlete/counselor bias, tenure protection), and mandatory financial burdens (tuition, non‑optional raffles, coach payoffs), describing systemic governance and funding problems that square reviews typically do not raise.
candidate_defs.square entries portray more consistent,: Square reviews more often describe dependable, empathetic teachers, accessible counselors, sustained staff continuity, and clear college‑prep supports (counselor-led credit/opportunities), whereas circle reviews show far more variability and frequent complaints about teacher departures or apathy — e.g., square statements like 'Staff and Administration... fantastic' and 'The Guidance counselor here is very helpful' contrast with many circle reports of high turnover and uneven teacher quality.
candidate_defs.circle entries exhibit pronounced intern: Circle reviews frequently contain starkly conflicting accounts (elementary vs. high‑school quality, severe negatives alongside five‑star praise, recent improvement after prior crises, department‑by‑department contrasts), producing a pattern of high intra‑school heterogeneity and temporal shifts that square entries rarely display, which are instead more uniformly consistent.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: This bucket groups reviews that report concrete curricular depth and outcomes in circle schools — AP/IB/honors availability, magnet/academy tracks, dual‑credit/college courses, high scholarship totals and reported college preparedness or test-score gains (examples: '8 AP courses...college credit in science, French, Spanish', 'Last year's class won over $28,000,000 in scholarships', 'IB program and AP classes are excellent'). These items focus on program breadth and documented student postsecondary success rather than classroom conduct or facilities.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reviews describing ongoing safety incidents and a poor climate in circle schools — frequent fights, police/security presence, sexual assaults, tolerated slurs/substance use and reviewers saying administration ignores or protects offenders (examples: 'bullying out of control...swept under the rug', 'at least 2 fights a month', 'many sexual assaults...not taken care of', 'students followed home and threatened'). It unifies evidence about incidence frequency, supervision failures, and ineffective or preferential discipline.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more teacher/sta: This bucket groups reports of instructional practice and staff responsiveness problems in circle schools — frequent teacher absences, poor teaching quality or inadequate feedback, missing homework/assignment communication, unreturned calls, counselor dysfunction, and special‑education/IEP/504 implementation failures (examples: 'a lot of the teachers do not even show up', 'student does not receive homework assignments', 'Transition Planning Meeting...has yet to take place', 'no one answers the phone'). These items focus on day‑to‑day professional practice, academic support, and compliance with student‑support processes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more facility, ope: This bucket groups concrete, operational complaints about building condition and resource management in circle schools — overcrowded cafeterias/buses, sewage/mold/heat problems, dirty custodial conditions, expired or unsafe food, fees excluding participation, and perceived misallocation of funds toward athletics or cosmetic items (examples: 'SEWAGE smell...mold in the music building', 'lunches aren’t even meals...found a bug in their food', 'lunch room line is horrible', '$250 fee keeps kid from homecoming', 'money spent on big screen TV while lacking textbooks'). It covers physical plant, health/sanitation, capacity, and budgeting/pricing practices rather than pedagogy or community culture.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger communi: This bucket collects reviews that emphasize social-network gatekeeping, alumni/parent influence, church/donation-based preferential treatment, tuition/faith-based governance or selective admissions in circle schools (examples: 'teacher's children received special treatment', 'must go to church with a teacher/coach', 'daily devotions and weekly chapel', 'tuition is expensive...feel like a family', 'selective magnet with admissions requirements'). These items are about how community ties, governance model, or religious/tuition status shape access, discipline, and opportunity — distinct from instructional quality, safety, or facilities.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student safet: These reviews describe concrete safety and climate harms at circle schools—sustained bullying ignored by staff, on‑campus fights/drugs/weapons, multiple suicidal or self‑harm incidents, and poor nurse/counseling follow‑up (examples: 'literally wanted to kill myself', weapons/lockdowns reported, 'students bringing weapons', 'cyber‑bullied' and 'police had to be involved'). This bucket captures reports about student misconduct, violence, victimization, and failures of behavioral/mental‑health protection and response.
candidate_defs.circle entries exhibit more administrati: These reviews document governance and office breakdowns at circle schools—frequent principal/teacher turnover, nepotism/donor/athlete favoritism, policy violations or manipulative metric practices, poor parent communication, and concrete operational mistakes (attendance/records/transfers, bus/drop‑off failings) (examples: 'favoring wealthy parents and athletes', 'they purged failing students to clear classes', 'calls/emails ignored', 'moved problem administrators here'). This bucket captures systemic leadership, policy, staffing and process failures that shape daily school operation and equity.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger in‑clas: These reviews highlight that circle schools more often report higher curricular rigor, explicit AP/honors/accelerated programs or magnet/academic‑center pipelines, college‑prep supports and named matriculations/scholarship totals (examples: 'many Advanced Placement classes available', 'Lane Tech Academic Center with high‑school credits', 'graduating class earned about eight million dollars in scholarships', 'students sent to Stanford/Yale/MIT'). This bucket covers classroom curriculum strength, alignment to college pathways, and concrete post‑secondary results.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader extracurri: These reviews emphasize program breadth outside core classes at circle schools—robust music/band/drama, specialized career academies and on‑site real‑world facilities, vocational/shop options, many clubs and community/alumni involvement (examples: 'working bank in the school', 'awesome band program', 'majors in Computer Science, Engineering, Legal', 'amazing PTSA and parent forum'). This bucket groups availability of extracurriculars, arts, vocational training, and the organized parent/alumni structures that sustain them, and also notes whether access is inclusive or gatekept.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive low: Square reviews more often describe weak day‑to‑day instruction and outcomes—low student engagement, classes not meeting state standards, reduced AP/honors offerings, alumni reporting college unpreparedness or remedial work, and teachers who fail to challenge students (examples: 'This school is not very engaging', 'less than half of Brewer graduates are proficient', 'AP and Honors cut back', 'completely unprepared for college classes'). This bucket captures complaints about instructional quality, insufficient rigor, and measurable underperformance in academic standards at square schools.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: These reviews describe concrete program strength (many APs, dual‑credit classes, students entering college with sophomore standing, national merit scholars, quantifiable rankings and high AP/SAT/ACT performance), e.g. “took 10 AP courses…31 credits,” “AP test scores and college placement successes are outstanding,” which square reviews do not match (square focuses on mixed rigor and limited advanced outcomes).
candidate_defs.circle entries document more consistentl: Multiple circle reviews praise teachers and counselors who provide one‑on‑one remediation, mentoring and explicit IEP accommodations—e.g. “Before I came…now I'm passing every class,” “administration has been very accommodating…placing her in advanced classes ahead of schedule,” and “Extra help is always available”—while square reviews more often report teachers who are uninterested, unhelpful, or unresponsive.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviewers recount frequent principal turnover, part‑time/interim heads, centralized decision blocks (Superintendent approval needed), poor follow‑through, threats to critics, and board dysfunction—e.g. “fourth principal in five years,” “interim leader…less than 3 days/week,” and administrators who “threaten to sue you for speaking up”—issues that are far less prominent in square reviews, which often note engaged or improving leadership.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive pee: Circle contains repeated, detailed accounts of bullying, fights, cyberbullying, racial/homophobic incidents, socioeconomic exclusion and staff complicity or inaction (police reports with no remedy, security failures, favoritism for athletes), e.g. “Lots of bullying…they do not do ANYTHING,” “belt fights on the bus,” and “athletes don't always have to follow guidelines,” whereas square reviews are comparatively less likely to describe sustained, unchecked safety problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader physical: Circle reviews frequently mention campus expansions, new or pro‑level athletic facilities, many clubs/teams, active alumni and parent programs, and specific facility improvements (or construction-in-progress)—e.g. “one of the largest and newest schools,” “pro football teams have used it for practice,” and long lists of clubs—while also raising funding/fee/transparency questions; square reviews rarely document that same scale of facilities, extracurricular variety, or organized alumni/parent programming.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: These reviews document concrete peer‑safety harms and harmful outcomes attributed to inadequate remediation: gang and drug violence, frequent fights, widespread bullying, student substance‑use and even multiple suicides, plus victims told to 'deal with it' or with no counseling — e.g., claims of an 'infested with gangs, drugs, and gang violence' campus, 'many students are on drugs all the time,' and 'the number of suicides... are absolutely shocking.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: These reviews cite formal advanced pathways and quantified results that square reviews lack, such as IB/AP and STEM academies, named university partnerships and large dual‑credit offers, expanded AP programs, rising test scores and ACT/college‑readiness metrics — e.g., 'offers great STEM programs, IB or AP courses,' 'over 60 free college hours through Morehead State,' and 'average ACT score of 23 for 85% of the seniors.'
candidate_defs.circle entries describe richer, better‑r: Reviewers point to extensive, high‑quality arts, clubs and extracurricular access and long‑term family/alumni ties: Broadway‑level theater, strong music/choir programs, 'a ton of clubs' that are 'very welcoming,' multi‑generation families and staff continuity — e.g., 'Broadway‑quality theater,' 'the choir is very well put together,' and 'Our family has been a part of the MaST family for well over 10 years.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report more punitive, exc: These reviews describe explicit administrative policies and abuses that exclude or punish students and families, and governance favoritism: locked bathrooms and denied accommodations, behavior contracts/exclusion from class, fines/withheld transcripts, nepotism and retaliation — e.g., 'students cannot use the restroom during class,' 'holding his transcripts hostage because I refuse to pay,' and 'this entire school system is run by a select group... Parents are retaliated against.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more visible admin: Square reviews repeatedly point to leadership and operational failures — absent or complacent principals, poor SAT/logistics planning, lost attendance/record errors, unreturned calls and counselor inaction — for example: 'The principal has zero communication,' 'HSPVA did not plan an alternative... construction... one call from the principal could have eliminated the noise,' and 'the teachers and counselors do not return phone calls.'
candidate_defs.circle entries document stronger, concre: These reviews report that circle schools list explicit AP/IB/dual‑enrollment offerings, structured ACT/SAT and test‑prep, vocational academies with industry certifications, and named scholarship/college matriculation totals (e.g., “over $9 million in scholarships,” students admitted to Columbia/Duke/Stanford, associate degrees on graduation), while square reviews lack comparable outcome evidence or only give generic academic praise.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Circle reviews contain repeated concrete safety incidents (weapons, stabbings, hospitalizing assaults, frequent fights, visible drug use, theft) and claims that staff/administration failed to intervene or selectively enforced discipline, whereas square reviews either omit such severe incidents or describe a safer, more orderly environment.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive tea: Square reviews repeatedly allege teachers who 'don't teach,' watch media in class, or are there 'for the paycheck,' plus accounts that administration protects staff (e.g., 'administration feel they are untouchable'), a pattern of low instructional accountability and administrative shielding not present in the same degree in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater on‑the‑gro: Circle reviewers frequently describe concrete student supports—after‑school tutoring, teachers available by phone until 9pm, Zero Hour, small class size/individual attention, and active principal visibility credited with school culture—while square reviews rarely document these sustained teacher‑led supports and instead emphasize in‑school-only help or lack thereof.
candidate_defs.circle entries document larger, concrete: Circle reviews include both vivid complaints about deferred maintenance, overcrowding, levy/political funding conflicts, punitive fee practices and also explicit infrastructure/technology investments (1:1 laptops, LEED campus, major renovations), showing strong variability and governance tension over resources; square reviews rarely show that same mix of extreme underinvestment or visible capital projects.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: These reviews describe concrete programmatic strength (extensive AP/IB/honors lists, dual‑enrollment, Blue Ribbon recognition, rising test scores, Gates scholarships, 100% graduation/college‑acceptance claims and explicit college‑prep structures like block scheduling) that square reviews generally do not document; examples include repeated circle claims of many AP/IB courses, dual‑enrollment pathways, honors cohorts and measurable test/college outcomes while square reviews rarely cite comparable program inventories or outcome metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe worse student sa: Circle reviewers recount frequent bullying, physical assaults, vaping/drug problems, suicidality-linked crises and concrete emergency failures (coaches or staff ignoring injured students, poor crisis follow‑through), whereas square reviews more often report a safe, quiet environment or only isolated behavior issues; representative evidence includes circle accounts of ignored attacks, police presence, drug/alcohol reports and students driven to transfer for safety.
candidate_defs.square entries portray more consistent,: Square reviews commonly describe reachable, caring teachers and effective guidance counselors who proactively contact families, whereas circle reviews oscillate between praise and sharp critiques—many circle reports name teachers who ‘go the extra mile’ but also highlight unqualified instructors, favoritism, and midyear turnover or non‑grading practices; examples include square statements that teachers "reached out" and circle allegations of teachers who "don't even grade" or hire‑by‑connections favoritism.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviews frequently document scheduling/enrollment breakdowns, lost or manipulated records, nepotism, retaliatory or exclusionary parent policies, and funding/priority choices (e.g., money routed to athletics over academics), while square reviews rarely describe comparable systemic operational failures; illustrative items include circle reports of multiple principals over short periods, schedules released late or wrong, alleged record tampering, and board/administration favoritism.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize broader extracu: Many circle reviews highlight award‑winning arts, magnet or vocational programs (pre‑professional arts, FFA/agriculture, health/tech magnets), one‑to‑one device programs and new technical centers, presenting a wide extracurricular and program mix that square reviews do not detail to the same extent; examples include circle mentions of orchestras, arts conservatories, magnet curricula, vocational career centers, MacBook rollout and new technical facilities.
candidate_defs.Circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews report concrete, school-level academic rigor and pathways—AP/IB/dual-enrollment, measurable college placements, exit-exam pass rates, and selective admissions—that square reviews generally do not. Examples: circle cites “Plenty of AP options,” on‑campus dual enrollment and Ivy acceptances (“Brown, Yale”), Newsweek rankings, and claims like “Every year all of our Seniors pass the EXIT EXAM,” whereas square tends to show mixed or limited AP/college prep evidence.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report broader, higher‑pr: Circle reviews frequently list extensive arts, music, theater, band, and varsity athletics with regional/state recognition and named programs, while square reviews usually mention only a single program or limited extracurriculars. Examples: circle names “orchestra, choir and theater programs,” “well recognized state wide…football and basketball,” award‑winning bands and JROTC accolades; square often cites just one strong program (e.g., music or baseball) or few clubs.
candidate_defs.Circle entries describe more frequent an: Circle reports concrete safety incidents and enforcement failures—fights, stabbings, drug use on campus, racial slurs, ignored bullying, metal‑detector deployment, and alleged police/administrative mishandling—whereas square contains far fewer or milder safety complaints. Examples: circle notes students “have taken and bought marijuana at school,” “After the stabbing last year,” and “bullied with zero action,” contrasted with square’s lack of comparable severe safety incidents.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more administrativ: Reviews in circle document systemic governance and personnel problems—tenure‑protected problematic staff, nepotism/insider favoritism, cover‑ups of incidents, widespread unresponsiveness, outsource/outdated curriculum, substitute instability, low pay driving turnover, and parents required to fund programs—claims that square reviews raise less often. Examples: circle alleges a teacher “boasted” about being protected by tenure, principals who “tried to cover the incident up,” dead FLVS links and “teachers that do NOT respond to emails,” and reliance on boosters to fund activities.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe more consistent: Square reviews more often emphasize attentive one‑on‑one support, proactive counseling, inclusive special‑education interactions, effective remediation, and pastoral care that improves student outcomes—features that circle reviews either criticize or report inconsistently. Examples: square includes statements like “Whenever I was having a bad day…someone would always notice and help me out,” “Mr. Kenny…is really exceptional!” and “The students here get along with the special education students,” while circle contains more reports of failed accommodations and hostile counseling.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, more num: This bucket captures program-level academic strength and verifiable outcomes: circle reviews repeatedly name IB/DP, extensive AP/dual-credit partnerships, high ACT/standardized test recognition, alumni scholarships and selective‑college matriculation (examples: 'DP/IB program...many teachers are adjuncts so students enter college with 40 credits', 'Bandys named an Honor School of Excellence...over 91% at or above grade level', 'Cox Mill brought in almost 5 million in scholarship funds'), whereas square reviews lack comparable metrics and focus more on limited AP/honors availability or declining academic performance.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups accounts of physical fights, routine bullying, drugs/vaping, sexual-assault allegations, special‑needs restraint incidents, and administrative nonresponse: circle reviewers cite 'fights are common', 'several past and current cases of students who have been sexually assaulted', 'code greens...special needs student needs restraining', and 'bullying is swept under the rug', while square reviews generally do not describe pervasive violence or institutional tolerance of bullying.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more visible gov: This bucket covers structural/leadership-level dysfunction: circle reviews allege governance shifts or secret boards, nepotistic hiring (coaches hired for friendships), favoritism by family names, heavy church influence, and complaints about superintendent/principal incompetence or administrative bloat (examples: 'run by a secret board', 'hired her own personal friends to coach', 'you’re either rich, religious, or you’re nobody', 'leadership is totally unsatisfactory'), whereas square reviews make fewer or no such governance/favoritism claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pronounced re: This bucket captures descriptions of skewed spending and program-level resource disparities: circle reviewers report well‑funded tech/athletics or one‑to‑one devices alongside underfunded arts/mechanics/theater, removed library books after laptop rollouts, parking or overcrowding issues, and both modern remodels and chronic funding cuts (examples: 'computer programs...have all the best software' vs 'underfunded theater program', 'they gave each student a Macbook Pro... removed all the books', 'we are facing budget cuts'), while square reviews rarely describe such concentrated funding imbalances.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent, o: This bucket captures steady, positive reports of teacher professionalism, parent communication, counselor/helpful administration, and predictable classroom instruction: square reviewers frequently praise 'caring and supportive faculty', 'excellent teaching staff', and responsive counselors, whereas circle reviews are more polarized—some praise dedicated teachers and outreach but many also allege unresponsiveness, inconsistent grading, or hostile staff—making square the group with more consistent staff-driven support in the data.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews emphasize concrete, formal academic pathways and credentials at circle schools — multiple AP/IB/dual‑enrollment offerings, Running Start/college credit, career‑technical programs and certifications (CNA, CPR, West Side CTC), JROTC, STEM academies, and frequent named college acceptances — while square reviews lack comparable breadth or document fewer AP/dual enrollment/vo‑tech pathways.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more consistent,: Circle reviews repeatedly report staff who stay late, provide individualized help, counsel students on course/college plans, run summer‑bridge orientations, and rally the community (e.g., principals/staff credited with turnaround), whereas square reviews more often describe unhelpful or apathetic teachers, weak counseling, and staff churn.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent seve: Circle reviewers provide concrete safety claims — repeated fights, daily gang bullying, weapon/ gun‑pulling allegations, near‑weekly lockdowns, teacher sexual arrest, and parents reporting unanswered safety complaints — and say the school/district often fails to remediate; square reviews contain fewer or less severe safety incidents and less evidence of systemic non‑response.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more administrativ: Circle reviews frequently accuse administrators of favoritism toward athletes/wealthy families, nepotistic selections for teams/leadership, punitive public shaming by principals, arbitrary expulsions/IEP denials, and GPA/athletics‑based exclusion — patterns of unequal enforcement and discriminatory discipline not present in square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more resource shor: Square reviews more often cite concrete funding and resourcing problems — no textbooks/handouts, cancelled programs/extracurriculars, staff layoffs, growing class sizes/overcrowding, and mandatory/unmanaged fees — whereas circle reviews more often describe up‑to‑date tech, available electives, or maintained facilities.
candidate_defs.circle entries have broader, better-docu: These reviews repeatedly point to concrete programmatic strengths at circle schools—more AP/CTE/IB options, vocational/shop and FFA tracks, award‑winning music, state athletic championships, SciTech/magnet programs, dual‑enrollment and college-credit pathways, device deployments (iPads/Chromebooks), certification opportunities and documented college scholarships/admissions—e.g., 'students can graduate with certifications,' 'Chromebooks available in every classroom,' 'accepted into SciTech,' and alumni claiming strong college placements.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Many circle reviews describe repeated or serious safety incidents, tolerated peer and staff bullying, on‑campus substance use, gang/drug pressure, violent attacks and threats, and disciplinary failures (zero‑tolerance punishments, staff inaction, or staff protecting popular athletes)—examples include accounts of 'fights almost daily,' 'alcohol and other substances are taken into and used at school,' a student concussed after an attack that staff ignored, and 'over 40 school shooting threats made by one student.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviews more often allege concrete operational failures—lost or denied credits, unapproved online recovery courses, transcripts/scheduling chaos, canceled programs, board nepotism/corruption and poor facilities management—e.g., 'credits from his previous school somehow got lost,' 'they actually lost my transcripts,' use of 'E2020' that universities won't accept, calls to replace school board members, and 'crammed...schedules into three days.'
candidate_defs.square entries describe more consistentl: Square reviews more often portray stable, responsive adults and parent‑facing systems—praised principals and vice‑principals, teachers who 'know our child personally,' effective grade/portal communication, and engaged counselors—evidenced by comments like 'The teachers and staff members are wonderful,' 'The principal and vice principals are incredible,' and 'grades are actually watched by the school and by parent portal (which I love)'.
candidate_defs.circle entries show greater polarization: Circle reviews frequently juxtapose extremes about the same school—high academic reputation or excellent programs alongside accounts of poor instruction, unsafe climate, or favoritism—producing highly variable narratives rather than a uniform picture (examples: the same school called 'one of the best in Ohio' and also 'students treat each other horribly,' or 'amazing teachers' vs 'some of my teachers bully students').
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced/: These entries describe concrete programmatic strength at circle—named STEM/Engineering/IB/AP/early‑college tracks, 1:1 student laptops, documented higher test/EOC/ACT scores and alumni graduate/advanced‑degree placement—claims that square reviews do not make (e.g., “Engineering Class and Independent Research Program,” “nearly 98% go on to advanced education,” “IB program,” “1:1 technology”).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These items document frequent serious safety problems at circle (physical fights, death threats, tobacco/drug use, metal detectors, cyber‑bullying) plus repeated accounts that staff or leadership ignore, under‑respond, or inconsistently discipline perpetrators—examples include ‘DEATH threats from varsity football players,’ ‘lots of drugs…even in 7th and 8th grade,’ and ‘staff do nothing to help a child being bullied,’ whereas square reviews describe fewer incidents and more prompt responses.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: These entries allege concrete staff misconduct and governance problems at circle—gossiping, teachers on cell phones, rudeness to parents/students, nepotism/wealth‑based favoritism, selective discipline, record‑keeping or residency fraud, and administrative indifference or retaliation (e.g., ‘staff gossips,’ ‘if you are a parent with deep pockets they will do anything for you,’ ‘principal does nothing, superintendent doesn’t care’), claims that square rarely makes and often contrasts with square’s reports of engaged staff.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute facilit: These entries cite tangible physical and budgetary deficits at circle—HVAC/boiler failures, mold, trailers, unclean bathrooms, missing textbooks, levy failures and planned deep cuts that eliminate programs or fire staff (e.g., ‘no working AC…rooms reach 95°F,’ ‘hard time passing levies…cut band…fire half the staff,’ ‘most students went a semester without books’), whereas square tends to report fewer or different facility complaints.
candidate_defs.circle entries show greater variability: These entries contain sharply conflicting reviewer accounts about the same circle school—high praise alongside severe condemnation within or across reviews (e.g., one review calls it ‘one of the best schools’ and elsewhere ‘a drop out factory’), indicating inconsistent student experiences, teacher quality, and outcomes; square reviews are comparatively more consistent in their assessments.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more personalized,: These reviews describe routine one‑on‑one availability (teachers staying before/after school, formal tutoring like a ‘9th hour’, named teacher endorsements, heavy parent volunteering and alumni engagement) and small‑school, family‑like cohorts that produce individualized help—examples include teachers ‘made themselves available…before school, after school,’ parent volunteers running programs, and repeated named teacher praise, whereas Square reviews lack comparable evidence of schoolwide personalized access.
candidate_defs.Square entries document more pervasive a: Square reviewers repeatedly flag inactive or indifferent leadership, unresponsive counselors, and leadership that fails to fix recurring problems (e.g., ‘Poor leadership’, ‘they didn't have time for you or your child’, guidance not sending transcripts), describing a pattern of managerial inaction and weak follow‑through that is less commonly asserted in Circle reviews.
candidate_defs.Circle entries describe more pervasive s: Many Circle reviews report rampant bullying, physical fights, homophobic/racist/sexist student behavior, drug use, and either harsh/dehumanizing discipline (demerit/ humiliation) or inconsistent enforcement (suspensions for trivial infractions or ignored bullying), while Square reviews rarely portray this level of widespread student misconduct or combined punitive/inconsistent disciplinary culture.
candidate_defs.Circle entries describe broader and more: Circle reviews list substantial program breadth and college prep supports (multiple AP/advanced courses, academies/magnet programs, A+/dual‑credit pathways, strong college‑counselor activity, expanded science/arts offerings and 1:1 student devices), whereas Square reviews more often note limited advanced options and fewer systemic college‑prep resources.
candidate_defs.Circle entries show greater internal str: Circle contains repeated reports of a pronounced two‑tier school (top students with scholarships and national recruiters vs many students needing tutors or failing tests), plus sharply conflicting reviewer narratives about safety, staff competence, and outcomes; Square reviews are comparatively more consistent in portraying a narrower set of programmatic or operational problems rather than this kind of deep stratification and reviewer polarization.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reports that circle schools describe repeated on‑campus fights, gang affiliation, widespread drug use/dealing, sexual activity, thefts and threats alongside ineffective security or inconsistent discipline (e.g., “Majority of the students here are gang affiliated,” “kids jumping others for juuls,” “fights all the time,” and “security isn't good; they get paid for standing in the halls”). These items contrast with square entries, which rarely describe pervasive safety crises and tend to report isolated incidents or addressed threats rather than ongoing, systemwide safety failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups reviewer claims about leadership and front‑office misconduct: public shaming by principals, administrators favoring athletes or insiders, nepotistic hiring/selection, withholding diplomas/yearbooks over fees, billing/record errors, and poor responsiveness (examples: “the principal called a girl... a baby,” “they will hold your child back... because Johnny Jr/Sally's Dad works here,” and “they refused to pull up the book returned list; I was forced to pay $119”). Square entries, by contrast, contain far fewer allegations of these kinds of punitive or unethical administrative behaviors and more often praise effective leadership.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger small‑sch: This bucket covers concrete evidence that circle schools are described as close‑knit, multigenerational communities with high volunteer participation, parent involvement, alumni continuity, and visible school pride (e.g., “As a 3rd generation student,” “Fantastic parent involvement. I can walk in and know the kids by name,” and “Gotta love the jacket pride!”). Square entries typically emphasize larger, more diffuse populations and do not emphasize sustained multigenerational parent/alumni investment to the same degree.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more concrete pr: This bucket groups concrete program and outcome evidence in circle reviews: nationally recognized arts/band achievements, IB and dual‑enrollment pathways, CTE certifications and industry licensure, ROTC/aviation magnets, and named college admissions/scholarships (examples: “IB program… Bright future scholarship,” “nation’s only high school where a student can earn a Private Pilot’s license,” “Band & Choir travels to New York,” and alumni getting into competitive colleges). Square entries rarely provide the same density of concrete credentialing pathways or named program outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more tangible faci: This bucket captures operational and infrastructure evidence in circle reviews: large enrollment and overcrowding (“we need to make a new high school… 4,000 students”), requests for new facilities or AC, descriptions of recent rebuilds/renovations, 1:1 laptop rollouts or tech problems, schedule changes/late starts, parking shortages and persistent fundraising demands. Square entries focus less on these concrete facility/enrollment logistics and more on classroom programs and staff behavior.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger academi: These reviews report concrete program strength and outcome metrics (AP/IB/honors, dual‑credit/early‑college diplomas, high graduation/college‑matriculation rates, state rankings and AP scores) that square reviews typically list as course availability or critique as poor college preparation; examples include circle notes of AP success, IB programs, >90% graduation rates and ‘98% go to college’ versus square’s lack of outcome metrics and statements like ‘doesn’t prepare you for college.’
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe safety: Circle reviews contain repeated accounts of pervasive student misbehavior and safety incidents (weapons/shooting threats, bomb threats, frequent fights, widespread bullying, vaping/drug/alcohol use and inconsistent enforcement) and claims that staff/administration tolerate or mishandle them, whereas square reviews rarely describe such systemic, violent or weaponized safety problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: These comments center on governance and staff behavior—explicit nepotism, coach/athlete favoritism, arbitrary rule‑making, management motivated by money, suppression of negative reviews, nonlocal/unreachable administration, hostile responses to parents and guidance‑office failures—while square reviews more often praise responsive principals and counselors.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more facility, fun: Circle reviewers repeatedly cite underfunding and tangible facility/resource problems—missing books, antiquated or inconsistent tech, no/poor heating or AC, pest and cleanliness issues, pay‑to‑play cuts, limited transportation, crowded halls or class capacity—whereas square reviews more often describe adequate or newly renovated facilities and fewer chronic resource shortages.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger extrac: Circle reviews frequently describe wide extracurricular breadth and high‑level achievements (state championships, nationally ranked arts, many clubs, mission/travel programs), strong community/booster support, and also complaints that athletes or donors receive preferential treatment—while square reviews seldom make the same claims of elite arts/athletics or the same degree of sport‑centered favoritism.
candidate_defs.Circle entries describe far worse studen: This bucket captures patterns about student conduct and campus safety: Circle reviews repeatedly report pervasive bullying, gang fights, widespread drug/alcohol exposure, racial and homophobic slurs, sexualized incidents, and repeated lockdowns (e.g., 'Bullying is the norm,' 'there is a lot of gang activity,' 'Drugs and alcohol are widespread,' 'students who “dressed up as nazis and haven't been punished”'), whereas square reviews do not describe these severe safety problems.
candidate_defs.Square entries depict stronger, more con: Square reviews emphasize reliable college prep and measurable successes (e.g., 'Academically, MHS is rated one of the top HS,' 'many college acceptances,' 'FULL RIDE to USC'), while Circle reviews more often show uneven or deficient academics—slow pacing, promotion/grade inflation, manipulated grades, illiteracy claims, or scheduling/credit mismanagement (e.g., 'one step above illiterate,' 'they might have been taking test 2-3 times until he passes,' 'delays in graduating due to mismanagement').
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more staff and lea: This bucket groups evidence about adults’ behavior and institutional accountability: Circle reviews contain many accounts of rude front‑office staff, administrators accused of abuse or dictatorship, threats to call CPS, favoritism in discipline/admissions, high principal/teacher turnover and inconsistent teaching quality (examples: 'Front office staff is VERY RUDE!!!', 'My child was abused ... by the principal', 'It's the NAME GAME around here!', 'teachers are leaving'), whereas square reviews show fewer systemwide accusations of abusive governance and more consistent leadership praise.
candidate_defs.Circle entries emphasize broader, more v: Circle reviews frequently list extensive after‑school options, celebrated music/athletics achievements, formal partnerships and postsecondary pipelines (e.g., 'Many of the school’s sports teams end up winning the state championships,' 'NAVY JROTC program,' 'students graduated with 50 college credits,' '12th grade project...helped him get a job'), while square reviews include fewer or less‑centralized descriptions of organized, award‑winning extracurricular pipelines.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more conspicuous f: This bucket groups physical‑infrastructure and resourcing signals: Circle reviews mention large capital projects and visible security practices (e.g., '$70Million building that didn’t fix education', 'last year they put cameras everywhere,' 'K9 thing along with random searches'), overcrowding or aging facilities, environmental contamination claims, and contested spending priorities (e.g., plasma screens vs textbooks), whereas square reviews more often report constrained funding but fewer dramatic facility/security contrasts.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: This bucket captures reviews that describe frequent physical fights, gang/drug activity, opioid/overdose incidents, widespread bullying (including of neurodivergent students), and even high teen‑pregnancy reports — plus repeated claims that teachers/principals failed to intervene or follow up (e.g., “bullied from kindergarten...teachers nor principal did anything,” “last year a kid overdosed in class,” “Asperger's child...constantly bullied but the bully wasn't [disciplined]”). These accounts contrast with square entries that largely omit safety/bullying crises or explicitly describe safe, supportive peer and staff climates.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger/formal: This bucket groups reviews highlighting formal rigor and programmatic college-prep (AP/IB/Scholars/STEM/academies, weighted classes, dual‑enrollment, JROTC, career academies) plus high test/college-placement metrics and scholarship outcomes (e.g., “college preparatory school,” “30–40 kids get into top colleges,” “AP pass rate, top SAT scores,” “Hope Scholarship”), whereas square entries more often complain about poor college readiness, remediation needs, or lack of advanced offerings.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more individualize: This bucket covers evidence of low student‑to‑teacher ratios, frequent one‑on‑one help (before/after school, texting teachers), strong counseling/targeted remediation, and proactive parent outreach (e.g., “teachers stay in contact with me by text,” “guidance staff is amazing…qualified for the Hope Scholarship,” “continuous open door policies — early morning, after school and weekend tutoring”), in contrast to square entries that describe counselors/teachers as unavailable or unable to provide individualized help.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more politicized,: This bucket captures reviews alleging administrative/political dysfunction — entrenched favoritism/nepotism, hiring/promotions based on connections, athletic/parent cliques, refusal to enforce attendance/discipline, authoritarian principals or threats, and community‑level politicking (e.g., “they play politics…who you know matters,” “principal shows favoritism,” “keep calling the BOE and get nowhere,” threats to call AG) — distinguishing leadership/policy failures from ordinary operational problems described in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, better‑re: This bucket groups items naming abundant and organized extracurriculars, successful arts/music/FFA/JROTC programs, strong athletics traditions/championships, specialized academies and vocational shops, or recent major capital projects and facility upgrades (e.g., multi‑million dollar stadium, brand‑new $75M building, large FFA greenhouse and animals), whereas square reviews typically lack such breadth or note limited extracurricular options and weaker facility investment.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews report concrete program offerings and outcomes (AP, IB, dual‑enrollment, college credits, high AP participation and students entering college with credits), e.g. 'they offer honors, AP and IB classes,' 'graduated with 21 college credits,' and 'students take AP exams and gotten college credit,' whereas square reviews rarely cite AP/IB/dual credit and instead emphasize students 'not prepared for college.'
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, higher‑: Circle reviews repeatedly list award‑winning, competitive activities across many domains (band, choir, theater, robotics, state champion teams and multiple sports championships), e.g. 'Award winning Math program, nationally ranked show choir and 2013 state champion football team' and 'excellent music program,' while square reviews rarely name such a breadth of award‑winning extracurriculars and focus more narrowly on a few sports or on academics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more on‑campus saf: Many circle reviewers describe pervasive student misconduct and weak physical/security controls—explicit bullying (including staff‑enabled), drugs/vaping, thefts, students sneaking out, and no cameras or unlocked doors (e.g. 'the people here are druggies... constantly trying to sell to my child,' 'they do not have the investments for installing security cameras,' 'students sneak out at their own will'), whereas square reviews do not document this constellation of routine safety and security failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more proactive, pe: Circle reviews cite concrete individualized supports and outreach—voluntary tutoring, Link Crew/freshman supports, academic dean monitoring, small class sizes and one‑on‑one remediation (e.g. 'Tutoring even for students not traditionally offered tutoring,' 'They caught him up and work one on one with him teaching him,' 'Class size was only 3 in one class'), while square reviews rarely describe this level of routine, structured individualized intervention.
candidate_defs.square entries report more systemic admi: Square reviews more often attribute problems to district governance, declining enrollment, budget/leadership failures and punitive administrative actions (e.g. 'Our school District is struggling with declining enrollment,' 'administration's solution was to withdraw my child from the class with no credit,' 'the latest principal is in over his head,' and complaints about program cuts and transportation), whereas circle reviews less frequently frame issues as broad district governance or the specific punitive/district exclusion practices described in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews report concrete programmatic rigor and results (AP/IB offerings, early‑college/dual‑enrollment, college credits, named AP passes, 100% selective matriculation claims, explicit GPAs and IB diploma counts) that square reviews do not; examples include claims of AP/IB curricula, associate‑degree pathways, students entering college with semester‑advances, and named college acceptances vs square’s lack of comparable measurable college‑prep evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more pervasive s: Circle reviews contain multiple firsthand accounts of violent threats, guns not resulting in expulsions, rampant bullying, drugs/tobacco on campus, gang formation, pest/food‑safety hazards and explicit failures to protect or discipline students, whereas square reviews largely omit repeated, systemic safety/weapon/drug allegations.
candidate_defs.square entries report more effective, st: Square reviews frequently credit responsive principals/counselors, active parent outreach (PTA/booster activity, mailings, Facebook updates) and clearer family–school communication, while many circle reviews complain about unresponsive administration, leadership turnover, poor counselor support, and breakdowns in parent communication.
candidate_defs.circle entries portray an athletics/ROTC: Circle reviews repeatedly allege that JROTC/football and athletes receive outsized social status, funding and preferential discipline/playing time (out‑of‑zone transfer athletes, donor/nepotistic favoritism, major budget shifts toward football), and report abusive or unethical coaching behavior—issues square reviews do not emphasize.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete oper: Circle reviews include detailed, tangible complaints or upgrades about physical plant and operations (aging/obsolete textbooks and computers, wifi failures, gross bathrooms, food poisoning, long charter‑bus commutes, confusing fees and paid parking, dress‑code suspensions, parents barred from bringing forgotten items, and both reports of facility renovations and of severe underfunding), while square reviews rarely present this breadth of specific operational detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reviews that describe recurring violence, weekly fights, gang activity, racialized bullying, lockdowns, pervasive harassment on buses/hallways, and students roaming unsupervised—e.g., multiple circle reviewers cite ‘weekly fights,’ ‘kids are getting assaulted every single day,’ gang presence, lockdowns every other week, and race‑based harassment—conditions square entries generally do not report.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more administrat: Includes critiques of leadership practices and operations such as cover‑ups, ignored parental complaints, missing transcripts/grades, rudely managed front offices, mass/ mid‑year teacher departures, local‑hire nepotism, and fear of retaliation—for example circle reviewers recount ‘superintendent did not hold administrators accountable,’ ‘front office loses paperwork,’ ‘half the teachers left in three years,’ and alleged donor/family favoritism, contrasts square’s fewer such allegations.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: Groups pieces that list explicit advanced-program access and outcomes—IB, many APs, dual enrollment/college credits, higher SATs, documented college acceptances and credits to skip freshman year—e.g., circle reviews recommend joining the IB program, note 40+ college credits and free dual enrollment or cite alumni accepted to multiple colleges, claims that square reviews typically lack or dispute.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader and more: Covers reporting of abundant clubs, standout band/arts programs, statewide athletic dominance, donor/alumni fundraising and tangible boosters (Annual Fund, alum support), and outreach to community arts organizations—for example circle reviewers praise ‘AMAZINGGGG band,’ state top‑ranked teams, robust donor giving, and partnerships with youth orchestras while square reviews do not emphasize such breadth or fundraising.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more chronic facil: Encompasses concrete, recurring operational deficits: overcrowded cafeterias/classrooms, broken HVAC for years, pest infestations, missing textbooks/equipment, required costly fees and opaque charging practices (e.g., pay for temporary IDs), and poorly maintained buildings—circle reviewers repeatedly cite no A/C, rats, peeling paint, and opaque student fees whereas square reviewers seldom raise those exact resource failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger formal: This bucket captures reviews that report concrete curricular offerings and outcomes — e.g., circle reviewers list multi-level courses, IB and AP programs, dual‑enrollment/college credits ("graduating with 18 credits"), specialty centers and vocational pathways, and alumni who matriculated to selective colleges — while square reviews generally lack comparable named advanced programs or measurable college-credit outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This groups reports of frequent and severe student-safety incidents and inaction — e.g., gang and fight reports, daily bullying, sexual harassment, rampant drugs, and claims that administration 'brushes it under the rug' — whereas square reviews do not contain the same breadth/intensity of violent or tolerated-misconduct accounts.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more systemic gove: This bucket covers allegations about how the school is run and who benefits — examples include favoritism to donors or athletes, nepotism, counselors' biased placement decisions, selective discipline, high teacher turnover and low morale — contrasted with square entries which do not primarily allege these coordinated governance or equity failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe richer, better‑r: This groups evidence of extensive out‑of‑class programming and community support — e.g., numerous named clubs, state championships and nationally ranked bands, strong parent fundraising (Shark Fund), peer tutoring and external partners — while square reviews typically do not enumerate comparable breadth, achievement, or organized parent/alumni investment.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete oper: This bucket collects practical, day‑to‑day resourcing and operations complaints — such as 30+ class sizes, ten‑year‑old textbooks, broken labs, only two janitors, attendance mis-marking, long uniform wait times, and threatened program eliminations — which are more frequently documented in circle reviews than in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews emphasize concrete program breadth and results: named AP/STEM teachers and courses, expanding AP/dual‑enrollment and magnet/pathway programs (e.g., Pathways to Engineering, Marine Studies), documented graduation/college‑acceptance improvements and scholarship offers, and explicit rating gains (e.g., D→B). Square entries typically lack comparable course‑level detail or outcome evidence and sometimes allege lowered standards or grade‑inflation instead of measurable college preparedness.
candidate_defs.circle entries report smaller class size: Multiple circle reviews cite very small graduating cohorts, low student:teacher ratios, teachers who stay after school or provide routine tutoring, principals who know students by name, and explicit one‑on‑one help; square reviews more often imply larger scale and less-consistent individualized attention.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more severe stud: Circle reviews frequently recount pervasive bullying, repeated physical fights/assaults, substance use (vaping, drugs), and administrative failures to protect students (suppressed referrals, ignored complaints), while also documenting authoritarian enforcement of minor infractions (locked doors, suspensions for phones, strict attendance/exam penalties and heavy punishments), creating a pattern of both unsafe student behavior and inconsistent/harsh discipline; square reviews do not present this same mixture of recurring severe violence plus these enforcement contradictions.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize an athletics‑fi: Circle reviewers repeatedly frame school priorities around sports—large on‑campus athletic facilities, athletic capital projects and recruitment, scholarship athletes, selection/leadership favoring athletes, and board/administrative spending choices privileging athletics—whereas square reviews rarely present athletics as the dominant institutional priority.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute facilit: Circle reviews include concrete maintenance/health failures (bed bugs, mold, worms in food, sulfurous water, leaking ceilings, unusable bathrooms), chronic overcrowding and lack of basic labs, unreliable transportation, and examples of misallocated/high‑cost low‑impact purchases (underused specialty labs vs. unrepaired basics); square reviews rarely document this cluster of acute facility/health hazards or the same scale of resource mismanagement.
candidate_defs.circle entries report a more pervasive u: This bucket captures safety and disciplinary practice: circle reviews describe tolerated bullying and racist incidents that go unaddressed, lax enforcement for high‑status students (e.g., “Bullies get away... especially if they are on the football team”), rampant cellphone noncompliance, and inconsistent rule application, whereas square reviews describe isolated fights and active administrative/parental involvement rather than a pervasive unsafe culture.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize structured acad: This groups material about instructional structure and outcomes: circle reviews repeatedly describe Houses/SLCs, block scheduling that aids learning and sports balance, cited performance metrics and awards (e.g., high scores, scholarship winners), and recent improvements over the last two years, while square reviews focus less on these structured academic supports and more on other concerns.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe tuition/status‑d: This bucket captures how resources and access are distributed: circle reviewers report pay‑to‑play dynamics, country‑club style status gating, and that attention/resources flow to honors/AP/athletes/magnet programs (e.g., “the school only cared for the Honor students, AP students, and athletes”), plus multigenerational alumni loyalty that reinforces exclusivity—patterns not present in square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries describe clearer active p: This groups family‑facing communication practices: square reviews cite concrete tools and habits (Parent Portal app, teacher emails, timely notifications) and responsive contact from teachers, whereas many circle reviews complain they “never know about important dates,” lack web/phone notifications, or report administrative unresponsiveness around outreach.
candidate_defs.circle entries report worse institutiona: This bucket covers school viability and staffing trends: circle reviews explicitly link recent levy/budget issues to program and staff losses, describe a growing budget deficit and a long decline with high turnover (“revolving door of teachers”), while square reviews do not report similar fiscal deterioration or chronic staff instability.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: These entries describe concrete, high‑severity safety incidents (sexual assaults, frequent fights, gangs, threats, weapons, racist harassment, food‑throwing) and also note staff/administration failing to address them (e.g., 'sexual assaults within the school with no action from the staff', 'Bullying occurs at every grade level and nothing is done'). They capture both the harmful events and the school's weak or denialist response, a pattern rarely present in square entries which report milder or no comparable safety crises.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more problems and: Many circle reviews focus on special‑education access and integration failures (denied services leading to lawsuits, students 'pushed thru the system', daily 'code greens' and restraints, lack of SSD integration and separate buses), whereas square entries either praise special‑ed progress or do not raise these systemic special‑needs problems. This bucket groups concrete operational failures, exclusion, and legal disputes tied to special education and neurodivergent students.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger/expanded: Circle reviews repeatedly name AP/Pre‑AP, dual‑credit/early‑college diplomas, Saturday Regents prep, and heavy AP workload/stress (e.g., 'variety of AP classes', 'majority entered college with...college credits', 'curriculum is challenging and definitely college preparatory'), while square reviews less often document that level of advanced coursework or exam‑prep intensity. This bucket captures substantive program-level academic rigor and structured college pathways.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviewers more often allege churn and incompetence (frequent principal/teacher turnover, calls for 'complete overhaul', lost transcripts, opaque rulemaking, 'good ol boy' favoritism, punitive restroom/tardy policies, teacher protests), whereas square reviews more often assert stable or improving leadership. This bucket groups governance, staffing, and operational failures distinct from individual classroom instruction or safety incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader specialize: Circle entries frequently list a wide array of identifiable programs and achievements (band/orchestra champions, NJROTC recognitions, arts magnet pipelines, career magnet strands, internships, many clubs and travel opportunities) and also describe concrete facility/resource stories (recent $23M upgrades or renovated campuses, specialized labs underused vs. basic facilities in disrepair, cafeteria and sanitation complaints). Square entries rarely combine both detailed program breadth and such specific facility/resource allocation claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries report worse student safe: These reviews describe concrete safety failures at the school (daily fights, organized social‑media fights, visible drug dealing and on‑campus use, robberies, frequent thefts, pests) plus weak or selectively enforced discipline (bullies/athletes get away with behavior, staff tolerate vaping/loitering). Examples: 'Student fights are almost a daily occurrence,' 'I've been robbed, threatened and followed,' 'Drugs are everywhere…you can smell it,' and repeated reports of police presence or social‑media pages dedicated to fighting — contrasts with Square, which contains few comparable reports of violence or tolerated illicit activity.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger academic: These reviews list institutional academic strengths and verifiable offerings — expanded APs, full IB pathways, dual/concurrent‑enrollment, STEM and shop programs, 1:1 device rollouts, SAT/ACT and online test prep — and often cite college matriculation outcomes (Ivy/elite acceptances, testing out of gen‑ed).
