Examples: 'AP Statistics, AP Calculus…', 'graduated full‑IB…tested out of a few general education classes,' 'each student provided a laptop,' and 'nearly 90% of eligible juniors/seniors take college classes,' whereas Square lacks comparable claims of systematic advanced coursework or measurable college outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more staff/adminis: These reviews allege preferential treatment (athletes and insiders get better counselors, enrollment 'hardships', teacher/coach favoritism), nepotism, and leadership failures (board/superintendent apathy, misleading communication, politicized staffing), plus enforcement that prioritizes nonacademic rules over safety or learning. Examples: 'I truly believe athletes get preferential treatment,' 'teachers play favorites A LOT…many kids have parents working at the school,' and 'the board of ed…just dont care,' which are far more prominent than in Square.
candidate_defs.square entries describe weaker teacher q: Square reviews focus on instructional deficiencies and frontline staff problems — hit‑or‑miss teaching, teachers who 'should retire,' classroom disengagement, and alumni saying they were 'not prepared for college AT ALL' — portraying graduates and current students as academically under‑prepared. Examples: 'very hit or miss…some outstanding… many unhelpful,' 'graduates woefully unprepared for college,' and 'teachers cruise on the internet during class,' complaints that are more frequent in Square than in Circle.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger community: These reviews emphasize active parental involvement, sustained alumni identity, strong fan support, and a wide/award‑winning extracurricular slate (band, drama, athletics, debate), with examples like 'Their fan support is unlike anything I've seen,' 'parents still volunteering even 20 years after their kids have graduated,' and 'excellent visual and performing arts programs,' contrasts with Square's relatively muted or absent claims about deep community traditions and broad extracurricular prestige.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures reviews that allege unreachable or rude front‑office staff, principals who won’t meet parents, lost paperwork, long unreturned calls, bungled enrollment/credit transfers, bus‑card and attendance process failures, and refusals to cooperate with law enforcement or alumni—e.g. “Trying to meet with the Principal is like trying to make an appointment with the President,” a bus‑card logistics failure, and counselors taking 6+ months to transfer classes. These concrete process and responsiveness failures are repeatedly tied to 'circle' schools and contrasted with the smoother administrative access or responsiveness described in 'square' reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent stud: This groups reviews documenting sustained bullying (including physical assaults and PTSD), repeated on‑campus fights and property crime, pervasive drug/vaping smells, absent or ineffective security, and punitive policies that create logistical harm (e.g. phones confiscated and only returned to parents), contrasted with 'square' reviews that emphasize safer, cohesive student climates. It covers both the occurrence of harm and failures or misapplications in discipline and supervision (e.g. administrators defending bullying or failing to stop violence) that reviewers attribute to 'circle' schools.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more individualize: This bucket groups concrete evidence of one‑to‑one teacher work, small class sizes, effective IEP/504 outcomes, supportive guidance counselors, named teachers who mentor students, and formal conflict‑resolution or counseling programs (e.g. “The teachers work with students on a one to one basis,” successful IEP inclusion, CAP clinical counselors). These reviewer claims position 'circle' schools as providing closer day‑to‑day instructional and special‑needs support compared with the relative lack of individualized help and overloaded counselors described in many 'square' reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader extracurri: This bucket captures reviews that list award‑winning bands, FFA, debate, theatre academies, wide CTE/vocational pathways, alumni‑organized events, and townwide game‑time support, plus recurrent claims that athletics receive disproportionate funding (e.g. “All money goes to sports…football is glorified”), contrasted with 'square' reviews that typically single out a strong music/drama niche rather than the same breadth of community/alumni engagement. It therefore groups program diversity, public‑facing traditions, and resource prioritization toward extracurriculars as distinguishing features of many 'circle' schools.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, measurab: This bucket covers reviews that describe systematic honors/AP/IB offerings, dual‑credit partnerships, consistent AP/test results and National Merit recognition, clear engineering/CTE pathways, and explicit college‑readiness outcomes (e.g. students recruited by selective universities), which 'square' reviewers emphasize more often than 'circle' reviewers. It isolates programmatic, curriculum‑level strength and documented outcome claims (accreditation, rising test scores, large scholarship totals) as a distinguishing characteristic favoring the 'square' group.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews name concrete programmatic strengths (AP/IB/Honors, dual‑enrollment, named English/STEM programs, AP passes, high test percentiles, early graduation) and describe regular tutoring, counselor outreach, and individualized recovery plans—e.g., multiple circle reviewers cite IB/AP classes, 'passed two AP tests,' 'concurrently enrolled in college,' '99% nationally' test ranks and structured math tutoring—claims that are absent or weaker in square reviews which more often report lack of help, credit-recovery failure, or low preparedness.
candidate_defs.circle entries report pervasive student: Many circle reviews document concrete safety incidents (frequent fights, gang fights, drug deals, groping/sexual assaults, near‑weekly lockdowns, students locked in class), claims of staff/counselors shrugging off bullying, and allegations of cover‑ups; square reviews lack the same frequency/severity of violent incidents and instead focus on classroom or supervision concerns without comparable reports of systemic safety failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report administrative dys: Circle reviewers repeatedly allege unreturned emails and missed parent meetings, nepotistic hires, rigged team selections, corrupt budget allocations, billing lawsuits, and formal complaints/ACLU threats (e.g., 'principal hung up on a parent,' 'lawsuit filed for billing my son,' 'sister‑in‑law assistant principal'), while square reviews generally do not present the same pattern of governance corruption or documented legal/financial disputes.
candidate_defs.circle entries portray an athletics‑ and: Circle reviews frequently emphasize sports as a dominant priority—state championships, pro teams using facilities, athletic funding crowding out academics, athletes getting preferential treatment, mandatory fundraisers/fees and high‑end athletic facilities—whereas square reviews rarely describe this combination of program prominence, funding skew, and athlete privilege.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize a small, family: Multiple circle reviewers describe small class sizes, staff knowing students by name, strong parental involvement, alumni returning, and tightly knit peer support (‘staff treats you like family,’ ‘fantastic parent involvement,’ waiting lists), contrasted with square reviews that more often describe large, impersonal campuses and weaker parent/staff familiarity.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete safety incidents and a hostile peer climate in circle schools — e.g., repeated hallway/parking‑lot fights, fire‑alarm disruptions, phone and property thefts, drug busts and on‑site hospitalizations, rampant vaping, and both peer and staff‑on‑student bullying ('Bullying is the norm', 'kids pull the fire alarm and fight outside', 'two drug busts... one student to the hospital'). Square reviews rarely report these systemic safety/bullying patterns and instead describe fewer or isolated altercations.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, broader: This bucket captures circle reviews that list extensive advanced-course pathways and college prep supports — examples include claims of 'all AP class options', Early College/AA attainment, Running Start/dual‑enrollment credits, US News top‑7% ranking, and large scholarship totals ('earned three college credits by being duel enrolled', 'walk with her AA Degree'), whereas square reviews typically note limited or uneven college‑prep access and lower aggregate outcome evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize expansive extra: This bucket groups evidence that circle schools foreground a wide range of extracurriculars — award‑winning music/arts, extensive clubs and academic teams, formal mentorships and long‑running traditions ('marching band state finalists, award‑winning newspaper, over 30 clubs') — while also repeatedly reporting that athletics dominate resources or receive privileged treatment ('school revolves around sports', 'administration is all about the athletes'), a prominence far more consistently described than in square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistently: This bucket collects items where square reviewers emphasize dependable, student‑centered adults and good home–school coordination — e.g., 'teachers who really care and go out of their way', 'the counseling staff was amazing', 'communication and access to teachers and administrators is exceptional', and active PTSA/volunteer activity — evidence that square schools are described as having steadier day‑to‑day adult support than many circle descriptions.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers concrete managerial and governance criticisms in circle schools — nepotism/favoritism ('principal shows favoritism to certain staff' or favors athletes/donors), inconsistent rule enforcement and subjective discipline, accreditation or recordkeeping threats, boards ignoring parental concerns, and IEP/504 non‑compliance or forcing parents to fight for services ('Does not follow through with IEPs', 'school board simply makes decrees ignoring parental concerns') — problems invoked far more often for circle than for square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete safety incidents (kill/bomb lists, gang activity, frequent large fights, student assaults, drug problems, suicides/threats) plus staff/administration failing to stop or even protecting offenders (bullying swept under the rug, teachers who are bullies, reliance on police because school won’t act). Examples: 'Along with the kill lists and bomb threats…', 'Bullying is out of control…swept under the rug', 'The kids beat up teachers…', and 'had to pull child out…due to bullying issues and lack of administration support.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader and better: This bucket captures descriptions of concrete program breadth and pathways (many AP/honors and AP-intensity, dual-enrollment and early-college credit, vocational certifications, wide electives/arts/clubs, state-level competitions, structured tutoring and specialty centers) that circle reviewers emphasize relative to square. Examples: 'nearly 20 AP classes and take classes at 3 colleges', 'graduated with 21 college credits', 'band, choir, drama, E.P.I.C. service club…donated $4000', and 'free, after-school tutoring…Tuesdays and Thursdays 3–4PM.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report newer or better-ma: This bucket groups reviews that make specific claims about physical plant and capital investment (new campus, beautiful facilities, upgraded buildings, attractive campus) in circle versus concrete decay, leaks, pest problems, falling ceiling tiles, and unsafe infrastructure in square. Examples: 'Love the fact this is a new campus. The campus is beautiful.' contrasted with 'The whole entire school is falling apart…a ceiling tile fell off and hit a peer' and 'the ones open are filthy from over use.'
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more concrete admi: This bucket covers reviews naming specific administrative misconduct or opaque governance—claims that scholarships/placements go to insiders, 'who you know' intake, misdirected funds to athletics, administration refusing to validate discipline, debt/curriculum-policy controversies, and broken accommodation/504 follow-through. Examples: 'Follow the money. Scholarships go to well connected rich insiders,' 'Who You Know Policy…for the intake process,' 'money that goes to the sports program,' and 'I received no help with getting my daughter's 504 plan accommodations.'
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger communi: This bucket groups evidence that circle schools more often report active parent/PTA involvement, alumni returning to teach, organized campus ministry or religious mission, high school spirit/mascot pride, and structured community partnerships that support students. Examples: 'Parental and community involvement…parent-run groups raise funds,' 'I'm a former student that has returned to teach…love the hometown feel,' 'The Jesuits…Campus Ministry is unsurpassed,' and 'i love this school so much… GO TROJANS.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe frequent physical fights, weapons/gang incidents, on-campus drug use, and rampant bullying — often paired with staff/security indifference or biased responses (e.g., ‘saw security take a gun out of a locker,’ ‘40+ fights last year,’ ‘Drugs are used very often,’ and ‘They handle bullying by telling the child being bullied to go on independent study’). By contrast square entries emphasize a safer, more orderly learning environment or only isolated incidents, so this bucket groups chronic safety problems plus failures of school discipline/response.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: Many circle reviews list robust AP/IB/dual-enrollment offerings, named career academies and hands‑on/STEM pathways, internships and industry partnerships, and explicit post‑secondary outcomes (e.g., ‘IB/AP classes,’ ‘free dual enrollment,’ ‘Sports Medicine Academy,’ ‘TRANSTEM Academy,’ and ‘99% of grads go on to college / Ivy placements’), whereas square reviews lack comparable advanced-program breadth or outcome statistics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent fail: Circle reviewers repeatedly recount inadequate or refused testing accommodations, absent summer remediation, poor IEP/504 advocacy, and weak mental‑health support (e.g., ‘They receive no support,’ ‘This school even refuses to give extra time,’ ‘You can forget a 504 or IEP’ and ‘GARBAGE at supporting a student’s mental health’), while square reviews more often describe available, responsive supports.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater administra: This covers leadership failures and politicized governance (unqualified principals, frequent principal turnover, ‘administration backs the teacher 100%,’ hidden politics, half‑hearted reforms, tuition/fee pressure, and budget-driven cuts) and related operational issues (late buses, scheduling nightmares, school-of-choice impacts), e.g., ‘One principal does not even have an administrative certificate,’ ‘Attempts to change are half‑hearted,’ and ‘they have changed it to pay to play.’ Square reviews do not present this cluster as consistently.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger or mor: Circle reviews frequently cite high-performing sports teams, state championships, celebrated band/arts programs, volunteer coach culture, pay-for-access booster activities, and explicit athletic prioritization or favoritism (e.g., ‘won three state football championships,’ ‘Band is fantastic,’ ‘the school focuses more on sports than learning,’ and ‘coaches need to be screened better’), whereas square reviews do not argue that extracurricular/athletic identity and competitive success are as prominent.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: This bucket captures reviews where circle schools describe concrete advanced offerings and outcomes (many AP/IB/honors classes, early 9th‑grade college prep, high test scores, alumni matriculation to selective universities and scholarship wins) while square reviews lack comparable programmatic evidence or report students 'far behind'—examples: circle notes “variety of AP courses,” “prepare the kids for college at the beginning of 9th grade,” and alumni Harvard/USC/Cal Berkeley placements versus square’s claims of weak college prep and limited AP availability.
candidate_defs.circle entries report richer, more diver: This groups reviews that describe broad extracurricular & CTE breadth at circle schools—multiple clubs (DECA, FBLA, robotics), career/technical pathways, student boards and organized leadership, thriving band/theatre—contrasted with square reviews that emphasize few electives, sport‑only priorities, or lost funding for activities; representative evidence: circle: 'ROTC, DECA, FBLA, robotics, mock trial' and 'Junior leaders won $5,000...' vs square: 'The only redemption... band which is extremely good but has lost almost all funding' or 'They only care about football.'
candidate_defs.circle entries provide more concrete, si: This bucket covers reviews that name specific on‑campus resources and capital changes—1:1 devices, up‑to‑date STEM labs, MacBooks/3D printers, new wellness centers, building bonds or recent renovations—whereas square reviews tend to frame problems at the district/policy level ('ZERO funding for education') without listing campus hardware; examples: circle: 'Every student has an iPad... 3D printers... science labs are up to date' and 'just passed a building bond' vs square’s systemic funding/policy critiques.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive saf: This bucket groups reviews documenting repeated safety crises and poor enforcement—bullying, frequent fights, drug offers/overdoses, bomb threats/lockdowns, sexual harassment, students roaming halls and evacuation/security policy concerns—often paired with administrators failing to act; examples: square: 'Kids coming to school drunk and high... bomb threats and lock downs weekly/monthly' and reports that 'administrators failing to address bullying' in contrast to circle reviews that more often highlight safe or well‑disciplined environments.
candidate_defs.square entries portray more administrati: This bucket captures complaints about unresponsive guidance/counseling, broken promises, leadership apathy or incompetence, and generalized staff disengagement (missed calls, counselors 'useless', principals who 'blow the whole thing off'), whereas circle reviews more frequently describe approachable administrators and teachers who 'work with him individually'; examples: square: 'The counselors are terrible... admins don't know how to direct' vs circle: 'The principal is the best administrator I have seen' and 'teachers are always willing to dedicate their time.'
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger academi: This bucket captures reviews that point to concrete, school‑level academic strength—advanced placement, dual‑credit/college partnerships, accreditation and high college matriculation or rising test scores—present in circle reviews but absent in square ones (e.g., circle mentions multiple AP programs, WASC praise, dual‑credit with Ivy Tech, ‘95% move on to college’, and measurable score gains). It groups statements about rigorous coursework, magnet/Cambridge programs, and explicit college‑readiness infrastructure that reviewers cite as distinguishing school practice and outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups reviews alleging ongoing safety and climate failures in circle schools—routine bullying, racial/homophobic abuse, vaping/drugs, fights, gang presence, and unaddressed assaults—together with claims that staff/administration tolerate or fail to remediate those harms (examples: daily fights, racial slurs allowed in front of staff, rampant vaping/drug use, gang‑affiliated students and ignored assaults). It describes substantive onsite supervision, incident, and discipline patterns rather than reviewer tone.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize and document pr: This bucket groups reviews that foreground specialized, high‑profile extracurricular programs and how the school allocates resources to them—strong/award‑winning band programs, competitive athletics and football favoritism, conservatory arts tracks, CTE/FFA and vocational magnets—often with reviewers noting those programs’ successes or that resources are channeled to them (e.g., band state titles, magnet medical/graphic arts, CTE-paid work for special‑needs students; and conversely, drama cut for football).
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more administrat: This bucket captures reviews documenting concrete administrative practices: favoritism/nepotism (athlete or insider preference), punitive discipline (humiliating enforcement, prom cancellation, door/attendance policing), withholding records/tuition disputes, and frequent unreturned parent communications (parent portal failures, rude front office). These are actionable descriptions of leadership behavior and accountability problems that reviewers attribute to school governance.
candidate_defs.circle entries contain more concrete ope: This bucket groups reviews that focus on physical and operational resourcing—either positive (recent renovations, central air, school‑issued devices, smartboards) or negative (no textbooks, poor food, broken security equipment, crowded event seating, shuttle/parking dangers, budget cuts). It covers explicit, tangible resource and logistics evidence (1:1 device rollouts and failures, funding shortfalls, facility condition, library hours) that reviewers use to characterize how the school operates day‑to‑day.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student safet: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete safety/climate failures in the building — physical fights, stabbings, gang activity, rampant vaping/drug use, sustained cyberbullying and clique-driven exclusion — often paired with teachers/administrators who ignore, minimize, or fail to intervene (e.g., “beaten by other kids… bus driver watched and did nothing,” “fights occur almost every day,” “RACISM goes unchecked”). These items are about observable threats to student safety and the school’s failure to protect students, not writing tone.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, more exp: This bucket groups reviews that describe formal academies, many AP/Honors courses, college-credit in‑house programs, vocational/CTE pathways, and explicit outcome evidence (scholarships, high AP pass rates, college matriculation) — e.g., “more than twenty AP and honors courses,” “academies count as college credit,” and “earned nearly $1,000,000 in scholarships combined.” It captures program breadth, rigor, and documented post‑secondary success as school-level realities.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more active, organ: This bucket covers reviews emphasizing formal parent engagement (parent coordinators, mandatory volunteer hours, recurring parent‑teacher meetings), parent-organized volunteering, and parent-facing communication systems (Skyward, weekly updates) — e.g., “parents must volunteer for many hours,” “we get weekly updates from Skyward,” and “the parents really work together to volunteer.” These are concrete organizational practices that increase family involvement.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket collects critiques of governance and equity inside the school: nepotism, students being ‘bumped’ for revenue, administrators who are also coaches and thus unaccountable, selective enforcement of rules, and calls for board intervention — e.g., “nepotism and favoritism are beyond belief,” “How can coaches be reprimanded by administration when administration is a coach?,” and “rules only apply for certain people.” These concern fairness, accountability, and politicization of school decisions.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete stud: This bucket groups evidence of hands‑on, individualized supports: special‑education services and IEP implementation, para support, tutoring/after‑school remediation, formal mentoring programs, and college/counseling assistance (and conversely concrete failures of such services when present) — e.g., “My son was autistic and MTHS did everything (IEP, Para, Tutors),” “upper classmen mentor the freshman,” and “guidance counselors provided a lot of assistance with scholarships.” These items describe operational supports that directly affect individual students’ progress and inclusion.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe worse student sa: These reviews emphasize concrete safety/behavior breakdowns (frequent bullying, fights, gang and drug activity, sexualized harassment, shooting threats) and repeated staff/administrative inaction or victim‑blaming (e.g., “bullying happens every second…they do nothing,” “drug and gang problems…principal in denial,” “over 40 school shooting threats,” students selling bodies), whereas square reviews rarely report pervasive safety threats or systemic non‑response.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more extensive s: Many circle reviews list formal advanced programs and concrete outcomes — IB programs with scholarships, AP passes, dual‑enrollment, named academies (Biotech, Pre‑Law), vocational trades and CTA public‑safety pathways, and quantified college placements — while square reviews generally mention fewer formalized or documented postsecondary partnerships and less outcome evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more individualize: Circle reviewers repeatedly cite teacher availability, one‑on‑one tutoring, caring teachers, effective counselors and parent liaisons, and individual turnarounds (e.g., “teachers reserve time before and after school,” “counseling staff is great,” “before I came here I failed every class, now I'm passing”), whereas square reviews more often describe limited teacher/counselor time, unresponsiveness, or lack of individualized help.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater administra: Circle reviews provide concrete operational complaints—high leadership turnover, part‑time/interim principals, poor front‑office communication, enrollment surges/abandoned lottery, chronic HVAC or building issues, pay‑to‑participate fees and fundraising pressure, chaotic drop‑off/COVID screening logistics—while square reviews less frequently document this cluster of administrative instability and systemic operational failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more nepotism, ath: Circle reviewers frequently allege legacy/nepotistic treatment, preferential treatment for athletes/donors, parent‑clique/elitist cultures, and explicit exclusionary practices (race, religion, wealth, anti‑LGBT policies) — e.g., “kids who have been here their whole life get better positions,” “treated compared to kids that had rich parents who donated,” “Christianity is being shoved down their throats” — whereas square reviews do not substantively document this pattern.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more concrete ad: These reviews enumerate specific academic offerings, credentials and outcomes (AP/honors rosters, dual‑enrollment/college credit, named programs like PACE, vocational/technical academies, one‑to‑one device rollouts, stated AP/test/college admission statistics) while square entries rarely list such concrete program inventories or measurable postsecondary outcomes; examples include circle mentions of '5 AP courses,' 'direct admission into an architecture program,' 'one-to-one technology,' and explicit proficiency/AP/test-rate numbers versus square’s absence of comparable metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute safety: Multiple circle reviews describe severe incidents and institutional failure or concealment (students sent to ICU, active drug-dealing networks, pepper‑spray/chemical interventions, repeated drug‑dog lockdowns and claims that authorities protected dealers), allegations largely absent from square entries which describe behavioral problems more moderately.
candidate_defs.square entries report more chronic, inst: Square reviews repeatedly highlight ongoing peer bullying, classroom disruption and insufficient disciplinary response that harms instruction and drives families away (e.g., 'they have done absolutely NOTHING about it!', students planning to leave because of bad behavior, cliquey exclusion that undermines learning), whereas circle entries are more mixed on chronic bullying and often describe either effective discipline or different safety problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries show more frequent accoun: Circle reviews commonly describe proactive principals and responsive teachers/counselors, parent fundraising clubs, rapid teacher‑parent communication (email/Facebook homework posts), and visible administrative turnaround efforts (named principals praised), whereas square reviews less often report this sustained parent-facing responsiveness or organized fundraising activity.
candidate_defs.circle entries contain far more detailed: Circle reviewers supply granular IEP/504 narratives, transition‑planning breakdowns, calls for parent advocacy, both praise for attentive IEP staff and warnings about abandoned 504s and guidance mismanagement (e.g., 'Transition Planning Meeting at age 16 has yet to take place,' 'If your child has ADD/ADHD... they will develop a 504 plan but quickly abandon it'), while square reviews only rarely mention special‑education coordination.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews repeatedly report concrete advanced-course offerings, AP/IB/dual‑enrollment pathways, college credit accumulation, and higher-ranked/graduation metrics (e.g., “top AP school… students walked into college with 12 credit hours,” “recognized by U.S. News”), plus descriptions of heavier homework and intentional college‑prep rigor that are absent or weaker in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent stud: Many circle reviews document pervasive student misconduct and unsafe incidents (gang/drug use, after‑school fights, teen pregnancy, racial/physical attacks), often paired with ineffective enforcement or counselor nonresponse (e.g., “I was getting bullied… nothing was done,” “drugs are a horrible problem”), complaints that square reviews do not generalize to the same degree.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more explicit in: Circle reviewers frequently foreground faith‑based missions, Catholic/Christian identity and spiritual formation and also report religious conformity, intolerance of dissenting beliefs, and favoritism tied to church/staff relationships (e.g., “Catholic… many teachers don’t respect opinions that differ from a Catholic viewpoint,” “if you have an issue with a student related to a pastor good luck”), a pattern not present in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries surface more concrete fac: Circle reviews provide tangible descriptions of facilities and resource choices—new buildings, championship band/football fields, strong STEAM labs or conversely rotting infrastructure, pest infestations, broken toilets, and opaque fundraising/scholarship practices (e.g., “new football field” and also “infested with bats…where has the fundraising money gone?”)—whereas square reviews rarely present this same level of facility/resource detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries give more specific operat: Circle reviewers describe fine‑grained policies and services—magnet programs and internships, block scheduling, PLUS periods, transportation logistics and long bus rides, detailed IEP or counseling failures and also strong special‑education supports in other cases, and lottery/tuition/transfer access barriers (e.g., “magnet communications program… internships,” “Students with IEPs are set up to fail,” “lottery admission, long waiting list”), content that square reviews do not document as often.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger parenta: These reviews emphasize active parent volunteering, organized parent programs, tight alumni networks, small class sizes and counselors with smaller caseloads (e.g., parents observing classrooms, Parents in Partnership, alumni involvement, ’small class sizes allow them to actually get to KNOW each student’), whereas square reviews rarely report the same level of two‑way community involvement or schoolwide personalization.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviews contain repeated, concrete complaints about unresponsive or deceitful leadership, staff inaction during bullying, inappropriate staff behavior, and poor parent‑school communication (e.g., ‘school administration is horrible’, ‘teachers not once did they interfere’, ‘you are always lied to as a parent’), while circle reviews more often describe engaged or visible principals and proactive administrative initiatives.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, applied a: Circle reviews repeatedly describe hands‑on CTE/vocational programs, dual enrollment and IB/AP supports, school‑paid concurrent college classes, measurable scholarship/graduation statistics and college‑credit outcomes (examples: welding/culinary/Audio Production pathways, ‘associate degree while in high school’, $9M in scholarships, IB teacher exam prep), whereas square reviews rarely provide equivalent evidence of diverse CTE pathways or documented college‑credit/scholarship outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more entrenched: Many circle reviews allege preferential treatment tied to last names, donors, athletes, multi‑generational families, or shared faith—plus selective access to programs and arts funding (e.g., ‘if you don’t have the right last name…’, ‘donors get away with anything’, overt religious instruction claims)—whereas square reviews report cliques or athletic status but not the same degree of nepotistic, donor‑or faith‑based gatekeeping.
candidate_defs.circle entries provide far more concrete: Circle reviews frequently give detailed accounts of buildings, capital projects, 1:1 devices, or acute facility failures and overcrowding (examples: new oceanfront campus and SmartBoards; ‘more trailers than ever’, rats in the cafeteria, 4 bathrooms for 400+ students), while square reviews seldom include this level of detailed, concrete facility/resource reporting.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive on-: This bucket groups reviews that describe frequent fights, ongoing bullying/harassment (including racial and LGBTQ+ targeting), police/bomb-threat incidents, sexual/physical abuse and resulting psychiatric crises, and administrators who ignore or tolerate these safety problems (e.g., “police are there constantly, bomb threats,” “bullying is rampant,” “I was being bullied, sexually harrassed and physically abused…had to go into psychiatric care”).
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, higher‑le: This bucket captures reviews describing substantive program breadth and successes — multiple AP/dual‑enrollment pathways, specialized electives (organic chemistry, bio‑chem, app design, engineering), strong CTE/vocational and agricultural/FFA programs, award‑winning music/arts and national rankings, and measurable college‑credit outcomes (e.g., '26 and 32 hours of college credit,' 'award‑winning Drama Program').
candidate_defs.circle entries report more systemic inst: This groups descriptions of school‑level academic breakdowns and process failures such as frequent schedule/policy changes that harm learning, removed deadlines/credits, misplacement and unapproved credit recovery (E2020), year‑long teacher vacancies, poor curriculum/grading practices, and alleged special‑education/regulatory violations (e.g., 'constantly change schedules…doing away with deadlines', 'E2020…not approved', 'not having a Mandarin teacher for a whole year', 'Consultative model for special education - what.a.joke').
candidate_defs.circle entries report stricter, more pun: This bucket covers concrete accounts of heavy-handed or monetized enforcement — strict dress/grooming/ID rules, punitive attendance/credit removal, expulsions for off‑campus behavior, fines/withheld records or tuition differentials, and enforcement applied inconsistently or to punish broad groups (e.g., 'mandatory ID…harassed by the APs to cut my hair', 'credits removed because reviewer would not attend Saturday', 'holding transcripts hostage', 'punish both schools instead of the two students').
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger small‑tow: This bucket groups reviews that emphasize a family‑style, community/faith identity, active parent/alumni engagement, campus ministry/retreats, and frequent individualized teacher/counselor attention (e.g., 'Families first', 'Campus Ministry is amazing', 'you get the one on one time with the teachers', 'parents look out for one another'), signaling tighter local social oversight and personalized supports compared with square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reviews that describe frequent bullying, physical fights, gang pressure, homophobia/racism/sexism, and administrators or staff who fail to protect victims (e.g., “bullying non-stop…and not a thing was done,” “fights and drug use are everyday occurrences,” “Racism is the norm,” and officers making bullied students return to cafeteria instead of counseling). Square entries rarely make these broad claims and instead focus on isolated incidents or improved discipline, so any review alleging ongoing peer‑to‑peer harm and systemic failure to address it falls here.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups reviews alleging governance problems, secretive or dishonest leadership, misallocated spending, manipulated performance data, punitive policies, and nontransparent surveillance (examples: “superintendent will lie straight to your face,” “school data is not reliable…manipulation from new principal,” “substance abuse testing program that is not random or transparent,” and “withholding transcripts for financial reasons”). Square reviews generally praise or criticize only specific school leaders rather than alleging district‑level corruption or covert policy abuse, so reviews describing opaque, politicized, or retaliatory leadership behavior belong here.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, more e: This bucket includes reviews that list concrete rigorous coursework and measurable outcomes—many AP/Honors offerings, Scholars/STEM programs, IB references, Ivy/Intel/major scholarship claims, and documented alumni college progress (e.g., “they offer a LOT of AP classes,” “Scholars program…engineering offered to freshmen,” “students accepted into Ivy League…Bill Gates Millennium Scholarship,” and “many Intel finalists”). Square entries, by contrast, either omit these specific advanced-program details or report weaker college preparedness, so reviews supplying named advanced-program descriptions and cohort/award evidence are captured here.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize a stronger, vis: This bucket captures reviews focused on extracurricular breadth and local tradition: active community events, award‑winning music/arts, state champion teams, FFA scholarships, alumni networks, stadium culture, and claims that funding or attention is shifted toward athletics (examples: “orchestra and jazz orchestra competing nationally,” “state champion teams…one of the best softball programs,” “FFA scholarship,” “multi‑million dollar football stadium,” and “they play favorites with athletes”). Square reviews rarely enumerate the same breadth of traditions or named extracurricular accolades, so any review emphasizing visible community rituals, alumni engagement, or sports/arts‑first resource choices belongs here.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more inadequate su: This bucket groups reviews alleging refusal or inability to accommodate IEPs, pushing out low‑performing students to protect scores, minimal special‑education instruction, and lack of counseling/tutoring (e.g., “they could not help my son…did not have the staff,” “anything and everything…to get them out of the district so it doesn't bring down test scores,” “special education is more like babysitting than education,” and families paying for private tutors). Square entries rarely make these claims, so items describing denied services, procedural obstacles to IEPs, or systemic exclusion of vulnerable students are placed here.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader and strong: These reviews repeatedly name specific rigorous offerings and measurable postsecondary results (e.g., 25+ AP courses, IB/STEM academies, CTE trade certifications, 'over 60 free college hours' via a university partnership, and alumni at top universities), whereas square reviews typically note limited AP/honors access or lack of advanced-track detail and report under‑preparation for college.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more severe stud: Multiple circle reviews cite concrete safety incidents and systemic failures (stabbings, metal detectors, drugs in middle grades, racial/sexual harassment chants, staff‑perpetrated bullying, mediation instead of formal action, and ignored threat reports), portraying both higher-severity incidents and administration toleration that square reviews do not document.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more consistent: Square reviewers repeatedly praise professional, accommodating staff, functioning parent portals and device rollouts (e.g., Chromebook program), and proactive counselor outreach, while circle reviews more often report poor communication, lost credits, misallocated funds, or uneven recordkeeping as operational weak points.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize richer extracur: Circle reviews enumerate extensive, high‑quality extracurriculars (elite performing-arts claims, large band/orchestra, varsity sports milestones, extensive clubs, new fine-arts centers) and note active parent, alumni, and community investment (parents buying houses, alumni returning), whereas square reviews lack comparable program breadth and sometimes report athletic decline.
candidate_defs.circle entries report a smaller-school s: Many circle reviews highlight K–12 or small-district models, manageable class ratios, one-on-one teacher support, principals who 'know every kid,' and long enrollment continuity, while square reviews emphasize larger high‑school campuses, crowding, and a more competitive, less individualized environment.
candidate_defs.circle entries report far more pervasive: This bucket captures concrete reports that circle schools suffer recurring physical and psychological safety problems (e.g., 'Bullying is out of control,' 'Sexual assault, bullying, and racial bias are rampant,' 'GANG ACTIVITY... kids being assaulted,' reports of sex/drug use on campus and students driven to anxiety or depression), whereas square entries do not provide comparable allegations of sustained violence or campus‑wide safety crises.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more systemic admi: This groups claims about governance and fairness: circle reviews allege the system 'is run by a select group,' '85–90% of the coaches are alumni' who hand‑pick teams, administrators 'protect tenured teachers,' retaliate against parents, 'would rather believe rumors than investigate,' or block transfers/transcripts — problems that square reviews do not characterize at the same systemic level.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater staffing a: This bucket covers workforce and classroom delivery issues such as 'no science teachers... substitutes (babysitters) and virtual teachers,' 'a third of the faculty left,' 'teachers unqualified,' 'grading system is a mess,' and counselor failures to send college documents or to support special‑education needs — operational and instructional breakdowns largely absent from square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more concrete, n: This groups programmatic strengths and pathway evidence: circle reviews frequently list 'lots of AP and honors classes,' IB workload, dual‑enrollment and college partnerships, specialized curricula (Mock Trial, Social Justice, CTE pathways), and high‑achieving extracurriculars (national‑award choirs, robotics, state championships), while square reviews provide fewer specific advanced program partnerships or documented outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report worse physical fac: This bucket collects concrete facility and resourcing complaints: circle reviewers cite severe overcrowding ('2,200 kids in a school for 1,500,' 'classes of 45'), mobile classrooms by a sewage pond, filthy restrooms, cafeteria strikes, lack of books and program cuts, whereas square reviews rarely describe similar environmental or capacity hazards.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, specific: These reviews describe concrete curricular offerings and outcomes (IB/MYP, AP, dual‑credit, honors tracks, high ACT scores, full‑ride scholarships and named alumni college placements) that indicate an organized college‑prep pathway at circle schools; square reviews rarely name real programs or provide systematic metrics and often describe uneven or poor college preparation instead (examples: IB diploma, dual enrollment, 32 ACT, alumni at UNC/Boston University vs. square's vague AP mentions or claims of inadequate preparation).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Circle reviews frequently document violent or targeted incidents (death threats, students filmed in restrooms, repeated fights, racial and homophobic harassment) and describe staff/administration failing to contain or respond, whereas square reviews mention fewer or more isolated behavior problems and often note better day‑to‑day order or disciplinary clarity (examples: filmed restroom incident, death threats, staff inaction on bullying).
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader and better: Circle reviews list extensive non‑academic programs (marching band state championships, choir/performing arts, drama/production, culinary, broadcast, vocational shops, ROTC, robotics, strong CTE pathways and work‑study) and concrete extracurricular successes, while square reviews rarely enumerate such breadth or achievements and instead emphasize a narrower program mix or academic concerns (examples: state marching band wins, culinary/chef teachers, commercial baking, engineering programs, robotics placements).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: These items describe managerial and operational failures at circle schools—rude or unresponsive principals, lost records, deflection to websites, alleged cover‑ups, misused funds, fee mismanagement, and retaliatory behavior—that create systemic problems for families and staff; square reviews contain fewer of these organizational‑mismanagement claims and often highlight more effective leadership or clearer communication (examples: secretaries doing 'dirty work', administrators accused of taking raises while cutting electives, lost transcripts, demands for apology).
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger socioecon: Circle reviews repeatedly cite social stratification and exclusion driven by wealth, religion, race, or athletic status—wealthy/connected parents getting privileges, non‑Catholics feeling excluded, racial bias toward Black males, favoritism toward football players and other cliques—whereas square reviews rarely describe such systemic social gatekeeping and often emphasize more inclusive spirit or different social dynamics (examples: wealthy parents ensuring advantages, 'if you aren't Catholic you will be made to feel like an outsider', favoritism for athletes).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures reviews that describe chronic governance failures at the school/district level—frequent principal turnover, unresponsive or rude principals/superintendents, cover‑ups or unequal discipline, nepotism/good‑ol‑boy hiring, and politicized decision‑making (examples: “3 principals in 4 years,” “they cover up and hide student serious offenses,” “ran off the Good Ol' Boy system,” “principal was rude and disrespectful,” “Superintendent Aten is incompetent”). These items are about leadership, governance and how administrators handle policy, complaints, and staffing rather than classroom instruction or facilities.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups reviews reporting widespread student misconduct and a failure to protect students—peer racial/ethnic/sexual harassment, assaults, targeted searches, interschool fights, students with criminal records, sexual misconduct allegations, and staff enabling or ignoring victims (examples: “kids are racist…teachers do nothing,” “teacher assaulted a student and school refused to discipline,” “students making out in hallways,” “children with criminal records threatening…and no discipline,” “we had to threaten a lawsuit over blatant bullying”). These refer to on‑campus safety, peer harassment, and the school's (in)ability to investigate or intervene.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute facilit: This bucket covers concrete physical‑plant and resourcing failures described in reviews—aging or inadequate buildings, HVAC/boiler failures and extreme classroom temperatures, overcrowding/insufficient seats, missing athletic fields or cafeterias, pest/mold infestations, and contested spending choices (examples: “no working AC…rooms reaching 95°F,” “no cafeteria…no track on the field,” “overcrowded…students sit on the ground,” “riddled with roaches and rats,” “they put all of the money into the football program”). These items focus on infrastructure, capacity and how financial/resource choices affect facilities and student access to basics.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, more e: This bucket groups reviews that highlight substantive curricular breadth and student outcomes—named magnet/IB/VPA/STEM/medical academies, wide AP/dual‑credit offerings, early college credit, National Merit/college acceptances, scholarships and rising test scores (examples: “IB and VPA programs…prepared me well for college,” “state of the art STEM facilities allow students to earn college credit their freshman year,” “Both my sister and I were named National Merit Scholars,” “test scores have blossomed through the last 5 years”). These are structural academic assets and measurable outcomes (courses, pathways, scores, acceptances), distinct from interpersonal teacher support or administration behavior.
candidate_defs.square entries report more programmatic: This bucket captures reviews where square schools are described as having clear program structures (electives, pathways, year‑long research), accessible and responsive administration, praised guidance counselors, and evidence of recent academic gains (examples: “Administration is open to feedback and acts on it,” “many electives, pathways and year-long research” and “My grades improved dramatically,” “The counselors are always there to help you”). These items emphasize systematized supports, administrative responsiveness, and visible improvement rather than the facility, safety, or governance failures captured elsewhere.
candidate_defs.circle entries document stronger, named: These reviews repeatedly list AP/IB/dual-enrollment offerings, named academies/majors (Engineering, Health, DASH), high test rankings and concrete college placements (US News rank, API scores, scholarship/acceptances), and explicit college-prep supports—e.g., “International Baccalaureate…top classes…US News #5,” “many APs available,” and “both my children were accepted to great colleges.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Many circle reviews describe recurring fights, pervasive bullying (including race/LGBTQ+ harassment), substance incidents, ignored reports, and weak or permissive discipline—examples include “at least 2 fights a month,” “administration turned a blind eye,” and “racism is non stop…administration will do nothing,” whereas square reviews present fewer or more promptly handled safety incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe worse physical f: Circle reviewers cite leaking ceilings, mold in food, unflushed toilets, portable classroom pods and severe overcrowding/parking strain—e.g., “ceilings in classroom still leak,” “MAJOR COMPLAINT: This school is OVERCROWDED…pods used as classrooms,” and “mold in the applesauce,” while square reviews generally lack comparable facility or food‑safety reports.
candidate_defs.circle entries evidence more administrat: Circle reviews frequently allege nepotism, politicized hiring, enrollment/recordkeeping errors, placating parents, opaque selective admissions, and poor front‑office responsiveness—examples: “Nepotism, Politics, and Cliques run this school,” “constant change of faculty,” “we cannot get return calls from the principal,” and misplaced selective-admission slots—patterns square reviews do not describe as often.
candidate_defs.circle entries show greater intra-school: Circle content often contains both strong, named program/coach/teacher endorsements (award‑winning band, top varsity coaches, excellent math programs) and crisp complaints about other programs or departments, plus high turnover—e.g., “varied by shop…some amazing physics teachers” alongside “constant change of faculty” or “one of the best advanced math programs” — indicating sharper program-level splits than the more uniformly described staff quality in square reviews.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report stronger and more: These entries describe concrete curricular strength (IB/AP/honors/dual‑credit, wall‑to‑wall IB expansion, heavy homework/readings, AP credit leading to advanced college standing) and cite measurable outcomes (higher ACT/PSAT scores, high college‑acceptance/elite placements). Example evidence: “definitely a college prep school… Expect to read 3–4 classic books,” “Last year 98% of the students were accepted to college,” and “I went into college as basically a sophomore due to taking so many AP tests.”
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more serious and f: These entries document recurring, concrete safety problems—frequent fights/lockdowns, bomb threats, sexual activity on campus, pervasive bullying (including against autistic and Black students), and episodes of theft/record manipulation—that materially affect school climate and student safety. Example evidence: “They have lockdowns every other week,” “Autistic son… bullied constantly everyday,” “There are fights at least once a week,” and “if you're black… you need to have thick skin.”
candidate_defs.Square entries report more pervasive unq: Square entries more often allege systemic teacher problems—underqualified or disengaged staff protected by tenure, low instructional rigor for gifted students, frequent teacher inattentiveness or disrespect, and administrative inaction to hold poor teachers accountable. Example evidence: “Administrators are unqualified… Most teacher can't teach worth anything… because of tenure, they stay,” and “most of the teachers are unchallenging and unsupportive of intelligent students.”
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more robust extrac: These entries list concrete, well‑developed outside‑class opportunities—championship athletics, award‑winning bands/arts, active booster clubs and alumni involvement, strong vocational/Votech/ROTC programs, and regional/international competition or internships—often tied to visible outcomes. Example evidence: “we have just won a football and baseball 1‑A state championship,” “The band director goes above and beyond,” “Amazing FFA Chapter,” and “afforded me the chance to take courses at CCAC / internships.”
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more individualize: Circle reviews more often describe one‑on‑one registration counseling, accessible counselors and guidance, concrete IEP/medical accommodations, 1:1 device programs and school‑run college‑credit/A+ pathways, and active casework to keep students on track. Example evidence: “personal, one‑on‑one counseling when registering,” “she has an IEP… a 10 am late start IF NEEDED for her epilepsy,” “every student get a laptop,” and “My daughter graduated with many college credits. The A+ program is a big help.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe safety: This bucket collects reviews describing acute student safety and conduct failures at the school — frequent bullying, fights, drug use, riots/lockdowns, police presence, staff‑perpetrated bullying or active siding with perpetrators, and either no meaningful sanctions or punishment biased toward athletes; examples include accounts of students being beaten while teachers look away, regular police involvement, drug incidents, and parents saying administrators only require a verbal apology instead of suspension.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, more spe: This groups comments that describe concrete programmatic academic strength — thriving IB/AP/STEM/arts conservatory tracks, paid dual‑credit options, vocational/magnet offerings, documented scholarship and elite college matriculation — e.g., IB full‑diploma recipients, STEM labs, arts conservatory rigor, paid dual‑credit hours and named scholarships or university acceptances, contrasted with square’s weaker or declining academic claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more systemic admi: This bucket covers reviewer claims about leadership misconduct and decision practices — nepotistic promotions, money‑driven policies, blocking parent safety programs, favoritism toward athletes or out‑of‑district transfers, and opaque/exclusionary admission behavior; examples include allegations that hiring is denomination‑based, the superintendent resisted anti‑drug programs, and spots are saved for coaches’ friends or donors.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more special‑educa: This captures evidence that the school struggles to serve students with disabilities — staff/administration failing to honor IEPs, exclusionary practices, inadequate or retaliatory treatment of special‑needs students, and budget‑driven cancellation of services, as illustrated by parents saying administrators won’t comply with IEPs, special‑ed classes are misused, or special needs students are "squeezed out."
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete faci: This bucket groups reviews that supply specific, operational facts about the building and resources (e.g., brand‑new $75M facility, planetarium, 3D‑printing labs, or conversely mice/pool sanitation problems, trailers, overcrowding, scheduling mistakes, and documented tutoring/‘help night’ programs), which contrasts with square reviews that mostly mention general crowding or program-level claims without the same level of concrete facility/operational detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize broader, higher: This bucket groups raw terms where circle reviews describe conservatory‑style arts, award‑winning bands/drama, extensive music programs, no‑cut sports, frequent off‑campus trips, and championship‑caliber teams (e.g., “art school,” “3‑time national championship winning band,” “no cut sports, no pay to play,” band/fine‑arts trips) while square reviews lack comparable claims of arts/championship breadth or student‑led extracurricular scope.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: Includes items where circle reviewers cite AP/IB strength, dual‑credit/college partnerships (Kirkwood, Bucknell, U of I), high AP/ACT pass rates, quantified metrics and concrete college matriculation (e.g., 'entered college a full semester ahead with AP credits,' 'increase CCRPI by over 10 points,' '98% college placement'), whereas square reviews do not provide the same programmatic detail or measurable college‑prep outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Groups raw terms that describe square as having recurring safety and climate problems—bus fights, spit attacks, vaping, daily fights, racial bullying and harassment—and administrators who fail to resolve or respond effectively (e.g., 'bullying is an issue… bus bullying and spit attacks,' 'the staff does NOTHING about it'), whereas circle reviews more often describe anti‑bullying enforcement or safer/closeness claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more governance in: Covers raw terms reporting high principal turnover, weak/disconnected school boards, calls for investigations or administrative leave, adversarial parent‑administration relationships, suppression of protests (e.g., pulling a fire alarm), lawsuits, nepotism and secrecy ('6 or 7 different Principals in the last 5 years,' 'an impartial investigation at once,' 'the admin/board is comprised of the same people'), while square reviews rarely raise comparable governance‑level accusations.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more individuali: This bucket groups evidence where circle reviewers report frequent one‑on‑one interactions, teachers staying after for homework help, peer tutoring and mentoring programs, strong school‑to‑home communication, and responsive guidance (e.g., 'teachers are willing to stay after just to help,' 'popular and successful peer tutoring program,' 'The level of communication from school to home is by far the best'), whereas square reviews give fewer concrete examples of routine, individualized academic or emotional support.
candidate_defs.circle entries show stronger, documented: These reviews describe concrete academic strength at circle schools — AP/honors-heavy curricula, dedicated college counseling, internships/fellowships, measurable college admissions and scholarships, tutoring/after‑school help, and small-class/one‑on‑one teacher availability (examples: multiple circle reviews cite AP classes, 'got into 4 of 4 universities with partial scholarships,' active guidance counselors, zero‑hour tutoring and teacher availability before/after school).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent seve: Circle reviews contain repeated, specific allegations of bullying, daily racial harassment, frequent fights, drug/weapon incidents and staff or administrative failure to protect victims (examples: students 'fighting constantly and being weapons,' 'racist remarks are heard and NOT DEALT with,' parents withdrawing children after unaddressed assaults), often tying safety failures to administrators who are dismissive or slow to act.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more socioeconom: Many circle reviews document the school siphoning enrollment, selective admission/tuition pressures, favoritism toward wealthy/athletic families, entrenched alumni staffing/cronyism, and explicit push‑out practices (examples: claims that the school 'drains diversity and enrollment from local public schools,' 'good school if you're rich or athletic,' nepotistic hiring, and forcing struggling students into alternative placements).
candidate_defs.circle entries report worse physical con: Circle reviews frequently cite overcrowded classrooms and cafeterias, broken/unsanitary facilities and food‑safety issues (rats, rotten food), outdated/locked‑down technology, and visible or intrusive security practices (armed guards, K9 searches, random whole‑class searches), documenting tangible facility and security arrangements not described in square entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more instructional: Square reviews more often describe teachers who don't provide one‑on‑one help, unresponsive or negligent counselors/administration (e.g., poor handling of sexual‑assault/mental‑health concerns), a chaotic/undermining student atmosphere, and recurring parent suggestions to transfer or choose alternatives (examples: reviewers urging 'move/put them in online school/GED,' 'counselor was beyond ridiculous,' and 'not an inspiring learning environment').
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reviews describing physical fights, gang or probationer presence, widespread substance use, staff‑perpetrated abuse, and sustained race/sexuality‑based harassment (e.g., “fights everyday,” “haven for gang thugs,” easy on‑campus drug access, “i have been getting harassed... if you are not white,” and teacher abuse allegations) — contrasted with square reviews that either omit such violence or depict manageable, addressed incidents. Content belongs here when reviewers describe concrete safety threats, frequent physical fights, gang/drug exposure, or systemic failure to protect marginalized students.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, more doc: This groups reviews that cite AP/IB/dual‑enrollment offerings, state test and ACT/EOC metrics, rapid improvements, and concrete college/scholarship outcomes (e.g., “offers the third most dual enrollment courses,” “higher ACT/EOC scores,” “students accepted to Ivy/earned scholarships,” “College‑in‑High‑School credit”), whereas square reviews more often note absence of gifted programs, declining academics, or weak college preparation. Include any review that emphasizes program breadth/rigor, documented test/performance data, or tangible postsecondary results.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more individuali: This bucket covers reviewer claims of small classes, one‑on‑one teacher attention, frequent remediation/tutoring, and named teachers who personally supported students (e.g., “teacher to student ratio is nice and small,” “abundant opportunities for students to get help,” and multiple named teacher praises), while square reviews more often report mixed/unresponsive classroom practice and lack of individualized help. Use this label for content focused on teacher‑delivered instructional access, differentiated pacing, or sustained personal support from classroom staff.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader extracurri: This bucket groups reviews that list many clubs/athletics, modern facilities/1:1 laptops, expanded sports and career academies, or complaints that funding favors athletics over arts (e.g., “brand new and technologically advanced,” “tons of AP classes and many clubs,” and “they give all the funding to the sports teams… drama program cut”), whereas square reviews typically describe fewer programs or resource shortages. Apply this when a review’s primary evidence concerns physical facilities, technology, program breadth, or visible funding/prioritization tradeoffs.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger parental/: This bucket captures reviews describing concentrated parent or elite family influence, faith‑based institutional identity, lottery/selective admissions complaints, politicized school‑board/admin choices, and nepotistic discipline/extracurricular favoritism (e.g., “completely controlled by prominent families,” “academic excellence in a community of faith,” magnet admissions disadvantaging local students, withholding graduation regalia for unpaid fees, and parent‑run selection of teams), while square reviews do not foreground these governance/community power dynamics. Use this label for content that centers on who controls access/resources and how community/board/parent power and identity shape policies and student experience.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student-safet: These reviews describe concrete safety failures (frequent fights, code-red lockdowns, students bringing guns, sexual manipulation of younger students, recurring locker-thefts) coupled with ineffective or inconsistent enforcement (light or no punishment for athletes, suspensions as primary response, staff tolerance of bullying). Example evidence: "Too many code red this year," "students brought guns... were not expelled," and "bullying issues that STILL haven't been addressed," whereas square reviews rarely report weapons/frequent fights or systemic non-enforcement.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more special-educa: Many circle reviews cite lost records, failure to follow IEPs/504s, poor transition/read‑through of special‑education files, unsafe treatment of students with disabilities, and escalation to legal action; e.g. "they don't follow IEP'S AND 504'S," "lost his records... I had to do everything all over again," and "physically abused by at least 2 different CPS aids." Square reviews do not contain comparable clusters of special‑education noncompliance or record/legal failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries highlight more concrete a: Circle reviewers frequently enumerate named, structured offerings (AP/IB, dual-enrollment, Running Start, vocational tracks like culinary and healthcare, FFA, Girls Leadership Academy) and cite quantifiable outcomes (large scholarship totals, top-college matriculation, state athletic championships); examples include "more than 30 clubs," "a graduating class... earned about eight million dollars in scholarship money," and "culinary program... named chefs." Square reviews tend to reference fewer named programmatic pathways and provide less evidence of such measurable postsecondary/career outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more personalize: Numerous circle reviews describe smaller class sizes, one-on-one time, caring/identified teachers and deans who monitor progress and produce turnarounds (named teachers, academic dean interventions, students graduating early or improving dramatically after targeted support); e.g. "smaller class sizes... more one on one time," "The Academic Dean... continually monitoring students," and "My son went from possible drop‑out to all college‑bound classes." Square reviews more often report inconsistent or unavailable individualized help.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviews concentrate complaints about politicized boards, superintendent/principal incompetence or turnover, nepotism/union control, contested spending priorities, budget-driven program cuts, and operational breakdowns (busing, overcrowding, technology, lunch, maintenance); examples include "too many chiefs and not enough Indians," "waste of money on 3 flat screen plasmas," "busing is horrible…drivers hopping curbs," and repeated notes of budget cuts or construction halted—problems that square reviews mention far less or not at all.
candidate_defs.circle entries have more extensive advan: These reviews repeatedly describe concrete program breadth and measurable college-credit outcomes (AP counts, IB pathways, dual‑enrollment, High Tech Academy, aviation/CTE magnets and National Merit recognition) that square entries do not (examples: “offer many AP as well as concurrent college credit… graduate with over 40 hours of college credit,” “access to High Tech Academy,” “The IB Program is exceptional,” and numerous CTE/magnet certification claims). Falling into this bucket means the school review emphasizes institutionalized advanced-course pathways, formal college credit accrual, or vocational-to‑certification pipelines as a dominant feature.
candidate_defs.circle entries report smaller enrollment: Many circle reviews highlight small graduating classes, close-knit alumni/teacher ties, families moving or choosing the district for the school, mandated/structured volunteer programs, and intensive parent involvement (examples: “graduating class … less than 45,” “moved to this area specifically,” “lottery based” and “parents serve 10 hrs/year”), whereas square reviews more often imply larger scale and less of that intimate community model. This bucket groups reviews that foreground small‑school personalization and active community/parent partnership as a core operational trait.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: Multiple circle reviews document grave safety and wellbeing concerns—student suicides, weapons, gang activity, repeated fights, drug problems, bomb/shot threats, and diagnosed depression tied to on-campus bullying (examples: “number of suicides… absolutely shocking,” “students bringing weapons,” “every week there are at least 3 to 5 fights,” and students diagnosed with depression forced into homeschooling) — problems that square entries rarely describe at that severity. Reviews in this bucket center the school's climate around chronic/serious safety or mental‑health crises and ineffective mitigation.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive tea: Square reviews more often describe passive in‑class practices, teachers who ‘don’t teach’ or give busywork, uneven grading and low expectations, and advice to look elsewhere for academic challenge (examples: comments that academics “is certainly not its strong point,” teachers who ‘give you a worksheet…or put on a movie,’ and warnings “if you want to be academically challenged, you should look elsewhere”). This bucket captures reviews that portray instructional neglect, chronic low rigor, or widely inconsistent classroom practice as the defining academic problem.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Many circle reviews allege concrete governance and operational breakdowns—unresponsive principals, nepotism/political hiring, bungled transfers/records, withheld report cards for meal debt, misplaced buses/trips, and gaming of awards (examples: “principal is uninvolved and will NOT return parents' phone calls,” “they even flat lied saying my student had been withdrawn… kept my student active,” “horrendous nepotism,” and “pulled teachers to fill out Blue Ribbon paperwork”). This bucket groups reviews that emphasize systemic administrative misconduct, poor operations, or institutional corruption as the salient organizational issue.
candidate_defs.circle entries report far more pervasive: This bucket describes reviews that recount routine physical fights, drug activity, racial slurs, homophobic/sexist harassment, threats or suicide-related incidents and claims that staff either ignore complaints or mete out uneven punishments (e.g., “a lot of bullying happens… teachers and counselors do diddly squat,” “my son has been beaten up four times,” “kids doing drugs in the bathroom or on the bus,” favoritism protects bullies). These items emphasize on-campus safety breakdowns and inadequate or discriminatory adult responses, in contrast to Square reviews that generally describe safer or better‑managed student behavior.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more extensive f: This bucket captures reviews that list concrete program infrastructure and outcomes—multiple AP/IB offerings, dual‑enrollment/Running Start, named career academies and industry certifications, internships with partner companies, large scholarship totals and college recruitment/acceptances (e.g., 'offers more AP courses than any other school', 'over $16 million in scholarships', 'Running Start and Sno‑Isle technical programs'). These items focus on formal program breadth and documented college/career outcomes, a set of concrete offerings and metrics reported far more often in Circle than in Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups reviewer claims about leadership and district failures—frequent principal/superintendent turnover, secretive or arbitrary firings, nepotism/favoritism, deliberate image‑management or suppressed complaints—and related operational breakdowns such as lost transcripts, scheduling errors, inaccessible counselors, 50% grading policies, and intentional credit manipulation (e.g., 'They keep everything a secret... fired a great teacher,' 'Counselors are never available,' 'lost testing scores,' 'some teachers are purposely failing the students meaning more money for the school'). These are governance and service-delivery problems distinct from classroom instruction and are reported more often in Circle.
candidate_defs.circle entries provide far more concrete: This bucket covers reviews giving specific, tangible accounts of the physical plant and resourcing choices—new renovations and domes, AstroTurf and field spending versus cuts to orchestra/Latin, crowded/locked restrooms, expired milk and long cafeteria lines or tiny portions, school bus routes, security staff presence, and active fundraising/tuition demands (e.g., 'huge expenditures on new fields', 'one slice of pizza and a milk carton', '$300 raffle tickets and $700+ monthly tuition'). These material, logistical, and funding-level details appear substantially more often in Circle reviews than in Square.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger teacher c: This bucket collects reviews that emphasize a demanding, fast‑paced instructional model with teachers who push students, expect ownership, provide regular help (extra help at lunch, consistent progress communication), and sustain academic accountability (e.g., 'The teachers won't baby you… students do have to take ownership,' 'The commitment of faculty and staff is tremendous,' 'Counselors are top notch… teachers usually keep in touch'), positioning classroom practice and staff dedication as the school's primary strengths relative to Circle.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger academic: This bucket groups raw items where reviewers say the circle school provides real academic rigor and pathways (AP/IB/Honors/Dual enrollment, early‑college partnerships, high test scores, scholarship dollars, concrete selective college acceptances and vocational certifications) that square reviews do not document; examples include claims of Ivy/MD/engineer matriculation, ‘millions in scholarship money annually,’ IB/early college programs, and robust AP/honors options versus square’s reports of restricted AP access and students unprepared for college.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reviews that describe frequent/serious student misconduct (bullying, gang formation, mass fights, sexual assaults, weapon incidents) combined with staff/administration failing to stop or actively mishandling incidents; illustrative evidence includes statements like ‘the bullying is out of control,’ ‘gangs are formed,’ ‘17 fights in one day,’ and ‘teachers/administration just look the other way’ which square reviews generally do not assert.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more facility, mai: This grouping gathers items about physical-plant and operational breakdowns at circle schools—poor cleanliness (no soap, roaches/rats), torn‑down labs, lack of air conditioning, severe overcrowding, restricted restrooms causing health issues, and bus/commute failures—contrasted with square reviews that tend to describe functioning or recently upgraded facilities.
