candidate_defs.circle entries report greater extracurri: This bucket groups reports that circle schools offer a wide range of well‑resourced extracurriculars (award‑winning arts, nationally ranked athletics, strong vocational/shop programs, robust band/drumline, internships/community partnerships) and sometimes explicitly prioritize athletics over academics or reallocate facilities for sports; examples include high‑profile athletic rankings, fully equipped automotive and shop programs, well‑funded arts, and claims that ‘the football team gets all the funding’—features not emphasized in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This theme covers concrete governance and personnel problems alleged about circle schools—pay/turnover issues, crony hiring and favoritism, punitive discipline and threats (CPS or expulsions), mishandled records/billing, PR solicitation, politicized district decisions, and generally rude or inaccessible front‑office staff—often described with specific incidents (withheld diplomas, lost transcripts, ‘good old boy’ hiring) that square reviews do not make.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced-: This bucket captures reviews that describe concrete curricular strength and postsecondary success at circle schools — e.g., multiple mentions of heavy AP/Honors enrollment, Dual Enrollment college credits (‘my daughter graduated with four college classes completed through Dual Enrollment’), large scholarship totals (‘Students have earned over 3 million dollars in scholarships’), and Ivy/merit acceptances — contrasted with square reviews that describe low rigor, falling rankings, or students being "just passed along" and lacking clear college-readiness programs.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent stud: This bucket groups reviews documenting unsafe student behavior and ineffective remediation at circle schools — examples include regular fights and police presence (‘there's always lots of security and police due to the fights’), racial slurs and staff inaction (‘N-word at least 3 times a week’, 'staff do nothing'), anti-trans and disability-targeted abuse, and claims that bullying is ignored — whereas square reviews generally lack comparable reports of sustained violence, racialized harassment, or systemic non-response.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe higher teacher e: This bucket collects concrete reports of teacher availability and active mentorship at circle schools — e.g., teachers staying after school, availability by phone until 9pm, named mentors/advisors who 'truly cared', teacher-led AP program development, and examples of dramatic grade turnaround — contrasted with square reviews that more often report teachers who 'don't care', are 'overworked', or provide limited extra help.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers specific management and office failures emphasized in square reviews: examples include administration almost costing a diploma by missing a required English course, month‑long unanswered principal communications, broken parent message delivery (‘office staff is completely RUDE… important msg… wont reach your kids’), and counseling/IEP process breakdowns; comparable, repeated examples of these operational errors are less frequent or are counterbalanced by positive admin reports in circle entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, better‑or: This bucket groups concrete claims that circle schools offer extensive clubs/arts/band/athletics and either well‑maintained facilities or tuition/fundraising models that enhance programs — e.g., robotics, multiple bands, top‑notch choral and drama programs, D‑1 athlete pipelines, active parent fundraising ('huge support by the parents via The Shark Fund'), and tuition/LEED campus investment — while square reviews tend to mention fewer organized extracurriculars, more limited facilities claims, or public‑funding shortfalls.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more individualize: These entries describe teacher-level warmth, one-on-one outreach, and small-class mentoring (e.g., “teachers go above and beyond,” “every teacher’s door is open,” “small class size allows teachers to remain vested,” and frequent parent contact), contrasted with square entries that more often describe disengaged or inconsistent teacher responsiveness.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger formal ac: These items emphasize program structures and measurable college outcomes—AP/dual‑credit offerings, academy/magnet pipelines, and high matriculation claims (e.g., “students are able to earn associate’s degrees,” “The AP classes are top notch,” “97% of Seniors went on to college”)—whereas square reviews more often lack comparable program detail or report weaker/uneven college‑prep supports.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more chronic stude: These entries document pervasive safety and behavior problems plus ineffective responses (e.g., “full of drugs and violence,” “bullied everyday,” “There are no consequences for chronic absences,” and administrators who “just sweep it under the rug”), while square reviews are less likely to characterize the school as persistently violent or discipline‑neutral at that scale.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: These entries focus on operational and people‑process failures—unresponsive counselors/administrators, missing transcripts, ignored parent emails and zero follow‑through (e.g., “If you send email or call they will not respond,” “her transcript was never sent…,” “There is ZERO accountability”), contrasted with square entries that more often note accessible staff or resolved administrative actions.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater athletic p: These entries allege explicit preferential treatment and resource emphasis for athletes—grade leniency for players, special perks, budget/attention skewed to sports, and gender inequities in athletics (e.g., “Teachers will give students good grades if they are in the football team,” “sports are prioritized above all other activities,” and large athletic funding decisions), whereas square reviews do not present the same consistent pattern of athlete-first favoritism.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe richer/clearer s: This bucket groups reviews that report concrete course pathways, AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, career‑technical shops/academies, certification/ROTC pipelines and explicit outcome metrics (college acceptances, US News rankings) — e.g., circle reviewers cite AP classes, dual enrollment, ‘Pathways to Engineering,’ ‘13 academies,’ strong AP/AP exam scores and graduates admitted to Ivy/other selective colleges; Square reviews lack that program detail or measurable schoolwide outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: This bucket captures accounts of peer misconduct and school safety failures (identity‑based slurs, sexual harassment, fights, drugs, gang presence, unlocked doors) plus claims that discipline and adult intervention are weak or inconsistent — e.g., circle reviewers describe homophobia/racism in earshot of teachers, ‘drugs and gangs,’ unlocked middle‑school doors, bathroom substance use, and administration failing to stop assaults; Square reviews do not make comparable safety/discipline severity claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, more p: This bucket groups reviews emphasizing one‑on‑one teacher help, tutoring/extra‑help, active parent notification systems and tangible family supports (bookstore, clothing closet, counselors, success coordinators, special‑needs accommodations) — e.g., circle mentions teachers who ‘bend over backwards,’ Powerschool/email outreach, on‑site clothing/food support and superb counseling, whereas Square typically lacks these concrete support program descriptions.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize recent school i: This bucket bundles square reviews that highlight upward academic trends, A+/improved ratings, caring teachers/guidance staff and good outcomes even with limited funding — e.g., Square reviewers cite ‘Jackson is now an A+ school,’ ‘teachers try very hard,’ strong guidance/IB support and district stewardship under tight budgets; Circle reviews do not consistently present that same recent, district‑level improvement narrative.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more administrativ: This bucket contains criticisms of leadership behavior and governance (administrators on ‘power trips,’ favoritism by last name/athletes, retained problematic staff, alleged grade‑altering, lost credits, retaliatory firings and explicit calls to close or totally re‑staff the school) — e.g., circle reviewers report principals who ‘yell,’ excuse abusive staff, keep arrested principals, instruct grade changes, or provoke parents to demand school closure; Square reviews do not raise that same pattern of systemic governance abuse.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, named a: These reviews report concrete program breadth and measurable academic results (AP/IB/Cambridge/AICE, STEM academies, dual‑credit/early‑college, vocational shops, award‑winning band/theater, JROTC, large marching bands) and cite alumni/graduate outcomes (associates degrees, university placements, higher SAT/college completion), whereas square entries tend to list fewer named programs and offer weaker or anecdotal outcome evidence (occasional AP/IB mentions without broad dual‑credit or alumni metrics). Examples: circle cites Cambridge/AICE, 'graduated with associates,' 'marching band 225 members'; square only mentions single programs or mixed AP results.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Many circle reviews include explicit safety incidents (gang activity, drug solicitation, students stabbed with pencils, property theft, bus accidents) and allege administration/staff do not effectively stop bullying or violence; square entries more often report few fights, faster staff intervention, or only routine discipline problems. Illustrative evidence: circle notes 'bullying... teachers don't stop it,' 'kids ask where to get drugs,' 'cell phone stolen'; square says 'little to never any fights' and 'faculty is on top of it.'
candidate_defs.circle entries document more explicit sp: Circle reviews frequently name IEP/504 implementation issues (misapplied plans, denied placements), specific successful disability accommodations, schoolwide mental‑health commitments, scheduled tutoring, Saturday programs, ESL/immigrant supports, and wraparound family services; square reviews rarely mention special‑education, mental‑health, or systematic wraparound services. Examples include circle accounts of denied reassignment for ADHD students, 'mental health is a cornerstone,' 'Saturday tutoring and one‑on‑one tutoring available,' and both praise and criticism of IEP handling.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger teacher: Circle reviews commonly portray teachers as mentors and parental figures, name specific beloved staff, describe multi‑generational family attendance, and cite active parent/alumni advocacy; square reviews more frequently recount mixed teacher effectiveness, burnout, poor communication, or an aloof/arrogant administration. Examples: circle statements like 'faculty was like parents to me,' 'we are parents of three alumni,' and named teachers (Mrs. Longshore/Mrs. Treva Reid); square cites 'teachers are unprofessional,' 'admin is very arrogant,' and 'guidance counselors provide no guidance.'
candidate_defs.circle entries raise resource, facility: Circle reviews both praise and criticize concrete resource decisions—documenting new construction, stadiums, or 'state‑of‑the‑art' facilities as well as funding shortfalls, costly tech mandates (iPads), athletic spending imbalances, program cuts, and alleged nepotism or school‑board coverups—while square reviews rarely cluster this full set of operational/governance details. Representative items: circle mentions 'millions on athletics but not winning,' 'parents forced to buy $700 iPad,' 'new library/field house,' 'school board covers for colleagues' and 'reinstated student due to donor/alumni influence.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: These reviews describe concrete, school‑level academic resources and results (AP/IB/Honors breadth, dual‑enrollment/college credit, test‑prep, high SAT/ACT averages and documented college matriculation/scholarships) that are more frequently asserted in Circle than in Square—for example, claims of “40+ college credits by graduation,” named AP/STEM teachers and AP 5 scores, “100% college placement” or specific SAT/ACT averages. Falling here means the review emphasizes institutional course offerings, test prep, honors/AP/IB structure, and verifiable college outcomes as central strengths or evidence of academic rigor.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: These reviews recount concrete safety incidents and climate failures (daily fights, gang activity, drug incidents, sexual misconduct, self‑harm mishandling, racist harassment) plus descriptions of punitive/rigid or non‑protective discipline (zero‑tolerance suspensions, failure to investigate, victim‑blaming) far more often in Circle than Square—for example, reports of students being jumped with no follow‑up, kids selling drugs on campus, and administration keeping bullied students separated while ignoring self‑harm. Membership means the review documents on‑campus violence/bullying/criminal risk and describes discipline as ineffective, arbitrary, or actively harmful.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: These reviews emphasize leadership and operational dysfunction (revolving principals, nepotism among central office staff, donor/connected‑family favoritism, budget misallocation) together with logistics and facilities problems (bus cancellations, food shortages, crowded classrooms, safety closures, deferred maintenance) more often in Circle than Square—for example, alleges the assistant superintendent married to the special‑ed coordinator, buses cut with one day notice, hot lunch running out, and a school closed over ceiling safety hazards. Inclusion here means the review cites governance or operational breakdowns—favoritism, misallocated funds, or concrete transportation/facilities failures—rather than instructional detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more extensive ext: These reviews provide concrete, programmatic evidence of rich out‑of‑class opportunities and communal ties (strong sports programs and on‑site athletic facilities, marching band and music achievements, many clubs and travel trips, faith formation and daily prayer, multi‑generational alumni involvement and parent volunteerism) more often in Circle than Square—for example, descriptions of an outstanding water polo program, yearly all‑school masses, extensive club lists and alumni returning to tutor. A review falls in this bucket when it foregrounds broad extracurricular breadth, athletics/arts success, faith programming, or sustained parent/alumni community engagement as central features of the school.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pronounced pr: These reviews focus on concrete special‑needs and student‑support practices—frequent allegations of unmet IEPs, staff ignorance about accommodations, and mishandled mental‑health crises, alongside some reports of effective IEPs, targeted tutoring, or successful remediation/turnarounds—appearing more often and more vividly in Circle than Square—for example, claims of daily fights plus ‘they don't give neurodivergent students the help that they need,’ parents fighting to get IEPs honored, and teacher‑led Saturday tutoring that improved outcomes.
